After teaching history at Harvard and Princeton, this American scholar was nominated by Ronald Reagan and unanimously confirmed to lead a major federal cultural institution for over four decades — who was he?

A Scottish biologist, classicist and mathematician who pioneered theoretical biology, he's remembered for his 1917 book On Growth and Form, which opened the way to explaining how patterns and body structures take shape — who was he?
D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson: Scottish biologist, mathematician, and classics scholar

With co-researcher James Cronin, this American nuclear physicist won the 1980 Nobel for a 1964 K-meson experiment proving certain subatomic reactions aren't indifferent to time — discovering CP violation. Who was he?
Val Logsdon Fitch: American nuclear physicist

A Manhattan Project veteran, this American physicist won a share of the 1975 Nobel Prize for proposing that not all atomic nuclei are spherical — an idea later confirmed by Aage Bohr and Ben Mottelson. Who was he?
A pharmaceutical chemist with a Dartmouth Ph.D. by day, this American has chaired Anthrocon — one of the world's largest furry conventions — since 1999. Who is he?
Samuel Conway: American chemist and furry fandom personality
Named from the Greek for an infinite carbon chain it would ultimately become, this class of organic compounds strings together alternating single and triple bonds. What is it called?
Polyyne is any organic compound with alternating single and triple bonds; that is, a series of consecutive alkynes, (CC)n with n greater than 1.
Born to Belarusian Jewish immigrants and a diva of the Golden Age of Argentine cinema, she studied under poet Alfonsina Storni as a child and earned acclaim for 1942's La guerra gaucha — who was she?

After winning a 1936 'Miss Radio' contest, this Filipina was actually turned away by LVN Pictures before becoming the highest-paid star and a box-office queen of romantic musicals on either side of the war — who was she?

Named her league's most valuable player six times, this Canadian forward played in the first-ever women's world championship in 1987 and suited up for Team Canada at the inaugural IIHF World Women's Championship in 1990 — who is she?
Angela James: Canadian ice hockey player (born 1964)

Towering at 6-foot-2 and whirling his arms wildly, this Australian spin bowler disguised leg breaks, googlies, and top spinners with no change in his action — and later became a respected cricket writer. Who was he?
William Joseph O'Reilly was an Australian cricketer, rated as one of the greatest bowlers in the history of the game.

Begun by Giovanni Bellini as his last major work in 1514 — then reworked in the landscape by Dosso Dossi and Titian — this rare mythological canvas now hangs in Washington's National Gallery of Art; what's the painting?
The Feast of the Gods: Painting by Giovanni Bellini

This English actor-manager and Poet Laureate wrote 25 Drury Lane plays and a rambling 1740 memoir, yet earned the scorn of Pope and others for his 'miserable mutilation' of Moliere and Shakespeare — who was he?
Colley Cibber: English actor-manager, playwright, and poet laureate
A self-taught Dominican nun in a Florence convent, shaped by Savonarola's teachings, this artist is celebrated as the first known female Renaissance painter of Florence — who was she?
Founder of Polish academic sociology, this philosopher-turned-sociologist co-wrote 'The Polish Peasant in Europe and America,' often called the foundation of modern empirical sociology — who was he?
Florian Znaniecki: Polish and American philosopher and sociologist (1882–1958)
Second head of a renowned school of Japanese woodblock artists, this ukiyo-e master made his name with vivid kabuki actor prints and lifted his school to lasting fame — who was he?
Played by students from grade school to university across several continents, this academic competition pits teams of four against a moderator and a lockout buzzer system. What is it called?

Quiz bowl (quizbowl, scholars' bowl, scholastic bowl, academic bowl, academic team, academic challenge, etc.) is a family of quiz-based competitions that test players on a wide variety of academic subjects.
This Palestinian-American philosopher of religion pioneered the 'Islamization of knowledge' and built a worldview around tawhid, the universal concept of divine unity. Who was he?
Ismail al-Faruqi (January 1, 1921 - May 27, 1986) was a Palestinian-American Muslim philosopher and scholar of religion.

For over 30 years this American editor ran St. Nicholas Magazine, coaxing Mark Twain, Robert Louis Stevenson and Tennyson into writing for children — though she's best remembered for her own novel Hans Brinker. Who was she?
Mary Mapes Dodge: American children's author and editor (1831–1905)

A member of the Blue Stockings Society whose children's primers set the model for more than a century, this English poet and essayist proved a woman could be engaged in the public sphere — who was she?

Artist, poet, nurse, sole police officer and ham radio operator of a remote South Pacific British territory, she co-wrote with the island's six children the first book ever published in both English and the Pitkern creole — who is she?
Meralda Warren: Nurse, poet and artist (born 1959)
Teaming with Ludovic Halévy on Offenbach's comic operas, this prolific French librettist also helped write the words for Bizet's 'Carmen' and Massenet's 'Manon.' Who was he?

Henri Meilhac (French; 23 February 1830 - 6 July 1897) was a prolific French playwright and opera librettist, known for his collaborations with Ludovic Halvy on comic operas with music by Jacques Offenbach.

Ranked alongside Turgenev and Dostoyevsky in the late 1850s before a feud with Sovremennik magazine wrecked his reputation, this Russian — with Aleksandr Ostrovsky — first put ordinary people on the Russian stage. Who was he?
Aleksey Pisemsky: Russian novelist and dramatist (1821–1881)
A co-founder of the satirical magazine Punch in 1841, this English journalist also surveyed the city's poor in the groundbreaking three-volume London Labour and the London Poor — who was he?
Henry Mayhew: British writer and activist (1812–1887)

She founded the New York chapter of the Daughters of Bilitis in 1958 and joined Frank Kameny on the first picket lines protesting the U.S. government's ban on employing gay people — this American LGBTQ activist was who?
Barbara Gittings: Librarian, LGBT rights activist (1932–2007)
A New Yorker staffer since 1996, this American critic specializing in classical music wrote 'The Rest Is Noise' and 'Wagnerism.' Who is he?
Alex Ross (born January 12, 1968) is an American music critic and author who specializes in classical music.
Though his writing career lasted barely a decade, this Elizabethan-and-Jacobean playwright is remembered for an energetic, often obscure style and an idiosyncratic vocabulary. Who was he?
John Marston was an English playwright, poet and satirist during the late Elizabethan and early Jacobean periods.

A self-taught poet and house painter who fought on the June Days barricades in 1848 and was later imprisoned and exiled for his verse, this Frenchman's experiences radicalised him toward anarchism — who was he?

This New Zealand author of over 100 picture books wove supernatural elements into stories about growing up, and won the British Carnegie Medal twice — for The Haunting and The Changeover. Who was she?
Margaret Mahy: New Zealand children's writer (1936–2012)

Widely considered Africa's first modern poet and the greatest literary artist of Madagascar, he was raised impoverished under French colonization, never finished secondary school, and taught himself by devouring both French literature and traditional Malagasy oral poetry. Who was he?
Rated by the National Trust as one of Australia's 100 Living Treasures, this poet published nearly 30 volumes of verse and was called the leading Australian poet of his generation. Who was he?
Leslie Allan Murray was an Australian poet, anthologist and critic.

Apprenticed as a teenager to a farmer-apothecary he resented, this English poet and clergyman became known for an early, realistic narrative style depicting middle- and working-class life — who was he?
George Crabbe: English poet, surgeon, and clergyman (1754–1832)
Writing under a pen name, this Japanese novelist's 1958 WWII bestseller The Human Condition became the basis for Masaki Kobayashi's film trilogy — who was he?

A friend of Samuel Johnson who moonlighted as a magazine pseudonym called 'Mrs. Mary Midnight,' this English poet was notoriously confined to an asylum by his father-in-law over an alleged religious 'mania' — who was he?
This Romanian Symbolist poet pioneered the local detective story and is best remembered for 'Craii de Curtea-Veche,' a portrait of fading boyar descendants around World War I — who was he?
Mateiu Caragiale: Romanian poet and prose writer (1885–1936)

Unsure of her standing with Christ, this English hymn writer poured that doubt into a verse of assurance that became 'Just as I Am' — translated into nearly every living language of her day. Who was she?
Charlotte Elliott: English poet and hymn writer (1789–1871)
Born in England, she married the future first president of Botswana and went on to serve as that nation's inaugural First Lady from 1966 to 1980. Who was she?
Ruth Williams Khama: First Lady of Botswana from 1966 to 1980

A fierce 1930s champion of fighter aircraft when the U.S. Army favored high-altitude bombing, this American aviator retired in 1937 to advise China — then led the legendary 'Flying Tigers.' Who was he?
Claire Lee Chennault (September 6, 1893 - July 27, 1958) was an American military aviator best known for his leadership of the "Flying Tigers" and the Chinese Nationalist Air Force in World War II.

A limestone slab inscribed in Brahmi script, found in 1931, dates this fortified Maurya-era city — the earliest urban archaeological site yet found in Bangladesh — to at least the 3rd century BCE. What site is it?
Mahasthangarh is the earliest urban archaeological sites discovered thus far in Bangladesh.
As baseball's first commissioner, this stern federal judge restored public faith in the game by expelling eight Chicago White Sox players for throwing the 1919 World Series — who was he?
Kenesaw Mountain Landis: American judge and first commissioner of baseball (1866–1944)
This Russian nihilist preached revolution "by any means necessary" and fled the country in 1869 after taking part in the murder of a former comrade who'd dared to disagree with him — who was he?
Known as the "Alter Rebbe," this 18th-century rabbi founded the Chabad branch of Hasidic Judaism and authored the Tanya — who was he?
Shneur Zalman of Liadi: Hasidic rabbi and first rebbe of Chabad
Born in Calcutta, she didn't pick up a camera until age 48 — a gift from her daughter — yet her soft-focus close-ups made her one of the 19th century's great portraitists. Who was she?
Julia Margaret Cameron (ne Pattle; 11 June 1815 - 26 January 1879) was an English photographer who is considered one of the most important portraitists of the 19th century.

Enforced through everything from separate schools and transit to anti-miscegenation laws barring interracial marriage, what was this legally and socially mandated separation of Black and white Americans called?
Racial segregation in the United States
Racial segregation in the United States
history of racial segregation in the United States

Racial segregation in the United States was the legally and/or socially enforced separation of black people from white people, as well as the de facto separation of other ethnic minorities from majority communities.
Racial segregation in the United States
Hitler called him one of his best field commanders and kept dispatching him to salvage collapsing fronts — which hard-driving German field marshal became famous as a master of defensive warfare?
The son of a cooper who enlisted as a cavalryman just before the French Revolution, this soldier rose to become one of Napoleon's original Marshals of the Empire — who was he?

Beginning in 73 BCE with about 70 gladiators escaping a school in Capua, this slave revolt swelled to 120,000 people and became the only such uprising to directly threaten the Roman heartland — what was it called?
Third Servile War: 73–71 BCE Roman slave rebellion
Which political stance sits between left and right, favoring gradual change and a welfare state with moderate redistribution rather than strong alignment to either wing?
Centrism: Political alignment in the middle of the left–right political spectrum
Mixing anti-elitist rhetoric with neo-nationalism, social conservatism, and a vow to defend national culture from outsiders — which political ideology is this?
Educated at Sandhurst in England, this man returned home in 1966 and ruled for nearly half a century, becoming the longest-serving leader in the Arab world at his death — which sultan?
Qaboos bin Said: Sultan of Oman from 1970 to 2020
Centered on the River Trent with no fixed capital, this Anglo-Saxon kingdom held "supremacy" over the Midlands for three centuries — King Offa favored Tamworth within it. What was it?

Across Hinduism, Jainism, Buddhism and Sikhism, this term names liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth — in Hindu tradition the highest of life's four aims, beside dharma, artha and kama. What is it?
Moksha: Spiritual liberation in Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism
Turning colorless in acid and a fuchsia pink in base, this phthalein dye is a favorite indicator for acid-base titrations — what is it?
Phenolphthalein: pH indicator that turns pink in basic solution
A shrub-like bush of western South America with oval leaves and small red berries, its leaves are chewed or brewed as a mild stimulant and famously contain a notorious alkaloid — which plant is it?
Coca: Plant in the Erythroxylaceae family

A natural cross between the pomelo and the wild mandarin, this Southeast Asian citrus is too sour to eat off the tree — but the Seville variety is exactly what British cooks prize for their breakfast preserve. What fruit is it?
This wingless insect spends its entire life on the human scalp, sipping blood, and can neither fly nor jump — its short stumpy legs can't even walk well on a flat surface. What tiny freeloader is it?
Head louse: Insect parasite of humans
The heaviest member of its family, this Southeastern U.S. reptile sees males stretch up to 15 feet and tip 1,000 pounds — and it's the larger of just two surviving species in its genus. What is it?
American alligator: Crocodilian native to the Southeastern United States
Caused by too little of the enzyme lactase, this condition brings on bloating and discomfort thirty minutes to two hours after dairy — yet, notably, it never damages the gut. What is it?
Lactose intolerance is a lessened ability or a complete inability to digest lactose, a sugar found in dairy products.

Among the longest of all living crocodilians, this fish-eater wields a slender snout lined with 110 interlocking teeth, and the males sport a bulbous, pot-shaped bump on the tip that gives the animal its name. What is it?
Gharial: Crocodilian native to the Indian subcontinent
A hygroscopic crystalline powder (formula NaNO2) and the most industrially important salt of its kind, this compound is most familiar to us cured into processed meats. What is it?
Drafted second overall by the Giants in 1981 and Defensive Rookie of the Year that same season, which linebacker nicknamed 'L.T.' is widely called the greatest defensive player of all time?

Lawrence Taylor (born February 4, 1959), nicknamed "L.T.", is an American former professional football linebacker who played in the National Football League (NFL) for 13 seasons with the New York Giants.
Created by Tina Fey and named after a New York address, this satirical sitcom drew on her years as head writer for a live NBC sketch show — what is it?
He acted and directed only as an amateur until age 33, when he co-founded the Moscow Art Theatre — but his lasting fame rests on a 'system' of actor training; who was this Russian practitioner?
Dubbed "the next Seinfeld" by Time, this deadpan stand-up built a career on surreal one-liners and an unconventional stage presence before his death in 2005 — who was he?

Once empty heathland frequented only by fishermen and smugglers, this Dorset coastal resort was founded in 1810 and now draws over five million visitors a year to its beaches and nightlife. Which town is it?

Carved into an Afghan valley cliff around the 6th century, these two monumental sandstone figures — the taller standing 180 feet — were dynamited into rubble by the Taliban in March 2001. What were they?
Buddhas of Bamiyan: Sculptures in Afghanistan before 2001

Spanning southern Missouri, northern Arkansas, and bits of Oklahoma and Kansas, this highland region holds the Boston and St. Francois ranges, topping out at Wahzhazhe Summit's 2,561 feet. What plateau is it?
Ozarks: Highland region in central-southern United States
These islands are governed by Taiwan, yet sit just 6 miles off the Chinese city of Xiamen and a full 116 miles from Taiwan itself — a strategic outpost also known as Quemoy. What are they?
Nicknamed 'Rocket' across 24 big-league seasons, which pitcher racked up 4,672 strikeouts and a record seven Cy Young Awards?

Roger Clemens (born August 4, 1962), nicknamed "Rocket", is an American former professional baseball pitcher who played 24 seasons in Major League Baseball (MLB), most notably with the Boston Red Sox and New York Yankees.
On the very first Baseball Hall of Fame ballot in 1936, the "Georgia Peach" pulled 222 of 226 votes — a percentage no player would top until 1992. Which Detroit Tigers center fielder was it?
Ty Cobb (December 18, 1886 - July 17, 1961), nicknamed "the Georgia Peach", was an American professional baseball center fielder.
A flamboyant World No. 1 from a gifted golfing family, this Spaniard won 90 tournaments and helped revive European golf, claiming The Open three times and the Masters twice — who was he?
"Sweetness" carried the ball for 13 seasons after the Bears took him fourth overall in 1975, winning the 1977 MVP — which Jackson State running back is widely called one of the greatest ever?
Walter Payton (July 25, 1953 - November 1, 1999) was an American professional football running back who played in the National Football League (NFL) for 13 seasons with the Chicago Bears.
Born from African-American musicians in the 1970s and known for lush vocal arrangements, melisma, and hip-hop-inspired beats, which genre blends rhythm and blues with disco, funk, and soul?
Contemporary R&B: Rhythm and blues music genre
Originally named for Minnesota's mining and manufacturing, this conglomerate makes over 60,000 products and gave the world Scotch Tape and Post-it notes — which company is it?
One of the most famous works by French composer Maurice Ravel, this 1928 piece for large orchestra was among his last before illness ended his composing — what is it?
Boléro: Orchestral composition by Maurice Ravel

Despite a battle with Austrian censors who nearly killed it under its original title 'The Curse,' this Verdi opera about a hunchbacked court jester triumphed at Venice's La Fenice in 1851 — what is it?
This Russian poet lived through the 1917 Revolution and the Moscow famine — losing a daughter to starvation — before years of poverty in Paris, Berlin and Prague; who was she?
An unnamed narrator insists on his own sanity even as he describes murdering an old man over a filmy "vulture-eye" and hiding the body beneath the floorboards — which 1843 Poe short story?
The Tell-Tale Heart: 1843 short story by Edgar Allan Poe

A Stanford grad with an Oxford doctorate in political science, this commentator was the first openly lesbian host of a major US prime-time news show and even won a Grammy for an audiobook — who is she?
Rachel Maddow: American television host and commentator (born 1973)
Having survived multiple concentration camps and a death march, this Austrian devoted the rest of his life to tracking down fugitive Nazi war criminals so they could face trial — who was he?

After publicizing the Gold Rush and founding San Francisco's first newspaper, this Latter-day Saint became California's first millionaire — before his vigilance-committee actions got him disfellowshipped — who was he?
An anti-imperialist independence hero, this politician guided the Maldives to freedom and became the first president of its Second Republic in 1968 — who was he?
Ibrahim Nasir: President of the Maldives from 1968 to 1978
Wounded at Gallipoli before entering politics, this businessman led the Nationalist Party as the eighth prime minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929 — who was he?
The Right Honourable The Viscount Bruce of Melbourne
Stanley Melbourne Bruce, 1st Viscount Bruce of Melbourne
Stanley Bruce: Prime Minister of Australia from 1923 to 1929
This Spanish expedition's captain made the first recorded European passage through the strait separating mainland Australia from New Guinea — a strait that now bears his name — who was he?
Luís Vaz de Torres: 16th- and 17th-century Galician maritime explorer

Arguing that cheaper letters would mean more letters and thus higher profits, this English teacher and reformer championed a Uniform Penny Post and is credited with inventing the postage stamp — who was he?
Rowland Hill (3 December 1795 - 27 August 1879) was an English teacher, inventor and social reformer.
For three decades this Malagasy statesman served as prime minister and co-king of Madagascar, succeeding his own older brother in the role — who was he?
Rainilaiarivony: Prime Minister of Madagascar from 1864 to 1895
Generally hailed as the first major investment banker in the United States, he helped finance the Union war effort and then the postwar push of railroads into the Northwest — who was he?

Jay Cooke (August 10, 1821 - February 16, 1905) was an American financier who helped finance the Union war effort during the American Civil War and the postwar development of railroads in the northwestern United States.

Ruling a swath of southeastern Britain around AD 9 to 40, this pre-Roman king minted coins by the score, was dubbed 'King of the Britons' by Suetonius, and later surfaced in legend as the Welsh Cynfelyn — who was he?
A barrister who founded his own Democratic Party, this politician stepped up after Makarios III's death to lead his Mediterranean island nation as president from 1977 to 1988 — who was he?
Spyros Kyprianou: President of Cyprus from 1977 to 1988

Born a peasant and once a schoolmaster, this politician from Dahomey — today's Benin — rose through regionalist politics to serve in the French National Assembly and become his country's leader at independence; who was he?
Hubert Maga: Dahomey politician, former president (1916–2000)
This small evergreen citrus tree is actually a hybrid of the citron and the bitter orange, and its juice runs about 5–6% citric acid — sour enough to anchor lemonade and meringue pie. What is it?
Lemon (Citrus limon) is a species of small evergreen tree in the Citrus genus of the flowering plant family Rutaceae.
The heaviest and largest members of the squirrel family, these 15 species of grazing ground-dwellers vanish each winter to hibernate underground — what are they?
Marmot are large ground squirrels in the genus Marmota, with 15 species living in Asia, Europe, and North America.
The only member of its genus and the most adapted to ground life of all lemurs, this highly social Madagascar primate is instantly known by its long black-and-white banded tail — which species is it?

The ring-tailed lemur (Lemur catta) is a medium- to larger-sized strepsirrhine (wet-nosed) primate and the most internationally recognized lemur species, owing to its long, black-and-white, ringed tail.

This Japanese biologist used diffusion equations to calculate how likely a gene is to take over a population, and in 1968 proposed the "neutral theory" that genetic drift, not just selection, drives molecular evolution — who was he?
A 1983 MacArthur Fellow, this American mathematician's work on Hilbert's tenth problem proved crucial to its eventual resolution — now known as the MRDP theorem. Who was she?
Working in Feynman's group on the Manhattan Project before co-detecting an elusive elementary particle with Clyde Cowan, he won the 1995 Nobel for catching the neutrino — who was he?

A British physicist who hauled a captured German thermionic valve back from the Western Front, he won the 1947 Nobel for mapping the ionosphere — work that paved the way for radar and shortwave radio. Who was he?
A pioneer of industrial toxicology, this American physician trained at Michigan, worked out of Hull House in Chicago, and led the fight to curb lead poisoning in the workplace — who was she?
Alice Hamilton (February 27, 1869 - September 22, 1970) was an American physician, research scientist, and author.

This Dutch microscopist showed that an insect's egg, larva, pupa, and adult are all one animal, pioneered the microscope in dissections, and in 1658 became the first to observe red blood cells — who was he?
Jan Swammerdam: Dutch biologist and microscopist (1637–1680)
This Canadian atmospheric scientist holds a chair in public policy at Texas Tech and in 2021 became chief scientist of the Nature Conservancy — who is she?
This British-American theoretical physicist at the University of Illinois won the 2003 Nobel Prize for pioneering work on superfluidity and the quantum physics of low-temperature helium — who was he?
Among the first women in Canada to earn a medical doctorate, this physician-chemist is best known for her 1913 work with Leonor Michaelis on enzyme kinetics — who was she?
Maud Menten: Canadian physician and chemist (1879–1960)
After reading the religious poet George Herbert, this Welsh metaphysical poet and physician renounced "idle verse" and poured his convictions into the 1650 collection Silex Scintillans — who was he?
Elected to the Royal Society in 1714 as Isaac Newton's experimental assistant, this French-born clergyman became a Grand Master of London's first Masonic Grand Lodge — who was he?
The first woman admitted to MIT, this environmental chemist was the first to apply chemistry to nutrition and founded the home economics movement — who was she?
Ellen Swallow Richards: American engineer and chemist (1843–1911)

Historian Anthony Slide called her, alongside D. W. Griffith, American cinema's first true auteur — a silent-film director who wrote, produced, and starred while putting her own social ideas on screen — who was she?
Lois Weber: American actress and film director
So beloved that her young female fans were nicknamed "Gerry-flappers," this American lyric soprano was prized for her beauty and acting and even succeeded in silent films — who was she?
Geraldine Farrar: American opera singer and actress (1882–1967)
Trained by Ellen Terry, this English actress married Alfred Lunt in 1922, and together — celebrated on both sides of the Atlantic as "The Lunts" — they co-starred for four decades — who was she?
Half of the Broadway-and-West-End partnership nicknamed "the Lunts," this American actor nearly always shared the stage with his wife, especially in light comedies by Noël Coward — who was he?

Considered the successor to the great clown Tarlton, this comic English actor was one of five shareholders in the Lord Chamberlain's Men alongside Shakespeare and may have originated Falstaff — who was he?
William Kempe: English actor and dancer (c. 1560–c. 1603)
This veteran Nigerian actress starred opposite Colin Firth in 'The Secret Laughter of Women' and, with husband Olu Jacobs, founded the Lufodo Group and its academy of performing arts — who is she?
Joke Silva: Nigerian actress and director
Across a 60-year career, this British film editor won an Oscar for cutting David Lean's 'Lawrence of Arabia' and earned later nods for 'The Elephant Man' and 'Out of Sight' — who is she?
Anne V. Coates: British film editor (1925–2018)
At just 35 the highest-paid executive in Hollywood and the first female executive at Metro/MGM, this screenwriter discovered Rudolph Valentino and penned 'Blood and Sand' — who was she?
June Mathis: American screenwriter, producer and film studio executive
The sixth-largest city in Ghana, this cocoa-growing capital of the Bono Region sits about 105 miles northwest of Kumasi — what is it?
Sunyani: City in Bono Region, Ghana
Home to "salt-water people" of the Langa Langa Lagoon and the second most populous island in the Solomon Islands, its capital is Auki — which island is it?
Malaita is the primary island of malaita Province in Solomon Islands.
Nicknamed 'Simmo,' this Australian batsman and brilliant slip fielder came out of a decade's retirement at 41 to captain his country during World Series Cricket — who was he?
Robert Baddeley Simpson, known as Simmo, was an Australian cricketer who played for New South Wales, Western Australia and the Australian national team.

Batting at number three for a perennially weak West Indies side, this one world-class cricketer carried the team almost single-handedly before World War II, averaging nearly 70 across all first-class play — who was he?
George Headley (30 May 1909 - 30 November 1983) was a Jamaican cricketer who played 22 Test matches, mostly before World War II.
This Cuban patriotic song sets a poem by José Martí to music; a 1966 version by the Sandpipers, built on a Weavers arrangement, turned it into an international hit. What's the song?

Eubie Blake called this pioneering ragtime and early-jazz bandleader the "Martin Luther King of music" for being among the first African-American musicians to win mainstream recognition in 1910s New York — who was he?
James Reese Europe: American jazz musician and US Army officer (1880–1919)

Affectionately crowned the "Queen of the Music Hall," this English singer drew both praise and outrage for the cheeky double entendre in songs like "The Boy I Love Is Up in the Gallery" — who was she?
Marie Lloyd: English singer, comedian and actress (1870–1922)
A Flemish High Renaissance composer who carried the Franco-Flemish polyphonic style south into Italy, this musician founded the Venetian School — who was he?

A central figure of the Burgundian School, this Franco-Flemish composer born in Mons was prized as a miniaturist and melodist of short secular chansons, ranked alongside Du Fay and Dunstaple — who was he?

Written in 1962 for MIT's PDP-1, this dogfight between two ships — 'the needle' and 'the wedge' — circling a star's gravity well was the first to be played at multiple computer installations. What's it called?
A leading poet of the imagist school, this American writer won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1926 — the year after her death — who was she?

W. H. Auden said he knew no American who wrote better prose than this food writer, who explored eating as one of the "arts of life" in books like Consider the Oyster and How to Cook a Wolf — who was she?
Mary Frances Kennedy Fisher Parrish Friede
M. F. K. Fisher: American food writer (1908–1992)
A physician, painter, and inventor, this American went on to design the United States Capitol and serve as the first Superintendent of the Patent Office — who was he?
William Thornton: American inventor and architect (1759–1828)
A contemporary of Brunelleschi, Ghiberti, and Donatello, this Italian sculptor was a major figure of the Early Renaissance — who was he?
This British philosopher didn't publish her first book until her late fifties, then wrote over fifteen more — on ethics, animal rights, and her fierce opposition to scientism — who was she?

This Australian writer's debut novel Monkey Grip, published in 1977, instantly marked her as an original voice and is now considered a classic — known for weaving her own life into her fiction, who is she?
Dubbed "the Napoleon of the South," this Māori warlord and Ngāti Toa chief waged a war of conquest during the Musket Wars that stretched his people's authority across Cook Strait — who was he?
Te Rauparaha: Māori chief and war leader of Ngāti Toa (1760s–1849)
This American writer was a member of the Beat Generation and is reputed to have coined the very term "Beat" — who was he?
Herbert Huncke: American writer and poet
A pioneer archaeologist and folklorist, this English antiquary systematically examined the Avebury henge, and a ring of pits at Stonehenge is named for him — who was he?
John Aubrey: English writer and antiquarian

The first writer to record the lives of women who contributed to the American Revolution, this American historian and poet was also entangled in a notorious scandal involving Edgar Allan Poe — who was she?
Elizabeth F. Ellet: American writer, poet and translator (1818–1877)
This English poet and Renaissance historian, married with children, openly championed male love, which he called "l'amour de l'impossible" — the love of the impossible — who was he?
John Addington Symonds: English poet, literary critic and cultural historian (1840–1893)

The first significant British painter of nudes, this Yorkshireman left school at twelve to be a printer's apprentice before training at the Royal Academy, where he was admired for his realistic flesh tones — who was he?

Hailed as a cornerstone of modern East African literature with his 1970 debut 'From a Crooked Rib,' this novelist left his homeland in the 1970s and has since taught across the US, Europe, and Africa — who is he?
A prolific woodblock printmaker of Japan's Meiji era, this artist was better known to his contemporaries by the art-name Yoshu — who was he?
Toyohara Chikanobu: Japanese samurai and artist (1838–1912)
The 'Sweet Singer of California' and a niece of Mormon founder Joseph Smith, she became the first poet laureate of any American state — who was this San Francisco literary figure?
Ina Coolbrith (born Josephine Donna Smith; March 10, 1841 - February 29, 1928) was an American poet, writer, librarian, and a prominent figure in the San Francisco Bay Area literary community.

One of the first formally trained professional architects to land in the newly independent United States, this British-American neoclassicist designed the US Capitol and the Old Baltimore Cathedral — who was he?
One of the most significant Argentine writers of his era, this novelist and poet is best remembered for his 1926 gaucho novel 'Don Segundo Sombra' — who is he?
Ricardo Güiraldes: Argentine novelist and poet (1886–1927)
Ranked number 89 among the millennium's 1,000 most influential people, this American architect-engineer is credited with building the very first skyscraper, in 1884 — who was he?
William Le Baron Jenney: American architect and engineer
This American journalist and feminist wrote a 1975 book on rape that the New York Public Library later named one of the 100 most important books of the 20th century — who is she?
Susan Brownmiller: American journalist, author and activist (1935–2025)

A close friend of Percy Bysshe Shelley and an East India Company official, this English novelist wrote satires that all shared one setting: characters around a table picking apart the philosophies of the day — who was he?
Thomas Love Peacock: English novelist and poet (1785-1866)

Convinced that Protestants and the Catholic majority had to make common cause against the Crown, this revolutionary helped found the Society of United Irishmen in 1791 and became an icon of Irish republicanism — who was he?

Largely self-taught and grinding his own lenses from spare parts on a Kansas farm, this astronomer's homemade skills landed him at Lowell Observatory — where his 1930 survey turned up the first known body in the Kuiper belt; who was he?

Clyde Tombaugh (February 4, 1906 - January 17, 1997) was an American astronomer and telescope maker, best known for discovering Pluto in 1930, marking the first detection of what would eventually be recognized as the Kuiper belt.

Beloved by biologists for its wild morphological variation and elaborate nest-building, this northern fish tolerates big swings in salinity, living in the sea but breeding in fresh water — what is it?
Three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) is a fish native to most inland and coastal waters north of 30N.
Having spent years building theremins, this engineer debuted the first commercial synthesizer in 1964 and later the portable Minimoog — earning a spot in the Inventors Hall of Fame. Who is it?
Robert Moog: American electronic music pioneer (1934–2005)
The only person ever to run the 800 metres under 1:41, this Kenyan holds the three fastest times in history at the distance — each a world record when set; who is he?
David Rudisha (born 17 December 1988) is a retired Kenyan middle-distance runner who is the world and Olympic record holder in the 800 metres.
What single word names the practice of banning by law the making, selling, and drinking of alcoholic beverages?
Organized after Russia's 1917 October Revolution and global by the Cold War, this stance has been claimed across the spectrum — by anarchists, fascists, liberals and libertarians alike. What is it?
Anti-communism is political and ideological opposition to communist beliefs, groups, and individuals.
Castrated as a child by a rival's successor, he nonetheless reunified Iran, made Tehran the capital, and founded a dynasty as its first Shah. Who was he?
Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar: Shah of Iran from 1789 to 1797

It began as a Cold War quarrel over how to read Marx — Mao branding Moscow's de-Stalinization and 'peaceful coexistence' as revisionism — and slowly froze relations between two communist giants. What is this rift called?
Sino-Soviet split: Conflict between communist blocs
Blinded in one eye by childhood smallpox, he fought his first battle at ten and went on to found the Sikh Empire, capturing Lahore and ruling as its first maharaja. Who was he?
From the French word for 'equal,' this school of political philosophy holds that all humans share the same fundamental worth and deserve equal rights under the law. What is it called?
Egalitarianism: School of thought favoring equality for all people
More than 80% of cases of this cancer — which grows in the thin lining covering the lungs and other organs — trace back to asbestos exposure. What is it?
Discovered in 1945 and first sold in 1964, this class of beta-lactam antibiotics was originally pulled from a fungus once known as Cephalosporium — what's the family called?
A colorless gas that throws off white fumes the moment it meets moist air, it turns into a familiar strong acid once dissolved in water — which compound, formula HCl?
A vitamer of vitamin B3 that the body can build from tryptophan, in large prescription doses it lowers LDL and raises "good" HDL cholesterol — what's this compound also called niacin?
Nicotinic acid: Organic compound and a form of vitamin B3

Madagascar's largest carnivore is a slender, long-tailed mammal that climbs down trees head-first and has convergently evolved so many cat-like features it's been likened to a small cougar — yet it's no cat. What is it?
Fossa (animal): Cat-like, carnivorous mammal endemic to Madagascar
A colorless, flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor, this N2H4 compound foams polymer plastics, fills airbag gas generators, and serves as a storable spacecraft propellant. What is it?
Hydrazine: Colorless flammable liquid with an ammonia-like odor
Discovered by a Swiss chemist in 1953 and sold as Tegretol, this anticonvulsant treats epilepsy and neuropathic pain and sits on the WHO's list of essential medicines. Which drug is it?

This widely used polar aprotic solvent dissolves both polar and nonpolar compounds, mixes with water, and — once absorbed through the skin — leaves a curious garlic-like taste in the mouth. Which organosulfur compound is it?
Dimethyl sulfoxide: Organosulfur chemical compound used as a solvent
A member of the crow family whose name simply mashes together "small" (jack) and an old synonym for itself, this grey-naped bird ranges across Europe and even into North Africa — which one is it?
The western jackdaw (Coloeus monedula), also known as the Eurasian jackdaw, the European jackdaw, or simply the jackdaw, is a passerine bird in the crow family.

One of the most colorful mammals alive, this west-central African monkey wears red and blue on both its face and its rump, with the brightest males being the biggest — long mistaken for a baboon, what is it?
Mandrill (Mandrillus sphinx) is a large Old World monkey native to west central Africa.
Found naturally in coffee, bread and ripe fruit, this aldehyde is produced when your liver partly oxidizes ethanol — making it a chief culprit behind the hangover. What is it?
This big, sociable black corvid is told apart from its relatives by a bare, whitish patch on its face, and it nests in noisy treetop colonies near farms and villages — which bird is it?
Rook (bird) — Rook (Corvus frugilegus) is a member of the family Corvidae in the passerine order of birds.
With over 800 species lugging borrowed snail shells to shield their soft, non-calcified abdomens, this crustacean is essentially homeless without a hand-me-down home. What is it?
A bitter, colorless alkaloid from the seeds of the nux-vomica tree, it kills birds and rodents by triggering muscular convulsions and asphyxia. Which poison is it?
Strychnine: Poisonous substance used as pesticide

After co-founding Asylum Records he launched his own eponymous label, then teamed with Spielberg and Katzenberg to start DreamWorks SKG — making him, per Forbes, the entertainment world's wealthiest figure. Who is he?
He co-hosted a Fox News debate show with Alan Colmes from the network's 1996 launch before going solo in 2009 with his own conservative commentary program. Which broadcaster is it?
Sean Hannity: American television host and political commentator (born 1961)
Nearly three-quarters of this Western state's residents live in a single county anchored by Las Vegas, and its nickname honors the metal that shaped its economy — which state is it?

A complex of 19 buildings between 48th and 51st Streets in Midtown Manhattan, its Art Deco core was built on land leased from Columbia University and split by a sunken plaza and a private street — what is this landmark?
Rockefeller Center: Skyscraper complex in Manhattan, New York
Named for the 48th state and commissioned in 1916, this Pennsylvania-class battleship even escorted President Wilson to the Paris Peace Conference before her Pacific Fleet years. Which ship is it?
USS Arizona: US Navy Pennsylvania-class battleship sunk in 1941
Arid, mineral-rich, and strategically prized, this historical region is split among Iran, Afghanistan, and Pakistan and named for the ethnic people who populate it — what is it?

A left-arm fast bowler so masterful with the moving ball that fans revered him as "The Sultan of Swing," he was the only Pakistani named in Wisden's 150th-anniversary all-time Test World XI — who is this cricketer?
Wasim Akram: Pakistani former international cricketer (born 1966)

Considered one of the greatest batters ever, this South African topped 9,500 ODI runs and 8,700 in Tests — averaging over 50 in both — while also keeping wicket and captaining his country. Who was he?
AB de Villiers (born (1984-02-17)17 February 1984) is a South African former professional cricketer, widely recognised as one of the greatest batters of all time.
Carl Orff built this 1935–36 cantata from 24 medieval poems, and its thundering opening movement "O Fortuna" became inescapable in film and ads — what's the work's title?
Carmina Burana is a cantata composed in 1935 and 1936 by Carl Orff, based on 24 poems from the medieval collection Carmina Burana.
Released in 1978 by the Village People, this disco anthem sold some 12 million copies and hit number one in the UK to become the group's biggest hit. Which song is it?
This Peruvian-American writer's bestselling books claimed to chronicle shamanic training under a Yaqui "Man of Knowledge" named Don Juan — now widely thought fabricated; who is he?
This Turkish Muslim scholar led a movement that built over 2,000 STEM-focused schools in more than 150 countries — and in 2017 his own government stripped him of his citizenship. Who was he?
Fethullah Gülen: Turkish scholar, theologian and dissident (1941–2024)
This Chinese official earned his jinshi degree in 1616 and rose to Supreme Commander over five provinces — but he's remembered for serving two rival dynasties, the Ming and then the Qing. Who was he?
Hong Chengchou: Chinese general and official (1593–1665)
A Scottish-born coal miner who emigrated to Australia, this Labor leader served three terms as prime minister and led his party to its first majority government in 1910 — who was he?
This Northern Irish peace activist co-founded a movement seeking a peaceful end to the Troubles, sharing the 1976 Nobel Peace Prize with Betty Williams — who is she?
Mairead Maguire: Northern Irish peace activist (born 1944)
The younger son of Neferirkare Kakai and Queen Khentkaus II, this sixth ruler of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty likely took the throne after his short-lived brother Neferefre. Which Old Kingdom king was he?
Nyuserre Ini: Ancient Egyptian pharaoh of the Fifth Dynasty
Ruling around 922–887 BC, this second king of Egypt's 22nd Dynasty held sway over much of the Levant. Who was he?
Osorkon I was an ancient Egyptian pharaoh of the 22nd Dynasty.
A PBS NewsHour anchor who moderated 12 U.S. presidential debates between 1988 and 2012, this American journalist also wrote novels drawn from his newsroom life — who was he?
Jim Lehrer: American journalist and writer (1934–2020)
During the War of the Spanish Succession in 1706, Prince Eugene of Savoy's relief of this besieged Savoyard capital — and the death of hero Pietro Micca — became legend; what's this military event?
Siege of Turin: 1706 battle of the War of the Spanish Succession
The first Australian woman to sit in a parliament, this social reformer for women and children has appeared on Australia's fifty-dollar note since 1995 — who was she?
Edith Cowan: Australian social reformer and politician (1861–1932)
Hailed as the "chief founder of England's naval supremacy," this Cromwell-era general at sea had his fame deliberately expunged after the Stuart Restoration — who was he?
General at Sea Robert Blake was an English naval officer who served as general at sea and the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports from 1656 to 1657.
He left school at 12 to work the family farm yet rose to become both prime minister and, uniquely in his country's history, also governor-general of New Zealand — who was he?
Breaking with tradition, this penultimate Fifth-Dynasty pharaoh declined to build a sun temple and likely reigned more than 40 years, succeeded by Unas — who was he?
Djedkare Isesi (known in Greek as Tancheres) was a pharaoh, the eighth and penultimate ruler of the Fifth Dynasty of Egypt in the late 25th century to mid-24th century BC, during the Old Kingdom.
This British lawyer-turned-diplomat was one of the architects of the League of Nations, and his lifelong defense of it earned him the 1937 Nobel Peace Prize — who was he?
Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Edgar Algernon Robert Gascoyne Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Robert Cecil, 1st Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood: British lawyer, politician and diplomat (1864–1958)
Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Nicknamed the "Redeemer of the Republic," this mulatto general helped overthrow Faustin Soulouque before becoming President of Haiti in 1859 — who was he?
Fabre Geffrard: President of Haiti from 1859 to 1867

Born in Lisbon days after his father died at the Battle of Badajoz, this British explorer went on to govern South Australia, Cape Colony, and New Zealand — twice — before becoming a New Zealand premier; who was he?
George Grey: British soldier, explorer, colonial administrator and writer (1812–1898)
This Portuguese explorer's far-fetched memoir Pilgrimage earned him a teasing nickname riffing on the verb "to lie" — who was this possibly-tall-tale-telling adventurer?
Fernão Mendes Pinto: Portuguese explorer and writer
A spherical, gram-positive bacterium that usually lives harmlessly on our skin and in our airways, this microbe can turn opportunistic and cause abscesses, sinusitis, and food poisoning — what is it?
Staphylococcus aureus: Species of Gram-positive bacterium
This Romanian mathematician-economist argued in his 1971 magnum opus that natural resources are irreversibly degraded by economic use, founding ecological economics — who was he?
Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen: Romanian mathematician, statistician and economist (1906–1994)
The second woman ever to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine — and the first American-born one — this physicist shared the 1977 award for developing the radioimmunoassay. Who was she?
Rosalyn Sussman Yalow: American medical physicist (1921–2011)
Considered the father of the exact and natural sciences in Armenia, this 7th-century polymath wrote the first known Armenian geographic work — who was he?
A Chinese economist and linguist who lived to 111, he's credited as the father of the romanization system China adopted in 1958 and the UN took up in 1986. Who was he?
Zhou Youguang: Chinese linguist and author (1906–2017)

This French mathematician, famous for his work in algebraic topology, came from an almost absurdly mathematical dynasty: son of mathematician Élie, nephew of mathematician Anna, and brother to a composer, a physicist, and yet another mathematician — who was he?
This American economist shared the 2012 Nobel for the theory of stable allocations and "market design" — applying economic theory to real-world matching problems; who is he?
Often called the founder of alpinism and modern meteorology, this Genevan scientist is also credited with building the first successful solar oven — who was he?
Horace Bénédict de Saussure: Genevan scientist and mountaineer (1740–1799)
In a 263 CE commentary on The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, this Chinese mathematician proved the Pythagorean theorem and improved on Archimedes's approximation of π — who was he?
Liu Hui: Chinese mathematician and writer
This Belgian-American physicist-mathematician is best known for wavelets that revolutionized image compression — a family of them even bears her name; who is she?
Ingrid Daubechies: Belgian physicist and mathematician (born 1954)
A founder of modern geometric analysis, this American mathematician won the 2019 Abel Prize for pioneering work in geometric partial differential equations and gauge theory — who is she?
This French mathematician ranged across number theory, complex analysis, and mathematical physics — and a crater on the Moon is named after him; who was he?
Element 124, also called eka-uranium, is a hypothetical g-block superactinide that may sit within the "island of stability" — what is its placeholder name?
Unbiquadium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 124 (Ubq)
This American psychologist completed every requirement for a Harvard Ph.D. in 1895 but was denied the degree because of her gender — who was she?
Mary Whiton Calkins: American philosopher and psychologist
This English physicist identified electromagnetic radiation independently of Hertz and built an early radio receiver he named the "coherer" — who was he?
Oliver Lodge: English physicist and electrical engineer (1851–1940)
A student of Marie Curie, this French physicist discovered the element francium in 1939 and later became the first woman elected to the French Académie des Sciences — who was she?

One of the first female interior decorators, this American actress-turned-designer swept away dark, cluttered Victorian rooms for light, simple layouts — and was proud to be called Lady Mendl; who was she?
Elsie de Wolfe: American interior decorator, author, and actress
Broadway's celebrated lyric-soprano ingénue of the 1950s, she won a Tony for The Music Man before reinventing herself as a cabaret and concert star — which singer?
Barbara Cook: American actress and singer (1927–2017)
The highest-earning actress of her day, she scandalized New York, London and Paris in the 1860s by appearing seemingly nude astride a horse onstage in the hippodrama "Mazeppa" — who was she?
Adah Isaacs Menken: American actress, dancer, painter, and poet (1835–1868)
A rodeo trick rider and vaudeville performer born Rose August Wenger, she's considered the first American professional stunt woman — who was she?

A three-time Tony winner who joined the Old Vic and the Royal Shakespeare Company, this American-born star of British and American theatre also won a BAFTA for the 1958 film "Orders to Kill" — who was she?
Dubbed "The King of Television" and a six-time Gold Logie winner, this Australian entertainer often paired with Bert Newton on In Melbourne Tonight — who was he?

Graham Kennedy (15 February 1934 - 25 May 2005) was an Australian entertainer, comedian and variety performer, radio and television host as well as a personality and actor of theatre, television and film.
Winner of Wimbledon in 1947 and a pioneer promoter who pushed tennis toward professionalism, this American ushered in the serve-and-volley era — who is he?
Serving as chief minstrel-poet to the Sasanian king Khosrow II, this barbat player is remembered as the most distinguished Persian musician of his age — who was he?
Barbad: Persian musician-poet under Khosrow II (r. 590–628)
Made Master of the Queen's Music in 2004, this English composer shocked audiences in 1969 with the monodrama Eight Songs for a Mad King — who was he?
Peter Maxwell Davies: English composer and conductor (1934–2016)

The earliest name in the Alexandrian canon of the Nine Lyric Poets, this 7th-century-BC Spartan wrote choral hymns in the Doric dialect that survive only in quotations and Egyptian papyrus scraps — who is he?
Alcman: Ancient Greek lyric poet from Sparta
A sculptor of the Harlem Renaissance whose studio launched a generation of Black artists, she fought for equal rights for African Americans in the arts — who was she?
Augusta Savage: American sculptor and teacher (1892–1962)
Working with his wife Marion, this American architect won a competition to draw an entire capital from scratch — Australia's Canberra. Which Prairie School designer was it?
Walter Burley Griffin: American architect and landscape architect (1876–1937)
A German dialect poet and Lutheran theologian, he's best remembered for Alemannic verse and a collection of tales called the "Treasure Chest of Rhenish Tales" — who was he?
After her 1908 debut novel, this Canadian writer turned to politics — winning a seat in Alberta's legislature and helping carry the famous Persons Case to court. Who was she?
Nellie McClung: Canadian author, activist, suffragist and politician (1873–1951)
Born Kathleen Ruska and once known as Kath Walker, this Aboriginal Australian activist became the first of her people to publish a book of verse — who is she?
Oodgeroo Noonuccal: Aboriginal Australian poet, artist, teacher and campaigner for Indigenous rights
A statesman and reformer who served some fifteen years as Chancellor of the Han state, this ancient Chinese thinker built a doctrine of governance around administrative technique — who was he?
Shen Buhai: Chinese philosopher and politician (c. 400–c. 337 BC)

This French thinker founded a school he called "eclecticism," blending German idealism with Scottish Common Sense — and shaped his nation's schools as its administrator of public instruction. Who was he?

Often called the first successful Black woman novelist living in Britain after 1948, this Nigerian writer drew on her own childhood for novels like "The Joys of Motherhood" and "Second Class Citizen" — who was she?
Thornton Wilder won a Pulitzer for this 1942 comedy-drama, a three-part allegory of all human history told through the Antrobus family of fictional Excelsior, New Jersey — what's its title?
The Skin of Our Teeth: 1942 play by Thornton Wilder

Known as the "Hoosier Poet," this writer penned most of his roughly 1,000 poems in dialect — including "Little Orphant Annie" — and got an early career boost from an endorsement by Longfellow. Who was he?
A former child actor turned radical feminist, this poet and Ms. magazine editor compiled the landmark 1970 anthology "Sisterhood Is Powerful" — who is she?
Robin Morgan: American poet, writer and activist (born 1941)
Painted by Thomas Gainsborough around 1750 and unknown to the public until a 1927 exhibition, this portrait of a couple amid their Suffolk estate now hangs in London's National Gallery — what is it?
Mr and Mrs Andrews: Painting by Thomas Gainsborough

Henri Rousseau's first jungle painting, this 1891 canvas shows a big cat lit by lightning, poised to pounce in a raging gale — it first hung at the unjuried Salon des Indépendants under the title "Surprised!" What is it?
Tiger in a Tropical Storm: Painting by Henri Rousseau
She edited the era's most widely read magazine, Godey's Lady's Book, wrote "Mary Had a Little Lamb," and campaigned tirelessly to make Thanksgiving a national holiday — who was she?
Sarah Josepha Hale: American writer and editor (1788–1879)
A Baltic German writer of the Sturm und Drang movement, he was born in 1751 and died young in 1792 — who was he?
Jakob Michael Reinhold Lenz: German playwright (1751–1792)
After dancing with Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, this Irish-born founder of The Royal Ballet became known as the "godmother" of English and Irish ballet — who was she?
Ninette de Valois (born Edris Stannus; 6 June 1898 - 8 March 2001) was an Irish-born British ballet dancer, teacher, choreographer, and director of classical ballet.
One of the most popular American women poets of her day, "Fanny" became famous for a flirtatious exchange of romantic verse with Edgar Allan Poe — who was she?
Lillian Hellman's 1939 drama about a scheming family fighting for control of a business in turn-of-the-century Alabama takes its title from a verse in the Song of Solomon — what's the play?
The Little Foxes: Play by Lillian Hellman

She ran a Baltimore girls' school until age 62, then launched a second career writing best-selling books on ancient Greece and Rome that made her one of America's most renowned classicists — who was she?
Edith Hamilton: American teacher and writer (1867–1963)

Compiled by Jiao Yu and Liu Bowen in the 14th-century early Ming dynasty, this Chinese military treatise — its name rendered in English as the "Fire Drake Manual" — illustrated early firearms. What is it?
Huolongjing: 14th-century military treatise from the early Ming dynasty (1368–1683)
This Pakistani dramatist's 1922 Urdu play about the legendary Anarkali was staged hundreds of times and helped inspire the epic Indian film "Mughal-e-Azam" — who was he?
Hailed by Time as a 2019 'Pioneer' yet condemned as a mad scientist, which Chinese biophysicist announced in 2018 that he'd created the first gene-edited human babies?
He Jiankui (pinyin: H Jinku HUH KWAY; born 1984) is a Chinese biophysicist known for his controversial first use of genome editing in humans in 2018.
From Japan and later China, this Vietnamese revolutionary launched the Đông Du movement and wrote tracts demanding independence from French rule — who was he?
Phan Bội Châu: Vietnamese nationalist and revolutionary

After Reinhard Heydrich's assassination, this Austrian SS official became the third chief of the Reich Security Main Office — overseeing the Gestapo, Kripo and SD — and was later convicted as a war criminal. Who was he?

This English mountaineer and his partner Sandy Irvine were last seen climbing toward Everest's summit in 1924, sparking a century of debate over whether they reached the top before they died. Who was he?
Nicknamed the "Land Cruiser War," this conflict erupted in Sudan in 2003 and led to President Omar al-Bashir being indicted for genocide by the International Criminal Court. What was it?
War in Darfur: Genocidal conflict in Western Sudan

One of the Three Kingdoms of Korea alongside Goguryeo and Silla, this kingdom in the southwest had the largest population of the three and was founded by Onjo near present-day Seoul. Which kingdom was it?
Paekche: Ancient Korean kingdom (18 BCE – 660 CE)
A rear admiral in the Austro-Hungarian Navy who fought at the Strait of Otranto, this man went on to rule his landlocked nation as regent from 1920 through most of World War II. Who was he?
Miklós Horthy: Regent of Hungary from 1920 to 1944
Begun with the 1947 partition and pitting India against both Pakistan and China, this territorial dispute has flared into three full wars — what is it called?
The Kashmir conflict is a territorial conflict over the Kashmir region, primarily between India and Pakistan, and also between China and India in the northeastern portion of the region.
It traces back to ancient myths of crafted beings, but the field formally began at a 1956 Dartmouth workshop where the Logic Theorist program debuted — what subject is being recounted?
The history of artificial intelligence began in antiquity, with myths, stories, and rumors of artificial beings endowed with intelligence by master craftsmen.

First described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, this family of over 2,000 araneomorph spiders includes the "cellar spider" and "vibrating spider" — and shares a famous leggy nickname with harvestmen and crane flies. What family is it?
Nocturnal, owl-faced, and unable to fly, this endangered New Zealand bird holds the title of the world's heaviest parrot. What is it?
Kākāpō: Parrot endemic to New Zealand

When a piece of one of these blood-vessel clots breaks free to travel the body it's called an embolus — and the original blockage can trigger a stroke or heart attack. What is this clot formation called?
Thrombosis: Formation of blood clots inside the blood vessels
Defined by an outer membrane that won't hold the crystal violet stain, this category includes E. coli and the plague bacterium Yersinia pestis — what are these microbes called?
Gram-negative bacteria are bacteria that, unlike gram-positive bacteria, do not retain the crystal violet stain used in the Gram staining method of bacterial differentiation.
Living up to 25 years and occasionally topping 50 kg, which widely-eaten fish ranges from the Bay of Biscay to the Arctic and around Greenland?
The Atlantic cod (pl.: cod; Gadus morhua) is a fish of the family Gadidae, widely consumed by humans.

Bounding the inner product of two vectors by the product of their norms, this much-used result carries the names of a Frenchman who published it for sums in 1821 and two others who tackled the integral version — what is it?
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality is an upper bound on the absolute value of the inner product between two vectors in an inner product space in terms of the product of the vector norms.
Awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2008 for his AIDS-relief work on PEPFAR, this immunologist directed the U.S. allergy and infectious-disease institute from 1984 to 2022. Who is he?
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
Cold-sensitive and tasting of sweet pine and citrus, this kitchen herb is so close to its cousin that in parts of the Middle East the two names are used interchangeably with oregano. What is it?
Sold as Thorazine, this drug was the first of the typical antipsychotics — used to treat schizophrenia and, oddly, hiccups that won't quit. What is it?
Dubbed "sea locusts" by the ancient Assyrians and "prawn killers" by others, these burrow-dwelling crustaceans are among the most important predators of shallow tropical seas. What are they?
Usually viral and often worse at night, this childhood respiratory infection swells the trachea and announces itself with an unmistakable barking, brassy cough — what's it called?
Croup: Respiratory infection often caused by a virus
Strawberries, blueberries, blackberries, and currants all fall under this small, pulpy, often brightly colored category of fruit — which Britain calls "soft fruit." What is it?
Berry: In the culinary sense, small edible fruit
This Asian canid stands apart from true dogs: a convex rather than concave skull, no third lower molar, and single-cusped upper molars — once it roamed into Europe. What is it?
Dhole (dohl; Cuon alpinus) is a canid native to South, East and Southeast Asia.
Before becoming TV's most famous bow-tied science educator, this Boeing mechanical engineer invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube for 747s, then quit to do sketch comedy. Who is he?
This reddish-brown, poisonous gas (formula NO2) is a key step in making nitric acid for fertilizer — and your gas stove quietly produces it while you cook. What is it?

Created by Reg Watson and on the air from 1985 to 2025, this Melbourne-set serial was cancelled by one network after just four months — then revived by a rival and grew into Australia's longest-running drama. What is it?

Praised for its realistic portrait of a working-class family in fictional Lanford, Illinois, this ABC sitcom hit No. 1 in the Nielsen ratings in its second season — then got a short-lived revival in 2018. What was it?
Before creating one of TV's most enduring science-fiction universes, this writer flew 89 combat missions in World War II, worked as a commercial pilot, and joined the LAPD. Who was he?
Gene Roddenberry: American screenwriter and producer (1921–1991)
A Canadian who became a U.S. citizen in 1998, this game-show host fronted the same syndicated quiz program for 37 seasons, from its 1984 revival until his death in 2020. Who was he?
Bordered by Lake Michigan to the east and Lake Superior to the north, this Upper Midwest state has 72 counties and its most populous city is Milwaukee — which state is it?
Whose name means "White Mountain" — a dormant Hawaiian shield volcano that, measured from its base on the ocean floor, towers more than 30,000 feet, a rise rivaled only by Everest?
The only German islands far from the mainland, this tiny North Sea archipelago was a British possession from 1807 until 1890. What is it?
Attached to the Doge's Palace at one end of a famous square, this Venetian cathedral holds the relics of the city's patron saint. What is it?
Patriarchal Cathedral Basilica of Saint Mark
The Patriarchal Cathedral Basilica of Saint Mark
St Mark's Basilica: Cathedral church in Venice, Italy

Born in Mexico in 1968 and now boasting over 25 million players, this racquet sport is played on a small enclosed court where solid, strapless paddles and walls of glass make it feel like tennis crossed with squash — what is it?
"Hammerin'" was the nickname, and for 33 years he held the career home-run record he took from Babe Ruth — until Barry Bonds passed him. Which right fielder?
Henry Louis Aaron, nicknamed "Hammer" or "Hammerin' Hank", was an American professional baseball right fielder who played 23 seasons in Major League Baseball, from 1954 through 1976.
Tracing its roots to a service called PlayNET, this web portal grew to about three million users by 1995, displacing rivals like CompuServe and Prodigy as the largest online service. What is it?
The first single released on the Beatles' own Apple label, this 1968 song spent nine weeks atop the Billboard Hot 100 — tying the all-time record at the time. What is it?
Hey Jude: 1968 single by the Beatles
Developed in 1965 by University of Florida researchers to replenish the electrolytes their student-athletes lost in sweat, this drink took its name from the school's team. What is it?
Gatorade: Brand of sports-themed beverages and food products
This Alsatian polymath was at once a theologian, organist, philosopher, and physician — and won the 1952 Nobel Peace Prize for his philosophy of "Reverence for Life." Who was he?
This Neo-Assyrian king destroyed Babylon in 689 BC and rebuilt Nineveh into a grand capital, but is most famous in the Hebrew Bible for his campaign in the Levant. Who was he?

This English explorer often journeyed alone through 1890s West Africa where Europeans rarely ventured, collecting zoological specimens for the British Museum and later writing 'Travels in West Africa' — who was she?
Mary Kingsley: English ethnographer, scientific writer and explorer (1862–1900)
Dubbed the 'Father of Federation,' this colonial Australian premier delivered an 1889 oration at Tenterfield that set the six colonies on the road to becoming one nation — who was he?
He left school at 13 after his father died and trained as a stonemason before emigrating from Scotland — then became Canada's first Liberal prime minister, taking office in 1873. Who was he?
Alexander Mackenzie (politician): Prime Minister of Canada from 1873 to 1878

A Brazilian naturalist who specialized in poison dart frogs — and has four frog species named after her — she also helped win women's suffrage in Brazil and signed the United Nations Charter. Who was she?
Bertha Lutz: Brazilian scientist and politician (1894–1976)
Once an Italian slave-girl gifted to Phraates IV, she had him poisoned and crowned herself co-ruler — becoming the first of only three women to reign as monarchs in Iranian history. Who was she?
Musa (also spelled Mousa), also known as Thea Musa, was the reigning queen of the Parthian Empire from 2 BC to 4 AD. Originally an Italian slave-girl, Augustus gifted her to Phraates IV.
He landed at Anzac Cove in 1915, distinguished himself planning the Battle of Pozières, and remains the only Australian ever to reach the rank of field marshal — who was he?

As Ulysses S. Grant's most trusted advisor and secretary of state, this New York statesman settled the Alabama Claims with Britain and helped pioneer the idea of international arbitration — who was he?
This Hyksos king ruled Lower Egypt during the Fifteenth Dynasty for some forty years, outliving his southern rival Kamose but not Ahmose I — the Greeks called him Apophis. What was his Egyptian name?
Apepi: Ruler of Lower Egypt during the Fifteenth Dynasty
Countess in her own right and queen consort to King Stephen, her courage and determination are credited by historians with keeping him on the English throne through the Anarchy. Who was she?
Matilda of Boulogne: Queen of England from 1135 to 1152

A former Tasmanian schoolteacher who'd led the state's Labor branch and been its premier, he later founded the United Australia Party and served as the tenth prime minister of Australia until his death in 1939 — who was he?
Joseph Lyons: Prime Minister of Australia from 1932 to 1939

Rising from vice president after Bingu wa Mutharika's death, she became the first female president of Malawi in 2012 and only the second woman to lead an African nation, after Liberia's Ellen Johnson Sirleaf — who is she?
Joyce Banda: President of Malawi from 2012 to 2014

An ethnic Tutsi army officer who'd helped crush a 1965 Hutu coup, he served as the very last Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Burundi before becoming his country's first president — and ruling as military strongman for a decade until his 1976 overthrow. Who was he?
Sparked after François Bozizé seized the presidency in 2003, this 2004–2007 civil war pitted UFDR rebels against government forces and displaced some 10,000 people. What conflict was it?
Central African Bush War: Civil war, 2004–2007
This towering annual in the daisy family yields the world's fourth most-used vegetable oil, plus snackable seeds and birdseed — and its wild cousins sprout multiple flower heads. What is it?
Common sunflower: Species of flowering plant in the family of Asteraceae
There are four living species of this medium-sized wild cat, including the bobcat, and its name traces to an Indo-European root for 'brightness' — a nod to its glowing, reflective eyes. What is it?
Lynx (links; pl.: Lynx or lynxes) is any of the four extant species (the Canada lynx, Iberian lynx, Eurasian lynx and the bobcat) within the medium-sized wild cat genus lynx.
Fill in the blank: “____ (Ophiophagus hannah) is a species complex of snakes endemic to Asia.”
King cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) is a species complex of snakes endemic to Asia.
This British physicist shared the 1951 Nobel Prize with Ernest Walton for first splitting the atomic nucleus — a feat that opened the way to nuclear power and weapons. Who was he?
This Czech chemist won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for inventing polarography — who was he?
Jaroslav Heyrovský: Czech chemist and inventor (1890–1967)

An American naturalist who surveyed wildlife in Labrador, he turned his observations into quick-freezing methods that launched the modern frozen food industry — and a famous brand bears his name. Who was he?
Clarence Birdseye: American inventor, entrepreneur, and naturalist

Dubbed the 'father of modern experimental optics,' this Scottish inventor discovered the angle and the photoelasticity that bear on polarized light — and improved the stereoscope along the way. Who was he?
David Brewster: British astronomer and mathematician (1781–1868)

This Canadian-American inventor pulled off the first transmission of speech by radio in 1900 and the first two-way radiotelegraphy across the Atlantic in 1906, racking up hundreds of patents — seven granted after his death. Who was this AM-radio pioneer?
Reginald Fessenden: Canadian-American electrical engineer and inventor (1866–1932)
A French economist who gave up accounting to lecture across France, he founded peace societies and the Inter-Parliamentary Union before sharing the very first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901. Who was he?
Frédéric Passy: French economist and pacifist (1822–1912)
This Zambian-born economist turned heads with four New York Times bestsellers, including "Dead Aid," which argues that foreign aid actually holds Africa back. Which author and life peer is it?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo: Zambian-born economist (born February 1969)

This Irish experimental physicist shared the 1951 Nobel with John Cockcroft for splitting the atom — the first nuclear transmutation, as the prize committee put it, "entirely under human control." Who was he?
A founder of modern topology who also wrote under the playful pen name "Paul Mongré," this German mathematician — Jewish and facing deportation — died by suicide with his family in 1942. Who was he?

Some scientists and sci-fi writers like Kim Stanley Robinson borrow the Greek word for the god of war to coin "areology" for this scientific field — the study of one particular planet's rocks and crust. What field is it?
The geology of Mars is the scientific study of the surface, crust, and interior of the planet Mars.

Writing under a pen name, this Belgian-Australian sinologist scandalized 1970s intellectuals with a trilogy denouncing China's Cultural Revolution and the West's idolizing of Mao. Whose pseudonym was it?
Simon Leys: Belgian-Australian writer, sinologist and essayist (1935–2014)
Credited as the first to create a transuranium element — neptunium — this Berkeley physicist shared the 1951 Nobel in Chemistry with Glenn Seaborg. Who was he?

This English silversmith-turned-industrialist partnered with James Watt to install hundreds of steam engines, then modernized the Royal Mint and struck millions of coins for Britain and beyond — who was he?
Matthew Boulton (3 September 1728 - 17 August 1809) was an English businessman, inventor, mechanical engineer, and silversmith.
An English mathematician who shaped matrix and invariant theory, he founded the American Journal of Mathematics while leading the field at Johns Hopkins — who was he?
Often called Trotula, this 12th-century medical writer practiced in a southern Italian coastal town whose school was among the first in Europe to admit women physicians. Who was she?
Trota of Salerno: 12th-century medical practitioner and writer
Fired from his Army astronomer post in 1957 during the Lavender Scare, this man turned his dismissal into a landmark fight that helped ignite a more militant gay rights movement. Who was he?
Frank Kameny: American gay rights activist (1925–2011)

Nicknamed "Chocolate Hero" for his charm and tender voice, this Pakistani actor produced Armaan — the first Pakistani film to do something notable — and became one of South Asia's most beloved stars. Who was he?
Waheed Murad: Pakistani actor, film producer and director

This English theatre critic championed Look Back in Anger at The Observer, but earned a different kind of fame in 1965 as the first person to deliberately say a notorious four-letter word on live British TV — who was he?
Kenneth Tynan: English theatre critic and writer (1927–1980)

This British actress had a commanding stage presence and a knack for powerful roles, but she's best remembered as the cobweb-draped Miss Havisham in David Lean's 1946 Great Expectations — who was she?
Dubbed the "Queen of the Serials," this American silent-film actress did most of her own stunts, never more famously than in The Perils of Pauline — who was she?
Its name means "Great Celebration" — a nod to the PRC's tenth anniversary — and this Heilongjiang city boomed into the "Oil Capital of China" after a 1959 strike. Which city is it?
Daqing: Prefecture-level city in Heilongjiang, China
The third-largest island of Indonesia's Maluku group, it sits between the Banda and Seram Seas, with port towns Namlea and Namrole serving its regencies. Which island is it?
Steep-sided and flat-topped, this 526-metre County Sligo mountain was carved as a nunatak in the last Ice Age and gives its name to "Yeats Country." What is this Irish landmark?
Benbulbin: Mountain in County Sligo, Ireland
A soccer player often recognized as the first Indigenous Australian man to graduate from a university, he led the 1965 Freedom Ride against rural racial discrimination — who was he?
Charles Nelson Perkins, popularly known as Charlie Perkins, was an Aboriginal Australian activist, soccer player, and public administrator.
A wildly popular prizefighter in 1790s Britain, he helped pioneer scientific boxing technique, even publishing two books on the art — who was this English boxer?
A WWII fighter pilot turned cricketer, this dashing member of the "Invincibles" was nicknamed "Nugget" and retired in 1956 with the best all-rounder stats in the game's history — who was he?
Keith Miller (28 November 1919 - 11 October 2004) was an Australian Test cricketer and a Royal Australian Air Force pilot during World War II.

Across five decades this composer-lyricist gave us the hit musicals 'Godspell' and 'Pippin' before defying gravity with 'Wicked,' plus film lyrics for 'Pocahontas' and 'The Prince of Egypt' — who is he?

Arriving in 1946 to lead a respected-but-undersized orchestra still reeling from the war, this Austro-Hungarian-born American conductor turned the Cleveland Orchestra into what critics called one of the world's finest. Who was the maestro?
George Szell: Classical conductor and composer (1897–1970)
She became the first U.S. women's all-around champion at a non-boycotted Olympics in 2004 — then traded the gym for a recording studio as a singer-songwriter. Who is she?
Carly Patterson: American singer and gymnast (born 1988)

Rare's inexperienced team, originally meant to make a side-scrolling platformer, spent two and a half years building this 1997 N64 first-person shooter — a movie tie-in famed for its split-screen deathmatch; what was it?
Sometimes called the "godfather of the Republican Party," this American journalist and politician co-founded both that party and a certain New York newspaper. Who was he?
Henry Jarvis Raymond: American journalist and politician (1820–1869)
