Fought between India and Pakistan from May to July 1999 high in the mountains of Ladakh along the Line of Control, this clash was code-named Operation Vijay by India — what is it known as?
Kargil War: 1999 conflict between India and Pakistan
Sold as Zithromax, this antibiotic tackles strep throat, pneumonia and traveler's diarrhea — but its tendency to cause QT prolongation keeps doctors watchful of the heart. Which drug is it?
Usually forming an S- or C-shaped curve with a rotational twist, this sideways irregular curvature of the spine sits alongside kyphosis and lordosis among the spine's abnormal curves. What is it?
Scoliosis: Left-right asymmetry of the spine's curvature

Believed to be the world's fourth-leading cause of disability, this degenerative joint disease comes from the breakdown of cartilage and bone, often striking the fingertips, thumb base, knees, and hips — what is it?
Osteoarthritis: Form of arthritis caused by degeneration of joints
Also called the bearcat, this dark, shaggy, tree-dwelling Asian viverrid sports a prehensile tail and musk glands that famously smell of buttered popcorn — what is it?
Binturong: Asian mammal also known as a bearcat
This chronic neurological disorder scrambles the sleep-wake cycle, bringing on excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis, and sudden episodes of muscle collapse called cataplexy — what is it?
Belonging to the genus Apis, this eusocial insect builds perennial nests of hexagonal wax cells and stores surplus food as a prized sweet — which creature is it?
A yellow-flowered perennial whose leaves look perforated by translucent glands, this plant is famed in folklore and traditional medicine under a saintly common name — what is its botanical name?
Hypericum perforatum: Flowering plant in the St John's wort family
This seagrass-grazing marine mammal is the lone survivor of its family — its closest cousin, Steller's sea cow, was hunted to extinction in the 1700s. Which coastal Indo-Pacific creature is it?
Dugong (dugong dugon) is a marine mammal.
Many of these 23 carrion-eating birds sport a bald head to stay clean while feeding, and cool off by urinating on their own legs — what kind of bird is it?
Vulture: Common name for a type of bird
A sympathomimetic stimulant often used to keep blood pressure up during anesthesia, this drug has also been tried for asthma, narcolepsy, and obesity — what is it?
This small southern-African mongoose has digging foreclaws and a knack for thermoregulating in harsh, dry country, living in tight packs of up to 30 — which sharp-eyed animal is it?
Meerkat (Suricata suricatta) or suricate is a small mongoose found in southern Africa.
This contagious bacterial skin infection most often shows up as yellowish crusts on a child's face, arms, or legs, and spreads easily in crowded day cares and contact sports — what is it?
Impetigo is a contagious bacterial infection that involves the superficial skin.
Native only to the wetlands of the Carolinas, which carnivorous plant snaps shut a 'jaw' formed from the tips of its leaves when an insect trips it?
Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) is a carnivorous plant native to the temperate and subtropical wetlands of North Carolina and South Carolina, on the East Coast of the United States.
The tallest and heaviest of all living penguins, this flightless Antarctic bird can top 45 kilograms and sports bright-yellow ear patches — which species is it?
Emperor penguin: Large flightless seabird endemic to Antarctica
Found naturally as the mineral sylvite, which white, odorless salt doubles as a low-sodium table-salt substitute, a fertilizer, and food additive E508?
Potassium chloride (KCl, or potassium salt) is a metal halide salt composed of potassium and chlorine.
First classified by Linnaeus in 1753, which herbaceous annual takes its specific name from the Latin for 'cultivated' and has long supplied fiber, seed oil, food and medicine?
Cannabis sativa is an annual herbaceous flowering plant.
This colorless solvent's sweet smell partly explains the aroma of gasoline and paint fumes, and its IUPAC name is simply methylbenzene — which aromatic hydrocarbon is it?
A longtime Harvard law professor, this American appellate lawyer won 13 of 15 murder cases and represented clients from Mike Tyson and Patty Hearst to Julian Assange — who is he?
Alan Dershowitz (born September 1, 1938) is an American lawyer and law professor known for his work in U.S.
In this 1990s NBC sitcom, a street-smart West Philadelphia teen is shipped off to live with wealthy relatives in Los Angeles — what's the show?
The Fresh Prince of Bel Air
The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air: American television sitcom (1990–1996)

George Miller's post-apocalyptic Australian franchise began in 1979 and runs through Fury Road and the 2024 spin-off Furiosa, with Mel Gibson, Tom Hardy, and Jacob Tomuri all playing its drifter hero — what is it?
First broadcast in 1973 and set in the fictional Genoa City, which long-running CBS soap opera grew from half-hour episodes to a full hour in 1980?
The Young and the Restless: American daytime television soap opera (since 1973)
Begun by Mehmed the Conqueror in 1459, this Istanbul complex was the Ottoman sultans' main residence and seat of power until the 1850s, and later took a name meaning 'Cannon Gate' — what is it?
Topkapı Palace is a large museum and library in the east of the Fatih district of Istanbul in Turkey.
Fill in the blank: “____ (d-) is a landlocked U.S.”
North Dakota (d-) is a landlocked U.S.
Fill in the blank: “____ (Siouan languages: Dakta itkaga) is a landlocked state in the North Central region of the United States.”
South Dakota (Siouan languages: Dakta itkaga) is a landlocked state in the North Central region of the United States.
A 110-story Chicago skyscraper that opened in 1973 as the world's tallest building, it still carries the name Sears for most locals and hosts the Skydeck observation level — what is it now called?
Willis Tower: Skyscraper in Chicago, Illinois
This isolated Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, prized for its high endemism, took its name from the day Captain William Mynors sighted it in 1643 — what is it?
Christmas Island: External territory of Australia

Nicknamed the 'Black Panther' and 'o Rei,' this Mozambican-born Portuguese striker banged in 733 goals and was the first man ever to win the European, World Cup, and European Cup Golden Boots — who was he?
Eusébio (European; 25 January 1942 - 5 January 2014), nicknamed the "Black Panther", the "Black Pearl" or "o Rei" ("the King"), was a Mozambican Portuguese footballer who played as a striker.
Raised in Lafayette, Louisiana, but competing for Sweden, this two-time Olympic champion holds the world record in his event at 6.31 metres — who is the pole vaulter nicknamed "Mondo"?
Armand Duplantis: Swedish and American pole vaulter (born 1999)
Born in the mid-1980s D.C. hardcore scene as "emocore" — pioneered by bands like Rites of Spring — this rock genre fuses punk's fury with confessional, emotional lyrics. What is it called?
Emo: Music genre derivative of punk rock
Named after a famous Manhattan neighborhood and built around macho costumed personas, this disco group was assembled by French producers Jacques Morali and Henri Belolo — who are they?
Formed in Chicago in 1969 by Maurice White, this 90-million-selling band fused funk, soul, and disco around a kalimba sound and a dynamic horn section — who are they?
Earth, Wind & Fire: American musical group
Headquartered in Philadelphia and owner of NBCUniversal at 30 Rockefeller Plaza, this conglomerate is the second-largest cable TV company by subscribers in the U.S. — what is it?
Comcast: American multinational telecommunications and media conglomerate

Born from a friendly competition between Percy Bysshe Shelley and Horace Smith over the ruins of pharaoh Ramesses II, this 1818 sonnet meditates on how time topples even the mightiest legacies — what is it?
Left unfinished at Puccini's death in 1924 and set in China, this opera sends Prince Calaf to solve three deadly riddles to win an icy princess's hand — which work is it?

Also called the War of Candia, this 24-year struggle pitted Venice and her allies — the Knights of Malta, the Papacy, France — against the Ottomans, mostly over Venice's richest overseas island. What conflict was it?
Cretan War (1645–1669): Conflict between the Republic of Venice and the Ottoman Empire (1645–1669)
This English aristocrat and writer spent two years in Ottoman Constantinople with her ambassador husband, chronicling life there as a woman — and became a noted medical pioneer. Who was she?
Lady Mary Wortley Montagu: English writer and poet (1689–1762)
An Australian mining billionaire who once listed litigation as a hobby in Who's Who, he founded his own political party in 2013 and won a Queensland seat in parliament. Who is he?
Clive Palmer: Australian businessman and politician (born 1954)
The 33rd king and founder of the Tibetan Empire, he formally brought Buddhism to Tibet, built the Jokhang, and moved his capital to Lhasa while his minister devised the Tibetan script. Who was he?
Songtsen Gampo: 1st Tibetan Emperor and 33rd King of Tibet (d.650)
Known as "Bill," this British field marshal led the so-called "forgotten army" in the Burma campaign before later serving as governor-general of Australia — who was he?
William Slim, 1st Viscount Slim: British Army field marshal, Governor-General of Australia, and author (1891–1970)

Famous for a lifelong lack of interest in politics and war, this Byzantine emperor — long overshadowed as co-ruler before finally reigning alone — held the throne for 66 years, the longest of any Roman emperor since Augustus — who was he?
Constantine VIII: Byzantine emperor from 962 to 1028

Elected by Ostrogothic nobles in 541 after his two predecessors were killed for trying to surrender to the Romans, this penultimate Gothic king reversed the tide of the Gothic War and recovered nearly all of Italy by 543 — who was he?
Totila, King of the Ostrogoths, d. 552
Totila: King of the Ostrogoths from 541 to 552

Designated to rule Ethiopia from 1913 to 1916, he is forever known by a title meaning "child" (especially one of royal blood) because he was never actually crowned and so never chose a regnal name — who is this would-be emperor?
Lij Iyasu: Uncrowned Emperor of Ethiopia from 1913 to 1916

A general of the Army of the Republic of Vietnam, this man led South Vietnam from 1964 to 1965 — bouncing between head of state and prime minister — before exile sent him to die in San Jose. Who is he?
Nguyễn Khánh (8 November 1927 - 11 January 2013) was a Vietnamese military officer and politician.
After a stint as a teacher, this man rose to become the first democratically elected president of Nigeria when the military handed over power in 1979, launching the Second Republic — who was he?
Shehu Shagari: President of Nigeria from 1979 to 1983
Reigning 51 years per the Turin King List, this sixth ruler of the 11th Dynasty reunited Egypt, ended the First Intermediate Period, and became the first pharaoh of the Middle Kingdom — who was he?
Mentuhotep II: Egyptian pharaoh of the 11th Dynasty
A Methodist minister and theologian, he became the first, largely ceremonial head of state of a newly independent African nation in 1980, later stepping aside for Robert Mugabe — who was he?
Canaan Banana: President of Zimbabwe from 1980 to 1987
After 16 distinguished years in Algeria, this French general briefly held the nation's executive power in 1848 during the Second Republic — who was he?
Louis-Eugène Cavaignac: French general and politician (1802–1857)

Likely first domesticated by Austronesian peoples in Maritime Southeast Asia, this herbaceous perennial is grown for the spicy rhizome that puts it in the same family as turmeric and cardamom — what is it?
Ginger: Species of plant used as a spice
A true thrush of Europe, western Asia and North Africa, the male of its nominate subspecies is entirely black — and depending on latitude it may stay put or migrate. What bird is it?
Common blackbird (Turdus merula) is a species of true thrush.
This small, wingless, primitive insect takes its name from its silvery grey color and darting, fish-like movements — and its scientific name hints at a diet of sugars and starches. What is it?
Silverfish (Lepisma saccharinum) is a species of small, primitive, wingless insect in the order Zygentoma (formerly Thysanura).

Discovered in 2013 deep in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system, this archaic human left behind over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, yet a tiny brain keeps its place in our family tree a puzzle — what species is it?

Homo naledi is an extinct species of archaic human discovered in 2013 in the Rising Star Cave system, Gauteng province, South Africa, part of the Cradle of Humankind, dating back to the Middle Pleistocene 335,000-236,000 years ago.
A towering 20th-century French mathematician known for foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry, he was a principal founder of the Bourbaki group. Who was he?

This English physician co-wrote the first English-language medical textbook on homosexuality in 1897, coined the term 'narcissism,' and penned an early public account of a mescaline trip he took on himself. Who was he?
Havelock Ellis: British physician, eugenicist, writer, and social reformer (1859–1939)

After more than 40 years at DuPont, this Polish-American chemist became the first woman to win the company's Lavoisier Medal — an honor that recognized her invention of a famously bullet-stopping fiber. Who was she?
Stephanie Kwolek (July 31, 1923 - June 18, 2014) was a Polish-American chemist known for inventing Kevlar (poly-paraphenylene terephthalamide).

In 1974 in Pacific Grove, California, this computer scientist demoed the first working prototype of CP/M and invented the BIOS, then founded Digital Research to sell his software — who was this PC-revolution pioneer?
Gary Kildall: American computer scientist and microcomputer entrepreneur (1942–1994)
When "Girl, Woman, Other" jointly took the 2019 Booker Prize alongside Margaret Atwood's "The Testaments," this English author became the first black woman ever to win it — who is she?
Bernardine Evaristo: English author and academic (born 1959)

In 1835 this Scottish polymath and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and she signed first on John Stuart Mill's 1866 petition for women's suffrage — who was she?

Germany's first professor of experimental physics is remembered both for the tree-like electrical discharge patterns named after him and for the witty posthumous notebooks he called "waste books" — who was he?
Georg Christoph Lichtenberg: German scientist and satirist (1742–1799)

This English aeronautical engineer wrote novels like "On the Beach" and "A Town Like Alice" under a pen name — dropping his surname so Vickers and fellow engineers wouldn't think him "not a serious person." Who was he?
After his Jewish family fled Germany, this engineer at Sanders Associates dreamed up playing games on a TV screen and built a 'Brown Box' that became the first home video game console — who is he?
Ralph H. Baer: American inventor and engineer (1922–2014)
Introduced to Noh theater as a boy by his actor father Kan'ami, this aesthetician and playwright so impressed the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu that the two formed a close relationship — who was he?
Zeami Motokiyo: Japanese aesthetician, actor, and playwright (c. 1363–c. 1443)

He joined the British Astronomical Association at age 11, compiled the Caldwell catalogue, and hosted the BBC's "The Sky at Night" — the longest-running TV series with its original presenter. Who was this English amateur astronomer?
Patrick Moore: English astronomer, broadcaster and writer (1923–2012)
Discovered by director Teguh Karya for a 1973 film and a six-time Citra Award winner, this Indonesian actress later took a minor role in Hollywood's Eat Pray Love — who is she?

Adapting Frank Norris's novel McTeague, this 1924 silent drama saw director Erich von Stroheim shoot roughly 85 hours of footage — including two grueling months in Death Valley for the finale. What film is it?
Greed (1924 film) — Greed is a 1924 American silent psychological drama film written and directed by Erich von Stroheim and based on the 1899 Frank Norris novel McTeague.
This American playwright and activist, who founded the V-Day movement, wrote a work the New York Times called "probably the most important piece of political theater of the last decade" — who is she?
Eve Ensler: American playwright, performer, feminist, and activist (born 1953)

Forgotten for millennia, this Chinese site — the final Shang capital, where oracle bone script first emerged — was rediscovered in 1899 after someone traced inscribed bones being sold nearby. What is it?
Yinxu: Site of the last capital of the Shang dynasty
This Washington quarterback led the NFL in completion percentage eight times — and, moonlighting as the team's punter, topped the league in punting average too. Who was this two-way star?
Sammy Baugh: American football player and coach (1914–2008)
The fifth IOC president and its only American leader, this fierce champion of amateurism is forever linked to the two Olympics he oversaw in Germany, in 1936 and 1972. Who was he?
Avery Brundage: President of the IOC from 1952 to 1972
A winger from Fredericton, New Brunswick, this player broke the NHL's colour barrier with the Boston Bruins and earned the nickname the "Jackie Robinson of hockey" — who is he?
Willie O'Ree: Canadian ice hockey player (born 1935)
Dubbed "Captain Clutch" for scoring the game-winner in three Olympic gold-medal games, this Canadian centre captains both the Montreal Victoire and her national team — who is she?
Marie-Philip Poulin: Canadian ice hockey player (born 1991)
A seven-time WNBL champion who carried the Opals to five Olympics and three silver medals, she's arguably Australia's most notable women's basketball player ever — who is she?

Public Enemy set out to make the hip-hop equivalent of Marvin Gaye's 'What's Going On' — faster than their debut and dense with social commentary — on this 1988 album built by the Bomb Squad. What's its title?
It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back
It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back
It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back: 1988 studio album by Public Enemy
It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back

A star of the Coupé-Décalé genre, this Ivorian DJ and singer behind hits like 'Jonathan' and 'Kpangor' built an international following in France and became an ambassador for African music. Who is he?
Ange Didier Houon, known professionally as DJ Arafat and various other stage names, was an Ivorian disc jockey and singer who made music in the Coupé-Décalé genre.

Crowned the third-greatest Indonesian musician of all time by Rolling Stone Indonesia in 2011, this progressive pop singer of Chinese-Indonesian descent started out playing bass in a band with his brother Joris — who was he?
His big break came when Stan Getz recruited his whole trio in 1950, and his bluesy piano and writing for Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers helped pioneer hard bop — which jazz pianist and composer was he?
Horace Silver: American jazz pianist and composer (1928–2014)
This Nigerian singer who performs in seven languages won the Peak Talent Show in 2009 and broke through with her 2014 hit "Johnny" — who is she?
Yemi Alade: Nigerian singer and songwriter (born 1989)

A Czech-born Austrian pianist beloved for his Beethoven, Schubert, and Liszt, he was the first ever to record Beethoven's complete works for solo piano — and recorded all 32 sonatas three times over. Who was he?
Alfred Brendel: Austrian composer and pianist (1931–2025)

The younger son of a famous Flemish Renaissance painter and a frequent collaborator with Rubens, this Baroque master painted lush flower still lifes, landscapes, and even scenes of hellfire. Who is he?
Jan Brueghel the Elder: Flemish painter (1568–1625)
This French critic and historian tried to put literature on a scientific footing, pioneering historicist criticism and shaping the naturalism that runs through Zola and Maupassant. Who is he?
Hippolyte Taine: French critic, historian, and philosopher (1828–1893)
A Harlem Renaissance poet and novelist, he also became the NAACP's executive secretary in 1920 and wrote 'Black Manhattan' on a Rosenwald fellowship. Who is this writer and civil rights leader?
James Weldon Johnson: American writer and activist (1871–1938)

Tied to the Beat Generation and dubbed the 'poet laureate of Deep Ecology,' this Pulitzer winner steeped his nature poems in Buddhist spirituality and translated from ancient Chinese and modern Japanese. Who is he?
Creator of the Dragonriders of Pern, she became the first woman to win a Hugo for fiction and the first to win a Nebula — and was later named a SFWA Grand Master. Who is she?
Anne McCaffrey: Irish science fiction writer (1926–2011)
One of the originators of photomontage in Weimar Germany, this Dada artist spliced together press photographs to pick apart the myth of the 'New Woman.' Who is she?
Nicknamed "the firebrand," this radical feminist helped found three New York organizations and in 1968 staged a symbolic "Burial of Traditional Womanhood" — who was she?
Shulamith Bath Shmuel Ben Ari Firestone

A leading authority on Lewis Carroll whose Annotated Alice sold over a million copies, this popular-math writer was also named one of the 100 most influential magicians of the 20th century — who was he?
Martin Gardner: American mathematics and science writer (1914–2010)

Rising to fame in the late 1960s with his wall drawings, this American conceptual and minimalist artist insisted on calling his three-dimensional pieces "structures" rather than sculptures — who was he?
A leading English Modernist sculptor, she worked alongside Ben Nicholson and Naum Gabo in the artists' colony at St Ives during the Second World War — who was she?
Barbara Hepworth: English artist and sculptor (1903–1975)

A leading figure in Reformed epistemology and longtime Notre Dame professor, this American philosopher is best known for his work in the philosophy of religion and the metaphysics of modality — who is he?
Jonathan Franzen's 2001 novel about an elderly Midwestern couple and their three adult children gathering for "one last Christmas" won that year's National Book Award — what's its title?
The Corrections: 2001 novel by Jonathan Franzen
Born in Santo Domingo and raised in New Jersey, this Dominican American writer and MIT professor created a recurring narrator named "Yunior" — who is he?
Junot Díaz: Dominican-American writer and academic (born 1968)
A printer of nearly 500 works, this English writer is remembered for three novels told entirely through letters, including Pamela and Clarissa — who was he?
Samuel Richardson: English writer and printer (1689–1761)
This American writer and illustrator, once a sought-after Brooklyn Daily Eagle reporter, is best known for Nightwood (1936), a cult classic of lesbian fiction — who is she?
Djuna Barnes: American Modernist writer, poet and artist (1892–1982)
A co-founder of the socialist Fabian Society, this English author wrote or collaborated on more than 60 children's books under her initialed name — who was she?
E. Nesbit: English author and poet (1858–1924)
This Irish furniture designer and architect, a pioneer of the Modern Movement, created the famous Roquebrune-Cap-Martin house known as E-1027 with Jean Badovici — who was she?
Eileen Gray: Irish architect and furniture designer
The most prominent modern Croatian sculptor, he studied at the Vienna Academy under the Secession and steeped himself in Michelangelo and Rodin — who was he?
Ivan Meštrović: Croatian sculptor and architect (1883–1962)
This English historian coined the phrase "history from below" and is best known for his 1963 work The Making of the English Working Class — who was he?
E. P. Thompson: English historian & activist (1924–1993)

An English social theorist who translated Auguste Comte and was rare among women writers in earning enough to support herself, she was invited to the young Princess Victoria's 1838 coronation — who was she?
Harriet Martineau: English writer and sociologist (1802–1876)

To escape an enslaver who threatened to sell her children, this North Carolina-born writer hid for seven years in a crawl space too low to stand up in — then published her story as 'Linda Brent.' Whose American classic is it?
Harriet Jacobs: African-American abolitionist and writer (d. 1897)

Her novel The Vegetarian became the first Korean-language book to win the International Booker, and in 2024 she became the first Asian woman to take the Nobel Prize in Literature — which South Korean writer?

Born into a wealthy Welsh family and once Cambridge's Public Orator, this priest of the Church of England is hailed as one of Britain's foremost devotional lyricists among the metaphysical poets — who is he?
George Herbert: English poet, orator and Anglican priest (1593–1633)
A pioneer of architectural functionalism, this Danish designer won worldwide fame less for his buildings than for a few impossibly simple, well-made chairs — who is he?
A librarian in ancient Alexandria, this Cyrene-born poet reportedly wrote over 800 works and lent his name to an entire aesthetic philosophy that shaped Roman poetry — who was he?
Callimachus: 3rd-century BCE Greek poet, scholar and librarian
Legend credits this man with toppling Rome's last king after the suicide of Lucretia and becoming one of the Republic's first two consuls — who was he?
Lucius Junius Brutus: Semi-legendary 6th-century BC founder of Roman Republic
Scottish-born to Irish parents, this socialist and union leader founded Ireland's first socialist party before being executed for his role in the 1916 Easter Rising. Who was he?
James Connolly: Irish republican, trade unionist and revolutionary (1868–1916)
Famous for its revolving turret, this Union ironclad fought the CSS Virginia to a stalemate at the Battle of Hampton Roads in 1862 and lent its name to a whole class of warship — what was it?
USS Monitor: First ironclad of the US Navy, 1861–1862
Ruling his principality for nearly 56 years, this sovereign transformed its economy from casino gambling toward a tax-haven and cultural destination — who was he?
Rainiero Louis Henri Maxence Bertrand Grimaldi
Rainier III was Prince of Monaco from 1949 to his death in 2005.
Ruled from Cairo by a military caste of freed slave-soldiers, this state overthrew the Ayyubids in 1250 and held Egypt and the Levant until the Ottomans conquered it in 1517 — what was it called?
Mamluk Sultanate: State in Egypt, Hejaz and Syria (1250–1517)

On 15 March 2019, a gunman attacked two New Zealand mosques during Friday prayer, killing 51 people in the first far-right terror attack to be successfully live-streamed on Facebook. What is this atrocity called?
Christchurch mosque shootings: 2019 terrorist attacks in New Zealand
Founded in 1919 and now owned by Stellantis, this French automaker made its name in 1934 with the Traction Avant, the world's first mass-produced car of its kind — what's the brand?
Citroën: French car brand of Stellantis

In Hindu cosmology this is the fourth, shortest, and worst of the four world ages — said to have begun at Krishna's death in 3102 BCE and to be the conflict-ridden era we live in now. What is it called?
Kali Yuga, in Hinduism, is the fourth, shortest and worst of the four yugas (world ages) in a Yuga cycle, preceded by Dvapara Yuga and followed by the next cycle's Krita (Satya) Yuga.

Marked by severe food restriction and an overwhelming desire to be thin despite usually being underweight, the DSM-5 frames this eating disorder around a 'disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced' — what is it?

Anorexia nervosa, commonly referred to as anorexia, is an eating disorder characterized by predominant food restriction, body image disturbance, fear of gaining weight, and an overwhelming desire to be thin.
About 90% of cases trace to a herniated spinal disc pressing on a nerve root, producing a shooting pain that runs from the lower back down one leg — what's the condition?
Sciatica: Lower-back pain that can extend down the leg
Native to Southeast Asia and a close relative of the lychee and longan, this medium-sized tree lends its name to a hairy-skinned tropical fruit — what is it?
Named for the English physician who first described it in 1832, this cancer is defined by multinucleated Reed–Sternberg cells in the lymph nodes — what is it?
Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of blood and immune-system cancer
Despite the zebra-like stripes on its legs, this shy mammal of the northeastern Congo is actually the giraffe's only living cousin — and the sole other member of the family Giraffidae. What is it?
Okapi (Okapia johnstoni), also known as the forest giraffe, and zebra giraffe, is an artiodactyl mammal that is endemic to the northeast Democratic Republic of the Congo in central Africa.
In this inherited blood disorder, faulty haemoglobin warps red cells into a rigid crescent shape that can't bend through capillaries, causing painful blockages — what is it?
An English GP convicted in 2000 of murdering 15 patients, he's reckoned one of history's most prolific serial killers with an estimated 250 victims — who was he?
Harold Shipman: English doctor and serial killer (1946–2004)
A catecholamine whose very name nods to the kidney, it acts as both a hormone and neurotransmitter and is called "noradrenaline" outside the US — what is it?
A sessile marine arthropod related to crabs and lobsters, folklore once claimed geese hatched fully formed from one variety of it — what creature is it?
Barnacle: Subclass of sessile marine crustaceans

In this condition, tiny arteries spasm and starve the fingers of blood, classically turning them white, then blue, then a burning red as flow returns. It's named for the physician who first described it in 1862 — what is it?
Raynaud syndrome: Medical condition in which spasm of arteries causes episodes of reduced blood flow
The smallest fox species, this North African desert dweller sports oversized ears that both dump body heat and pick up the sound of prey moving underground — which fox is it?
The fennec fox (Vulpes zerda) is a small fox native to the deserts of North Africa, ranging from Western Sahara and Mauritania to the Sinai Peninsula.

He co-founded Microsoft with his childhood friend Bill Gates in 1975, then stepped back from daily work in 1983 after a Hodgkin lymphoma diagnosis and later launched Vulcan Inc. with his sister. Who was he?
Odorless, colorless, and dangerously sweet-tasting, this viscous compound goes into polyester fibers and antifreeze — and has even been spotted in outer space. What is it?
First described by Linnaeus in 1758, this medium-sized spotted cat of the Americas is a skilled climber, leaper, and swimmer that hunts armadillos and opossums by night — which cat is it?
Ocelot (Leopardus pardalis) is a medium-sized spotted wild cat that reaches 40-50 cm (16-20 in) at the shoulders and weighs between 7 and 15.5 kg (15 and 34 lb) on average.

This rapid, irregular quivering of the heart's upper chambers can be entirely silent or bring palpitations and fainting — and it sharply raises the risk of stroke, dementia and heart failure. What is this arrhythmia?
Atrial fibrillation: Irregular beating of the atria of the heart
A pioneer of women in comedy who started in Greenwich Village beside Carlin and Pryor, she made her name with a blunt, acerbic, self-deprecating New York persona — who was she?
Joan Rivers: American comedian and television host (1933–2014)
After years fronting American Idol and Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve, this host took over a beloved game show in September 2024, replacing Pat Sajak. Who is he?
Ryan Seacrest: American television and radio host (born 1974)
Across 33 years and 6,080 episodes, this NBC-then-CBS host surpassed his friend and mentor Johnny Carson to become the longest-serving late-night talk show host in American TV history. Who is he?
David Letterman: American comedian and television host (born 1947)
The only U.S. state that divides itself into "parishes" instead of counties, this Deep South state wears its French heritage proudly, from Baton Rouge to New Orleans — which state is it?
Culturally and legally split into three "Grand Divisions" — East, Middle, and West — this landlocked Southern state is anchored by its capital and largest city, Nashville. Which state is it?
Recorded in the Domesday Book as "Brighthelmstone," this East Sussex seaside resort 47 miles south of London boomed as a boarding point for boats to France — which town is it?
Brighton: Seaside resort on the south coast of England
A UNESCO biosphere reserve just 60 miles off the coast of North Africa, this Spanish island in the Atlantic is the second largest of the Canary Islands. Which island is it?
Fuerteventura is one of the Canary Islands, in the Atlantic Ocean, geographically part of Macaronesia, and politically part of Spain.
Formed where Broadway meets Seventh Avenue and 42nd Street, this bowtie-shaped Midtown plaza is a hub of the Theater District blazing with digital billboards — what is it?
Times Square: Intersection and area in Manhattan, New York
Widely called the greatest leg-spinner ever, this Australian took 708 Test wickets and later captained Rajasthan Royals to the inaugural IPL title — who was he?
This left fielder holds the single-season home run record of 73, set in 2001, plus a record seven NL MVP awards across stints with the Pirates and Giants — who is he?
Barry Bonds (born July 24, 1964) is an American former professional baseball left fielder who played 22 seasons in Major League Baseball (MLB).
Across 20 NFL seasons he won three Super Bowls with San Francisco and ranked second only to Jim Brown on The Sporting News' 1999 greatest-players list — who is this receiver?
Jerry Rice (born October 13, 1962) is an American former professional football wide receiver who played for 20 seasons in the National Football League (NFL).
The first airline to fly worldwide, it pioneered the jumbo jet and computerized reservations, and its blue globe logo was nicknamed "The Blue Meatball" — which carrier was it?
Pan Am: Airline of the United States (1927–1991)
Before TV stardom, this cartoonist sold a strip called "Life in Hell" that caught producer James L. Brooks's eye — who is the creator of The Simpsons?
Matt Groening: American cartoonist and animator (born 1954)
This Austrian literary-critic-turned-occultist founded the esoteric movement anthroposophy and claimed to be clairvoyant — who was he?

Obscure in her short life but later one of the most beloved saints in the church, this French Carmelite is known the world over as the "Little Flower" for her simple, practical path to holiness. Who was she?
Saint Therese of the Child Jesus and the Holy Face, O.C.D.
St Theresa of the Child Jesus
Thérèse of Lisieux: French Discalced Carmelite nun and saint (1873–1897)
He commanded Bosnian government forces defending the surrounded Srebrenica enclave during the Bosnian War, and was later tried at The Hague over the treatment of detainees — which officer was he?

Naser Orić (born 3 March 1967) is a Bosnian former officer who commanded Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina (ARBiH) forces in the Srebrenica enclave in eastern Bosnia surrounded by Bosnian Serb forces, during the Bosnian War.
He led the first government of Bangladesh as prime minister during the 1971 War of Independence and is seen as one of the most instrumental figures in the nation's birth — who was he?
Tajuddin Ahmad: Prime Minister of Bangladesh from 1971 to 1972
This 30th U.S. vice president, serving under Coolidge, also won a Nobel Peace Prize for the WWI reparations plan that bears his name — who was he?
Charles G. Dawes: Vice President of the United States from 1925 to 1929
Nicknamed for both his towering height and his 23-year run, this architect of the 'Swedish Model' welfare state holds the record as his country's longest-serving prime minister — who was he?
Tage Erlander: Prime Minister of Sweden from 1946 to 1969
Crowned king of the Franks as an infant under his mother Fredegund's regency, he pursued her feud with Queen Brunhilda to a brutal end — her execution by dismemberment in 613. Which king?
Known as 'the Great Fifth,' this 17th-century figure was the first to hold both Tibet's spiritual and political leadership, unifying the land under the Ganden Phodrang — who was he?
5th Dalai Lama: Spiritual and political leader of Tibet from 1642 to 1682

One of three brothers with distinguished military careers, this British general rose to Commander-in-Chief, America, during the War of Independence after famously scaling the cliffs at Quebec in 1759. Who was he?
William Howe, 5th Viscount Howe: British Army officer and politician (1729–1814)
As Lunar Module pilot on Apollo 15, this Air Force test pilot became the eighth person to walk on the Moon. Who was he?
James Irwin: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1930–1991)
Also called the ratel, this remarkably loose-skinned mammal — able to twist freely inside its own hide — is the largest land member of the weasel family in Africa. What is it?
The largest tree fruit on Earth can hit 120 pounds and 35 inches long — a 'multiple fruit' made of thousands of individual flowers, with a single tree bearing hundreds a year. What is it?
This German physicist won the 1914 Nobel for discovering how crystals diffract X-rays, then — a fierce opponent of Nazism — helped rebuild German science after the war. Who is he?

This American Nobel laureate coined the term 'bioorthogonal chemistry' for reactions that work inside living systems, building chemical tools to study the cell-surface sugars called glycans. Who is she?
Awarded a gas-attack Iron Cross in WWI before sharing the 1925 Nobel with Gustav Hertz for the laws of how an electron strikes an atom — who was this German-American physicist?

This American physicist dared to drop the wave-function-collapse postulate, proposing a 'relative state' theory that became the basis of the many-worlds interpretation — largely ignored until quantum decoherence vindicated him. Who is he?
Sometimes called the founder of pneumatic chemistry, this 17th-century Brussels physician coined the word 'gas' and ran a famous five-year willow-tree experiment. Who was he?
Jan Baptist van Helmont: Chemist and physician (1580–1644)
This Turing Award winner brought order to the chaos of distributed computing — and, on the side, created the document-preparation system LaTeX and wrote its first manual. Who is he?
Leslie Lamport: American computer scientist and mathematician (born 1941)
This British mathematician and logician coined the phrase 'mathematical induction' and gave his name to a pair of laws relating conjunction, disjunction, and negation. Who was he?
Augustus De Morgan: British mathematician and logician (1806–1871)
This Italian-American physicist discovered two elements, technetium and astatine, plus the antiproton — the last earning him a share of the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. Who was he?
Emilio Segrè: Italian-American nuclear physicist and radiochemist (1905–1989)
A Boston physician, medical reformer, and 'fireside' poet, this polymath delighted readers with his 'Breakfast-Table' series begun in 1858. Who was he?
Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.: American poet, essayist, physician (1809–1894)
Dubbed 'the Edgar Allan Poe of cinema,' this former carnival sideshow performer turned director gave us Dracula (1931) and Freaks (1932) — who is he?
A Cahiers du Cinéma critic turned French New Wave director, he was famed for improvisation and marathon runtimes in films like Out 1 and Céline and Julie Go Boating — who is he?
Jacques Rivette: French film director, screenwriter and film critic
A contemporary of Satyajit Ray, this Bengali filmmaker was largely ignored in his lifetime but is now ranked among the greats for his work on partition, feminism, and social reality — who is he?
Ritwik Ghatak: Indian Bengali filmmaker and script writer (1925–1976)

After running away to Chicago at 16 to haunt "whorehouses, police stations, courtrooms... saloons, slums, madhouses," this journalist-turned-screenwriter went on to write some seventy films and earn six Oscar nominations — who was he?
Ben Hecht: American writer, director, and producer (1894–1964)

Billy Wilder and Raymond Chandler adapted James M. Cain's novel into this 1944 film noir, whose title refers to an insurance clause doubling a payout when death occurs in a statistically rare way — what's the movie?
Double Indemnity: 1944 American film by Billy Wilder
Belgium's most populous municipality sits on the river Scheldt, which links it to the North Sea, and lies about 40 km north of Brussels and just south of the Dutch border — what city is it?
Antwerp is a city and a municipality in the Flemish Region of Belgium.
Nicknamed "Mother of the Colonies" and founded in 1878 with help from Edmond Rothschild, this is now Israel's fourth-largest city, just east of Tel Aviv — which one?

Founded in 1748 and once ruled by its own Nawabs, this Pakistani city sits at the edge of the Cholistan Desert as the gateway to Lal Suhanra National Park, rich with princely-era monuments. Which city is it?
Before twice holding a WBA super-middleweight boxing title, this Australian played professional rugby league — and stoked heated feuds with Danny Green and Daniel Geale. Who is he?
Anthony Mundine: Australian boxer, rugby league footballer, and rapper (born 1975)
This Cleveland Browns quarterback reached his league's championship game every single year he played — ten straight appearances, seven of them won. Who was he?
Otto Graham: American football player, coach, and executive (1921–2003)
The first woman to play full-time pro men's hockey outside the goal crease, she captained Canada to four Olympic golds and is her national team's all-time points leader — who is she?
Hayley Wickenheiser: Canadian ice hockey player (born 1978)
Ranked the world's number one male professional from 1952 to 1961, this American won 15 major singles titles, including back-to-back U.S. National Championships in 1948 and 1949 — who was he?
Crowned 'Shahenshah-e-Ghazal' — Emperor of Ghazal — this Pakistani playback singer with a haunting baritone carried ghazal to a worldwide audience — who is it?
A chart-topping Turkish pop singer who debuted in the early 2000s, she's known for constantly reinventing her image and a brief detour into electronic music — who is she?
Hande Yener: Turkish singer and songwriter (born 1973)

Music historians crown this fiddle-playing Texas bandleader the founder of Western swing, though a rival named Spade Cooley kept trying to steal his 'King' nickname — who punctuated his songs with a trademark 'ah-haa'?
Bob Wills: American musician and Western swing bandleader
She sang 'Stormy Weather' and 'His Eye Is on the Sparrow,' then made history as the first African American to star in her own television show — who was this blues-and-Broadway pioneer?
Ethel Waters: American vocalist and actress (1896–1977)

A protégé of Gustav Mahler, this German conductor ran Berlin's avant-garde Kroll Opera before the Nazis drove his Jewish family out — bouncing him from Germany to the U.S., Hungary, and finally Britain. Who is it?

Often called the most-performed opera composer of the entire nineteenth century — the bridge from Mozart to Wagner — this German gave 'grand opera' its decisive character with Robert le diable. Who is he?
Recorded in New York in 1968, this Van Morrison record blended folk, blues, jazz and classical into a hypnotic song cycle — a radical swerve from his earlier hit "Brown Eyed Girl." Which album is it?
Astral Weeks: 1968 studio album by Van Morrison

Crowned the 'King of Country Music,' this fiddler led the Smoky Mountain Boys and joined the Grand Ole Opry in 1938 — so big that Hank Williams ranked his drawing power in the South as 'then God.' Who is he?
Roy Acuff: American country music singer and fiddler (1903–1992)
The first Australian to win international fame as a classical musician, this coloratura soprano took her stage name from her home town of Melbourne. Who was she?
This 18th-century Bengali Shakta poet-saint wrote devotional songs — still sung in Bengal today — mostly addressed to the goddess Kali. Who was he?
Ramprasad Sen: Shakta poet of eighteenth century Bengal

A bebop pioneer born during the Harlem Renaissance, this jazz pianist broke from the stride and ragtime tradition with an attacking right-handed style that reshaped how the instrument was played. Who was he?
Bud Powell: American jazz pianist and composer (1924–1966)
Tomohiro Nishikado drew on Breakout and The War of the Worlds to design this 1978 Taito hit — the first fixed shooter, with waves of descending aliens and endless play; what was it?
Before writing spy thrillers like The IPCRESS File, he illustrated the cover of the first UK edition of Kerouac's On the Road — which British author who also penned cookery books?

This Pictures Generation artist is famous for black-and-white photos overlaid with bold declarative captions in white-on-red type, often jabbing at power and consumerism with words like 'you' and 'we' — who is she?
Co-founder of Sierra On-Line, her 1980 debut Mystery House is credited as the first graphic adventure game, and she went on to create the King's Quest series — who is she?
Roberta Williams: American video game designer (born 1953)
Counted among the four great Polish Romantic poets, this poet, painter, and sculptor lived a life of poverty and isolation abroad, debated even today as late-Romantic or early-modernist — who was he?
Written in the 2nd century AD by Lucian of Samosata as a spoof of tall travelers' tales, this work is the earliest known fiction to feature outer space, aliens, and interplanetary war — what is it?
A True Story, also translated as True History, is a long novella or short novel written in the second century AD by the Syrian author Lucian of Samosata.
Delacroix's four-meter-tall canvas of suffering on a northern Aegean island is striking for offering no heroic figure to balance the despair — almost no hope amid the ruin. Which painting?
Escenas de las masacres de Quíos
The Massacre at Chios: Painting by Eugène Delacroix
This Ming-dynasty novelist and poet is credited by many as the author of one of the Classic Chinese Novels, Journey to the West — who was he?
Wu Cheng'en: 16th-century Chinese novelist and poet
Counted among Japan's four great haiku masters alongside Bashō, Buson and Shiki, this poet took a pen name meaning 'Cup-of-tea' — who was he?
Kobayashi Issa (June 15, 1763 - January 5, 1828) was a Japanese poet.

This 1932 Southern Gothic novel weaves together a pregnant white woman and a man who passes as white but believes himself of mixed race, exploring race and religion in the American South — which Faulkner work is it?
Light in August: 1932 novel by William Faulkner

Built from interviews Alex Haley conducted between 1963 and 1965 and published months after its subject's assassination, this conversion narrative champions Black pride and pan-Africanism — what book is it?
The Autobiography of Malcolm X is an autobiography written by Muslim American minister and activist Malcolm X in collaboration with American journalist Alex Haley.
This Japanese farmer-philosopher championed 'do-nothing' natural farming — no tilling, no herbicides, no pesticides — and inspired the natural food movement. Who was he?
Masanobu Fukuoka: Japanese farmer and philosopher (1913–2008)
This Columbus-born New Yorker humorist and cartoonist co-wrote a sex-manual parody, Is Sex Necessary?, with E. B. White — who is he?
James Thurber: American cartoonist, author, journalist, and playwright (1894–1961)
An abstract expressionist who exhibited for six decades, she was featured in Clement Greenberg's 1964 Post-Painterly Abstraction show that heralded color field painting — who is she?
A central figure of São Paulo's avant-garde and a pioneer of ethnomusicology, this Brazilian wrote the landmark 1922 poetry collection Hallucinated City — who was he?
Mário de Andrade: Brazilian writer, musicologist and photographer (1893–1945)
Hailed as 'The Great Citizen of the Americas,' this Puerto Rican educator, philosopher, and lawyer was a fierce advocate for the island's independence — who was he?
Eugenio María de Hostos y de Bonilla
Eugenio María de Hostos: Puerto Rican writer, activist and sociologist (1839–1921)
This Dominica-born British Creole novelist is best known for a 1966 prequel to Jane Eyre, written with a literary nudge from her mentor and lover Ford Madox Ford — who is she?

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's 2006 novel follows a houseboy, a revolutionary professor, and his beloved Olanna as the Nigerian Civil War upends their lives — what's the book, titled for an emblem of that breakaway state?
Half of a Yellow Sun: 2006 novel by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie

This late-Heian anthologist and critic is counted among Japan's greatest poets and perhaps the supreme master of the waka — the ancient five-line, 31-syllable form. Whose poetic ideas were studied right up to the Meiji era?
Fujiwara no Teika: Japanese poet and court noble
Known as 'Master of Art,' this Bangladeshi painter rose to fame in 1944 for his haunting series on the great Bengal famine — who was he?
Zainul Abedin (29 December 1914 - 28 May 1976), also known as Shilpacharya (Master of Art) was a Bangladeshi painter.
Born into one wealthy dynasty and married into another, this American sculptor used her fortune to found a New York museum of American art in 1931. Who was she?
Gertrude Vanderbilt Whitney: American sculptor, art patron and collector (1875–1942)
Dubbed the 'Iron Woman' and 'Mother of the Revolution,' this Yemeni journalist became the public face of the 2011 uprising and shared that year's Nobel Peace Prize. Who is she?
Tawakkol Karman: Yemeni-Turkish journalist, politician and human rights activist (born 1979)
H. Rider Haggard's wildly popular 1887 Gothic novel sends two adventurers to a lost African kingdom ruled by an immortal queen called She-who-must-be-obeyed — what's the book's title?
She: A History of Adventure: 1887 novel by H. Rider Haggard

A German doctor turned novelist whose half-century of work ranged from historical fiction to science fiction, he became a giant of German literary modernism — chiefly for his 1929 portrait of a great city, 'Berlin Alexanderplatz.' Who is he?
Alfred Döblin: German novelist, essayist, and doctor (1878–1957)
Also known as AZT, this was the very first antiretroviral drug used against HIV/AIDS, and can be given during birth to prevent mother-to-child spread — what is it?
Zidovudine (ZDV), also known as azidothymidine (AZT), was the first antiretroviral medication used to prevent and treat HIV/AIDS.

The last survivor of the 57 musicians in the 1958 photo 'A Great Day in Harlem,' this tenor saxophonist wrote standards like 'St. Thomas' and 'Oleo' — who was so often called 'the greatest living improviser'?
Sonny Rollins (September 7, 1930 - May 25, 2026) was an American jazz tenor saxophonist who is widely recognized as one of the most important and influential jazz musicians.
Mentored early on by Red Barber, this Bronx-born broadcaster called Dodgers games for 67 seasons across Brooklyn and Los Angeles, all in a lyrically descriptive tenor — who was he?
Vin Scully (November 29, 1927 - August 2, 2022) was an American sportscaster, best known for his broadcast work in Major League Baseball.
One of Stalin's closest allies and his long-serving foreign minister, this Soviet diplomat lent his name to an improvised incendiary weapon. Who is he?

Born from the First Crusade in 1099 and lasting nearly 200 years until the fall of Acre in 1291, this Crusader state was nearly wiped out by Saladin before the Third Crusade revived it. What was it called?
Kingdom of Jerusalem: Crusader state in the Levant from 1099 to 1291
As chief of the OKW, this German field marshal signed the criminal orders that fed countless war crimes — and was so deferential to Hitler that colleagues reviled him. Who was he?
This Italian statesman served five terms as prime minister and pursued a pro-Arab foreign policy before being kidnapped by the Red Brigades in March 1978 — who was he?
Aldo Moro (23 September 1916 - 9 May 1978) was an Italian statesman and prominent member of Christian Democracy (DC) and its centre-left wing.

Mark Twain's 1873 novel gave its name to this late-1870s-to-1890s American era of breakneck industrial growth and mass European immigration, slotted between Reconstruction and the Progressive Era — what's it called?
Gilded Age: Era of US history from the 1870s to the late 1890s
Fill in the blank: “____ (Delphinapterus leucas), is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean.”
Beluga whale (Delphinapterus leucas), is an Arctic and sub-Arctic cetacean.
Commonly found in nature as quartz and making up most of the world's sand, this oxide with the formula SiO2 is also the fundamental ingredient of glass. What is it?
Silicon dioxide, also known as silica, is an oxide of silicon with the chemical formula SiO2, and is commonly found in nature as quartz.
Also sold as Xylocaine, this amino-amide local anesthetic numbs in minutes and doubles as a treatment for dangerous ventricular heart rhythms — what is it?

Many people show no symptoms after catching this liver-attacking virus, but when signs do appear weeks later they can include nausea, yellowing skin, and fatigue — and an infection lasting past six months is deemed chronic. What is it?
Its explosive yield became the standard yardstick for comparing bombs and even asteroid impacts; chemists also use it to make charge-transfer salts — what's this nitro compound?
A purplish-black crystalline salt that dissolves into an intensely pink-to-purple solution, this strong oxidizer also appears on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines for wound care — what is it?
Sold as Lipitor, this first-line statin lowers cholesterol to fend off cardiovascular disease, with mild muscle aches among its better-known side effects — what's the drug?

When the thyroid produces too little hormone, the body slows down — cold intolerance, fatigue, constipation, weight gain — and worldwide too little dietary iodine is the leading cause. What's the condition?
Hypothyroidism: Insufficient production of thyroid hormones
This media executive succeeded Michael Eisner to run a famous entertainment company, retired in 2020, then was coaxed back by its board to lead it a second time — who is he?

Before winning six Emmys and three Grammys for his own comedy, this stand-up cut his teeth in the 1990s writing for the likes of David Letterman and Conan O'Brien — and directing surreal short films. Who is he?
Louis Alfred Székely (born September 12, 1967), known professionally as Louis C.K., is an American stand-up comedian, actor and filmmaker.
This American host took his religion-skewering satire to the 2008 documentary Religulous, hosted ABC's Politically Incorrect, and has fronted an HBO talk show since 2003 — who is he?
Bill Maher: American comedian and television host (born 1956)
After honing his on-air style at stations from Detroit to Washington, this American broadcaster built a syndicated morning show before moving to SiriusXM in 2006. Who is he?
Howard Stern: American radio and television personality (born 1954)
This landlocked Midwestern state borders eight others, counts St. Louis and Kansas City among its biggest cities, and governs from Jefferson City — what state is it?

The least populous state despite ranking tenth in size, this Rocky Mountain land splits between mountain rangelands in the west and High Plains prairie in the east, with Cheyenne as its capital — which state?
Nicknamed the Yellowhammer State after its state bird and also known as the "Heart of Dixie," this Deep South state runs from the mountainous Tennessee Valley down to Mobile Bay — which state is it?
Proclaimed by the Polisario Front in 1976, this partially recognized Maghreb state claims a former Spanish colony but controls only its easternmost fifth — what is it?
Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic: Partially recognised state in North Africa
Born of the 1707 Acts of Union joining England and Scotland under one Westminster parliament, this sovereign state lasted until the end of 1800 — what was it called?
Kingdom of Great Britain: Sovereign state in Western Europe (1707–1801)
Sprawling over roughly 27,000 acres near Orlando since 1971, this resort packs four theme parks, two water parks and four golf courses into one complex — what is it?
Walt Disney World: Entertainment resort in Orlando, Florida, US
Founded by the Romans around 47 AD as Londinium, this tiny 'Square Mile' is a ceremonial county all its own, governed by a Corporation led by its own Lord Mayor — what is it?
City and County of the City of London
The City of London (informally known as the City or the Square Mile) is a city, ceremonial county and local government district in England.

An eight-island archipelago of France sitting in the Atlantic just off Newfoundland, its roughly 5,500 residents are French citizens who even elect their own deputy to the National Assembly — what's this overseas collectivity?
Saint Pierre and Miquelon: Overseas collectivity of France
Nicknamed "the Dream," this Lagos-born center led the Houston Rockets to back-to-back NBA titles in 1994 and 1995 after starring in college for the University of Houston. Who is he?
Hakeem Olajuwon (born January 21, 1963), nicknamed "the Dream", is a Nigerian and American former professional basketball player who played 18 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA).

Born in London to Sri Lankan Tamil parents, this artist's stage name puns on both "Missing in action" and the neighborhood of Acton — and her music blends hip hop with world and electronic sounds. Who is she?
M.I.A. (rapper) — M.I.A. (born 18 July 1975), known as Maya and professionally as M.I.A.
Born Adam Wiles, this Scottish DJ and producer broke through with 'Acceptable in the 80s' and sometimes records under the alias Love Regenerator — who is he?
Robert Burns penned this Scots poem in 1788; set to a pentatonic tune in 1799, it's traditionally sung at the stroke of midnight to bid farewell to the old year — what's the song?
Auld Lang Syne: Robert Burns poem set to traditional melody
Originally called the "Seattle Sound," this mid-1980s Washington-born genre fused punk and heavy metal with distorted guitars and angst-filled, introspective lyrics — what's the style?
This New Haven-born sibling duo paired one's contralto vocals with the other's piano arrangements to define a soft musical style across 14 years and 10 albums — who were they?
This Saudi journalist and dissident, once editor of the progressive paper Al Watan, was assassinated inside his country's Istanbul consulate in October 2018 — who was he?
Jamal Khashoggi: Saudi journalist and dissident (1958–2018)
A Holocaust survivor and Viennese psychiatrist, he founded logotherapy and distilled his concentration-camp experiences into the bestseller 'Man's Search for Meaning' — who was he?

Collected by the Brothers Grimm in 1812, this German tale sends two abandoned siblings to a witch's house made of bread, cake, and sugar — until one of them shoves her into her own oven. What's the story?
Hansel and Gretel: German fairy tale
John Steinbeck drew on his teenage years among migrant farm workers for this 1937 novella, whose title comes from a Robert Burns line about the best-laid schemes going awry. What is it?
Of Mice and Men: 1937 novella by John Steinbeck
Of the four sacred Hindu Vedas, only one Shakha of this oldest collection of Sanskrit hymns survives intact today — the Śakalya Shakha; the rest are lost or hidden. Which canonical text is this?
Rigveda is an ancient Indian collection of Vedic Sanskrit hymns (sktas).
This Swedish explorer made the Transhimalaya known to the West, located the sources of the Brahmaputra, Indus and Sutlej, and titled one book 'From Pole to Pole' — who was he?
Sven Hedin: Swedish geographer, explorer, photographer, and illustrator (1865–1952)
Regarded as a founding father of geopolitics, this British geographer is credited with introducing 'manpower' and 'heartland' into English and led the early London School of Economics — who was he?
Halford Mackinder: English geographer and politician (1861–1947)
Armenia's first Defence Minister, he had just become prime minister in 1999 when he was assassinated that October — who was he?
Vazgen Sargsyan: Armenian military commander, politician (1959–1999)
Historians use this name for the wave of anticlerical violence — killings and church arson — carried out by leftist groups during the Spanish Civil War; what's it called?
Red Terror (Spain): Assassinations during the Spanish Civil War
This English Puritan lawyer led the first big wave of colonists to Massachusetts Bay in 1630 and cast it as a 'city upon a hill' — who was he?
John Winthrop: English leader of Massachusetts Bay Colony (1587–1649)
An aeronautical engineer and test pilot who later became a painter, he was the fourth person ever to walk on the Moon — which Astronaut Group 3 member?
Alan Bean: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1932–2018)
Nicknamed 'Fighting Bob,' this Wisconsin progressive served as governor and senator before running for president in 1924 on a party he made himself — who is it?
Robert M. La Follette: American lawyer and politician (1855–1925)
He became Byzantine emperor in 1042 by marrying the ruling empress Zoë, then proceeded to drain the treasury Basil II had left full — which prodigal 11th-century ruler?
Constantine IX Monomachos: Byzantine emperor from 1042 to 1055
Born Ong Boon Hua, this Maoist became a revolutionary at 15 and the longest-serving General Secretary of the Communist Party of Malaya — who is it?
This Harvard legal scholar founded Creative Commons and briefly ran for the 2016 Democratic presidential nomination before withdrawing — who is it?
Lawrence Lessig: American legal scholar and activist (born 1961)
Seeking to reconcile Irish nationalism and Ulster unionism while opposing 'armed struggle,' this SDLP founder won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1998 — who is it?
He served as Cameroon's first prime minister and then its first president from 1960 to 1982, knitting the French- and English-speaking halves into one state — who is it?
Ahmadou Ahidjo: President of Cameroon from 1960 to 1982

A former reporter and TV host turned premier of Quebec, he founded the Parti Québécois and became the first leader since Confederation to seek, by referendum, a mandate to negotiate the province's independence. Who was he?
René Lévesque (August 24, 1922 - November 1, 1987) was a Canadian politician and journalist who served as the 23rd premier of Quebec from 1976 to 1985.
A protégé of Colonel Arana, this far-right military officer seized power in a 1954 coup to become the 28th president of Guatemala — who is it?
Carlos Castillo Armas: President of Guatemala from 1954 to 1957

A Mediterranean shrub in the mint family, this plant bears fragrant, needle-like evergreen leaves and purple, white, pink, or blue flowers — and those leaves are a beloved cooking flavoring. What is it?
This British engineer rewrote Maxwell's equations into the form we use today and devised the telegrapher's equations — who was he?
Oliver Heaviside: British mathematician and electrical engineer (1850–1925)
Son of a bass-baritone and born into a family of engineers, this American built his first car at 19, won four F1 Grands Prix, and took Le Mans in 1967 — who was he?
Dan Gurney: American racing driver, engineer and motorsport executive (1931–2018)
This English anatomist coined the word 'Dinosauria' — 'terrible reptile' — yet remained an outspoken critic of Darwin's theory of natural selection — who is it?
Richard Owen: English biologist and palaeontologist (1804–1892)
Working under Tamerlane around 1400, this Persian astronomer and mathematician produced work that mostly never reached Europe and stays largely unpublished — who is it?
Jamshid al-Kashi: Persian astronomer and mathematician (c. 1380–1429)
A star of television's Golden Age of slice-of-life drama, he's the only person to win three solo Academy Awards for screenwriting — who is it?
Paddy Chayefsky: American playwright, screenwriter and novelist (1923–1981)
At just fourteen, this American dancer was hired by Walt Disney Studios to be a real-life dance model that animators traced for their films — who was she?
Marge Champion: American dancer and actress (1919–2020)
This family of Microsoft operating systems ran from 1995 to 2000, kept MS-DOS support for booting, and ended with the Me release before being superseded — what's the generic term for the line?
Windows 9x: Series of Microsoft operating systems
A onetime illustrator's model who became a Ziegfeld girl in 1915 and starred in over 20 silent films before dying at 25 in 1920 — which actress?
Olive Thomas: American actress and model (1894–1920)
Hired as an assistant cameraman at 17, this director went on to shoot the 'Our Gang' shorts and win Best Director Oscars for both 'A Place in the Sun' and 'Giant' — who is he?
This playwright earned an Oscar nomination for the 'Women in Love' screenplay, then ignited fury within the gay community with his blunt 1978 novel 'Faggots' — who was he?
Larry Kramer: American playwright and gay rights activist (1935–2020)
Twice Oscar-nominated for Best Director, this Austrian-American filmmaker is best remembered for his shadowy 1930s collaborations with Marlene Dietrich, including The Blue Angel. Who is he?
Josef von Sternberg: Austrian-American film director (1894–1969)

Home to 78 foreign embassies, the headquarters of its country's army, and landmarks like the Imperial Citadel of Thăng Long and Hoàn Kiếm Lake, this is the second-most populous municipality of Vietnam — what city is it?
Sitting on the banks of the Kaveri river and ringed by the Western Ghats, this is the seventh-largest urban agglomeration in Tamil Nadu — which city?
Erode: City in Tamil Nadu, India
Fill in the blank: “____ was a Sinhalese monarchy on the island of Sri Lanka, located in the central and eastern portion of the island.”
Kingdom of Kandy was a Sinhalese monarchy on the island of Sri Lanka, located in the central and eastern portion of the island.
Knighted in 1967, this former England defender is best remembered for managing the national side to its 1966 World Cup triumph — who was he?
In 1919 he co-founded a Wisconsin football team, then served as its first captain and player-coach, lining up at halfback — which NFL pioneer?
Curly Lambeau: American football player, coach, and executive (1898–1965)
Often called Australia's 'unofficial national anthem,' this bush ballad spins the tale of a swagman, a stolen jumbuck, and the troopers who pursue him — what song is it?
A child prodigy who conducted an operetta at twelve, this Austrian émigré became known as 'the father of film music' after moving to Hollywood in 1929 — who was he?
This avant-garde composer coined the phrase 'organized sound' and thought of his music in terms of crystallizing 'sound-masses' — who was he?
Edgard Varèse: French and American composer (1883–1965)
This American theatre composer wrote more than 700 songs — among them 'Ol' Man River' and 'Smoke Gets in Your Eyes' — across over 100 stage works — who was he?
One contemporary said his cornet tone was so pure it was like 'shooting bullets at a bell' — which influential 1920s jazz soloist behind 'Singin' the Blues'?
Bix Beiderbecke: American jazz cornetist, pianist and composer (1903–1931)
Fill in the blank: “____ is a song recorded by the American singer Elvis Presley.”
Heartbreak Hotel is a song recorded by the American singer Elvis Presley.
Formed at Liberty University in 1987, this trio was once dubbed 'the most popular overtly Christian act of all time,' evolving from hip-hop toward rock — who are they?
DC Talk: American Christian rap band
The first American woman to earn first-class honors at Oxford, she turned her Columbia doctoral dissertation into the second-wave landmark 'Sexual Politics' (1970) — who is she?
Kate Millett: American writer and artist (1934–2017)
This Australian-born critic made his name as The Observer's TV reviewer in 1972, famous for a wry, deadpan humor that carried him into his own British TV shows — who was he?
Clive James: Australian writer and broadcaster (1939–2019)
Appointed in 2009, this Scottish-born poet was the first woman — and first openly lesbian writer — to hold the post of Poet Laureate — who is she?
Carol Ann Duffy: Scottish poet and playwright (born 1955)
This Irish novelist wrote 'The Master,' a fictionalized inner life of Henry James, and 'The Magician,' which did the same for Thomas Mann — who is he?
Colm Tóibín: Irish novelist and writer (born 1955)
A celebrated social figure of the Roaring Twenties who sometimes wrote prose as 'Nancy Boyd,' this lyrical poet became the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry — who was she?
Edna St. Vincent Millay: American poet (1892–1950)
One of the first English women to live by her pen, this Restoration playwright wrote under the name 'Astrea' and even spied in Antwerp for Charles II — who was she?
Aphra Behn: English playwright, poet and spy (1640–1689)
A major figure of Russian symbolism, this poet married Dmitry Merezhkovsky in 1889 and later joined him in criticizing the tsarist government after the 1905 Revolution — who was she?
Born Everett Leroy Jones and once known as LeRoi Jones, this writer of plays and poetry produced texts scholars call defining works of African-American culture — who was he?
Said to have started writing at age four, this American author left Syracuse for reporting and penned the 1893 Bowery tale 'Maggie: A Girl of the Streets' before dying at 28 — who was he?
Stephen Crane: American novelist, short story writer, poet, and journalist
A Grand Master of science fiction who also wrote mysteries as 'Ellery Queen,' he won Hugo Awards for 'The Dragon Masters' and 'The Last Castle' — who was he?
A leading member of the Vienna Secession, this Austrian architect gave the city's Metro stations their floral Art Nouveau look starting in 1898 — who was he?
An early writer on autism, this Austrian-born psychologist directed Chicago's Sonia Shankman Orthogenic School for emotionally disturbed children and built his theories on Freud's — who was he?
Bruno Bettelheim: Austrian-American child psychologist and writer (1903–1990)

A Bauhaus student turned faculty member, this German-born artist became one of the most influential 20th-century art teachers in America — after a craftsman's childhood of engraving glass, plumbing, and wiring. Who is he?
A co-founder of Russian Symbolism and self-styled apocalyptic prophet, this novelist and his poet wife Zinaida Gippius were twice forced into political exile. Who was he?

Stephen Crane was born after the Civil War and had never seen battle, yet his 1895 novel about a young Union private fleeing the field — then craving a wound to redeem his shame — is celebrated for its realism. What is it?
The Red Badge of Courage: 1895 war novel by Stephen Crane
This Belle Époque French playwright, who organized his schoolmates into a drama troupe as a boy, became famous for the frantic farces he wrote between 1886 and 1914. Who is he?
This Danish-American muckraking journalist used pioneering casual photography to expose the plight of New York's tenement poor, championing 'model tenements' as urban reform. Who was he?
Jacob Riis: American photographer, journalist and activist (1849–1914)
Famously shy and reclusive, this English novelist pioneered the Gothic genre with suspenseful, exotic tales of seemingly supernatural events, most popularly The Mysteries of Udolpho. Who was she?
This American comic creator spun about 90 Scrooge McDuck tales built on Carl Barks's world, winning a 1995 Eisner Award for his 12-chapter Life and Times of the famous duck. Who is he?
Don Rosa: American comic book writer and illustrator (born 1951)
Going by the craft name Scire, this English author and amateur anthropologist founded a tradition of the modern pagan religion Wicca and wrote some of its definitive texts. Who was he?

She was the first living author to have her works gathered into the Library of America, and her Pulitzer came for The Optimist's Daughter — which Mississippi short-story writer and photographer of the South?
Eudora Welty: American writer and photographer (1909–2001)
He studied English literature at Berkeley before turning to art, then became famous for towering abstract sculptures built for the exact site they'd stand in — which postminimalist?
He invented a metrical idea he called 'sprung rhythm,' yet his poems went almost entirely unpublished until Robert Bridges shared a few after his death — which Jesuit priest and English poet?
Gerard Manley Hopkins: English poet and Catholic priest (1844–1889)
For most of his career this English philosopher of religion argued you should presuppose atheism until evidence for God turns up — who is it?
Antony Flew: English analytic and evidentialist philosopher (1923–2010)
A critic once called her 'perhaps the most purely gifted poet of the 20th century,' praising the miniaturist's care she brought to small things — which American poet, also a painter?
Elizabeth Bishop: American poet and short-story writer (1911–1979)

Fought almost entirely at sea from 1798 to 1800 after France started seizing American merchant ships, this undeclared conflict between the U.S. and the French First Republic goes by what fittingly half-hearted name?
Quasi-War was an undeclared quasi-war from 1798 to 1800 between the United States and the French First Republic.

He organized the 1978 Saur Revolution and co-founded the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan, but ruled as head of state for barely three months before being assassinated — which communist leader was he?

Hafizullah Amin (Dari/; 1 August 1929 - 27 December 1979) was an Afghan revolutionary and communist head of state, who served in that position for a little over three months, from September 1979 until his assassination.
With his group the Comets and the million-selling "Rock Around the Clock," this musician is credited by many as the first to popularize rock and roll in the early 1950s — who was he?
Bill Haley: American rock and roll music pioneer (1925–1981)
For more than 16 years, which lawyer-turned-journalist was the longest-serving moderator of NBC's Meet the Press, earning a 2008 spot on Time's 100 most influential people?
Tim Russert (May 7, 1950 - June 13, 2008) was an American television journalist and lawyer who appeared for more than 16 years as the longest-serving moderator of NBC's Meet the Press.
Whose documentary photography for the Farm Security Administration put a human face on the Great Depression and helped shape the whole genre?
Dorothea Margaretta Nutzhorn Dixon Taylor Lange
Dorothea Lange was an American documentary photographer and photojournalist, best known for her Depression-era work for the Farm Security Administration.
A self-taught Civil War nurse, former teacher and patent clerk, she did humanitarian and civil-rights work before women could even vote, and founded an American relief organization — who was she?
Clara Barton (December 25, 1821 - April 12, 1912) was an American nurse who founded the American Red Cross.

Founded in 1932 on land seized in Japan's invasion of Manchuria, this Axis-recognized "puppet state" was dressed up first as a republic and then a monarchy before dissolving in 1945 — what was it called?
Manchukuo: 1932–1945 Japanese puppet state in northern China

When the Tatmadaw seized power on 1 February 2021, the coup triggered mass protests and turned the country's longstanding insurgencies into open warfare — the exiled National Unity Government even tore up the 2008 Constitution. Which conflict is this?
Myanmar civil war (2021–present): Ongoing armed conflict in Southeast Asia
Hailed as the "Father of the Constitution" for shaping it and the Bill of Rights, this Virginia planter went on to become the fourth U.S. president — who was he?
It was the world's first fully electronic stock market and remains the second-largest by market cap — the Manhattan venue where most American tech giants choose to list. Which exchange is it?

A Navy man turned radio comic, he took over a late-night NBC show from Jack Paar in 1962 and hosted it for thirty years, racking up six Emmys and a Presidential Medal of Freedom along the way — who is he?
Johnny Carson: American comedian and television host (1925–2005)
Now branded simply by its two initials, this London-based network is one of the Big Four professional services firms alongside Deloitte, KPMG and PwC — which one?
Ernst & Young: Multinational professional services network

Traditionally blamed on Queen Catherine de' Medici, this 1572 wave of Catholic mob violence targeted Huguenots gathered in Paris for a royal wedding during the French Wars of Religion. By what name is it known?
St. Bartholomew's Day massacre: 1572 killing of Huguenots in France
This body of religious law, drawn from the Qur'an and hadith, refers to immutable divine law — distinct from fiqh, its human interpretation by scholars. What is it?
A self-taught Soviet tinkerer who later became a lieutenant general, he designed a famously reliable assault rifle but felt sorrow at how widely it spread — who was he?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele pinned down this gas's composition in 1777; it's flammable, smells of rotten eggs, and kills by blocking cellular respiration much like cyanide — what colorless compound is it?
Hydrogen sulfide: Poisonous and flammable gas
Sometimes called urticaria, this itchy rash of raised welts can flare for minutes or days, may follow an allergy or infection, and in half of all cases has no identifiable cause — what is it?
Hives is a kind of skin rash with red or flesh-colored, raised, itchy bumps.
Affecting roughly one in five people at some point and usually starting in childhood, this long-term itchy, red, cracked-skin condition is also simply called eczema — what's its formal name?
Atopic dermatitis: Long-term form of skin inflammation

The most common hormonal disorder in women of reproductive age, it's diagnosed by two of three signs — irregular periods, high testosterone, or many antral follicles — despite a name that misleadingly implies true cysts. What's its newer name?
Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome: Hormonal disorder in women
Nicknamed the "silent thief of sight" because it steals vision slowly, this group of eye diseases damages the optic nerve and is closely tied to raised pressure inside the eye — what is it?
Glaucoma: Group of eye diseases related to poor retinal and nerve perfusion
This North American wild cat earns its name from the black-tipped, stubby tail it sports, along with distinctive black bars on its forelegs — one of the four species of lynx. Which animal is it?
Bobcat: Medium-sized North American wild cat
