His Latin name meant "the Humble," yet this 6th-century Scythian monk in Rome quietly reshaped how nearly all of us label the year — by inventing AD dating, the numbering still used by the Gregorian calendar. Who was he?
Dionysius Exiguus: Byzantine monk, inventor of AD dating

Inducted into the U.S. Air Force Hall of Fame in 2018, this American mathematician modeled the precise shape of the Earth — work later baked into the Global Positioning System that now guides your phone. Who is she?

This Serbian polymath — mathematician, astronomer, civil engineer — explained Earth's long-term climate swings by tracking our planet's shifting position relative to the Sun, a theory of cycles that now bears his name. Who was he?
Milutin Milanković: Serbian scientist and professor (1879–1958)
This Soviet documentary pioneer and theorist helped inspire cinéma vérité, and critics in a 2012 poll voted his 1929 film the eighth-greatest movie ever made. Who was he?
Determined to act despite her parents' objections, this English dame held a leading place in British theatre for 50 years, much of it with the Old Vic and Gielgud's companies. Who was she?
Over a 70-year career this English actor and monologist became famous for one role above all — the dustman Alfred P. Doolittle in My Fair Lady. Who was he?
Stanley Holloway: British actor, singer and comedian (1890–1982)
Her nearly 80-year career included 1940's 'Pride and Prejudice,' but in the 1950s Hollywood executives blacklisted this American actress during McCarthyism — who was she?
Marsha Hunt was an American actress with a career spanning nearly 80 years.
This Canadian-American artist co-created one of comics' most enduring superheroes in Action Comics #1 in 1938, then spent years in legal battles over who owned him. Who was he?
Strumming a ukulele or banjolele through cheeky comic songs, this Wigan-born entertainer became the UK's highest-paid star via his films of the 1930s and '40s. Who was he?
George Formby: English actor, singer-songwriter and comedian (1904–1961)
Capping Andrzej Wajda's war trilogy, this 1958 Polish drama follows a Home Army veteran ordered to assassinate a Communist Party secretary in the unsettled days just after the war — which film?
Ashes and Diamonds is a 1958 Polish drama film directed by Andrzej Wajda, based on the 1948 novel by Polish writer Jerzy Andrzejewski.
This Hungarian-American producer made one of America's first feature-length films, 1913's The Prisoner of Zenda, and went on to co-found Paramount Pictures — who was he?
For Going My Way this Irish actor pulled off a feat never repeated — nominated for both Best Actor and Best Supporting Actor for the same role, winning the latter; who was he?
Perched on a plateau above the Tigris behind a historic fortress, this largest Kurdish-majority city in Turkey has been continually inhabited since around 8,000 BCE — what is it?
Once a British military base and later a Japanese POW camp, this island off Singapore's southern coast was renamed in the 1970s and turned into a popular tourist resort — what's it called?
Affectionately called "PJ," this Malaysian city in Selangor began life as a satellite township for Kuala Lumpur before earning city status in 2006 — what is it?
Petaling Jaya: City in Selangor, Malaysia
Which Japanese city, capital of Shiga Prefecture and home to around 344,000 people, sits just east of Kyoto?
Ōtsu: Prefecture capital and Core city in Kansai
Renowned for his backhand and a career stretching from the early 1950s into the 1970s, this Australian won 23 majors including a record 15 Pro Majors — who was he?
This Canadian winger set a rookie record with 53 goals, then anchored four straight Stanley Cups for the New York Islanders in the early 1980s — who is it?
Mike Bossy: Canadian ice hockey player (1957–2022)
Discovered by country star Hank Thompson after running her own Oklahoma City radio show, this singer earned the nickname "The Queen of Rockabilly" — who is she?
Wanda Jackson: American singer, songwriter, and musician (born 1937)
Raised in a musical Worcester, Massachusetts household and trained at Harvard, this American composer is celebrated above all for operas built around real historical events — who is he?
John Coolidge Adams (born February 15, 1947) is an American composer and conductor.
Largely self-taught, this Japanese composer scored more than ninety films and was admired for fusing sound with silence and Eastern with Western philosophy; who was he?
Tōru Takemitsu: Japanese composer and writer (1930–1996)
This French Romantic composer is best remembered for the ballets Coppélia and Sylvia and for the opera Lakmé, home of the famous 'Flower Duet'; who was he?
Released by King in 2012, this free-to-play hit has players swap colored candies to match three or more, with matches of four-plus spawning board-clearing power-ups — what's the game?

A self-proclaimed medium who appeared on Montel Williams and Larry King, she made many predictions later found false and pleaded no contest to securities fraud in 1992 — yet kept a huge following. Who was she?
A frontier farmer and writer, he helped found Vermont and seized Fort Ticonderoga during the American Revolutionary War. Who was he?
Ethan Allen: American farmer, military officer and politician (1738–1789)

Gustave Courbet shocked the 1850–51 Paris Salon by painting an ordinary provincial funeral with frank realism on the grand scale once reserved for heroic history scenes — a work that brought him instant fame. What painting is it?
A Burial at Ornans: Painting by Gustave Courbet, 1850–1851
With 91 million copies sold, this American author gave middle-class kids characters like Ramona Quimby and Henry Huggins's dog Ribsy, set in the Portland neighborhood where she grew up. Who was she?
A prominent figure in Berlin Dada and New Objectivity, this German artist skewered 1920s Berlin life in biting caricatures before emigrating to the United States in 1933. Who was he?
Writing sometimes as "Jan Sawa," this Polish poet and children's writer was a leading voice of her country's Positivist period and an activist for women's rights and Polish independence. Who was she?
Three Pulitzer Prizes went to one American writer — for the novel The Bridge of San Luis Rey and the plays Our Town and The Skin of Our Teeth. Who pulled off that hat trick?
Thornton Wilder: American playwright and novelist (1897–1975)

Which English playwright, a poster child for the confrontational "in-yer-face theatre" that drew on Jacobean tragedy, wrote with poetic intensity about love, torture, and death before dying at just 28?
Daughter of a detective novelist, she launched an 'alphabet series' starting with 'A' Is for Alibi, following PI Kinsey Millhone around the fictional Santa Teresa, California — who was she?

One of the few ukiyo-e masters famous across Japan in his own lifetime, this woodblock designer produced over 2,000 prints and was best known for his 'large-headed pictures of beautiful women'; who was he?
A trained neurophysiologist who later settled on Norfolk Island, this Australian wrote a 1977 novel that sold over 30 million copies and became a hit miniseries; who was she?

A Broadway success who was later blacklisted by Hollywood after refusing to answer the House Un-American Activities Committee, this playwright drew both praise and suspicion for her stance — who was she?

Lillian Hellman (June 20, 1905 - June 30, 1984) was an American playwright, prose writer, memoirist, and screenwriter known for her success on Broadway as well as her communist views and political activism.
Ranked between Pheidias and Myron in the ancient world, this 5th-century BCE Greek sculptor is famed for a lost treatise laying out the mathematical proportions of the ideal male body; who was he?
Polykleitos: Fifth century BCE Greek sculptor
His true name and dates unknown, this ukiyo-e designer of kabuki-actor portraits burst onto the scene and vanished after just ten prolific months in 1794–95 — who was the mystery artist?
Endemic to China and sporting a handy 'thumb' on its forepaw to grip bamboo, this black-and-white bear weighs in around 100 to 115 kg — what animal is it?

This German engineer invented the high-speed petroleum engine, working alongside his lifelong partner Wilhelm Maybach to build small, fast motors they hoped to mount on any kind of vehicle. Who was he?
Gottlieb Daimler: German engineer, industrialist and automotive pioneer (1834–1900)
With Emmanuelle Charpentier, this Berkeley biochemist proposed in 2012 that CRISPR-Cas9 could edit genomes — work that won them the 2020 Nobel in Chemistry; who is she?
Jennifer Doudna: American biochemist and Nobel laureate (born 1964)
Often called a "national treasure," this Irish broadcaster drew some eight million listeners to his BBC Radio 2 breakfast show and long fronted Children in Need — who is he?
Terry Wogan (3 August 1938 - 31 January 2016) was an Irish radio and television broadcaster who worked for the BBC in Britain for most of his career.
He won the 1960 Rome Olympic marathon running barefoot, then defended his title in Tokyo — both times in world-record time; which Ethiopian runner was it?
Abebe Bikila (August 7, 1932 - October 25, 1973) was an Ethiopian marathon runner who was a back-to-back Olympic marathon champion.
Usually unaccompanied and 'through-composed' so each line of poetry gets its own music, this secular vocal form flourished in the Renaissance and early Baroque — what is it called?
Madrigal is a form of secular vocal music most typical of the Renaissance (15th-16th centuries) and early Baroque (1580-1650) periods, although revisited by some later European composers.
Often made today with text-to-image models, this kind of visual work has stirred deep philosophical questions about the mind and the very nature of art — what is it?

AI art: Artificial intelligence visual art, or AI art, is visual artwork generated or enhanced through the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) programs, most commonly using text-to-image models.
Publishing a new scripture at age 24, this American founder of a major religious movement drew tens of thousands of followers before his death just fourteen years later — who was he?
Joseph Smith: Founder of the Latter Day Saint movement (1805–1844)
Nicknamed the 'Red Eminence' for his crimson robes, this French prelate became chief minister to Louis XIII in 1624 and held the post until his death — who was he?
Cardinal Richelieu: French statesman and clergyman (1585–1642)
Having lost two fingers at Tsushima and later studied at Harvard, this admiral commanded Japan's Combined Fleet until U.S. fighters shot down his plane over New Guinea in 1943 — who was he?
This decentralized movement against police brutality and racial inequality arose after the killings of Trayvon Martin, Michael Brown, and Eric Garner — what's its name?
Black Lives Matter: Social movement originating in the US

In faiths with a linear history this afterlife place can be eternal, while reincarnation-based religions treat it as merely a stop between lives — and it's often imagined beneath the Earth's surface; what is it?
Hell: Abode of the dead, in various cultures
A woody shrub native to South America, this starchy tuber yields tapioca and, when grated and toasted, becomes Brazil's farofa and West Africa's garri — what crop is it?
Their Latin name means 'those with shells,' and this mostly aquatic group includes crabs, lobsters, krill, barnacles, and mantis shrimp — what are they?
This Russian chemist's great law let him predict three undiscovered elements — germanium, gallium, and scandium — and a synthetic element now bears his name; who was he?
Across a 70-year career this American producer made over 100 TV shows, bringing political and social themes to 1970s sitcoms like Maude, The Jeffersons, and Good Times — who was he?
Norman Lear: American screenwriter and producer (1922–2023)
This Danish model shared the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue's 50th-anniversary cover with Chrissy Teigen and Lily Aldridge — who is she?
Discovered at 17 in a Düsseldorf nightclub and likened to Brigitte Bardot, this German supermodel became the face of Chanel in 1990 — who is she?
Claudia Maria Schiffer de Vere Drummond
This Australian entertainer is credited with inventing the wobble board and made the didgeridoo a pop instrument on hits like 'Tie Me Kangaroo Down, Sport' — who was he?
Jon Favreau created this Disney+ space Western as a 'Mandalorian' spin-off, following a famous bounty hunter as he muscles in on Jabba the Hutt's old turf — what's the title?
The Book of Boba Fett: American television miniseries
Before her own makeup brand and reality fame, this model got her start as Nicki Minaj's stunt double in Kanye West's 'Monster' video — who is she?
Blac Chyna: American model and socialite (born 1988)

Etched into a Peruvian desert floor between 500 BC and 500 AD by scraping away pebbles to reveal lighter dirt, these vast figures of animals and plants are still turning up by the hundreds thanks to drones — what are they?
The Nazca lines are a group of geoglyphs made in the soil of the Nazca Desert in southern Peru.

Invented in 1965 as a children's backyard game on a Washington island, this paddle sport — played with a perforated plastic ball over a low net — became Washington's official state sport in 2022. What is it?

Because real grappling was deemed too slow to draw a crowd, 19th-century American performers quietly began fixing their matches to add spectacular choreographed moves — what 'athletic theater' grew out of that?
Professional wrestling: Form of athletic theater
This Chicago snack giant was carved out of Kraft Foods in 2012, keeping the cookies-and-candy business while the grocery half spun off — which company is it?
Mondelez International: American multinational food and beverage corporation
Founded in Nanjing in 2008 as 'ZZKKO,' this fast-fashion e-commerce platform grew into the world's largest fashion retailer by 2022 before moving its headquarters to Singapore — what is it?
Formed in Braintree in 1990 and dubbed the "Godfathers of Rave," this English big-beat band — fronted by the late Keith Flint — emerged from the underground rave scene. Who are they?
The Prodigy: English electronic rave music group
Revived in 1998 as a Volkswagen Group subsidiary in Molsheim, this French maker of two-seater hyper-cars is now run by Mate Rimac — which marque is it?
Bugatti Automobiles: French high-performance luxury automobile manufacturer
Adopted by the Weimar Republic in 1922, this anthem set to a Hoffmann von Fallersleben poem now has only its third stanza sung since reunification — what is it?
An early-modernist of the École de Paris, this Vitebsk-born artist worked in everything from paint to stained glass, ceramics, and tapestries — who was he?

Borrowing a military term for 'advance guard,' this label marks art that's aesthetically ahead of its time — and initially unacceptable to the establishment, as the anti-novel and surrealism once were — what is it?
Avant-garde: Works that are experimental or innovative
Exiled from Iceland for three years, this Norse explorer — father of Leif Erikson — used the time to found the first European settlement in Greenland; by what color-coded nickname is he known?

One of the original five Marshals of the Soviet Union, this ex-tsarist officer was rare enough that the Red Army actually trusted him — and he commanded its Southern Front against the Whites in the Civil War. Who was he?
Raised on a farm outside Hamilton, she became New Zealand's fifth-longest-serving prime minister and only its second woman in the role, then went on to run the UN Development Programme — who is she?
The Right Honourable Helen Elizabeth Clark
Helen Clark: Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1999 to 2008
The longest-serving prime minister in his nation's history, this Melbourne lawyer led one party in the 1930s and then founded an entirely new one for his second, much longer stint — who was he?
The Right Honourable Sir Robert Menzies
Robert Menzies: Prime Minister of Australia (1939–1941; 1949–1966)
His brief 1982–83 turn as Guatemala's de facto president became one of the bloodiest chapters of its civil war, later drawing accusations of genocide — which former military academy director was he?
Efraín Ríos Montt: 38th President of Guatemala from 1982 to 1983
Born into an Anglo-Irish Protestant landowning family, this Home Rule leader held the balance of power in the Commons before a long-running affair toppled him at just 45 — who was he?
Holding the grim distinction of being the only British prime minister ever assassinated, this barrister was also the only attorney-general to reach the top job — who was he?
Spencer Perceval: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1809 to 1812

Fought as a guerrilla conflict between British colonists and Aboriginal Tasmanians from the mid-1820s to 1832, it nearly exterminated the island's Indigenous population — what's this dark chapter called?
Black War: War between British colonists and Aboriginal Tasmanians (1824–1832)
In a 1960 royal coup this king dismissed his government, jailed leaders, and imposed a Panchayat system that lasted until 1990, opening his Himalayan kingdom to the world — who was he?
Shri Panch Mahendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev, was King of Nepal from 13 March 1955 until his death in 1972.
The son of a shipping magnate who founded OOCL, this businessman became Hong Kong's very first Chief Executive when sovereignty transferred in 1997 — who was he?
Tung Chee-hwa: Politician and businessman from Hong Kong
Declared emperor by the Senate at nearly 66 after Domitian's assassination, this former servant of Nero who helped expose the Pisonian conspiracy ruled Rome only from AD 96 to 98 — who was he?
Nerva: Roman emperor from AD 96 to 98
A brigadier general who led El Salvador through most of World War II, he served as the country's 27th president until resigning in 1944 — which Salvadoran officer?
Maximiliano Hernández Martínez: President of El Salvador from 1931 to 1934 and 1935 to 1944
This Byzantine emperor from 741 to 775 exploited civil war in the Muslim world to secure his eastern frontier, then campaigned repeatedly against the Bulgars in the Balkans — who was he?
Constantine V: Byzantine emperor from 741 to 775
One of 24 Apollo astronauts to fly to the Moon, he commanded Apollo 10 and, with his crewmate, became the first to fly a Lunar Module in lunar orbit — which test pilot?
Thomas P. Stafford: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1930–2024)

The only pair skater to win 10 straight World Championships and three consecutive Olympic golds — and the first to take Olympic pairs gold with two different partners — who is this skater-turned-politician?
Irina Rodnina: Russian politician and figure skater

Element 101, first made in 1955 by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles, was the first that couldn't be produced by simply neutron-blasting a lighter element — and it honors the father of the periodic table. Which element is it?
Mendelevium: Chemical element with atomic number 101 (Md)
A synthetic group-7 transition metal made only in particle accelerators, this radioactive element honors a Danish physicist and sits at atomic number 107 — what is it?
Bohrium: Chemical element with atomic number 107 (Bh)
This Hungarian-American aerospace pioneer made crucial advances in supersonic and hypersonic airflow, and the agreed boundary of outer space — the "___ line" — bears his name. Who was he?
Theodore von Kármán: Hungarian-American mathematician, aerospace engineer and physicist (1881–1963)
Aboard Apollo 8, the first crewed mission to leave low Earth orbit, this astronaut snapped the iconic "Earthrise" photograph as the crew circled the Moon ten times — who took it?
William Anders: American astronaut and lunar explorer (1933–2024)
A largely self-taught naturalist and astronomer born to a free mother in Maryland, he helped survey the District of Columbia and corresponded with Thomas Jefferson — who was he?
Benjamin Banneker: American scientist, surveyor and farmer (1731–1806)
This Manchester physicist shared the 2010 Nobel Prize for his work on graphene — and is the only person to also hold an Ig Nobel, won for levitating a frog with magnetism. Who is he?
A British-American structural biologist who shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for revealing the structure of the ribosome, he later served as President of the Royal Society — who is he?
Called the "father of modern parasitology," this Italian physician-poet famously dismantled spontaneous generation by showing that maggots hatch from fly eggs — who was he?
Francesco Redi: Italian naturalist and poet

Karen Silkwood: Labor union activist and laboratory technician (1946-1974)
Crowned the "Queen of Philippine Cinema," this American-born actress appeared in more than 300 productions across seven decades as the country's biggest box-office star — who was she?
Gloria Romero: Filipino actress and model (1933–2025)
This English director gave us a string of 1930s horror classics — Frankenstein, The Invisible Man, Bride of Frankenstein — before also tackling the musical Show Boat. Who?
Sitting on the northwestern coast of Guadalcanal, this city of about 130,000 became a capital territory in 1983 and lies along the Kukum Highway — what's the largest city of the Solomon Islands?
Honiara: Capital city in Capital territory, Solomon Islands
Egypt's seventh-largest city sits midway between Cairo and Alexandria, capital of Gharbia Governorate and a cotton-ginning hub famed for its roasted-chickpea sweets — which city?
Born on the northern slopes of the Himalayas in Tibet and known as the Karnali once it reaches Nepal, this 1,080-km waterway is the Ganges' largest tributary by volume — which river is it?
Ghaghara: Asian river and tributary of the Ganges
Equally brilliant at centre-back or centre-forward, this Welshman starred for Leeds United and Juventus and is rated among the greatest all-round footballers Britain ever produced — who is he?
The inaugural women's tennis world No. 1 from 1921, she won five straight Wimbledon singles titles and was the first leading amateur to turn professional — which French star?
Nicknamed "Double X" and "the Beast," this first baseman retired with the second-most home runs behind only Babe Ruth and topped 30 homers in 12 straight seasons — who was he?
Honored as one of England's greatest composers, this Tudor-era master of choral music wrote primarily for voices and anchors anthologies of English church song — who is he?
Irving Berlin wrote this patriotic prayer of a song in 1918, then revised it twenty years later for Kate Smith, who made it her signature — what is it?
God Bless America is an American patriotic song written by Irving Berlin in 1918 during World War I and revised by him in 1938 in the period leading up to World War II.
Recorded at Electric Lady Studios with former Velvet Underground member John Cale producing, this 1975 debut fused punk minimalism with avant-garde improvisation — which album is it?
Horses (album) — Horses is the debut studio album by American musician Patti Smith, released on November 10, 1975 by Arista Records.
This French painter invented a bold, machine-age form of cubism nicknamed "tubism" that made him a forerunner of pop art — who is he?
Days before a scheduled lobotomy, this New Zealand author was spared when her debut story collection won a national prize — launching a celebrated literary career. Who is she?
Nominated three times for the Nobel Prize in Literature, this Austrian satirist and aphorist aimed his sharpest barbs at the press and at German and Austrian politics — who was he?
Karl Kraus was an Austrian writer and journalist, known as a satirist, essayist, aphorist, playwright and poet.
Editor of the feminist magazine Bluestocking, this Japanese anarchist was murdered alongside her lover Ōsugi Sakae during the Amakasu Incident in 1923 — who was she?
Itō Noe: Japanese editor and activist (1895–1923)
This German humorist's illustrated tale Max and Moritz inspired The Katzenjammer Kids, making him a founding father of the comic strip — who is he?
Wilhelm Busch: German humorist, poet, illustrator, and painter (1832–1908)
This American novelist won the 1968 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction for The Confessions of Nat Turner — who is he?
Famed for dense, allusive prose and his Catholic faith, this American writer's Book of the New Sun series earned him Grand Master honors in science fiction and fantasy — who is he?
Gene Wolfe: American science fiction and fantasy writer (1931–2019)
Best known for her 1899 novel The Awakening, this Louisiana author of Creole heritage is regarded as a forerunner of 20th-century feminist writing — who is she?

Believed to be the first known woman to paint nude self-portraits — and the first to depict herself pregnant — this early German Expressionist also became the first woman with a museum devoted solely to her art. Who?
Paula Modersohn-Becker: German expressionist painter and draftswoman (1876–1907)

His 1971 book "Rules for Radicals: A Pragmatic Primer" defended both confrontation and compromise, drawn from his work with Chicago's Industrial Areas Foundation organizing poor communities — which American activist wrote it?
Saul Alinsky: American activist and political theorist (1909–1972)
An early student of "the father of modern yoga," this Indian guru founded his own namesake style and wrote "Light on Yoga" — who popularized the practice from India to the wider world?
B. K. S. Iyengar: Indian yoga teacher and author (1918–2014)
This German hermeneutic philosopher held Hegel's old Chair in Philosophy at the University of Berlin and wrestled with whether history could count as a science — who was he?
A Dutch-born painter who settled in London, he became famous for languorous figures lounging amid marbled Roman luxury against dazzling blue Mediterranean skies — who was this Victorian artist?
The son of Spanish anarchists and one of the few to survive the Granma landing, this beloved commander was considered second only to Fidel Castro in the Cuban Revolution. Who is he?
Camilo Cienfuegos (6 February 1932 - 28 October 1959) was a Cuban revolutionary.
Discovered in 1807 and named for the Roman goddess of home and hearth, this is thought to be the second-largest asteroid and the only known rocky protoplanet still intact in the belt — which one?
Dubbed the "Flying Tailor," this inventor was so sure his wearable parachute would work that he leapt from the Eiffel Tower to test it himself — fatally. Who was he?

Running weekly from 1964 to 2006, this BBC chart show — the world's longest-running weekly music programme — opened its very first episode with Dusty Springfield's 'I Only Want to Be with You'; what was it?
Top of the Pops is a British record chart television programme, made by the BBC and broadcast weekly between 1 January 1964 and 30 July 2006.
Nicknamed "Monsieur Chrono" for his peerless time-trialing, this Frenchman became the first cyclist ever to win the Tour de France five times. Who is he?
Jacques Anquetil (8 January 1934 - 18 November 1987) was a French road racing cyclist and the first cyclist to win the Tour de France five times, in 1957 and from 1961 to 1964.
This Congress politician led his party to victory in the 2023 election and became the second Chief Minister of Telangana — who is he?
Revanth Reddy: Chief Minister of Telangana (born 1969)
This Spanish construction magnate, who heads the ACS engineering group, also launched the star-studded 'Galácticos' era as president of Real Madrid — who is he?
One of the Celtic nations, this rural ceremonial county at England's southwestern tip is bordered by the Atlantic and the English Channel, with Truro as its city — which county?
Often starting as a blood clot in the leg that travels to the lungs, this blockage can cause chest pain on breathing in, coughing up blood, and sudden death — what is the condition?
Pulmonary embolism: Blockage of an artery in the lungs
Caused by a Corynebacterium bacterium, this infection can spin a tough grey 'pseudomembrane' across the throat that slowly chokes off the airway — what is it?
Diphtheria is an infection caused by the bacterium Corynebacterium diphtheriae.
Sold as Aleve, this NSAID eases pain, fever, and menstrual cramps for up to twelve hours, and also comes in a more soluble sodium form — which drug?
Naproxen: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to treat pain

Marked by an IQ below 70 and deficits in everyday adaptive skills first apparent in childhood, this neurodevelopmental condition was formerly called 'mental retardation' in the U.S. — what is it now called?

There's a large introduced population of this small carnivorous mammal in Hawaii, though its family — split into the Herpestinae and Mungotinae — is native to southern Europe, Africa, and Asia — what animal is it?
Mongoose: Family of mammals in Africa and Asia
Spurred by the 1980 failure of Operation Eagle Claw, this American tiltrotor blends a helicopter's vertical takeoff with a turboprop's long-range cruise — what aircraft is it?
Bell Boeing V-22 Osprey: Military transport tiltrotor
Nicknamed the 'Dragon Lady,' this single-engine American spy plane flew covert missions above 70,000 feet over the Soviet Union, China, and Cuba from the 1950s — what is it?
This Arabic word for a 'report' refers to the Islamic oral tradition of anecdotes preserving the words and deeds of Muhammad, ranking second only to the Quran in authority — what is it?
Hadith: Collections of sayings and teachings of Muhammad
A cousin of the tomato and potato, this European nightshade is so toxic — via atropine and scopolamine — that even handling it can harm you; its other common name is "belladonna." What's the plant?
Atropa bella-donna: Deadly nightshade, a flowering plant
Affecting some 280 million people worldwide, this state of low mood saps motivation and the pleasure once taken in activities — what is it?
Depression (mood) — Depression is a mental state of low mood and aversion to activity.
Caused by the bacterium Neisseria gonorrhoeae and colloquially called 'the clap,' this sexually transmitted infection can pass from mother to child during birth — what is it?
Better known as "pink eye," this inflammation of the clear layer over the white of the eye can leave a lid stuck shut by morning — what's the medical name?

In the British Isles this small insectivorous flycatcher is known simply as the redbreast, its orange face and breast identical in male and female, while juveniles are freckled brown — which bird is it?

The European robin (Erithacus rubecula), known simply as the robin or robin redbreast in the British Isles, is a small insectivorous passerine bird belonging to the Old World flycatcher family Muscicapidae.
This Oracle co-founder owns 98% of the Hawaiian island of Lānaʻi and briefly became the world's richest person in September 2025 when his company's stock spiked — who is he?
As owner of Hopetown Entertainment, this American manager has steered the careers of her two daughters, Miley and Noah, from the very start — who is she?
Tish Cyrus (ne Leticia Jean Finley; born May 15, 1967) is an American manager and producer.
The very first primetime series on the brand-new Fox network, this Chicago-set sitcom about a hard-luck former football player ran a decade — what was it?
Born in Johannesburg, this South African comedian took over a satirical Comedy Central news show in 2015, won two Emmys, and made Time's 100 most influential — who is he?
Standing over seven feet tall due to acromegaly, this Indian-born wrestler became WWE's first Indian-born world champion in the mid-2000s — who is he?
The Great Khali: Indian-American professional wrestler (born 1972)
After Yale, he shot war-zone footage before joining CNN in 2001 to anchor a show bearing his own name and "360°" — and moonlighted for two decades on 60 Minutes. Which journalist?

Drawing on Patrick Radden Keefe's reporting and Barry Meier's book, this American drama miniseries dramatizes the birth of the opioid crisis and Purdue Pharma's aggressive marketing of OxyContin — which series is it?
Painkiller (TV series) — Painkiller is an American drama television miniseries created by Micah Fitzerman-Blue and Noah Harpster.
One of the Four Corners states, this landlocked Mountain West state packs roughly two-thirds of its people into the Wasatch Front around its capital. Which state is it?
It's the largest state by total area east of the Mississippi, with Lansing as its capital and Detroit as its biggest city — which Great Lakes state is it?
Twelve grand avenues radiate like a star from the plaza at the western end of the Champs-Élysées, all meeting at one famous monument honoring France's war dead — what is it?

Typically about two-thirds copper and one-third zinc, which prehistoric substitutional alloy differs from bronze, which swaps in tin instead of zinc?
Brass: Alloy of copper and zinc
Derived from a French word meaning 'watcher' and linked to the 'Peeping Tom' of the Lady Godiva legend, which behaviour does the DSM classify as a paraphilia?
Voyeurism: Sexual interest in or practice of spying on people engaged in intimate behaviors
Generally colourless, hydrophobic, and faintly gasoline-scented, which organic compound is made entirely of hydrogen and carbon and includes everything from methane to paraffin wax?
Hydrocarbon: Organic compound consisting entirely of hydrogen and carbon

Founder of the Janasena Party and a Telugu cinema star with a famously 'cult-like' fanbase, which actor-turned-politician became Deputy Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh in 2024?
Pawan Kalyan: 11th Deputy Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh since 2024
Nicknamed "The Hoff," this American actor and singer drove a talking car as Michael Knight before patrolling the sand as lifeguard Mitch Buchannon on Baywatch — who is he?
David Hasselhoff (born July 17, 1952), nicknamed "The Hoff", is an American actor, singer, and television personality.
Sharing the Four Corners with Arizona, New Mexico, and Utah, which eighth-largest U.S. state encompasses most of the Southern Rocky Mountains?

The World Bank sorts the world's economies into high, upper-middle, lower-middle, and low income, but there's no universal agreement on which nations belong in this broader, lower-HDI category. What's the term?
Developing country: Nation with a relatively low living standard

He won every one of the three marathons he ever ran, each under 2 hours and 2 minutes, and was the top-ranked men's marathoner in the world when he died in early 2024 — which Kenyan runner held that crown?
Born in 1957, this infielder spent his Nippon Professional Baseball career with the Hanshin Tigers and Orix BlueWave before later managing — which Japanese star is it?
Akinobu Okada (born November 25, 1957) is a Japanese former professional baseball infielder and manager.
At 29 she beat a 55-year-old in the 1973 "Battle of the Sexes," then founded the Women's Tennis Association and racked up 39 Grand Slam titles. Which equality-crusading champion?

Born in the African-American communities of New Orleans around the turn of the 20th century, this genre is built on swing, blue notes, call-and-response, and improvisation — what is it?
Emerging from Bronx block parties in the early 1970s, this genre counts turntablism, scratching, and beatboxing among its hallmarks — what is it?

Opera: Art form combining sung text and musical score in a theatrical setting

A Christmas Carol: 1843 novella by Charles Dickens

Jerry Rawlings: Leader of Ghana in 1979 and 1981–2001
This British-German-French philosopher's 1899 two-volume work attributed all of civilization's achievements to the Germanic race and went on to shape the antisemitism of Adolf Hitler — who was he?
Houston Stewart Chamberlain: British-German racialist philosopher (1855–1927)
Introduced to Marxism while imprisoned, he founded the Parcham faction of Afghanistan's communist party and led the country as its general secretary through the early 1980s. Who was he?

To prove bombers could sink battleships, this U.S. Army officer staged a series of bombing runs against stationary ships — relentless advocacy that made him a father of the U.S. Air Force and infuriated his superiors. Who was he?
Father of the United States Air Force
Billy Mitchell: United States Army general (1879–1936)

Taking his regnal name — which meant "the legitimate king" — from an ancient ruler of Akkad, this Neo-Assyrian monarch founded a new dynastic line and aspired to conquer the known world before dying in battle in 705 BC. Who was he?
Sargon II: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire

A Bourbon prince celebrated as one of France's greatest generals, he made his name routing the Spanish at the 1643 Battle of Rocroi during the Thirty Years' War. Known by an epithet meaning "the Great," who was he?
Louis, Grand Condé: French military leader (1621–1686)
A former Salesian priest who preached liberation theology, he served multiple stints as president of Haiti — twice driven into exile, in 1991 and again in 2004. Who is he?
Jean-Bertrand Aristide: Former president of Haiti (born 1953)

Fought in the 1820s between the Empire of Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata over a contested province, this conflict ended by birthing a brand-new nation: Uruguay. What was it called?
Cisplatine War: 1825–1828 war between Brazil and the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata
A towering figure whose political career spanned seven decades, this Greek statesman served four terms as prime minister and two as president of the Third Hellenic Republic — who was he?
These seed-loving rodents come in 19 species, the golden or Syrian variety being the one most often found in a child's bedroom cage — what are they?
Hamster are rodents (order Rodentia) belonging to the subfamily Cricetinae, which contains 19 species classified in seven genera.

Formally described only in 1983, this helical, flagella-driven bacterium burrows through the stomach's mucous lining and is the chief culprit behind gastric ulcers and some stomach cancers. What is it?

Native to the eastern Himalayas and southwestern China, this small mammal sports dense reddish-brown fur, a ringed tail, and curved semi-retractile claws for climbing — and was the original bearer of its famous name. What is it?
Red panda: Species of mammal in Asia
Normally circulating among fruit bats of the genus Pteropus, this zoonotic disease can turn a flu-like illness into fatal encephalitis and a coma within a day or two — what condition is it?
Nipah virus infection is a zoonotic viral disease caused by the Nipah virus.
A synthetic element named for a famous physicist, it's the first of the super-heavy transactinides and behaves chemically as the heavier cousin of hafnium in group 4 — which element?
Rutherfordium: Chemical element with atomic number 104 (Rf)
A West Point-trained engineer, this Confederate general fired the opening shots of the American Civil War at Fort Sumter — yet signed his letters "G. T.," rarely using his first name. Who was he?
P. G. T. Beauregard: Confederate States Army general (1818–1893)
First created in 1994 near Darmstadt, Germany, this extremely radioactive synthetic element is named for the physicist who discovered X-rays — which element is it?
Roentgenium: Chemical element with atomic number 111 (Rg)

Meitnerium: Chemical element with atomic number 109 (Mt)

This American physicist worked with Niels Bohr on nuclear fission and had a gift for coinages — "quantum foam," "wormhole," and the term that popularized "gravitationally collapsed objects." Who was he?
John Archibald Wheeler: American theoretical physicist (1911–2008)
This Stanford computer scientist built ImageNet, the vast labeled dataset that ignited the deep-learning revolution in computer vision in the 2010s. Who is she?

Seaborgium: Chemical element with atomic number 106 (Sg)
Hailed as "the Father of Indian cinema," he directed India's very first full-length feature, Raja Harishchandra, back in 1913 — who was he?
Dadasaheb Phalke: Indian film producer, director and screenwriter (1870–1944)
This British-Australian filmmaker cut his teeth directing episodes of EastEnders and Byker Grove before going on to win an Academy Award. Who is he?
Famous for her vocal range and belting, this Filipino singer endured an unorthodox childhood training method — singing while immersed neck-deep in the sea. Who is she?
Regine Velasquez: Filipino singer and actress (born 1970)
Crowned the "Queen of Fado," this artist did more than anyone to carry her country's mournful music to the world and remains the best-selling Portuguese recording artist in history. Who was she?
Hailed as "Hollywood's last romantic," this iconoclastic director clashed constantly with the studio system but left his mark with the 1955 film Rebel Without a Cause. Who was he?
Nicknamed "Bojangles," this tap dancer was the highest-paid Black entertainer in early-20th-century America and is credited with bringing tap up onto its toes. Who was he?
Bill Robinson: American dancer and actor (1878–1949)
He co-founded Maxis and, after a debut called Raid on Bungeling Bay, hit it big with a city-building simulation he followed with SimEarth and SimAnt — which game designer?
William Ralph Wright (born January 20, 1960) is an American video game designer and co-founder of the game development company Maxis, which later became part of Electronic Arts.
Though Amsterdam is the official capital, this North Sea coastal city has been the Netherlands' de facto seat of government since the Dutch Republic — which city is it?
The Hague: City and municipality in the Netherlands

Famed for its seventeen ancient norias — waterwheels said to date back to 1100 BC — this city on the Orontes is also known for a signature cheese dessert called Halawet el Jibn. What Syrian city is it?
Hama is a city on the banks of the Orontes River in west-central Syria.
Also known as Nellai and perched on the west bank of the Thamirabarani River, this Tamil Nadu city was a major town under the Early Pandyas during the Sangam period. Which city is it?
Tirunelveli: City in Tamil Nadu, India
Sitting in the Triângulo Mineiro and home to over 750,000 people, what is the second most populous municipality in Brazil's Minas Gerais state?
Uberlândia (Brazilian Portuguese) is a Brazilian municipality located in the interior of the state of Minas Gerais, in the region known as Tringulo Mineiro, Southeast Region of the country.
Nicknamed "the Big Train," this Washington Senators pitcher still holds the all-time record for career shutouts with 110 and sits second all-time in wins. Who was he?
Walter Johnson: American baseball player and manager (1887–1946)

Highway 61 Revisited: 1965 studio album by Bob Dylan
This Vietnamese singer-songwriter launched his own label, M-TP Entertainment, and built his career on self-written hits like "Lạc trôi" and "Nơi này có anh" — who is he?

This Chilean comedian became the first YouTuber ever to earn two Diamond Play Buttons, first famous for his everyday-life humor channel before his gaming channel overtook it — who is he?
Germán Garmendia: Chilean YouTuber, comedian, and writer (born 1990)
Known as "The Singing Brakeman" and "America's Blue Yodeler," this Meridian, Mississippi native is widely hailed as the "Father of Country Music." Who was he?

George M. Cohan: American actor, singer, composer and playwright (1878–1942)

Built single-handedly over five years by indie developer "ConcernedApe," this 2016 game hands you a dilapidated farm inherited from your grandfather to clear, plant, and bring back to life — what is it?

Conceived by Shigeru Miyamoto during the making of Star Fox, this 1996 Nintendo 64 launch title was the first in its franchise to go fully 3D, sending its hero into worlds hidden inside magical paintings — which game is it?

Robert's Rules of Order: Book on parliamentary procedure by Henry Martyn Robert

This English writer published two landmark books within a single year — an attack on political institutions and an early mystery novel — and is counted the first modern proponent of anarchism. Who is he?
William Godwin: English philosopher and novelist (1756–1836)

Constantine VII: Byzantine emperor from 913 to 959

Sudirman: First commander-in-chief of the Indonesian armed forces

Tiradentes: 18th-century Brazilian revolutionary and national hero

Born in Singapore in 1983, this former Xiaomi finance chief has run a wildly popular ByteDance-owned video app since 2021 — who is he?
Shou Zi Chew: Singaporean business executive (born 1983)

Aneurysm: Bulge in the wall of a blood vessel

Jawed Karim: American entrepreneur and software engineer (born 1979)
An eight-year MADtv cast member turned podcaster, he co-hosts 'Bad Friends' and 'TigerBelly' and played the burned-out Dr. Kang on 'Reservation Dogs' — who is this comedian?

Sitting on the Ganges and also known as Kashi or Benares, this northern Indian city holds a central place in Hindu traditions of pilgrimage and mourning — which city is it?
Varanasi: Metropolis in Uttar Pradesh, India

Crowned as a child after his father died at the siege of Roxburgh Castle, this unpopular King of Scots faced two major rebellions and died at the Battle of Sauchieburn in 1488 — who was he?
James III of Scotland: King of Scots from 1460 to 1488

Anna Jagiellon (18 October 1523 - 9 September 1596) was Queen of Poland and Grand Duchess of Lithuania from 1575 to 1587.

Tiberius Gracchus: Roman politician and social reformer (163 – 133 BC)

Morihei Ueshiba was a Japanese martial artist and founder of the martial art of aikido.
Before becoming Australia's 23rd prime minister, this Rhodes Scholar led the Australian Council of Trade Unions — who was he?
Bob Hawke: Prime Minister of Australia from 1983 to 1991

Set off by the gold rush's flood of settlers, this 19th-century campaign killed thousands of the region's Indigenous people through massacre, starvation, and forced labor between 1846 and 1873. What is this dark chapter called?
The California genocide was a series of genocidal massacres of the Indigenous peoples of California by United States governments, soldiers and settlers during the 19th century.

Trained in the Soviet NKVD's methods in Moscow, this Chinese Communist official and calligrapher ran the party's security and intelligence apparatus at the height of the Cultural Revolution — who was he?

Sirimavo Bandaranaike: Prime Minister of Sri Lanka (1916–2000)

Paul Keating: Prime Minister of Australia from 1991 to 1996

Thutmose I: Third Egyptian Pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty (c. 1506 – 1493 BC)
One of the widest-ranging mammals on Earth, this adaptable suid native to Eurasia and North Africa has turned invasive wherever people introduced it — what is it?

HIV (HIVs) are two species of Lentivirus (a subgroup of retrovirus) that infect humans.

Sophie Germain: French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher
This Hungarian-American theoretical physicist won the 1963 Nobel for applying fundamental symmetry principles to the atomic nucleus and elementary particles — who was he?
Eugene Wigner: Hungarian-American physicist and mathematician (1902–1995)
An Olympic gold medallist and political activist, this pediatrician told mothers 'you know more than you think you do' in a 1946 book that sold 50 million copies — who was he?
Benjamin Spock: American pediatrician, political activist, and writer (1903–1998)

Lawrencium: Chemical element with atomic number 103 (Lr)

Gunpei Yokoi: Japanese video game designer (1941–1997)

A major figure of Hong Kong's cinematic Golden Age, this filmmaker directed the Once Upon a Time in China series and Green Snake, and produced A Better Tomorrow and A Chinese Ghost Story — who is he?

Mark Millar: Scottish comic book writer (born 1969)
Once an assistant to Abbas Kiarostami, this Iranian New Wave director won the Caméra d'Or at Cannes with his debut The White Balloon — who is he?
Jafar Panahi: Iranian filmmaker and actor (born 1960)

Trujillo is a city in coastal northwestern Peru and the capital of the Department of La Libertad.

Huangshan: Mountain range in southern Anhui, China
