Sihanoukville: City in Preah Sihanouk province, Cambodia
A Parisian watchmaker's son who was also at various times an inventor, spy, arms dealer, and revolutionary, this Enlightenment Frenchman is best known for his three Figaro plays — who was he?
Pierre-Augustin de Beaumarchais: French playwright and diplomat (1732–1799)
A pioneer of rockabilly, this American's 1956 hit 'Be-Bop-a-Lula' with his Blue Caps became an early landmark of the style — though he charted bigger in the UK than at home. Who was he?
As the house band for Stax Records in Memphis, this instrumental group backed Otis Redding, Wilson Pickett and Sam & Dave while also cutting hits under their own name — who were they?
Booker T. & the M.G.'s: American R&B/funk band

Brian Wilson built this Beach Boys single from dozens of recorded "modules" and promoted it as a "pocket symphony," inspired by the idea of extrasensory perception; topping charts in 1966, what is the song?
Good Vibrations is a song by the American rock band the Beach Boys, produced and composed by Brian Wilson with lyrics by Mike Love and, in some published versions, by Tony Asher.
Valve's 2013 sequel grew out of a community-made Warcraft III mod, pitting two teams of five hero-controlling players against each other to destroy the enemy base — which MOBA?
Founding director of Oxford's Future of Humanity Institute, this philosopher wrote Superintelligence and is known for his work on existential risk and the anthropic principle — who is he?
Which 19th-century Russian poet, later known as Shenshin, is regarded as the finest master of lyric verse in all of Russian literature?
Nabokov built this 1962 novel as a 999-line poem by a fictional poet, wrapped in a foreword, commentary, and index by his self-appointed neighbor — together forming the story. Which book?
Pale Fire: 1962 novel by Vladimir Nabokov

Henry Fuseli's 1781 painting shows a sleeping woman with a demonic incubus crouched on her chest while a ghostly horse looks on — its overt sexuality scandalized critics and made his name. Which work?
The Nightmare: 1781 painting by Henry Fuseli
Held in high esteem by Tolstoy, Chekhov, and Gorky, this Russian master of short forms wrote Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk, later made into a Shostakovich opera — who is he?
Nikolai Leskov: Russian writer and novelist (1831–1895)
Which Austrian writer, born in 1874, worked across novel, poem, drama, essay — and made his name as a librettist?
Hugo Laurenz August Hofmann von Hofmannsthal
Hugo von Hofmannsthal: Austrian novelist, librettist, poet, dramatist (1874–1929)
This English novelist and critic, born Antonia Susan Drabble, wrote under her former married name and saw her books translated into more than thirty languages — who is she?

This Danish architect won a 1957 international competition with a design that became one of the world's great landmarks — and was only the second person, after Oscar Niemeyer, honored with a World Heritage Site in his own lifetime. Who is he?
Considered by some the greatest lawyer of the 20th century, this ACLU leader argued the Leopold and Loeb case and the Scopes 'monkey' trial — who is he?
Clarence Darrow: American lawyer and politician (1857–1938)
A supreme colorist of the Venetian Late Renaissance, this painter of enormous canvases like The Wedding at Cana made up a "great trio" alongside Titian and Tintoretto — who is he?
A Savoyard lawyer and diplomat who championed monarchy after the French Revolution and served as ambassador to Russia, he's remembered as a forefather of modern conservatism — who is he?
Joseph de Maistre: Savoyard political philosopher (1753–1821)
Taught as a boy by his illustrator father N. C., this American realist painted the land and people of Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania — though he oddly insisted he was an "abstractionist." Who is he?

Adapted from a 1967 Mel Brooks film, this Broadway musical follows a producer and his timid accountant who scheme to get rich by overselling shares in a show designed to flop — until it's a hit. What is it?
The Producers is a musical comedy with music and lyrics by Mel Brooks and a book by Brooks and Thomas Meehan.
Fill in the blank: “____ was a medieval monarchy in the Iberian Peninsula founded by the nobleman Pelagius.”
Kingdom of Asturias was a medieval monarchy in the Iberian Peninsula founded by the nobleman Pelagius.
Native to India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka and listed as Near Threatened as its deciduous forests vanish, this is one of the entire cat family's tiniest members — which feline is it?
The rusty-spotted cat (Prionailurus rubiginosus) is one of the cat family's smallest members.

The largest land bird in North America went fully extinct in the wild in 1987 when every survivor was captured for breeding — which critically endangered vulture has since returned to the Grand Canyon and beyond?
California condor (Gymnogyps californianus) is a New World vulture and the largest North American land bird.

Aristotle studied here for twenty years before founding his own rival school, and it's regarded as the first institution of higher education in the West — what was this Athenian school founded around 387 BC?
Platonic Academy: Educative center founded by Plato
From 431 to 404 BC, two leagues fought for control of Ancient Greece — and it took the Persian Empire backing Sparta to finally crush Athens. What is this drawn-out conflict called?
The Peloponnesian War was fought in the Eastern Mediterranean between the Athenian-led Delian League and the Spartan-led Peloponnesian League from 431 to 404 BC for hegemony over Ancient Greece.
It's the season when the earliest sunrises and latest sunsets crowd around a single solstice — and when half the planet swelters, the other half shivers. Which season is it?
Summer: Hottest of the four temperate seasons

A former police officer turned serial killer, this Californian terrorized the state from 1974 to 1986 under a chilling roster of nicknames — the East Area Rapist, the Original Night Stalker, the Visalia Ransacker. Who is he?
Joseph James DeAngelo: American serial rapist and serial killer (born 1945)
Surprisingly, the closest living relatives of birds are a clan of semiaquatic predators that includes alligators, caimans, and the long-snouted gharial. What is this reptile order?
Fill in the blank: “____ (COPD) is a long-term lung condition that makes it progressively harder to breathe.”
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a long-term lung condition that makes it progressively harder to breathe.
Prescribed for ADHD and narcolepsy but also misused as a euphoriant, this fixed-dose pill packs four different amphetamine salts into one tablet. What is its brand name?
Adderall: Drug mixture used mainly to treat ADHD and narcolepsy
Extracted and refined from either sugarcane or sugar beet, this disaccharide of glucose and fructose is the main ingredient in ordinary white sugar. What is it?
Sucrose: Disaccharide made of glucose and fructose
Caused by a toxin that thrives in low-oxygen conditions — the same one sold cosmetically as 'botox' — this rare illness brings blurred vision and creeping paralysis but rarely a fever. What is it?
Botulism is a rare and potentially fatal illness caused by botulinum toxin (commonly referred to as botox), which is produced by the bacterium Clostridium botulinum.

Numbering 126 species, these are the largest order of marsupials in the Western Hemisphere — and only one of them, the Virginia variety, made it as far north as the United States and Canada. What animal is this?
Its name comes from Greek roots meaning 'chief' and 'creator,' and historians often identify whole vanished civilizations by what survives of this visual art. What is it?
Architecture: Art and technique of designing buildings
Taking its name from the Latin for 'weasel,' this is the largest family in the suborder Caniformia — gathering otters, badgers, martens, and wolverines under one roof. What is it?
Caused by a group of enteroviruses, this common infection opens with a fever and then sprinkles blistering spots on exactly the three body parts named in its label. What is it?
Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is a common infection caused by a group of enteroviruses.

This catch-all name covers over 7,000 squamate species on every continent but Antarctica — from finger-length geckos to the three-meter Komodo dragon, with a few 'legless' lineages thrown in. What is it?
A former Miss Georgia USA contestant who later launched her own yarn brand, this television personality has co-hosted the same letter-turning game show since 1982 — who is she?
Vanna White (ne Rosich; born February 18, 1957) is an American television personality.
Known by his initials GSP, this Canadian became a two-division UFC champion, holding the welterweight title three times and ranking #1 in the world for years. Who is he?
Georges St-Pierre: Canadian mixed martial arts fighter

This fourth-largest state splits its personality down the middle — Rocky Mountain ranges to the west, prairie and badlands to the east — with Helena as its capital but Billings as its biggest city. Which one is it?
Carved from old stone quarries to relieve the city's overflowing graveyards, this underground ossuary now cradles the bones of more than six million people. What is it?
The Catacombs of Paris are underground ossuaries in Paris, France, which hold the remains of more than six million people.
Begun in AD 122, this stone barrier with ditches stretched clear across northern Britain, dotted with forts and milecastles whose gates may have doubled as customs posts. What Roman landmark is it?
Hadrian's Wall: Defensive fortification in Roman Britain
Italy's largest carmaker traces its roots to 1899 and its very first model, the 4 HP; today it's a subsidiary of Stellantis. Which automaker is it?
Born in 1847 as a Berlin telegraph workshop, this German conglomerate is now Europe's largest engineering company and a global leader in industrial automation. What is it?

Its words began as a poem a lawyer scribbled in 1814 after watching Fort McHenry survive a British bombardment — then got set to the tune of a London gentlemen's-club drinking song. What is this anthem?
The Star-Spangled Banner: National anthem of the United States

He joined a famous funk-rock band at just 18 after the previous guitarist's death, debuting on 1989's Mother's Milk before their breakthrough Blood Sugar Sex Magik — then quit, overwhelmed by fame. Who is this guitarist?
Emerging mid-20th century as a skeptical reply to modernism, this movement prizes the instability of meaning, distrusts grand narratives, and gleefully blends styles. What is it?
Postmodernism: Artistic, cultural, and theoretical movement
Fill in the blank: “____ was a fifth-century Romano-British Christian missionary and bishop in Ireland.”
Saint Patrick was a fifth-century Romano-British Christian missionary and bishop in Ireland.
With her debut cookbook 'Mastering the Art of French Cooking' and the 1963 TV show 'The French Chef,' this American brought French cuisine into ordinary kitchens. Who was she?

First surfacing in Paris just before World War I, this sleek style took its name from a French phrase for 'decorative arts' and went on to shape everything from skyscrapers to vacuum cleaners. What is it?
Art Deco: 20th-century architectural and art style

The first governor-general of Bengal, he and Robert Clive are credited with laying the foundation of British India — then in 1787 he was impeached for corruption, only to be acquitted in 1795. Who is it?
Commander of the Indonesian Armed Forces during the country's 1998 transition from authoritarian rule, this retired general later chaired the Presidential Advisory Council — who is it?
Codenamed Operation Marita, this April 1941 World War II assault followed Italy's failed 1940 attack and culminated in airborne landings on Crete — which campaign is it?
German invasion of Greece: World War II military campaign in 1941
Known for fiery anti-Catholic sermons, this Northern Irish loyalist co-founded the Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster and led the DUP from 1971 — who is it?
Ian Richard Kyle Paisley, Baron Bannside
Ian Paisley: Northern Irish politician and religious leader (1926–2014)
Before becoming President of India in 1977, this politician had been chief minister of Andhra Pradesh and a two-time Speaker of the Lok Sabha — who is it?
Neelam Sanjiva Reddy: President of India from 1977 to 1982
The exiled spokesman for East Timor's resistance during the Indonesian occupation, he shared the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize and later became his nation's president — who is it?
José Ramos-Horta: President of East Timor (2007–2012; since 2022)
Nicknamed 'electric brain' for his calm under pressure, this U.S. admiral commanded Task Force 16 at Midway, where American dive bombers sank four Japanese fleet carriers — who was he?
Raymond A. Spruance (July 3, 1886 - December 13, 1969) was a United States Navy admiral during World War II.
This US Army general led the 82nd Airborne in Sicily, Italy and Normandy, later commanded a corps at the Battle of the Bulge, and went on to be Supreme Allied Commander Europe — who was he?
Matthew Ridgway: United States Army general (1895–1993)

When Theodosius I died in 395, the Roman Empire split between his two sons: Honorius took the west, while which eldest son — long remembered as a weak ruler dominated by his ministers and his wife Aelia Eudoxia — took the east?
By the time he stepped down in 2017 after 38 years leading the MPLA, which man was Africa's second-longest-serving president, behind only Equatorial Guinea's Obiang?
José Eduardo dos Santos: President of Angola from 1979 to 2017

The seventh pharaoh of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty inherited a vast kingdom from his father Thutmose III but fought far less, his reign seeing hostilities with Mitanni effectively cease — which ruler was he?
Amenhotep II: Seventh Pharaoh of the Eighteenth dynasty of Egypt
This three-time Conservative prime minister, who doubled as Foreign Secretary for most of his tenure, championed a foreign policy he called 'splendid isolation' — who was he?
Robert Arthur Talbot Gascoigne Cecil, Marquis of Salisbury
Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 3rd Marquess of Salisbury: British prime minister (1885-86; 1886-92; 1895-1902)
Only about 35 atoms of this synthetic element (number 116) had ever been made as of 2020 — and it's named for the California national laboratory that helped discover it. Which element?
Livermorium: Chemical element with atomic number 116 (Lv)
Discovered in Dubna in 1999, this superheavy synthetic element (number 114) honors a Russian physicist whose name in Cyrillic explains why its spelling swaps a 'yo' for an 'e' — which element?
Flerovium: Chemical element with atomic number 114 (Fl)
Her famous experiment proved parity is not conserved — earning Lee and Yang the 1957 Nobel while she received the inaugural Wolf Prize in Physics instead. Which Manhattan Project physicist was she?
First created near Darmstadt in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th anniversary, this synthetic element (number 112) is so volatile it may even be a gas — which element?
Copernicium: Chemical element with atomic number 112 (Cn)
Crowned 'El Rey de los Timbales' — the King of the Timbales — this Latin jazz and mambo bandleader still found time to guest on Sesame Street and The Simpsons' 'Who Shot Mr. Burns?' — who is it?
Tito Puente: American Latin jazz and mambo musician (1923–2000)
Bob Kane privately admitted this co-creator of Batman was responsible for 50 to 75 percent of the creativity, yet he was long stuck with mere 'ghostwriter' status — who is it?
A former bank clerk turned comic, this Englishman starred in Porridge, Open All Hours, and a famous double act billed as "The Two" of his first name — who was he?
Ronnie Barker: English actor, comedian and writer (1929–2005)
Home to three railway stations and a 75-hectare former rail-yard district now being reborn, which is the second-largest city in the Dutch province of North Brabant?
Tilburg: City in North Brabant, Netherlands
Designed by Pierre L'Enfant as a democratic 'Grand Avenue' — deliberately unlike the palace gardens of Versailles — this Washington park draws some 24 million visitors a year. What is it?
National Mall is a landscaped park near the downtown area of Washington, D.C., the capital city of the United States.
Widely called the greatest fast bowler of the modern era, this South African paired rare late swing with high pace and took 78 wickets at an average of 16.24 in 2007–08 — who is he?
Dale Steyn (born 27 June 1983) is a South African former professional cricketer who played for the South African cricket team.
Across 22 NHL seasons — 21 with the New Jersey Devils — this Canadian goaltender stacked up three Stanley Cups and two Olympic gold medals for Canada. Who is it?
Martin Brodeur: Canadian-American ice hockey player (born 1972)
Recorded over three days in 1969 and pieced together by producer Teo Macero, this Miles Davis album traded traditional jazz rhythms for loose, rock-influenced electric improvisation — what is it?
Bitches Brew: 1970 studio album by Miles Davis
This German-born composer's most famous collaboration with Bertolt Brecht gave the world The Threepenny Opera and the ballad 'Mack the Knife' — who is it?
Nicknamed 'El Potro' — the Colt — this charismatic Argentine singer carried cuarteto music to the national stage before his death at 27 in 2000 — who is it?
A three-time Grammy winner with 45 Dove Awards, this artist crossed over to mainstream in 1991 when 'Place in This World' hit No. 6 on the Billboard Hot 100 — who is it?
Bob Dylan's seventh studio album, this 1966 double LP finally clicked when he decamped to Nashville's CBS studios with Al Kooper and Robbie Robertson — what is it?
Blonde on Blonde: 1966 studio album by Bob Dylan

Starting around 1885, a cluster of music publishers on West 28th Street in Manhattan came to dominate American popular song — and earned a nickname now marked by a plaque and a co-named street. What is it?
Tin Pan Alley: Group of music publishers and songwriters in New York City
Regarded as one of the 20th century's greatest symphonic conductors, this German led the Berlin Philharmonic from 1922 to 1945 and again from 1952 until his death — who was he?
Gustav Heinrich Ernst Martin Wilhelm Furtwängler
Wilhelm Furtwängler: German conductor and composer (1886–1954)
This 2007 first-person shooter drops you into Rapture, an underwater utopia built by a business magnate and undone by ADAM, a genetic material granting superhuman powers. What's the game?
Japan's first professional woman writer of modern literature, this Meiji-era master of short stories and poetry was later honored on the 5000 yen banknote — who is it?
Born Wesley Cook and a Black Panther at 14, this journalist wrote about the justice system from death row before his sentence was commuted to life in 2011 — who is it?
A founder of the group Die Brücke — 'The Bridge' — that helped launch Expressionism, this German painter saw the Nazis brand his work 'degenerate' and sell or destroy over 600 pieces — who is it?
Ernst Ludwig Kirchner: German expressionist painter (1880–1938)
This WWII veteran turned historian, a self-described 'something of an anarchist,' wrote the best-selling A People's History of the United States — who is it?
Howard Zinn: American historian and socialist philosopher (1922–2010)
From 1967 onward a prominent advocate of a two-state solution, this Israeli novelist saw his 40 books published in 45 languages — more than any other Israeli writer. Who is it?
Amos Oz: Israeli writer, journalist and intellectual (1939–2018)
After three years in the Parliamentary Army during the English Civil War, this tinker-turned-preacher wrote the Christian allegory The Pilgrim's Progress — who is it?
John Bunyan: English writer and preacher (1628–1688)
Sold into slavery in West Africa as a child and brought to Boston, she became, in 1773, the first African-American author of a published book of poetry — who is it?
This British-American novelist, who began writing at 19 to support her family, gave us Little Lord Fauntleroy, A Little Princess, and The Secret Garden — who was she?
This 19th-century French writer and diplomat penned An Essay on the Inequality of the Human Races, helping invent the notion of an Aryan master race — who was he?
Arthur de Gobineau: French diplomat and writer (1816–1882)
This French Renaissance poet wrote Les Amours de Cassandre and the Sonnets pour Hélène before a hearing impairment ended his diplomatic career — who was he?
Best known for her novels of life on the Great Plains like My Ántonia and O Pioneers!, this writer won the 1923 Pulitzer for One of Ours — who was she?
A Rotterdam-born painter who emigrated to the US in 1926, this "action painting" abstract expressionist belonged to the New York School alongside Pollock and Rothko — who was he?
Willem de Kooning: Dutch-American abstract expressionist artist (1904–1997)
A founding figure of sociology, this German thinker asked "What is society?" in deliberate echo of Kant, and wrote "The Metropolis and Mental Life" — who was he?
Georg Simmel: German sociologist and philosopher (1858–1918)
Author of Red Cavalry and Odessa Stories and hailed as "the greatest prose writer of Russian Jewry," this writer was executed by the NKVD on fabricated charges in 1940 — who was he?
Isaac Babel: Russian writer and journalist (1894–1940)
First published in Finnish in 1945 by Mika Waltari, this historical novel about a man named Sinuhe remains the only Finnish novel adapted into a Hollywood film — which book is it?
The Egyptian: 1945 novel by Finnish author Mika Waltari
Inspired early by Le Corbusier, this Japanese architect rebuilt postwar cities and designed the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Park — who was he?
In 2017 he was called "probably the most famous literary critic in the English-speaking world" — a Yale Sterling Professor who wrote over 40 books of criticism; who was he?
Harold Bloom: American critic, scholar, and writer (1930–2019)

Born John Chapman, this American pioneer nurseryman planted seed-grown apple trees across Pennsylvania, Ohio and beyond, becoming a folk hero in his own lifetime for his kindness and conservation. By what nickname do we know him?
Before taking the throne in 2020, this leader had served as his country's minister of interior, minister of defense, and crown prince under his half-brother. Which Emir of Kuwait is this?
Nawaf Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah: Emir of Kuwait from 2020 to 2023

Launched in 2017 by Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman at the northern tip of the Red Sea, this 26,500-square-kilometer megaproject was widely mocked as unrealistic before being scaled way back. What is it?
Neom is a megaproject in Tabuk Province in Saudi Arabia.
Its Sanskrit name literally means 'wheel' or 'circle,' and it refers to a psychospiritual energy-center in the subtle body used as a meditation aid in Hindu and Buddhist tantric practice. What is it?
Chakra: Subtle body centers in esoteric traditions
Trusted fully by George Washington and given command of West Point, this Continental Army major general plotted to hand the fort to the British in 1780 before fleeing to their lines. Who was he?
A real estate magnate and Spanish–American War officer worth roughly $87 million, he was the richest passenger aboard the Titanic — and went down with it in 1912. Who was he?
John Jacob Astor IV: American businessman and Titanic passenger (1864–1912)
A broad-spectrum member of the tetracycline class, this antibiotic treats everything from acne and chlamydia to Lyme disease and cholera — though it'll make you sunburn more easily. Which drug?
Found on every continent but Antarctica, these flowers can lure pollinators by mimicking female insects, and their tiny seeds depend on fungal partners just to sprout. What plant family is this?
Orchid: Family of flowering plants in the order Asparagales
Humphry Davy coined this colorless gas's cheerful nickname for the euphoria it brings, and it still earns a spot on the WHO's Essential Medicines list for dentistry and surgery. What is it?
Nitrous oxide: Colourless non-flammable greenhouse gas
Known for flamboyant ring attire and a raspy voice, this former pro baseball player became a wrestling legend whose ring name announced he was a "Macho Man." Who was he?
Dan Harmon spun his own time at a real junior college into this NBC ensemble sitcom set in fictional Greendale, Colorado, famous for its meta-humor and film-trope homages — which series?
This Japanese system of close combat, usable defensively or offensively, seeded a whole family of modern arts including judo, aikido, sambo, and the Brazilian style that bears its name — what is it?

Nicknamed 'the Monster of the Reiwa Era,' this pitcher set a Japanese high-school record with a 101-mph fastball before the Chiba Lotte Marines took him first overall and the Dodgers signed him in 2025 — who is he?

Roki Sasaki (born November 3, 2001), nicknamed "the Monster of the Reiwa Era" (Reiwa no Kaibutsu), is a Japanese professional baseball pitcher for the Los Angeles Dodgers of Major League Baseball (MLB).
Founded in 1856 to bankroll the building of Switzerland's railways, this Zurich institution became famous for ironclad client confidentiality before its collapse — which bank?
Credit Suisse: Defunct Swiss multinational bank
Often dubbed a 'guitarist's guitarist' and ranked among the top five ever by Rolling Stone, this Yardbirds alumnus later went instrumental, roaming from blues rock to jazz fusion — who was he?
Voted the world's number-one DJ in DJ Mag's poll five separate times, this French producer behind 'When Love Takes Over' has racked up more than 30 billion Spotify streams. Who is he?
Born into a literary London household — her sister was the painter Vanessa Bell — this English modernist helped pioneer the stream-of-consciousness narrative; who is she?
Virginia Woolf ("wolf"; ne Stephen; 25 January 1882 - 28 March 1941) was an English writer and one of the most influential 20th-century modernist authors.
Hebrew honors this Hungarian-born journalist and lawyer as 'Visionary of the State,' and Israel's Declaration of Independence names him the spiritual father of the Jewish state — who was he?
Theodor Herzl: Father of modern political Zionism (1860–1904)

This French civil engineer made his name building railway bridges like the Garabit Viaduct and later helped erect the Statue of Liberty, before retiring to study meteorology and aerodynamics — who was he?
Described in Genesis as the source of four rivers and also called the Terrestrial Paradise, this biblical place has been variously located at the head of the Persian Gulf or in Armenia — what is it?

The Garden of Eden, also called Garden of God or the (Terrestrial) Paradise, is the biblical paradise described in Genesis 2–3 and Ezekiel 28 and 31.
The location of Eden is described in the Book of Genesis as the source of four tributaries.
A close associate of Gandhi and a founder of Jamia Millia Islamia, this Berlin-educated educationist rose to become president of India, dying in office in 1969 — who was he?
Zakir Husain: President of India from 1967 to 1969
This French Romantic writer and historic-monuments inspector penned the novella that became Bizet's opera Carmen, and translated Pushkin and Gogol into French — who was he?
Prosper Mérimée: French writer, archaeologist and historian (1803–1870)
This German industrialist who organized the WWI war economy became foreign minister and negotiated the 1922 Treaty of Rapallo, only to be assassinated months later — who was he?
Walther Rathenau: German businessman and politician (1867–1922)
Born to a poor farming family in Haeju and revered in South Korea today, this independence activist led the Korean Provisional Government against Imperial Japan — who is he?
A Damascus-born philosopher who studied at the Sorbonne, this thinker is considered by many the principal founder of Ba'athist thought — who is he?
Michel Aflaq: Syrian philosopher, sociologist and Arab nationalist (1910–1989)
The first Canadian prime minister to hold a PhD, this Liberal racked up 21 years and 154 days in office across three non-consecutive terms — the longest tenure in the country's history; who is he?
William Lyon Mackenzie King: Canadian prime minister (1874–1950)
As Lincoln's Secretary of State this anti-slavery Republican steered Union diplomacy through the Civil War and negotiated the treaty to buy the Alaska Territory — who is he?
Once called 'perhaps the most famous singer alive' in much of Africa, this Senegalese star helped develop the mbalax genre and even served as his country's Minister of Tourism — who is he?
Youssou N'Dour: Senegalese politician and musician (born 1959)
This British Labour politician sat in the Commons for 47 of 51 years and later presided over the Stop the War Coalition — though for a stretch he was known as The Viscount Stansgate — who is he?
Tony Benn: British politician and activist (1925–2014)
It erupted in 1989 when Charles Taylor's NPFL invaded from Ivory Coast to topple President Samuel Doe, who was soon captured and executed by a splinter faction — which conflict is this?
First Liberian Civil War: 1989–1997 war in West Africa
Its name means 'river horse' in Ancient Greek, yet this semiaquatic sub-Saharan giant — the largest even-toed ungulate alive — is more closely tied to pigs than to horses; what is it?
Hippopotamus: Species of large semi-aquatic mammal
Nicknamed "Marvellous Merchiston," this 16th-century Scottish laird discovered logarithms and popularized the decimal point — who was this mathematical wizard?
This German chess player, mathematician and philosopher held the world title for 27 years — the longest reign ever — partly by a famously "psychological" approach to rattling opponents; who was he?
Despite the name, this gold-brown-eyed black-and-white bird of Australia isn't related to its Eurasian namesake at all — it's a butcherbird cousin in its own genus. What is it?
Australian magpie (Gymnorhina tibicen) is a black and white passerine bird native to Australia and southern New Guinea, and introduced to New Zealand, and the Fijian island of Taveuni.
This French mathematician and physicist wrote Institutions de Physique, a work translated into German and Italian that sparked heated 18th-century debate — who is she?
Émilie Le Tonnelier de Breteuil, marquise du Châtelet
Gabrielle-Emilie de Breteuil Marchioness du Chatelet
Gabrielle-Émilie Le Tonnelier de Breteuil du Châtelet
Émilie du Châtelet: French mathematician, physicist, and author (1706–1749)
Nicknamed 'Apung Dadong' and father of a future president, this ninth president of the Philippines held doctorates in both civil law and economics — who is he?
Diosdado Macapagal: President of the Philippines from 1961 to 1965
Honored with both the Padma Shri and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, this Indian actress appeared in over 85 films including Teesri Manzil and Love in Tokyo — who is she?
One of only 22 people to win an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony, this producer of No Country for Old Men and eight Wes Anderson films stepped back from his projects in 2021 — who is he?
Scott Rudin: American film, television, and theater producer
A matinee idol of 1910s silent Hollywood, this Japanese actor became the first performer of Asian descent to reach leading-man stardom and an early male sex symbol — who is he?

A production of Hamlet in Brighton turned this man from an artistic-but-untheatrical background into one of the trinity of English actors who, with Gielgud and Olivier, ruled the 20th-century stage — who is he?
Famous for playing strict, no-nonsense characters across the Carry On films, this English comedy actress first found fame on BBC radio alongside Tony Hancock and Tommy Handley — who is she?
Selznick's go-to director for literary adaptations like Little Women and David Copperfield, this filmmaker was famously replaced partway through Gone with the Wind — who is he?
George Cukor: American film director and producer (1899–1983)
Debuting in 1952 as the very first program of its kind anywhere in the world, this NBC morning show has been waking up America for over seven decades — what is it?
Today (American TV program) — Today (also called The today Show) is an American morning television show that airs weekdays from 7:00 a.m.
Warner Bros. lured this Hungarian to Hollywood in 1926 when he'd already directed 64 European films; he'd go on to direct 102 more, becoming one of the most prolific directors in history — who is it?
Michael Curtiz: Hungarian and American director (1886–1962)
A port since the Middle Ages, this city on the River Usk near the Severn Estuary saw the largest population growth of any Welsh unitary authority between 2011 and 2021 — which Welsh city is it?
Newport is a city and county borough in Wales, on the River Usk near its confluence with the Severn Estuary, approximately 12 mi (19 km) northeast of Cardiff.

Once called Pitic, this city in the center of Mexico's northwestern state of Sonora is its capital, largest city, and an automotive-industry hub repeatedly ranked among the country's best for quality of life — which is it?
Sitting in the northern part of Iran's Isfahan province, this is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world — what is it?

First identified from an 1856 fossil in a German valley, this group of archaic humans roamed Europe and Asia until vanishing around 40,000 years ago as modern humans arrived — who were they?
RIKEN has been trying to synthesize this hypothetical element 119 since 2018 — the lightest element not yet made and the first of the eighth period. What is it?
Ununennium: Theoretical chemical element with atomic number 119 (Uue)
This British-American theoretical physicist lent his name to a hypothetical genetically engineered 'tree' and a transform used in additive number theory — who was he?
Freeman Dyson: British theoretical physicist and mathematician (1923–2020)
Element 99 was first discovered in the radioactive debris of the very first hydrogen bomb explosion in 1952 — what synthetic actinide is it?
Einsteinium: Chemical element with atomic number 99 (Es)
Caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides and spread through food tainted with eggs, this infection most often hits children and is symptomless in over 85% of cases — what is it?
Ascariasis: Disease caused by the parasitic roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides
Dubbed the 'First Lady of American Theatre,' she was the first woman to win the EGOT and gives her name to an annual D.C. theatre awards — who was she?
A record-setting competitive swimmer turned MGM star, she swam alongside Tarzan actor Johnny Weissmuller in Billy Rose's Aquacade before Hollywood scouts found her — who was she?
Esther Williams: American swimmer and actress (1921–2013)
Nicknamed "the Golden Arm," this Baltimore Colts quarterback was a three-time MVP often called the prototype of the modern marquee passer. Whose 18-season legend is this?
Fellini called this 1954 Italian film "a complete catalogue of my entire mythological world"; it follows simple Gelsomina, sold to a brutish strongman who takes her on the road — what's the title?
La Strada: 1954 Italian road tragedy film directed by Federico Fellini
Satyajit Ray's 1955 directorial debut and the first film of The Apu Trilogy, it follows young Apu and his sister Durga through rural Bengali poverty — what's this landmark of Indian cinema?
Pather Panchali: 1955 film by Satyajit Ray
This American voice actor won the 2007 American Anime Award for Best Actor for voicing Edward Elric in Fullmetal Alchemist, part of a 100-plus title résumé — who is he?
England's northernmost city grew from a Roman site called Pons Aelius and took its name from a castle built in 1080 — once one of the world's great shipbuilding centres. Which city?
Newcastle upon Tyne: City in England
Once capital of the Bagratuni Armenian kingdom, this ruined medieval city in Turkey was nicknamed the "City of 1,001 Churches." What is it?
Nicknamed the "Gateway of Northeast India," this West Bengal city sits in the Himalayan foothills near the borders of Nepal, Bangladesh, and Bhutan. What is it?
Siliguri: City in West Bengal, India
Sitting at 1,650 metres in the eastern Himalayas, this capital became a Buddhist pilgrimage hub after the 1840 Enchey Monastery. Which Indian city is it?
Gangtok: Capital city of Sikkim, India
Sitting near the geographic center of its state, this New England city is nicknamed the "Heart of the Commonwealth" and even uses a heart as its official symbol. Which city is it?
Worcester, Massachusetts (locally) is a city in the U.S.

Founded during the 1849 Gold Rush by Charles Maria Weber, this Central Valley city sits on a river delta so sprawling it's practically cut off from its neighbors like Sacramento and the Bay Area. What is it?
Stockton is a city in and the county seat of San Joaquin County, California, United States.
Famed for its cuisine, limestone caves and conserved British colonial architecture, this Malaysian city on the Kinta River is the capital of Perak — what is it?
Ipoh: State capital city in Perak, Malaysia
This British player won three straight Wimbledon titles in the 1930s and was the only British man to complete a Career Grand Slam — until Andy Murray. Who was he?
Nicknamed 'Mr. Basketball,' this 6-foot-10 Minneapolis Lakers pioneer wore thick round spectacles and redefined the game with an ambidextrous hook shot — who was he?
Recorded after a bout of writer's block, the Clash's 1979 double album blended punk with reggae, ska, and rockabilly. What's its title?
London Calling: 1979 studio album by the Clash
The son of a sharecropper, this Detroit bluesman built a driving-rhythm boogie style and recorded "Boogie Chillen'" in 1948. Who was he?
John Lee Hooker: American blues musician (1912 or 1917–2001)
South African Solomon Linda's 1939 song "Mbube" became a worldwide hit after the Tokens added English lyrics in 1961. By what name is it best known today?
The Lion Sleeps Tonight: 1939 song by Solomon Linda and the Evening Birds
Written by Mick Jagger, this acclaimed Rolling Stones track opens their 1968 album Beggars Banquet. What's its title?
Sympathy for the Devil: 1968 song by the Rolling Stones
Built on a signature five-accent 'hambone' beat and African rhythms, this guitarist's sound shaped Buddy Holly, the Beatles and the Stones during the leap from blues to rock and roll — who was he?
Bo Diddley: American guitarist and singer (1928–2008)
This American soprano has won five of her 18 Grammy nominations and collected honors from the Légion d'Honneur to a 2023 Kennedy Center tribute — who is she?
Renée Fleming (born February 14, 1959) is an American soprano and actress, known for performances in opera, concerts, recordings, theater, film, and at major public occasions.
A pioneer of breakbeat DJing, this artist turned his street gang, the Black Spades, into the Universal Zulu Nation to spread hip-hop culture worldwide — who is he?
Afrika Bambaataa: American DJ, rapper and producer (1957–2026)

Originally titled 'Puck Man' in Japan, this 1980 Namco maze game was designed by Toru Iwatani specifically to appeal to women — and its dot-munching hero turns the tables with Power Pellets. What's the game?

Inspired by the Japanese film Battle Royale and grown from Brendan Greene's earlier mods, this 2017 game drops up to a hundred parachuting players onto a shrinking island to scavenge and survive — what is it?
In this 1997 PlayStation epic, mercenary Cloud Strife joins an eco-terrorist cell to stop a megacorporation from draining the planet's life essence for energy — which game?
This Indian-Canadian poet rose to fame on Instagram, then went viral after the platform deleted her photos of menstrual blood stains taken for a university course. Who is she?
Set on the icy planet Gethen, this 1969 novel followed an envoy named Genly Ai and cemented Ursula K. Le Guin's status as a major science fiction author. What's its title?
The Left Hand of Darkness: 1969 science fiction novel by Ursula K. Le Guin
As of 2024, only one writer has won a Hugo and a Nebula in two consecutive years — for a novel and its sequel about gifted children making high-stakes choices. Who is it?
Orson Scott Card: American science fiction novelist (born 1951)
The New York Times called this Chilean novelist "the most significant Latin American literary voice of his generation," honoring his epic 2666 after his death. Who was he?
This English novelist courted scandal with a story titled "Why I Want to Fuck Ronald Reagan" and a novel about car-crash fetishists called Crash. Who is he?
When Blizzard first showed this real-time strategy game at E3 in 1996, critics panned it as a Warcraft II clone — so the team overhauled it entirely before its acclaimed 1998 release. Which game?
StarCraft (video game) — StarCraft is a real-time strategy video game developed and published by Blizzard Entertainment for Microsoft Windows.
The last of the three Milesian thinkers regarded as the West's first philosophers, he taught that air is the arche, the basic element of everything. Who was he?
Anaximenes of Miletus: Ancient Greek philosopher (c. 586 – c. 526 BC)
This medieval English friar earned the title Doctor Mirabilis and was later remembered as a wizard famed for a story about a mechanical brazen head. Who was he?
Roger Bacon: English polymath, philosopher and friar (c.1219/20–c.1292)
This American game designer founded the Gen Con convention, launched The Dragon magazine, and co-created a pioneering tabletop role-playing game with Dave Arneson. Who was he?
Gary Gygax: American game designer and author (1938–2008)
A French Jesuit priest and paleontologist, he helped uncover the Peking Man fossils while weaving evolution together with Christian mysticism — sometimes to charges of pseudoscience. Who was he?
Pierre Teilhard de Chardin: French philosopher and Jesuit priest (1881–1955)
One of only four writers ever to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction more than once, this American novelist spun his most famous work into a four-book 'Rabbit' series — who is he?
The leading figure of Britain's 1960s satire boom, this English comedian co-created the revue 'Beyond the Fringe' with Alan Bennett, Jonathan Miller and Dudley Moore — who was he?
Peter Cook: British comedian, actor, satirist (1937–1995)
Chief of the German General Staff from 1933 to 1938, he grew disillusioned and became a main conspirator of the 20 July plot to kill Hitler — which general was he?
Han dynasty Chinese practiced it during New Year celebrations and ancient Egyptian children were depicted leaping over vines — what playground equipment, also a competitive sport, is this?
A skipping rope (or jump rope) is equipment used in sport and play that involves rhythmically jumping over a rope swung underfoot and overhead.
George Gershwin's English-language opera made the daring 1935 choice to cast classically trained African-American singers, with a libretto from DuBose and Ira — what work is it?
Porgy and Bess ( PORG-ee) is an English-language opera by American composer George Gershwin, with a libretto written by author DuBose Heyward and lyricist Ira Gershwin.
Astonishingly prolific with over 225 novels, this American romance author also writes sci-fi-tinged police procedurals under the pen name J. D. Robb — who is she?
A founder of the NAACP, this investigative journalist documented lynching across the 1890s in pamphlets like 'Southern Horrors' and 'The Red Record' — who was she?
Ida B. Wells: American journalist and civil rights activist (1862–1931)
At 2,962 metres, this Wetterstein peak is Germany's highest mountain, straddling the Austrian border and hosting the country's two largest glaciers on its flanks — what is it?
Zugspitze: Highest peak of the Wetterstein Mountains (Eastern Alps)
A daughter of Peter the Great, she ruled from 1741 to 1762 and stayed beloved partly for a remarkable vow: not to execute a single person during her reign — which empress?
Fought on and off from 1927 to 1949 between a Kuomintang-led government and a Communist Party that eventually seized the mainland, which long conflict is this?
The Chinese Civil War was fought between the Kuomintang - led government of the Republic of China and the forces of the Chinese Communist Party.

Founded in France in 1899, this automaker has built not just cars and vans but trucks, tractors, tanks, buses, and even aircraft engines, and now anchors an alliance with Nissan and Mitsubishi — which company?
Fill in the blank: “____ was fought from 21 February to 18 December 1916 on the Western Front in France.”
Battle of Verdun was fought from 21 February to 18 December 1916 on the Western Front in France.
It usually causes no symptoms at all, yet this persistently elevated arterial pressure is a leading cause of stroke, heart failure and premature death worldwide — what's the medical name for it?
Hypertension: Long-term high blood pressure in the arteries

A subdiscipline of metaphysics, this philosophical study of being asks what reality's most general features are, sorting things into particulars like Socrates and universals like the color green — what is it?

Coming on slowly it brings vague fatigue and breathlessness; arriving suddenly it can cause confusion and fainting — and only when it's severe does a person look pale — which blood disorder reduces the blood's oxygen-carrying ability?
Anemia: Reduced ability of blood to carry oxygen
NATO calls it 'Frogfoot' but its Soviet designers named it after the rook; this subsonic twin-engine jet first flew in 1975 to give close air support to ground forces — which aircraft?
Sukhoi Su-25: Soviet attack aircraft introduced 1978
Sold as Seroquel and prescribed for schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, this atypical antipsychotic is also widely (and questionably) used as a sleep aid for its tranquillizing effect — which drug?
Fill in the blank: “____ is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7.”
Citric acid is an organic compound with the formula C6H8O7.
Named for a Native American war chief, this four-blade, twin-engine utility helicopter beat the Boeing Vertol YUH-61 in a 1976 fly-off to replace the Army's UH-1 Iroquois — what is it?
The Sikorsky UH-60 Black Hawk is a four-blade, twin-engine, medium-lift military utility helicopter manufactured by Sikorsky Aircraft.

Often making people tall and thin with long fingers and very flexible joints, this connective-tissue disorder carries serious risks to the heart and aorta — caused by a mutation in the FBN1 fibrillin gene — which condition?
Marfan syndrome: Genetic disorder involving connective tissue

The most widely cultivated species of its genus, this bulb vegetable counts garlic, leeks and chives among its close relatives, and the shallot was reclassified as merely a variety of it in 2011 — what is it?
From Greek for 'arrangement' and 'method', this science names and classifies organisms into ranked groups — domain, kingdom, phylum, and on down to species — what is the field?
Larry David plays a cranky, fictionalized version of himself across 12 seasons of HBO improv-driven comedy, with celebrity guests often appearing as themselves — which series is it?
Curb Your Enthusiasm: American television sitcom (2000–2024)
Born in 1974, this comedian moved to LA at 21 chasing stand-up, joined Saturday Night Live in 1998 and co-anchored Weekend Update before becoming an NBC late-night host — who is he?
Jimmy Fallon: American comedian and television host (born 1974)
Dubbed a 'comedian's comedian' and crowned by Rolling Stone the 'heavyweight champ of rage-fueled humor,' this stand-up tackles social issues with sharp confrontational wit — who is he?
Its name means 'Mount Charles,' and though only about 3,500 people live in this ward of Monaco, its famous casino draws far more — which place?
Monte Carlo: Quarter and ward of Monaco
This volcanic archipelago straddling the equator belongs to Ecuador and teems with endemic species that Charles Darwin studied in the 1830s, inspiring his theory of natural selection — what is it?
Carved from limestone bedrock with a human head on a lion's body, this east-facing monument — likely from the reign of Khufu or Khafre — is Egypt's oldest known monumental sculpture — what is it?
The Great Sphinx of Giza is a limestone statue of a reclining sphinx, a mythical creature with the head of a human and the body of a lion.

Rooted in military obstacle-course training and martial arts, this self-led practice has you vault, climb, and roll through urban spaces, seeing buildings as things to flow over and under — what is it?
After winning the Heisman and a national title at LSU, this quarterback went first overall in 2020 and ended Cincinnati's longest-in-sports playoff drought on the way to a Super Bowl — who is he?
Joe Burrow (born December 10, 1996) is an American professional football quarterback for the Cincinnati Bengals of the National Football League (NFL).
A lightly recruited prospect who started at a junior college before Wyoming, this quarterback went seventh overall in 2018 and has since piloted Buffalo to five straight division titles — who is he?
Josh Allen (born May 21, 1996) is an American professional football quarterback for the Buffalo Bills of the National Football League (NFL).
His six-volume "A History of Australia" earned him the title of his country's most famous historian — and plenty of fire from conservative critics. Who wrote it?

Manning Clark (3 March 1915 - 23 May 1991) was an Australian historian and the author of the best-known general history of Australia, his six-volume A History of Australia, published between 1962 and 1987.
The 2014 lead single from To Pimp a Butterfly, it re-recorded the Isley Brothers' 'That Lady' with Ronald Isley himself and won Best Rap Performance and Best Rap Song — which Kendrick Lamar track?
I (Kendrick Lamar song) — I (stylized in lowercase or as "") is a song by American rapper Kendrick Lamar.
This Greek writer from Halicarnassus chronicled the Greco-Persian Wars in his 'Histories,' earning from Cicero the lasting title 'Father of History' — who is he?
Herodotus: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC)
Nicknamed "the Captain," this shortstop spent all 20 of his big-league seasons with one team and entered the Hall of Fame on 396 of 397 votes — who is he?
Derek Jeter (born June 26, 1974), nicknamed "the Captain", is an American former professional baseball player, businessman, and baseball executive.
Recognizable by her pageboy bob and dark sunglasses, this editor-in-chief ran Vogue from 1988 to 2025 and has chaired the Met Gala since the 1990s — who is she?
Anna Wintour: British and American media executive (born 1949)
He founded the anti-trafficking group Operation Underground Railroad, and his exploits inspired the 2023 film Sound of Freedom — though he was later ousted amid misconduct accusations — who is he?
Tim Ballard: Founder and former CEO of Operation Underground Railroad

As royal midwife to Marie de Medici, she delivered the future Louis XIII and five more royal siblings, and became France's first woman to publish a medical text — who was this largely self-taught pioneer?
Louise (Bourgeois) Boursier was royal midwife at the court of King Henry IV of France and the first female writer in that country to publish a medical text.
Earning the title "Supreme Combatant" for ending France's 75-year protectorate, this Paris-trained lawyer became the first president of an independent North African nation in 1957 — who is he?
Habib Bourguiba: President of Tunisia from 1957 to 1987
A glider pilot who flew 705 combat missions and survived being shot down four times, this Luftwaffe ace racked up 104 aerial victories, all against the Western Allies — who is he?
Adolf Galland: German World War II flying ace and general
A lawyer, poet and writer, he stepped up from vice president to become Brazil's 37th president in 2016 after the Senate voted to remove Dilma Rousseff from office — who is he?
Michel Temer: President of Brazil from 2016 to 2019

Sparked in 1991 when the Revolutionary United Front — backed by Liberia's Charles Taylor — moved to topple the Momoh government, this nearly 11-year conflict displaced some 2.5 million people. Which war is it?
Sierra Leone Civil War: 1991–2002 war in West Africa
A queen of Halicarnassus who personally commanded warships for Xerxes at Artemisium and Salamis, she comes down to us mainly through the writings of Herodotus — who is she?
Artemisia I of Caria: Ancient Greek queen of the 5th century BC
Born in Shawinigan Falls, Quebec, this Liberal first entered the Commons in 1963 and served under Pearson and Trudeau before becoming Canada's 20th prime minister in 1993 — who is he?
Jean Chrétien: Prime Minister of Canada from 1993 to 2003
After a 1969 coup, this army commander became Somalia's third president and reconstituted the country as a one-party Marxist-Leninist state — who is he?
Siad Barre: President of Somalia from 1969 to 1991

Nicknamed "the Quarrelsome," this short-reigning French king emancipated serfs willing to buy their freedom and readmitted Jews to the kingdom — and his first wife was famously caught up in the Tour de Nesle scandal. Who was he?
Louis X, known as the Quarrelsome, was King of France from 1314 and King of Navarre (as Louis I) from 1305 until his death.
An English archaeologist and traveller who mapped the Middle East, she became so trusted by British officials that she helped shape borders at the 1921 Cairo Conference. Who was she?
Gertrude Bell: English traveller and writer

Drawing on anthropology, paleontology and genetics, this field studies how our species gradually gained bipedalism, dexterity and complex language — and shows our past was weblike, with interbreeding among archaic humans — what is the subject?
Human evolution: Homo sapiens is a distinct species of the hominid family of primates, which includes all the great apes.

This Harvard political scientist coordinated security planning for Jimmy Carter's National Security Council, but he's best remembered for a 1993 theory arguing future wars would be fought between cultures rather than countries — who was he?
Samuel P. Huntington: American political scientist and academic (1927–2008)
This Austrian-School economist founded anarcho-capitalism and called the state "the organization of robbery systematized and writ large" — which libertarian theoretician?
This American experimental physicist won the 1968 Nobel Prize for discovering resonance states using the hydrogen bubble chamber — who was he?
Luis Walter Alvarez: American physicist, inventor and professor (1911–1988)
This synthetic element 113 was claimed by both a Russian-American team at Dubna and, in 2004, a Japanese team at Riken. What's its name?
Nihonium: Chemical element with atomic number 113 (Nh)
An Oscar winner and six-time Emmy recipient, he's best remembered as sewer worker Ed Norton on The Honeymooners — which actor?
Art Carney: American actor and comedian (1918–2003)

A nineteen-year-old Ziegfeld Follies performer who caught the eye of newspaper tycoon William Randolph Hearst, she became his mistress and the film star whose career he financed and promoted — who is she?
Born in British India, this Irish comic was the co-creator and main writer of the radio classic The Goon Show — playing Eccles and Minnie Bannister — and the last surviving Goon. Who is he?
Spike Milligan: Irish comedian and writer (1918–2002)
Canada's southernmost major city sits on the south bank of the Detroit River, directly across from a famous American metropolis — what is it?
Windsor is a city in southwestern Ontario, Canada.
Two ancient Greek sites sit within the modern Turkish city of İzmir, one of them linked to the founding hand of Alexander the Great — by what name was this Aegean port known before 1930?
Smyrna: Ancient Greek city, currently İzmir, Turkey
Founded in 1856 as the village of Lancaster on a stretch of wild salt marshes, this state capital was renamed for a U.S. president and became the seat of government in 1869 — which city?
Lincoln, Nebraska is the capital city of the U.S.
The first major singles champion born in Asia, this trailblazer won the 2011 French Open and reached a career-high world No. 2. Who is she?
Named after the singer's age during production, this 2011 album of heartbreak and forgiveness leaned into country and Southern blues she discovered while touring America — which record is it?
21 (Adele album) — 21 is the second studio album by the English singer-songwriter Adele.
Formed in San Francisco in 1966, this funk-and-soul outfit was the first major American rock group with a racially integrated, mixed-gender lineup — which band?
Sly and the Family Stone: American funk and soul band
Known as the "Barefoot Diva" for performing without shoes, this Cape Verdean Grammy winner sang morna in her native Creole and even influenced Madonna — who is she?
Almost entirely written and produced by its star after her band the Fugees went on hiatus, this 1998 neo-soul concept album about love features Santana, Mary J. Blige and D'Angelo — what is it?
The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill is the debut solo studio album by the American rapper and singer-songwriter Lauryn Hill.
She won the 1950 Best Actress Oscar reprising her stage role as Billie Dawn in Born Yesterday, and later took a Tony for the musical Bells Are Ringing — who is this actress?
This Danish-French actress was an early muse of New Wave director Jean-Luc Godard — her first husband — starring in A Woman Is a Woman, Band of Outsiders and Alphaville. Who is she?
Anna Karina: Danish and French actress (1940–2019)
Inspired by the teachings of guru Meher Baba, Pete Townshend wrote this 1969 double album — an early rock opera following a fictional boy's rise to messianic figure. Which album?
Tommy (The Who album) — Tommy is the fourth studio album by the English rock band the Who, released on 19 May 1969.

He conducted a rotating crew called the Magic Band, cut 13 albums of blues-meets-free-jazz weirdness, and ran his musicians with dictatorial control while inventing myths about his own life — which avant-garde frontman?
Nominated for eighteen Academy Awards (winning for The Omen), this composer scored five Star Trek films and three Rambos across nearly 50 years. Who was he?
This Estonian composer invented a chant-inspired technique he called tintinnabuli, and for years has ranked as the most performed living composer in the world. Who is he?

A Roman senator and polymath of the early Middle Ages, he was central to translating the Greek classics into Latin and is honored alongside Cassiodorus as a leading 6th-century Christian scholar — who was he?
Boethius: 6th-century Roman senator and philosopher (480–524 AD)

Born Tomáš Sträussler and brought out of Czechoslovakia as a Jewish child refugee, this knighted playwright became one of his generation's most performed dramatists, compared to Shakespeare and Shaw — who was he?

His gritty 1993 debut about working-class Scottish life became a cult classic in both print and on film, and later ranked 7th in a poll of the best Scottish novels ever — which Scottish novelist wrote it?
Nicknamed the "Gandhi of grain" for her anti-GMO activism, this Delhi-based ecofeminist and food-sovereignty advocate has written more than 20 books — who is she?
Vandana Shiva: Indian philosopher, scientist and environmentalist
Its author died in 1969, but his mother and the writer Walker Percy got this picaresque novel published in 1980 — and it won a posthumous Pulitzer. Which book is it?
A Confederacy of Dunces: 1980 novel by John Kennedy Toole

Decorated for bravery on the Western Front, this English war poet then made a lone written protest against the war in 1917 — and was packed off to Craiglockhart hospital, where he befriended Wilfred Owen. Who was he?
Siegfried Sassoon: English war poet and writer (1886–1967)

Between 1908 and 1912, his Cubist canvases were so close to Picasso's that they were indistinguishable for years — yet his quiet temperament left him overshadowed. Which French painter was Picasso's co-pilot in Cubism?
Georges Braque: French painter and sculptor (1882–1963)
A writer, folklorist and anthropologist who researched Hoodoo and Caribbean Vodou, she's best remembered for the 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God — who is she?
Zora Neale Hurston: American author, anthropologist, filmmaker (1891–1960)
This New Testament book names no author — though most ancient Greek manuscripts file it among Paul's letters, modern scholarship mostly rejects Pauline authorship. Which text is it?
Epistle to the Hebrews: Book of the New Testament
Before becoming Colombia's 32nd president in 2002, this leader of the right-wing Democratic Center party served as mayor of Medellín, then governor of Antioquia — who is he?
Álvaro Uribe: President of Colombia from 2002 to 2010

Robert Heinlein's 1961 novel follows Valentine Michael Smith, a human born on Mars and raised by Martians who comes to transform Earth's culture — and its title is lifted straight from the Book of Exodus. Which novel?
Stranger in a Strange Land: 1961 science fiction novel by Robert A. Heinlein
A student of Parmenides, this pre-Socratic from southern Italy defended monism by inventing a famous series of paradoxes meant to prove that space, time and motion are impossible — who is he?
Zeno of Elea: Greek philosopher (c. 495 – c. 430 BC)
A Greek-Irish journalist who worked in Cincinnati and New Orleans before moving to Japan, becoming a citizen, and introducing the West to Japanese ghost stories like Kwaidan — who is this writer?
Plato credits this pre-Socratic with inventing the role of the professional sophist, and he stirred ancient controversy declaring that "Man is the measure of all things" — who is he?

In 1874 this French painter abandoned the esteemed Paris Salon to join the "rejected" group exhibiting alongside Cézanne, Degas, Monet and Renoir at their very first show — making her one of the founding Impressionists. Who is she?

Avenging the slain Husayn at Karbala, this pro-Alid revolutionary led a rebellion from Kufa against the Umayyads in 685 and ruled most of Iraq for eighteen months during the Second Fitna — who was he?

His orchestral and string arrangements, piano playing, and taste for novel recording tricks shaped every original Beatles album — earning this English producer the nickname 'the fifth Beatle.' Who is it?
After years of royal suspicion, this 17th-century Frenchman finally won a seat in the Académie Française, and his collection of Fables became the model fabulists across Europe would copy. Who was he?
Jean de La Fontaine (8 July 1621 - 13 April 1695) was a French fabulist and one of the most widely read French poets of the 17th century.
Born in the late 19th century and often hurled as an insult, this contested political stance pits the so-called 'common people' against a perceived elite — what is it?
Populism: Political ideology emphasising the "common people"

Fluent in Cherokee, Choctaw, and several other Native languages, this man escaped slavery and went on to rack up over 3,000 arrests as one of the first Black deputy U.S. Marshals west of the Mississippi — who was he?
Rising through party posts in Wenzhou, Zhejiang and Jiangsu, this politician became the premier of China and the second-ranking member of the Politburo Standing Committee — who is he?
Li Qiang: Premier of China since 2023
A Hindu monk who became Uttar Pradesh's longest-serving and first two-term chief minister, he won five straight terms from Gorakhpur after entering parliament at just 26 — who is he?
Yogi Adityanath: Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh since 2017

During the 1972 Summer Olympics, eight Black September militants infiltrated the Olympic Village and seized members of the Israeli team, who all died in a failed rescue — what is this attack known as?
Munich massacre: 1972 Summer Olympics terrorist attack

Commissioned into a light horse unit his own father raised, he became the first Australian to reach lieutenant general and led the Desert Mounted Corps to one of military history's fastest pursuits. Who was this WWI commander?

Harry Chauvel (16 April 1865 - 4 March 1945) was a senior officer of the Australian Imperial Force who fought at Gallipoli and during the Sinai and Palestine Campaign in the Middle Eastern theatre of the First World War.
Painlessly swollen lymph nodes, drenching night sweats, and unexplained weight loss point to this family of white-blood-cell cancers, split mainly into Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin types — what is it?
Lymphoma: Hematologic cancer that affects lymphocytes

Marketed as Wellbutrin, this atypical antidepressant doubles as a stop-smoking aid and stands out for not causing sexual dysfunction or weight gain — what is this norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor?
Bupropion: Medication mainly used for depression and smoking cessation
Built to replace the AH-1 Cobra, this twin-turboshaft attack helicopter packs a nose-mounted 30 mm chain gun and Hellfire missiles, with a two-person tandem cockpit — which aircraft is it?
Boeing AH-64 Apache: U.S. attack helicopter
This chronic autoimmune disorder causes patches of skin to lose their pigment, and in antiquity it was so misunderstood that it was often confused with leprosy — what is it?
Vitiligo: Skin condition where patches lose pigment
Sold as Voltaren and taken by mouth, suppository, injection, skin gel, or even eye drops, this NSAID eases pain and inflammation like gout for up to eight hours a dose — what is it?
Spanning five films and two TV series and grossing over $2.5 billion, this Legendary-produced shared universe pits Godzilla against King Kong — what's it called?
An NPC Mr. California winner who became a YouTube star, this larger-than-life bodybuilder was famous for his over-the-top personality and unusual candor about steroid use — who was he?
Rich Piana: American bodybuilder and internet personality (1970–2017)
Co-created by Donald Glover, this dark-comedy miniseries follows Dre, whose obsession with a pop star sends her down a sinister path — and earned Dominique Fishback an Emmy nod. What's the show?
Swarm (TV series) — Swarm is an American satirical dark comedy television miniseries created by Janine Nabers and Donald Glover.
Fill in the blank: “____ is an American biographical crime drama television miniseries directed by Andrs Baiz and produced by Eric Newman and Sofa Vergara.”
Griselda (miniseries) — Griselda is an American biographical crime drama television miniseries directed by Andrs Baiz and produced by Eric Newman and Sofa Vergara.
The only Hawaii-born player ever to win the Heisman Trophy, this quarterback went second overall in the 2015 draft to Tennessee before stints with the Raiders and Falcons — who is he?

Born Rakhshandeh in 1907, this celebrated Iranian wrote in Persian and died young in 1941 — which 20th-century poet is it?

A leading figure of the Frankfurt School who earned his PhD under Martin Heidegger, this philosopher argued that capitalism, technology, and popular culture had become new forms of social control — who is he?
Herbert Marcuse: German–American philosopher, sociologist, and political theorist (1898–1979)
This Czech writer's 1920 play 'R.U.R.' gave the world the word 'robot,' yet despite seven Nobel nominations he never won the prize — who is he?
Karel Čapek: Czech science fiction writer and playwright (1890–1938)

Robert E. Howard: American pulp fiction writer (1906–1936)

Rejected twice before being published posthumously in 1958, this Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa novel of Sicilian life during the Risorgimento went on to become the best-selling novel in Italian history — which book is it?
The Leopard: 1958 novel by Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa
This American writer, primarily known for horror and mystery, packed six novels, two memoirs, and over 200 short stories into a career of just two decades — who is she?
Shirley Jackson: American novelist, short-story writer (1916–1965)
This New York-born poet, once U.S. Poet Laureate, won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Literature for a voice the judges said 'makes individual existence universal' — who was she?
Louise Glück (GLIK; April 22, 1943 - October 13, 2023) was an American poet and essayist.
This American writer dreamed up John Carter of Mars and a jungle hero who starred in twenty-four of his books and became a lasting cultural icon — who was he?
Blurring high and low art, this Japanese contemporary artist designed album covers for Kanye West's Graduation and Kids See Ghosts — who is he?

Writing under a pen name in 19th-century Germany, this Hegel-attending philosopher of self-consciousness and egoism is seen as a forerunner of nihilism, existentialism, and individualist anarchism — who was he?
This former First Lady of the Philippines was famous for an "edifice complex" of grandiose buildings raised in impossibly short order with public funds — who is she?
Imelda Marcos: First Lady of the Philippines from 1965 to 1986
Founder of Black Hole Recordings, this Dutch DJ was voted "The Greatest DJ of All Time" by Mix magazine and is widely called the "Godfather of EDM" — who is he?
Tiësto: Dutch DJ and record producer (born 1969)

Shaped by liberal ideas and the non-aggression principle, this political philosophy prizes liberty and personal sovereignty above all, holding you may live as you choose so long as you don't force or defraud others — what is it?
Libertarianism: Political philosophy based on liberty
She graduated cum laude in economics from Penn, converted to Judaism before marrying Jared Kushner, and later served as an advisor in her father's first administration — who is she?

He swapped political-science studies at Amherst for the bobsleigh track, competing in five Winter Olympics before taking a throne in 2005 and becoming an outspoken environmentalist — which reigning royal is this?

Albert II (Albert Alexandre Louis Pierre Grimaldi; born 14 March 1958) is Prince of Monaco, reigning since 2005.
Born at the Prince's Palace of Monaco, Albert is the second child and only son of Prince Rainier III and Princess Grace.
The Soviet probe Luna 2 got there first in 1959, but it took a crewed Apollo mission a decade later to pull off the human version — what milestone are we describing?
A Moon landing or lunar landing is the arrival of a crewed or robotic spacecraft on the Moon.

Geological history of oxygen is the most abundant element in Earth's crust, due to its high reactivity it mostly exists in compound (oxide) forms such as water, carbon dioxide, iron oxides and silicates.
Twice captured by pirates and sold into slavery as a boy, he rose to lead the Dutch navy through the Eighty Years' War and the First Anglo-Dutch War — which admiral?

Maarten Harpertszoon Tromp, also known as Maarten van Tromp, was an army general and admiral in the Dutch navy during much of the Eighty Years' War and throughout the First Anglo-Dutch War.
Born in Brielle, the son of a ship's captain, Tromp spent much of his childhood at sea, during which time he was twice captured by pirates and sold into slavery.

Produced in the hypothalamus and nicknamed for its role in love and social bonding, this peptide hormone also doubles as a pharmaceutical that speeds up childbirth by triggering uterine contractions — what is it?
Whether a milk board's 'Got Milk?' campaign or a city pitching itself as a tourist destination, this discipline boils down to acquiring, satisfying, and retaining customers — what is it?
Marketing: Study and process of exploring, creating, and delivering value to customers
A pale-blue gas with a chlorine-like pungent odour, this unstable three-atom cousin of oxygen forms by UV light and electrical discharges and shields us high in the stratosphere — what is it?

Often tangled up with mood, temperament, and creativity, these neurophysiological states carry a degree of pleasure or displeasure — yet scientists still can't agree on a single definition. What are they?
Affecting roughly 10% of women of reproductive age — nearly 200 million worldwide — this disease occurs when tissue like the uterine lining grows on the ovaries, bowel, or elsewhere. What is it?
Its very name comes from the Arabic for 'the kohl,' and chemically it's any compound carrying a hydroxyl group on a saturated carbon — a family that ranges from methanol to cholesterol. What is it?
Alcohol (chemistry): Organic compound with at least one hydroxyl (–OH) group
Their 'lady' actually refers to the Virgin Mary, and their cheerful red-and-black warning colours tell predators they taste terrible — what is this 6,000-species family of small beetles?
At just 37 this American biologist won a 1975 Nobel for discovering reverse transcriptase, later running Caltech and founding the Whitehead Institute — who is he?
David Baltimore: American biologist and Nobel laureate (1938–2025)
This Norwegian shared the very first Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, and we owe him the words 'econometrics,' 'microeconomics,' and 'macroeconomics' — who was he?
Ragnar Frisch: Norwegian economist and Nobel Laureate (1895–1973)

An ungoverned Chinese enclave inside British Hong Kong, by 1987 this 2.6-hectare warren packed in some 33,000 people, making it one of the densest places on Earth before it was demolished in the 1990s — what was it?
Kowloon Walled City: Former slum in Hong Kong
Stretching 2,448 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica, this 1926 highway carried Dust Bowl migrants west before the Interstate system left it behind — what is it?
U.S. Route 66: Former US Highway between Chicago and Santa Monica
Nicknamed 'GGG' or 'Triple G,' this Kazakhstani boxer reigned as a two-time unified middleweight champion before retiring in 2022 — who is he?
Gennady Golovkin (also spelled Gennadiy; born 8 April 1982), often known by his nickname "GGG" or "Triple G", is a Kazakhstani former professional boxer who competed from 2006 to 2022.
This Italian manager won back-to-back Coppa Italia titles at Roma and a Serie A crown at Napoli before taking charge of the national team in 2023 — who is he?
An 11-time All-Star and three-time AL MVP, this Angels outfielder even captained Team USA at the 2023 World Baseball Classic and is hailed as the best of his generation — who is he?
Mike Trout (born August 7, 1991) is an American professional baseball outfielder for the Los Angeles Angels of Major League Baseball (MLB).

Nicknamed 'Cholo,' this Argentine has managed Atlético Madrid since 2011 — making him one of the longest-serving bosses in Europe — after a playing career across Argentina, Italy, and Spain. Who is he?
He embodied 'everything in punk that was dark, decadent and nihilistic,' served as the Sex Pistols' second bassist, and died at just 21 in 1979 — under what stage name is this Englishman known?
Nicknamed the 'Sorcerer of the Guitar,' this Congolese rumba master led TPOK Jazz for over 20 years — making it the most popular African band of its time. Who was he?
François Luambo Makiadi Lokanga La Djo Péné
Franco Luambo: Congolese musician and cultural revolutionary (1938–1989)

A horseman of the Quraysh's Banu Makhzum clan, he first fought against Muhammad before converting and leading Muslim armies through the Ridda Wars and the conquest of Byzantine Syria — who was this 7th-century commander?
Khalid ibn al-Walid (died 642) was a 7th-century Arab military commander.
Hans Christian Andersen's 1837 tale follows a young sea princess willing to trade her ocean life for a human soul — and scholars still debate why he gave it such a tragic ending. Which story is it?
The Little Mermaid: 1837 fairy tale by Hans Christian Andersen
This Danish realist shared the 1917 Nobel Prize for Literature for his "authentic descriptions of present-day life in Denmark" — who was he?
Henrik Pontoppidan: Danish writer, Nobel Laureate

Harold Harefoot: King of England from 1037 to 1040

Emmerson Mnangagwa: President of Zimbabwe since 2017

Martti Ahtisaari: Finnish politician and diplomat, President of Finland (1937–2023)

Albrecht von Wallenstein: Bohemian military leader and statesman (1583–1634)

Peng Dehuai: Chinese politician and general (1898–1974)

Nguyễn Văn Thiệu: President of South Vietnam from 1967 to 1975

Omar Bongo: President of Gabon from 1967 to 2009

Khosrow II: Emperor of the Sasanian Empire from 590 to 628

John C. Calhoun: Vice President of the United States from 1825 to 1832
The largest wild member of the dog family, it can still breed fertile hybrids with coyotes and jackals, and counts the domestic dog and dingo among its many subspecies — what animal is it?

Whale shark: Largest living species of fish

Muhammad Yunus: Bangladeshi economist and statesman (born 1940)

Giardiasis: Parasitic disease that results in diarrhea
This English actor broke through in the Apple TV+ series 'See' before landing roles in 'Midsommar,' 'Gran Turismo,' and 'Saltburn' — who is he?
This American actress created and starred in the web series The Guild, loosely based on her own life as a gamer, and later hosted Critical Role — who is she?
Before winning seven Emmys as creator and head writer of an HBO mob drama that ran from 1999 to 2007, this writer cut his teeth on The Rockford Files and Northern Exposure — who is he?
David Chase: American writer, director and producer (born 1945)
Astonishingly prolific with over 100 films across every genre, this Japanese director is best known for horror like Audition and Ichi the Killer plus samurai epic 13 Assassins — who is he?
This American actress, famed for playing women based on true stories, traveled to Hollywood in 1937 to audition for Scarlett O'Hara and later earned five Best Actress nominations — who is she?

Frankenstein (1931 film) — Frankenstein is a 1931 American pre-Code horror film directed by James Whale and produced by Carl Laemmle Jr..

Inspired by linking two Game Boys with a cable and by his childhood love of insect collecting, this Japanese designer co-founded Game Freak and spent six years creating a now-global franchise — who is he?
Satoshi Tajiri: Japanese video game designer (born 1965)

Misty Copeland: American ballet dancer and author (born 1982)

Al Franken: American comedian and politician (born 1951)

Aguirre, the Wrath of God: 1972 film by Werner Herzog

Faten Hamama: Egyptian actress and producer (1931–2015)

Columbia, South Carolina is the capital city of the U.S.

Merv: Ancient major city in Central Asia

Key West: Island and city in Florida, United States

Republic of Florence: City-state on the Italian Peninsula (1115–1569)

Isle of Skye: Island of the Inner Hebrides, Scotland

Jan Mayen: Norwegian island in the Arctic Ocean

Mircea Lucescu: Romanian football player and manager (1945–2026)

Tarkan (singer) — Tarkan (Turkish; born 17 October 1972) is a German-born Turkish singer-songwriter.

To Pimp a Butterfly: 2015 studio album by Kendrick Lamar

Daniel Padilla: Filipino actor and singer (born 1995)

The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim: 2011 video game

Jean Baudrillard: French sociologist and philosopher (1929–2007)

Nan Goldin: American photographer and activist

Simone de Beauvoir wrote this groundbreaking 1949 work of feminist philosophy in about 14 months, and the Vatican promptly banned it — what is it?
The Second Sex: 1949 book by Simone de Beauvoir

Jesuits: Male religious congregation of the Catholic Church

2006 Lebanon War: Armed conflict primarily between Israel and Hezbollah

Political science (sometimes abbreviated as poli sci) is a field which aims to study the scientific aspect of politics.

Nostradamus: French apothecary, astrologer and seer (1503–1566)

Anthrax: Infection caused by Bacillus anthracis bacteria

Astronomy: Scientific study of celestial objects
