Citric acid cycle: Interconnected biochemical reactions releasing energy

Owl: Birds from the order Strigiformes
Colorless, odorless, and practically non-toxic, this organic compound is the main nitrogen-bearing substance in mammal urine — fittingly, its name traces back to the Greek word for urine. What is it?
Deafened by childhood illness and rerouted from competitive diving, she became a Hollywood stunt pioneer and earned the title 'the fastest woman in the world.' Who was she?
Kitty O'Neil: American stuntwoman and racer (1946–2018)

After (film series) — After consists of American romantic dramas based on the Anna Todd-authored after novels.
Ninth-smallest U.S. state by land area, this place wraps around Washington, D.C. to its southwest, keeps its capital at Annapolis, but parks its biggest city in Baltimore — which state?
Nicknamed 'the City of Gold' and 'Jozi,' South Africa's most populous city sits on the mineral-rich Witwatersrand and hosts the country's Constitutional Court. Which city is it?
Johannesburg (joh-, US also -HAHN-), colloquially known as Jozi, Joburg or "the City of Gold", is the most populous city in South Africa.
A right-handed top-order batter, this cricketer captained Pakistan in all three formats and helped his country win the 2017 ICC Champions Trophy. Who is he?

Rob Gronkowski (born May 14, 1989) is an American former professional football tight end who played in the National Football League (NFL) for 11 seasons.

Book of Genesis (from Greek, Gnesis, 'Origin'; Biblical

A British journalist who once anchored China Central Television's main evening news, he became the UN's first UNAIDS goodwill ambassador for China in 2009. Who is he?
James Chau: British journalist and TV presenter (born 1977)

War and Peace: 1869 literary work by Leo Tolstoy

Severus Alexander: Roman emperor from 222 to 235
A royalist commander who once defeated the very insurgents he'd later side with, this criollo crowned himself the first Emperor of Mexico in 1822 — only to abdicate a year later. Who was he?
Agustín de Iturbide: Mexican army officer and politician

Eadred: King of the English from 946 to 955

Gustav Vasa: King of Sweden from 1523 to 1560

Agnes Chow: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist (born 1996)

Yitzhak Shamir: Prime Minister of Israel (1983–1984; 1986–1992)

Raúl Alfonsín: President of Argentina from 1983 to 1989

Alan Greenspan: American economist and financial advisor (born 1926)

John Carmack: American computer programmer and video game developer (born 1970)
This computer scientist led the on-board flight software for NASA's Apollo Guidance Computer and is credited with coining the very term 'software engineering' — who is she?
Margaret Elaine Hamilton is an American computer scientist.
Nicknamed "the comedian of feelings," this Italian actor and director was posthumously nominated for two Oscars for the 1994 film Il Postino: The Postman — who was he?
Massimo Troisi: Italian actor, film director, and poet (1953–1994)

Vyjayanthimala: Indian actress, dancer and parliamentarian (born 1933)

Jim Nabors: American actor and singer (1930–2017)
One of India's highest-paid television actresses, she won acclaim for playing Akshara in Yeh Rishta Kya Kehlata Hai and was a runner-up on two seasons of a reality show — who is she?

Zhao Wei: Chinese actress, singer and filmmaker (born 1976)
Premiering on CBS in 1972, this pricing-game show summons contestants from the studio audience with the announcer's famous cry of 'come on down!' — and Bob Barker hosted it until 2007 — what is it?
The Price Is Right: American television game show
Set in the 2060s and brought to life with electronic marionette puppetry dubbed 'Supermarionation,' this 1960s British sci-fi series came from Gerry and Sylvia Anderson — what was it called?

Thunderbirds (TV series) — Thunderbirds is a British science fiction television series created by Gerry and Sylvia Anderson, filmed by their production company AP Films (APF) and distributed by ITC Entertainment.
Home to the Jasna Góra Monastery and its famous Black Madonna, this southern Polish city sits on the Warta in the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland. Which city is it?

Built up from a small Kashubian fishing village starting in 1926, this is the largest city in Poland that isn't a voivodeship capital, forming a Baltic "Tricity" with Sopot and Gdańsk — which seaport is it?
Gdynia: City in Pomeranian Voivodeship, Poland
The fourth-largest city in Scotland, perched on the north bank of the Firth of Tay, this east-coast trading port became the center of the global jute industry in the 19th century — what is it?
Dundee: City and council area in Scotland
Ranked by RSSSF as the third-most prolific scorer in history with over 950 goals, this Austrian-Czech striker netted 591 alone for Slavia Prague — who is he?

Recorded over ten months around Detroit with Dr. Dre producing, this 2000 album of introspective, transgressive hip-hop reflects on its rapper's rise to fame and family estrangement. Which record is it?
The Marshall Mathers LP: 2000 studio album by Eminem
Famous for moulding his voice to whichever actor was lip-syncing on screen, this Indian playback singer won six Filmfare Awards and a Padma Shri across genres from qawwalis to ghazals. Who was he?

With 31 Latin Grammys and a style fusing merengue with Latin pop, this Dominican musician became one of the best-selling Latin artists of recent decades. Who is he?

Formed in Washington, D.C. in 1986, this post-hardcore band was as famous for its DIY ethics and contempt for the music industry as for its style-transcending sound. Which band, on indefinite hiatus since 2003?
Founded in Delaware back in 1802 by a French-American chemist, this company makes Tyvek packaging and TYCHEM protective suits across its healthcare, water and industrial markets — what is it?
E. I. DuPont de Nemours & Co.
He won an Oscar, a Tony, a BAFTA and a Golden Globe all for playing the same role — the leering Master of Ceremonies in Cabaret on stage and in Bob Fosse's 1972 film — who is he?
Joel Grey: American actor, singer, dancer, director, and photographer (born 1932)
A leading Soviet Armenian composer raised in Tbilisi, he enrolled in music school with no prior training and went on to write celebrated Piano, Violin and Cello concertos — who was he?

The second-most-recorded jazz composer in history after Duke Ellington, this pianist's angular style leaned on dissonances, flat fifths and unexpected chromatic notes — and gave us 'Round Midnight' — who was he?
Thelonious Monk: American jazz pianist and composer (1917–1982)
Formed in San Francisco in 1978 with frontman Jello Biafra, this punk band helped define the American scene and released the acclaimed album Fresh Fruit for Rotting Vegetables in 1980 — who are they?
Fill in the blank: “____ was an American alternative rock band formed in Los Angeles, California, in 1989.”
Hole (band) — Hole was an American alternative rock band formed in Los Angeles, California, in 1989.

As a member of The Weavers, he scored a number-one hit with Lead Belly's "Goodnight, Irene" in 1950 — then got blacklisted in the McCarthy era before returning as a beloved voice of protest and civil rights. Which folk singer-songwriter and activist was he?
Pete Seeger: American musician and social activist (1919–2014)

A Brown-trained physicist turned composer, this musician helped Robert Moog develop his first commercial synthesizer, then put it on the map with the 1968 album Switched-On Bach — who is the electronic-music pioneer?
Wendy Carlos: American composer and electronic musician (born 1939)

At Rutgers he was the only African-American student, a two-time All-American footballer, and class valedictorian — and he went on to a Columbia law degree, NFL play, the Harlem Renaissance stage, and a career as a famed bass-baritone. Which multi-talented activist was he?
Paul Robeson: American singer, actor, political activist, and athlete (1898–1976)
Released in 1979, this was Michael Jackson's first album with producer Quincy Jones and his first on Epic, blending disco, funk and Broadway ballads — which album?
Off the Wall: 1979 studio album by Michael Jackson
The U.S. Treasury once listed this dancer and pin-up as America's highest-salaried woman, and her 1940s films grossed over $100 million — who was she?
Betty Grable: American actress and pin-up girl (1916–1973)

Ralph Nader: American lawyer and activist (born 1934)
Modelled by Elizabeth Siddal and now in Tate Britain, this 1851–52 Millais painting depicts a drowning Shakespearean noblewoman amid a lush natural landscape — what is it?
Ophelia (painting) — Ophelia is an 1851-52 painting by British artist John Everett Millais in the collection of Tate Britain, London.
A leading Pop Art figure, this American painter made his name with comic-book-inspired works featuring bold outlines, flat colors, and hand-painted Ben-Day dots — who was he?
A "romantic communist" praised for his lyrical flow, this Turkish poet was repeatedly jailed or exiled for his beliefs, yet his verse has been translated into more than 50 languages — who was he?
Nâzım Hikmet: Turkish communist poet, playwright and novelist (1902–1963)

A Stoic and famously incorruptible orator of the late Roman Republic, this conservative senator rallied a following against powerful generals like Caesar and Pompey in defense of traditional liberty — who was he?
Cato the Younger: Roman politician and Stoic (95–46 BC)
A 19th-century Muslim reformer and educationist in British India, he's widely credited as the father of the two-nation theory that underpinned the Pakistan movement — which figure was he?
Syed Ahmad Khan: Indian reformer and social activist (1817–1898)

His 1992 book argued that the global spread of liberal democracy and free-market capitalism might be the final step in humanity's political evolution — "the end of history." Which American political scientist made that controversial claim?
Francis Fukuyama: American political scientist, economist, and author (born 1952)

His 1975 book argued for vegetarianism, and his essay "Famine, Affluence, and Morality" insisted we're morally obligated to help the world's poor — all from a secular, utilitarian view. Which Australian moral philosopher is this?
The youngest of the famous literary siblings of Haworth, she wrote Agnes Grey and The Tenant of Wildfell Hall, the latter hailed as one of the first feminist novels — who is she?
Anne Brontë: English novelist and poet (1820–1849)

A clinical-psychologist-turned-novelist, this Polish writer won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Literature for an 'encyclopedic' imagination, and her novel Flights took the Man Booker International that same year — who is she?
Olga Tokarczuk: Polish writer and activist (born 1962)

Samantha Smith: American child peace activist (1972–1985)

Classically, one form of this condition wakes you at night with upper abdominal pain that eases when you eat, while another flares up after meals — and a third of older sufferers feel nothing at all. What is it?
acute peptic ulcer with hemorrhage and perforation
Peptic ulcer disease refers to damage of the inner part of the stomach's gastric mucosa (lining of the stomach), the first part of the small intestine, or sometimes the lower esophagus.

Walled off to the east and south by the Carpathians and to the west by the Apuseni Mountains, this historical region sits in central Romania and goes by Erdély in Hungarian and Siebenbürgen in German. What is it?
Transylvania: Historical region in Central Europe
Founded in 1961 to spur economic progress and world trade, this 38-member intergovernmental forum unites high-income, advanced economies committed to democracy and the market economy. What is it?
Appointed to lead the Bureau of Investigation by Calvin Coolidge in 1924, this man went on to run its successor agency for 37 more years, serving under eight presidents in all. Who was he?
J. Edgar Hoover: American law enforcement administrator (1895–1972)

Ruby Ridge standoff: 1992 siege and shootout in Idaho, US
In 1932, Australian artillery soldiers armed with Lewis guns were deployed against crop-raiding flightless birds in Western Australia — and lost. What did the media dub this campaign?
Emu War: 1932 Australian nuisance wildlife management campaign

Marked by at least two weeks of pervasive low mood and loss of pleasure, this condition was named by US clinicians in the mid-1970s and causes the second-most years lived with disability, after lower back pain. What is it?

Major depressive disorder, also known as clinical depression, is a mental disorder characterized by at least two weeks of pervasive low mood, low self-esteem, and loss of interest or pleasure in normally enjoyable activities.

From a Greek word meaning 'change,' this term covers the enzyme-driven reactions that turn food into usable energy and building blocks while excreting waste — letting organisms grow and reproduce. What is it?
Metabolism: Set of chemical reactions in organisms
Chairman of a sprawling Indian conglomerate from 1991 to 2012, this architecture graduate of Cornell received both the Padma Bhushan and the Padma Vibhushan. Who was he?
Ratan Tata: Indian industrialist and philanthropist (1937–2024)

As modern science emerged, this concept came to mean the passive reality moved by divine laws — and after the Industrial Revolution, the part of the world untouched by intentional human hands. What word is it?
Nature: Material world and its phenomena

A colorless, sweet-tasting, syrupy liquid, this sugar alcohol carries three hydroxyl groups, forms the backbone of triglycerides in fats and oils, and doubles as a food-industry sweetener. What is it?
Nicknamed the seven-year itch, this contagious skin condition is caused by a microscopic burrowing mite and thrives in crowded places like prisons and care homes — what is it?
Scabies (also sometimes known as the seven-year itch) is a contagious human skin infestation by the tiny (0.2-0.45 mm) mite Sarcoptes scabiei, variety hominis.
Nicknamed the 'winter vomiting disease' and spread by the fecal-oral route, this is the most common cause of gastroenteritis — what is it?
Norovirus: Type of viruses that cause gastroenteritis
Every animal in this group shares five telltale traits — including a notochord, pharyngeal slits, and a tail that extends past the anus — at some stage of life; which of these belongs to that phylum?
Chordate: Phylum of animals having a dorsal nerve cord
Named for the daring Doolittle airmen of World War II, this subsonic stealth flying wing is being built to replace the B-1 and B-2 by 2040 — which aircraft is it?
Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider: American stealth bomber aircraft
Useless against the cold, the flu, or any fungus, this kind of medicine works only by killing or stalling bacteria — what is it called?
Antibiotic: Antimicrobial substance active against bacteria

Nutria: Semi-aquatic rodent from South America
As chairman of Purdue Pharma, this physician-businessman oversaw the launch of OxyContin and was later portrayed in the miniseries Dopesick and Painkiller — who is he?
A member of the aminopenicillin class, this oral antibiotic is a go-to for ear infections, strep throat, and pneumonia — and is often paired with clavulanic acid. What is it?
Of the 68 species bearing this name, only the Aquilinae are genetically "true" ones — the rest just qualify as any bird of prey big enough to hunt sizeable vertebrates; what's the common name?
This Italian-American economist taught at MIT's Sloan School and Carnegie Mellon before collecting the 1985 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics. Who was he?
Franco Modigliani: Italian-American economist and Nobel Laureate (1918–2003)
Famously dubbed 'a show about nothing,' this NBC sitcom co-created by Larry David ran nine seasons around a Manhattan apartment shared in spirit by George, Elaine, and Kramer — which show is it?
Known as "the Demon" and famous for an extraordinarily long tongue, this Israeli-American bassist co-founded a face-painted hard rock band in 1973 — who is he?
Gene Simmons (born Chaim Witz;; August 25, 1949), also known by his stage persona "the Demon", is an Israeli and American musician.
Praised for its eerie atmosphere and historical accuracy, this 2019 HBO–Sky drama starring Jared Harris recreated a 1986 nuclear disaster across five episodes — which miniseries is it?
Chernobyl (miniseries) — Chernobyl is a 2019 historical drama television miniseries that revolves around the chernobyl disaster of 1986 and the cleanup efforts that followed.

The Continental: From the World of John Wick
The Continental: From the World of John Wick
The Continental: From the World of John Wick: 2023 American action miniseries
The Continental: From the World of John Wick
Debuting on the runway in 1999, this Brazilian became the longest-running Victoria's Secret Angel and was once crowned the brand's 'most valuable' Angel — who is she?
Nicknamed the Lone Star State, this place forms a natural border with Mexico along the Rio Grande and is the second-largest U.S. state by both area and population — which one is it?

Taken first overall in the 2016 draft, this quarterback led the Rams to Super Bowl LIII before a 2021 trade sent him to Detroit — who is he?
Jared Goff (born October 14, 1994) is an American professional football quarterback for the Detroit Lions of the National Football League (NFL).
Nicknamed "the Doctor," this Italian racer won nine Grand Prix motorcycle world titles and holds the premier-class records for victories and podiums — who is he?

Tim Tebow (born August 14, 1987) is an American former professional football quarterback who played in the National Football League (NFL) for three seasons, primarily with the Denver Broncos.
A favorite consort turned regent, this Ottoman power broker ruled during the minorities of her son and grandson before being assassinated in 1651 — who was she?
Kösem Sultan, also known as Mahpeyker Sultan, was the Haseki Sultan as a favorite consort and legal wife of Ottoman sultan Ahmed I, mother of Murad IV and Ibrahim, and grandmother of Mehmed IV.

Ivana Trump (ne Zelnkov; February 20, 1949 - July 14, 2022) was a Czech and American businesswoman, socialite, and model.

Nando Parrado: Survivor of the 1972 Andes flight disaster

Zoroaster: Iranian prophet and spiritual founder of Zoroastrianism

Roh Moo-hyun: President of South Korea from 2003 to 2008

Juan Manuel de Rosas: Argentine politician and general (1793–1877)

Stephen Harper: Prime Minister of Canada from 2006 to 2015
Triggered by Napoleon's invasion of Spain, this week of events in 1810 ousted a viceroy in Buenos Aires and installed the Primera Junta — what is this turning point named for the month it happened?
The May Revolution was a week-long series of events that took place from 18 to 25 May 1810, in Buenos Aires, capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata.
He served as Mexico's Secretary of Energy under Vicente Fox before winning the presidency himself in 2006 — and quit the PAN party after 30 years in 2018. Which Mexican president is this?
Felipe Calderón: President of Mexico from 2006 to 2012
Rising from a family of smallholders, this Roman general held the office of consul a record seven times — more than anyone else in the Republican period. Who was he?
Gaius Marius: Roman general and statesman (c. 157–86 BC)

Vicente Fox: President of Mexico from 2000 to 2006
"Keeper of greatness" was the meaning of his name — fitting for the 13th and final emperor of Vietnam's Nguyễn dynasty, who abdicated in August 1945 after Japan surrendered. Who was he?

A Baptist minister and founder of the National Action Network, this civil-rights activist ran for the 2004 Democratic presidential nomination and hosts the radio show "Keepin' It Real" — who is he?
Al Sharpton: American Baptist minister, activist and talk show host (born 1954)

Aarhus: City in Central Denmark Region, Denmark
He's the rare athlete who went from playing for a team to owning it — drafted first overall by the Penguins in 1984, he later took the franchise's reins in 1999. Which 'Magnificent One' is this?
Mario Lemieux: Canadian ice hockey player (born 1965)
Nicknamed "Mo" and "Sandman," this Panamanian-American closer is MLB's all-time leader in saves with 652 — who spent all 19 of his seasons in pinstripes?
Born in Haiti, this rapper-producer was the guitarist and lead producer of the Fugees, whose album 'The Score' became one of the best-selling of all time — who is he?

Chick Corea: American musician and composer (1941–2021)

Edward Hopper's 1942 portrait of four figures in a late-night diner, glimpsed through a vast glass window onto a deserted street, sold to the Art Institute of Chicago within months — what's the painting called?

Nighthawks (Hopper) — Nighthawks is a 1942 oil on canvas painting by the American artist Edward Hopper that portrays four people in a downtown diner late at night as viewed through the diner's large glass window.

This Italian far-right philosopher started as a Dada painter, abandoned the brush in his twenties, and after reading a Buddhist text became an esoteric mentor to the post-war militant right — who is he?
Julius Evola: Italian radical-right philosopher and esotericist (1898–1974)
Goya painted this 1814 canvas, now in the Prado, to commemorate Spanish resistance to Napoleon's troops during the 1808 occupation of Madrid — which work is it?
The Third of May 1808: 1814 painting by Francisco de Goya
Fill in the blank: “____ is a 2007 puzzle-platform game developed and published by Valve.”
Portal (video game) — Portal is a 2007 puzzle-platform game developed and published by Valve.
He spoke Spanish before English, did a stint at the CIA, then in 1955 founded National Review — which conservative writer and public intellectual?
William F. Buckley Jr.: American conservative author and commentator (1925–2008)
Born into a low-ranking samurai family, this Meiji-era reformer taught himself English, sailed on Japan's first mission to the U.S. in 1860, and founded Keio University — who is he?
Fukuzawa Yukichi: Japanese author, educator, and philosopher (1835–1901)
Born into an Igbo family in Enugu and a central voice in postcolonial feminist literature, this Nigerian writer often sets her novels in Nsukka — who is she?

Michelle McNamara: American true crime writer (1970–2016)
Prosecuted in 1877 for publishing a birth-control book, this English socialist and theosophist went on to become the first woman president of the Indian National Congress — who is she?
Annie Besant: English writer and activist (1847–1933)
Dubbed "the poet of apprehension" by Graham Greene, this American novelist gave the world five psychological thrillers about a charming killer named Tom Ripley — who is she?
Born Friedrich Stowasser, this Austrian artist-architect waged war on the straight line, weaving nature into buildings like Vienna's whimsical Hundertwasserhaus — who is he?
This speculative-fiction writer coined the word "cyberspace" and pioneered a "lowlife meets high tech" subgenre he keeps distancing himself from — who is he?
William Gibson: American-Canadian speculative fiction novelist (born 1948)
Poet Laureate for much of Queen Victoria's reign, this Englishman won Cambridge's Chancellor's Gold Medal in 1829 for a poem on "Timbuktu" and gave us "Mariana" — who was he?
Alfred, Lord Tennyson: British Poet Laureate (1809–1892)

Published after the author's death, this last completed Jane Austen novel reunites 27-year-old Anne Elliot with Captain Wentworth nearly eight years after she was talked out of marrying him — what is it?
Persuasion (novel) — Persuasion is the last novel completed by the English author Jane Austen.
Often traced to a 1973 Bronx party thrown by a brother-sister duo, this art movement is built on rapping, DJing, turntablism and breakdancing — what is it?
Hip-hop culture is an art movement that emerged in New York City, in the borough of the Bronx, primarily within the black community.
Beginning in September up north and March down south, this temperate season shortens the days and famously sets deciduous leaves ablaze with color — which one is it?
Autumn: One of Earth's four temperate seasons
This American billionaire co-founded and leads BlackRock, the world's largest money-management firm with over $10 trillion under management — who is he?

Sparked by British trade restrictions and the Royal Navy's impressment of sailors, this conflict was declared by the United States in June 1812 and dragged on even after the Treaty of Ghent — which war is it?
War of 1812: 1812–1815 conflict in North America
World chess champion from 1985 to 2000 and the game's top-ranked player for a record 255 months, this grandmaster later turned political activist — who is he?

Hoysala Kingdom was a prominent South Indian dynasty that ruled most of what is now Karnataka, as well as parts of Tamil Nadu and southwestern Telangana, between the 11th and 14th centuries CE.
A Burma Campaign veteran regarded as the founder of the Bangladesh Armed Forces, he served as commander-in-chief of the Bangladesh Forces in 1971 — who was this four-star general?
M. A. G. Osmani: Bangladeshi military general & revolutionary (1918–1984)
Its 41 living species boast the most varied fur patterns of any land carnivore, all armed with retractile claws and an obligate taste for meat — which family is this?
Estimated by one 2021 study to occur in about 2% of people, this paraphilia is often confused with bestiality but actually describes the attraction, not the act — what is it?
Zoophilia: Sexual fixation on non-human animals
Better known by the brand name Viagra, this drug treats erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension, kicking in within about twenty minutes — what is it?

He co-founded a certain search company with Sergey Brin, later led its parent Alphabet as CEO, and is now among the two wealthiest people on Earth — who is it?
Now the wealthiest Brazilian and the richest person in Singapore, this Facebook co-founder later started the venture firm B Capital — who is he?
These slow-moving South American mammals hang upside down in rainforest canopies, are kin to anteaters, and — despite the "two-toed" label — all have three toes on each rear limb; what are they?
Sloth: Group of tree dwelling mammals noted for slowness
First prepared in 1908 by biochemist Kikunae Ikeda as he tried to bottle the savory taste of kombu seaweed, this flavor enhancer is the original source of umami in cooking — what is it?
Monosodium glutamate: Flavor enhancer (621 or E621)
This four-engine American turboprop can land on dirt strips and unprepared runways, then moonlight as a gunship, a flying firefighter, or a weather scout — which versatile workhorse is it?
Lockheed C-130 Hercules: American military transport aircraft
Built atop an Ilyushin transport and nicknamed 'Mainstay,' this Soviet radar plane had its existence leaked to the West by a spy in 1978 — which aircraft is it?
Beriev A-50: Soviet airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft

Guinea pig: Domesticated rodent from South America
First flown in 1952, this nuclear-capable Soviet bomber is the only turboprop strategic bomber still flying — its contra-rotating propellers earning it the NATO nickname 'Bear.' What is it?
Tupolev Tu-95: Russian strategic bomber aircraft

Cashew: Flowering plant in the family Anacardiaceae

His 1962 book The Calculus of Consent launched a theory of how politicians' and bureaucrats' self-interest shapes their decisions, earning him the 1986 Nobel in economics — which founder of public choice theory is this?
James M. Buchanan: American economist and Nobel Laureate (1919–2013)
This Berkeley cognitive linguist argued in 'Metaphors We Live By' that the conceptual metaphors we choose quietly shape our lives — who is he?

George Lakoff (born May 24, 1941) is an American cognitive linguist and philosopher, best known for his thesis that people's lives are significantly influenced by the conceptual metaphors they use to explain complex phenomena.
Kicked off by WandaVision in January 2021, this was the first stretch of its blockbuster franchise to fold in Disney+ TV series and even animation — which film-and-show grouping is it?
Marvel Cinematic Universe: Phase Four: 2021–22 group of superhero media
David Letterman called this deadpan Canadian comedian — beloved for his folksy understatement and chaotic late-night appearances — simply 'the best.' Who is it?
It's the only U.S. state that's entirely an archipelago, the only one south of the Tropic of Cancer, and made of 137 volcanic islands — which state is it?

Sculptor Gutzon Borglum called this granite work the 'Shrine of Democracy' and spent 1927 to 1941 carving four 60-foot presidential heads into a Black Hills peak the Lakota call Six Grandfathers — what is it?

The Mount Rushmore National Memorial is a national memorial featuring a colossal sculpture carved into the granite face of Mount Rushmore in the Black Hills, about 2 mi (3 km) southwest of Keystone, South Dakota, United States.

Maus I, My Father Bleeds History
Maus: Graphic novel by Art Spiegelman
Smithsonian named her among the '100 Most Significant Americans,' and her grandson reckoned she reported over 2,000 visions — which co-founder and prophet of the Seventh-day Adventist Church?
Ellen G. White: American author and co-founder of the Seventh-day Adventist Church
Born Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, this British far-right activist co-founded and led the English Defence League from 2009 to 2013 — by what better-known name does he go?
A seven-time All-Star and Triple Crown winner whose durability earned him the nickname 'the Iron Horse,' this Yankees first baseman batted.340 over 17 seasons — who was he?
Henry Louis Gehrig was an American professional baseball first baseman who played 17 seasons in Major League Baseball for the New York Yankees.

One of the world's last absolute monarchs and reportedly worth $50 billion, he has reigned over a small, oil-rich nation since 1967 — making him the world's longest-reigning current monarch. Who is he?
Hassanal Bolkiah: Sultan of Brunei since 1967
Often used as a pejorative, this late-20th-century ideology champions free-market capitalism through lower taxes, privatization, and deregulation — what is it?
Neoliberalism: Political ideology promoting free-market capitalism
Heir to a former Maharaja and founder of the Lakshya Trust charity, he is widely considered the first openly gay prince in the world — who is he?
Manvendra Singh Gohil: Hereditary Prince of Rajpipla

In early Christianity, this label — from a Latin word for "rustic" — was pinned on anyone in the Roman Empire who didn't follow an Abrahamic faith, often spotted by their taking part in ritual sacrifice. What's the term?
A Princeton grad and former F-15 flight test engineer, he co-founded the deep-sea firm OceanGate and died in 2023 when its submersible imploded en route to the Titanic wreck — who was he?

Broadcast, print, digital, social, and streaming all fall under this umbrella term for the forms of communication that reach huge audiences at once — and which is often controlled by a few conglomerates. What is it?
Mass media refers to the forms of media that reach large audiences via mass communication.
A member of the ginger family native to the Indian subcontinent, its boiled and dried rhizomes are ground into a deep orange-yellow powder used to color and flavor curries — what is it?
Son of Taiwanese immigrants, this engineer launched the world's most valuable company from a Denny's restaurant in 1993 after earning a Stanford master's degree — who is he?
Jensen Huang: Taiwanese and American businessman (born 1963)

This group of neurological disorders is marked by recurrent, unprovoked seizures — sudden bursts of abnormal electrical activity that can range from brief lapses of awareness to full convulsions. What is it?
Epilepsy: Group of neurological disorders causing seizures

Marked by widespread chronic pain plus fatigue and foggy thinking, this condition affects 2 to 4% of people, more often women, and was first recognised in the 1950s but only defined in 1990 — what is it?
Listed by Ptolemy and named for a hunter in Greek myth, this winter constellation boasts the supergiant stars Rigel and Betelgeuse and a famous short, straight line of three stars — which is it?
Orion (constellation) — Orion is a prominent set of stars visible during winter in the northern celestial hemisphere.

Often defined as the normal functioning of the body free of disease, pain, or injury, this multidimensional state of well-being can be promoted by exercise and sleep and harmed by smoking or stress — what's the one-word concept?
Health: Desirable level of functional or metabolic efficiency of a living being
A key figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, this thinker is often called the "father of economics" and is best known for "The Theory of Moral Sentiments" and "The Wealth of Nations" — who is it?

Cuban-born and a former star of the Spanish teen drama "El Internado," this actress moved to Los Angeles and earned an Academy Award nomination after roles in "Knock Knock" and "War Dogs" — who is she?

Ana de Armas (Spanish; born 30 April 1988) is a Cuban-born actress holding Cuban,
Spanish, and American
citizenship.
Before owning an NBA team in Dallas and spending years as a "shark" on "Shark Tank," this Pittsburgh-raised entrepreneur got his start selling garbage bags door to door — who is he?
His grandfather, father, and uncle all wrestled before him, making this SmackDown star a third-generation grappler with one of the most world-championship reigns in WWE history — who is he?
Bordering Oregon, Nevada, Arizona, and sharing an international line with Mexico's Baja peninsula, this is the most populous U.S. state — which one?
This suspension span carries both U.S. Route 101 and California State Route 1 across a one-mile-wide strait, and engineers crowned it one of the Wonders of the Modern World — what is it?
The Golden Gate Bridge is a suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate, the one-mile-wide (1.6 km) strait connecting San Francisco Bay and the Pacific Ocean in California, United States.
A former track star nicknamed 'Cheetah' for his blazing speed, this wide receiver bounced from three colleges to a fifth-round draft and a Super Bowl LIV ring — who is he?
Tyreek Hill (born March 1, 1994) is an American professional football wide receiver.
A Portland girl who laced up skates at age three and later became both a U.S. figure-skating champion and a boxer — who is she?
A noted London session guitarist who joined the Yardbirds in 1966, he founded a legendary rock band when they broke up in 1968 — which guitarist is this?
Founded in 1946 as Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo by Masaru Ibuka and Akio Morita, this Tokyo conglomerate spans electronics, film, music, and video games — what is its modern name, adopted in 1958?
Headquartered in Ingolstadt and now a Volkswagen subsidiary, this German luxury carmaker traces its tangled roots to engineer August Horch and the 1932 founding of Auto Union — which brand?
Fill in the blank: “____ is a Spanish fast fashion retail subsidiary of the Spanish multinational fashion design, manufacturing, and retailing group Inditex.”
Zara (retailer) — Zara is a Spanish fast fashion retail subsidiary of the Spanish multinational fashion design, manufacturing, and retailing group Inditex.
He ran track under coach Bill Bowerman at Oregon, then teamed with that same coach to launch a footwear giant — and now owns the stop-motion studio Laika; who is he?
Phil Knight: American billionaire business magnate (born 1938)
Stitched together in Akkadian from older Sumerian poems about a king of Uruk, its oldest combined version opens with the line 'Surpassing All Other Kings' — what ancient work is it?
The Epic of Gilgamesh is an epic from ancient Mesopotamia.
Born Amonute and later baptized Rebecca, this Powhatan woman — daughter of a paramount chief — was captured by English colonists and is forever tied to the Jamestown settlement; who is she?
A yachtsman and musician as well as a politician, this son of a carpenter and chambermaid served as British Prime Minister from 1970 to 1974 — who was he?
Edward Heath: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1970 to 1974
As South Africa's last head of state under white-minority rule, this leader dismantled apartheid and introduced universal suffrage, later serving as deputy president under Mandela — who is he?
F. W. de Klerk: President of South Africa from 1989 to 1994
An Arizona senator and Air Force Reserve major general who rejected the legacy of the New Deal, this conservative was the Republican Party's presidential nominee in 1964. Who is he?
Barry Goldwater: American politician and military officer (1909–1998)

His name became a byword for traitor, but this Norwegian officer once worked alongside explorer Fridtjof Nansen on famine relief before heading the Nazi puppet government during Germany's occupation of Norway — who is it?
Vidkun Quisling: Norwegian politician and Nazi collaborator (1887–1945)
He joined the ANC at 17, spent ten years imprisoned on Robben Island, and went on to serve as president of South Africa from 2009 to 2018 — who is this leader known by his initials JZ?
Jacob Zuma: President of South Africa from 2009 to 2018
Carried out by Myanmar's Tatmadaw in phases since 2016, this campaign drove over a million Muslims into Bangladesh, creating the world's largest refugee camp — what is it called?
The Rohingya genocide is a series of ongoing persecutions and killings of the Muslim Rohingya people by the Tatmadaw (armed forces of Myanmar).
Nicknamed "The Kingfish," this populist Louisiana governor-turned-senator attacked FDR's New Deal for being too timid before his 1935 assassination — who was he?
Pakistan's longest-serving de-facto ruler, this general seized power in a 1977 coup and held it until his death in a 1988 airplane crash — who is he?
Zia-ul-Haq: 6th President of Pakistan from 1978 to 1988
A general and politician of the state of Cao Wei during China's Three Kingdoms period, he crushed Meng Da's rebellion and conquered the Liaodong commandery as regent. Who is he?
Sima Yi: Chinese general, politician and regent (179–251)
A Congress politician and former Governor of Rajasthan, she made history in 2007 as the first woman to become the President of India. Who is she?
Pratibha Patil: President of India from 2007 to 2012

The first person from West Bengal to become President of India, this longtime Congress leader had been Finance Minister just before his 2012 election and was awarded the Bharat Ratna in 2019. Who is he?
Pranab Mukherjee: President of India from 2012 to 2017
This Sapporo-born programmer rose to become Nintendo's fourth president, betting on novel, entertaining games over the most powerful hardware — who is he?
Satoru Iwata: Japanese video game executive (1959–2015)

He dreamed up an "impossible" triangle, traded ideas with M. C. Escher, and shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for proving black holes are a robust prediction of general relativity — who is this English mathematician?
Roger Penrose: English mathematician, mathematical physicist (born 1931)
Often called the frontman of Mexican neoliberalism, this economist-president from 1988 to 1994 formulated and signed NAFTA — though his election was dogged by fraud accusations — who is he?
Carlos Salinas de Gortari: President of Mexico from 1988 to 1994
In this autoimmune disease the body's own defenses destroy the insulin-making beta cells of the pancreas, bringing on thirst, frequent urination, and weight loss — what is it?
Type 1 diabetes, or type 1 diabetes mellitus, is an autoimmune disease that occurs when the body's immune system destroys beta cells in the pancreas that produce the hormone insulin.
Spread by the bite of phlebotomine sandflies in the tropics, this parasitic disease can show up as skin ulcers or, in its visceral form, fever and an enlarged spleen and liver — what is it?
Leishmaniasis: Disease caused by parasites of the Leishmania type
This American scholar of comparative mythology coined the term "monomyth" in The Hero with a Thousand Faces, describing the universal journey of the archetypal hero — who is he?
Joseph Campbell: American mythologist, writer, and lecturer (1904–1987)

Synthesized in 2003 at the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research in Dubna and named in 2016 for the Russian region around it, this element 115 has a most-stable isotope lasting just 0.65 seconds — what is it?
Moscovium: Chemical element with atomic number 115 (Mc)

Caused by a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin), this disease is remembered for its grim quartet of symptoms — inflamed skin, diarrhea, dementia, and mouth sores — striking sun-exposed skin first. What is it?
Pellagra: Human disease caused by a lack of vitamin B3
Also known as snail fever and bilharzia, this tropical disease is caused by a parasitic flatworm and can lead to bloody urine, liver damage, and even bladder cancer over time. What is it?
Schistosomiasis: Human disease caused by parasitic worms called schistosomes
Created by Mark Goodson, this game show pits two families against each other to name the most popular answers to survey questions, and is now hosted by Steve Harvey — what is it?
Family Feud: American television game show

With over 230 million copies in circulation from hits like "Urusei Yatsura" and "Inuyasha," this two-time Shogakukan Manga Award winner is among Japan's wealthiest and best-known manga artists. Who is she?
The only musician to top the Billboard Hot 100 both as a vocalist and as an instrumentalist, this trumpeter co-founded A&M Records and led a brass band in the 1960s. Who is he?
Shot partly on Long Island's South Fork, this 1977 romantic comedy stars its director as Alvy Singer puzzling over a failed romance with a role written for Diane Keaton — what film?
Annie Hall: 1977 film by Woody Allen
Dubbed the 'father of the zombie film,' this filmmaker's 'Night of the Living Dead' trilogy shaped the modern cultural image of the undead — who was he?
A reluctant heir to a great theatrical family who first chased a career as a visual artist, this actor's 1922 stage turn earned him the title 'greatest living American tragedian' — who was he?
Capital of its own medieval principality under the Lombards, this city on Italy's Tyrrhenian coast is now Campania's second-most populous after Naples — what is it?
Finland's oldest city, sitting at the mouth of the River Aura, was first mentioned by Pope Gregory IX in 1229 — the year now used for its founding. What is it?
Fill in the blank: “____ is the capital city of the U.S.”
Tallahassee, Florida is the capital city of the U.S.
This Devon port grew from a Bronze Age trading post and was the 1620 departure point for the Pilgrim Fathers to the New World — what is it?
Plymouth: City and unitary authority in England
The most populous inland city in the Nordic countries, this Finnish Lakeland hub sits in Pirkanmaa and ranks as the country's third-largest municipality — what is it?
Home to a famous Disney resort and both the Angels and the Ducks, which Orange County city is the most populous in its county?
Anaheim is a city in northern Orange County, California, United States, part of the Greater Los Angeles area.
Once the capital of a powerful medieval state, this Russian city sits where the Volga and Tvertsa rivers meet, about 110 miles northwest of Moscow — which is it?
Tver is a city and the administrative centre of tver Oblast, Russia.
Just 17 miles long and lying in the Mediterranean between Italy and Libya, which island — capital Valletta — is the largest of its archipelago?
Malta (island) — Malta is an island in Southern Europe.
Nicknamed "the Flying Scot," this driver won three Formula One titles with Tyrrell and retired holding the records for most wins and podiums — who is he?
A four-time Women's World Cup competitor who won it in 1991 and 1999, she was a founding player of the first U.S. professional women's soccer league — who is this soccer icon?
Nicknamed "the Say Hey Kid," this five-tool center fielder began in the Negro leagues with the Birmingham Black Barons before 23 MLB seasons with the Giants and Mets. Who is he?
This Malaysian shuttler held the world number one singles ranking for 349 weeks — including a 199-week streak — making him the only Malaysian to top the rankings for over a year. Who is he?
Lee Chong Wei: Malaysian badminton player (born 1982)
This American boxer was the undisputed middleweight champion from 2001 to 2005, racking up a record 20 title defenses before later claiming the light heavyweight crown. Who is he?

Until 1996 every member of this Florida-formed band took a stage name fusing a female sex symbol with a male serial killer; they were also the first act signed to Trent Reznor's Nothing Records — which band is it?
Marilyn Manson and the Spooky Kids
Marilyn Manson is an American rock band formed by namesake lead singer Marilyn Manson and guitarist Daisy Berkowitz in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, in 1989.
Behind soul hits like "Tired of Being Alone" and "Let's Stay Together," this Rock and Roll Hall of Famer later became an ordained pastor recording gospel in the 1980s — who is he?
Al Green: American soul singer, songwriter and pastor (born 1946)
This German Romantic — a jurist and composer as well as a writer — penned "The Sandman" and the novella behind Tchaikovsky's beloved Nutcracker ballet, who is it?
E. T. A. Hoffmann: German author (1776–1822)
Inspired by an Ed Sullivan Show performance at age ten, this Seattle-born saxophonist became the best-selling instrumentalist in history with over 75 million records — who is he?
Kenny G: American jazz saxophonist and composer (born 1956)
Recorded during a self-imposed Hawaiian exile after a notorious VMA interruption, this 2010 Kanye West album boasts guests from Nicki Minaj to Bon Iver to Elton John — what is it?
My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy: 2010 studio album by Kanye West
Set on the planet Azeroth and launched in 2004 for the franchise's 10th anniversary, this Blizzard MMORPG has spawned eleven major expansion packs — what is it?
His semi-autobiographical novels Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn, drawn from his life in New York and Paris, were banned in the United States until 1961 — who wrote them?
Nicknamed "The Lady in Gold," this Gustav Klimt canvas of a Viennese banker's wife — the crowning work of his golden phase — was stolen by the Nazis in 1941. What is it?
Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (Adele Bloch-Bauer I)
Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I: 1907 painting by Gustav Klimt
This pseudonymous Italian novelist, famous for the four Neapolitan Novels, has guarded her identity since her 1992 debut, insisting that books "have no need of their authors." Who is she?
Fill in the blank: “____ is a novel written by English author Jane Austen.”
Emma (novel) — Emma is a novel written by English author Jane Austen.

Defying his grandfather's wish that he practice law, this wealthy Indiana-born composer became a Broadway giant of the 1930s, and — unusually — wrote both the witty lyrics and the music for his songs. Who is he?
Cole Porter: American composer and songwriter (1891–1964)

This Irish-born British painter made raw, unsettling images of the human form — screaming popes, crucifixions, distorted friends — often working in triptychs, and destroyed many of his own canvases. Who is he?
Francis Bacon (artist): Irish-born British figurative painter (1909–1992)

This Salem-born author of "Twice-Told Tales" so disliked his first novel, 1828's "Fanshawe," that he later tried to suppress it entirely — who is the American writer of history, morality, and religion?
The Cornwall-loving English novelist behind "Jamaica Inn" and "My Cousin Rachel" also wrote two short stories — "The Birds" and "Don't Look Now" — that became famous films. Who is she?

A Danish painter who exhibited under the name Einar Wegener, this person became one of the earliest recipients of sex reassignment surgery, and her semi-autobiographical story was published in 1933 as "Man into Woman." Who is she?
Lili Elbe: Danish painter and transgender woman (1882–1931)

Conscripted as a poor peasant's son into the Imperial Russian Army, he rose to Marshal of the Soviet Union and served as Stalin's deputy commander overseeing the Red Army's biggest WWII victories — who was he?
In 1956, Britain, France, and Israel jointly invaded Egypt after Nasser nationalized a vital canal — what is this conflict commonly called?
Suez Crisis: 1956 British–French–Israeli invasion of Egypt
Fought from 1998 to 1999 between Yugoslav forces and an Albanian separatist militia, this conflict ended only after NATO air strikes drove Yugoslav troops out — which war is it?
Kosovo War: 1998–1999 armed conflict in the Balkans
The fifth governor of Roman Judaea under Tiberius, he presided over the trial of Jesus — and is so central to Christianity that he's named in both the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds; who is he?
Pontius Pilate: Roman governor of Judea and condemner of Jesus

Sometimes called the "Bonn Republic" after its capital, this Cold War state was assembled from twelve states across the American, British and French occupation zones and lasted until reunification in 1990. What was it?
history of West Germany from 1949 to 1990
West Germany was the common English name for the Federal Republic of Germany from its formation on 23 May 1949 until its reunification with East Germany on 3 October 1990.
Ectothermic four-limbed vertebrates whose only living members are frogs, salamanders, and the worm-like caecilians — what class of animal is this?
Sold as Zoloft, this SSRI antidepressant treats major depression, OCD, panic disorder, and social anxiety, with common side effects like nausea and insomnia — what is it?
Domesticated twice in the Neolithic — once near the Tigris Basin and once in China — this even-toed, hoofed omnivore is farmed mainly for pork; what is it?
Nicknamed the 'Bone,' this variable-sweep-wing heavy bomber was dreamed up to fuse the B-58's Mach 2 speed with the B-52's range and payload — which aircraft is it?
Rockwell B-1 Lancer: American strategic bomber
A rod-shaped gut bacterium that's mostly harmless or even helpful — some strains produce vitamin K2 and fend off nastier microbes — what is its name?

Fill in the blank: “____ is a British science fiction mystery thriller television miniseries primarily written and created for Netflix by Paul Tomalin and directed by Marco Kreuzpaintner and Haolu Wang.”

Bodies (2023 TV series) — Bodies is a British science fiction mystery thriller television miniseries primarily written and created for Netflix by Paul Tomalin and directed by Marco Kreuzpaintner and Haolu Wang.
Best known for hosting the motoring shows Top Gear and The Grand Tour, this English presenter also fronts Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? and a farming documentary series — who is he?
Jeremy Clarkson: English television presenter and farmer (born 1960)
A somma-stratovolcano on the Gulf of Naples whose 79 AD eruption buried Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Stabiae under stone and ash — what is it?
Mount Vesuvius: Active stratovolcano in the Gulf of Naples, Italy
Rising in the Swiss canton of Graubünden, this major European river traces stretches of the Franco-German border before turning west into the Netherlands and the North Sea — which river is it?
Rhine (RYNE) is one of the major rivers of Europe.

Sweden's second-largest lake is a long, finger-shaped sliver of fresh water whose deepest point sits 128 metres below sea level — and since 1832 the Göta Canal has linked it to the Kattegat. Which lake is it?
Vättern: Second largest lake in Sweden
Long before he became head coach of the U.S. men's national team, this Argentine centre-back helped Espanyol win their first trophy in 60 years — who is the manager?
Famed for seam, reverse swing, and a knack for the death overs, this Indian fast bowler also turns out for Bengal and the Lucknow Super Giants — who is he?
A left-handed bat who also bowls left-arm orthodox spin, this New Zealander has signed on with the Washington Freedoms and Kolkata Knight Riders — who is the cricketer?
Raised in Bakersfield and named MVP of the 2018 New Mexico Bowl with Utah State, which quarterback now lines up under center for the Green Bay Packers?
Jordan Love (born November 2, 1998) is an American professional football quarterback for the Green Bay Packers of the National Football League (NFL).

Headquartered in Issaquah, Washington, this membership-only big-box chain grew into the world's largest retailer of beef, poultry and wine — and sells its own "Kirkland Signature" house brand. What is it?
Costco: American multinational warehouse club chain
Begun in Landsberg Prison after a failed 1923 Munich coup and largely edited by Rudolf Hess, which two-volume manifesto of the 1920s spelled out its author's plans for Germany?
Mein Kampf: 1925 autobiography by Adolf Hitler
Rising from modest origins through the army's ranks, this third-century Roman emperor reunited a fracturing empire and earned the title Restitutor Orbis, "Restorer of the World" — who was he?
A former Fudan University law-school dean and professor of international politics, he became a leading Communist Party ideologist and now chairs the CPPCC — which Chinese politician?
Named Supreme Allied Commander on the Western Front in March 1918, this Marshal of France halted the German spring offensive and launched the counterattack that won the war — who was he?
Ferdinand Foch: French general and military theorist (1851–1929)
Prime Minister during the years Turkey joined NATO and fought in Korea, he became the last Turkish leader executed after a military coup, hanged in 1961 — who was he?
Adnan Menderes: 9th Prime Minister of the Republic of Turkey from 1950 to 1960
A writer who governed Tokyo from 1999 to 2012, this prominent ultranationalist was widely criticized for xenophobic and racist remarks against Chinese and Koreans in Japan — who was he?
A lawyer who entered politics during the Kaohsiung Incident, he became Taiwan's first president from the DPP in 2000, ending 55 years of Kuomintang rule — who is he?
Chen Shui-bian: President of the Republic of China from 2000 to 2008

Between 1885 and 1908, brutal rubber-collection policies under King Leopold II of Belgium — alongside famine and disease — caused a population collapse estimated at anywhere from 1.2 to 10 million. What is this dark chapter called?
Atrocities in the Congo Free State

From 1885 to 1908, many atrocities were committed in the Congo Free State (today the Democratic Republic of the Congo) under the absolute rule of King Leopold II of Belgium.
Atrocities in the Congo Free State
Son of Cnut the Great, this ruler was the last monarch of the North Sea Empire uniting England and Denmark before dying suddenly in 1042 — who was he?
Harthacnut Cnutsson, King of England and Denmark
Harthacnut: King of England (1040–42) and Denmark (1035–42)

This Colombian liberal politician and journalist, who founded the New Liberalism movement and declared himself an enemy of the drug cartels, was assassinated in 1989 before the presidential vote — who was he?
This retired military officer studied law in Rangoon, led the Tatmadaw from 2011, and has ruled his country since seizing power in a February 2021 coup — who is he?
Maha Thray Sithu Thiri Thudhamma Min Aung Hlaing
Senior General U Min Aung Hlaing
Maha Thray Sithu Min Aung Hlaing
Senior General Maha Thray Sithu Min Aung Hlaing
Min Aung Hlaing: Burmese politician and military officer (born 1956)
This New Zealand driver-engineer won the 1966 24 Hours of Le Mans and founded the racing team that still bears his name — winning his own team's first F1 race at Belgium in 1968 — who was he?
Bruce McLaren: New Zealand racing driver and motorsport executive (1937–1970)
Introduced to acting by his brother Germán "Tin-Tan" Valdés, this Mexican comedian is best remembered as Don Ramón on the sitcom El Chavo del Ocho — who was he?
A Groundlings alum, she turned her outsider status into back-to-back Emmys for a reality show literally titled "My Life on the D-List" — which comedian?
Kathy Griffin: American comedian and actress (born 1960)
Nicknamed "The Man of a Thousand Voices," he's widely regarded as the greatest voice actor of all time, famous for the Looney Tunes cast and his radio work alongside Jack Benny — who was he?
The Man of a Thousand Voices
Mel Blanc: American voice actor and radio personality (1908–1989)
One of the last surviving stars of Hollywood's golden age, this French ballerina-turned-actress made her film debut in An American in Paris and won a BAFTA playing an orphan in Lili — who is she?
Leslie Caron: French and American actress and dancer (born 1931)
She got her start by winning a Vogue essay contest in the 1950s, then chronicled California, the counterculture, and Hollywood as a pioneer of New Journalism — who is this writer?
A leading light of Indian parallel cinema known for portraying strong, independent women, she won two National Film Awards and the Padma Shri before dying tragically young at 31 — which actress?
He created and hosted American Top 40 and was also the first actor to voice Shaggy Rogers in Scooby-Doo — who was this disc jockey?
Casey Kasem: American disc jockey and actor (1932–2014)
This acclaimed German-speaking actor, whose family fled Austria for Switzerland in 1938, won the Best Actor Oscar for playing a lawyer on screen — who is he?
Maximilian Schell: Swiss actor, filmmaker, and theatre director (1930–2014)
This Russian actor and director, popular across Eastern Europe, starred in Vampire Academy and Soulless and appeared in the TV series Vikings — who is he?
Danila Kozlovsky: Russian film and theater actor and director
Over a career spanning eight decades, this Indian playback singer won a record seven Filmfare Best Female Playback awards and earned two Grammy nominations — who is she?
This Filipino pool legend with over 100 international titles was the first player to win world championships in two different pool disciplines — who is he?
A star of dozens of 1920s silent films, she earned her most famous Oscar nomination for Billy Wilder's Sunset Boulevard in 1950 — who is she?

The voice behind Homer Simpson — plus Grampa, Krusty, and Groundskeeper Willie — this actor also voiced Grandpa Phil on Hey Arnold! — who is he?
Ukraine's third-largest city, a Black Sea port whose 19th-century centre was declared a World Heritage Site in Danger in 2023 — which multiethnic city is it?
Odesa is the third-most populous city and municipality in Ukraine and a major seaport and transport hub located in the south-west of the country, on the northwestern shore of the Black Sea.
Famous for its Art Nouveau entrances and dense network of sixteen numbered lines — plus odd branches like 3bis and 7bis — which 245-km transit system serves a European capital?
The Paris Metro, short for Métropolitain, is a rapid transit system serving the Paris metropolitan area in Île-de-France, the region of France's capital.
The largest city in England's East Midlands and the county town of its shire, it has topped the Good Growth for Cities ranking for the region three years running — which city?
Leicester: City and unitary authority in England
The tenth-largest city in England sits on the River Sherbourne, has been a settlement for centuries, and won its formal city charter back in 1345 — which West Midlands cathedral city is it?
Coventry: Cathedral city in the West Midlands, England
Northern Ireland's second-largest city straddles the River Foyle, with its old walled core on the west bank facing Waterside on the east — which city, sitting close to the Donegal border, is it?
Fill in the blank: “____ is a city in the northwest section of the U.S.”
Reno, Nevada is a city in the northwest section of the U.S.
Sweden's largest island — home to the walled town of Visby and the nearby Karlsö and Fårö islets — which Baltic island is it?
Gotland: Island and historical province in Sweden

Born from a 1960s plan to relieve London's housing congestion, this Buckinghamshire new town was deliberately laid out as well-delineated neighborhoods, with a quarter of it parkland — which city is it?
Milton Keynes: City in Buckinghamshire, England
Nicknamed "The Manassa Mauler," this heavyweight champion from 1919 to 1926 was voted by the Associated Press the greatest fighter of the previous 50 years — who was he?
A sharpshooting guard who starred for Cibona and Real Madrid before reaching the NBA in 1989, he collected Olympic silvers and a 1986 World Championship MVP before dying at 28 — which Croatian great?
Liverpool's all-time leading goalscorer with 346 goals, this Welsh forward also long held his nation's scoring record with 28 goals — who is he?
Ian Rush: Welsh footballer and manager (born 1961)
Charismatic and famously outspoken, this English manager won back-to-back European Cups with unfancied Nottingham Forest and took the English league title with two different clubs — who was he?
Brian Clough: English football player and manager (1935–2004)
Pelé called him the greatest defender he ever faced — this West Ham captain lifted the 1966 World Cup as England's skipper — who was he?
She originated Anita in West Side Story and Velma Kelly in Chicago, and in 2002 became the first Latina to receive a Kennedy Center Honor — who was this Broadway legend?
Chita Rivera: American actress, dancer and singer (1933–2024)
