A Western European power whose territory extends from the Rhine to the Atlantic and from the Mediterranean to the English Channel, with overseas regions from South America to Oceania—which continental and overseas republic borders eight neighboring lands?
France: Country primarily in Western Europe

Straddling West Asia and Southeast Europe, mostly in Anatolia but with a foothold across the Bosphorus, home to over 86 million people including Turks and Kurds, with Istanbul as its economic beating heart—which country's capital sits inland in Ankara?
Turkey: Country in Southeastern Europe and West Asia

Eastern Europe's second-largest nation after one colossal neighbor, stretching from the Black Sea eastward with Kyiv as its gleaming capital and over 32 million residents—which country's waters touch both the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov?

The second-largest country by total area, stretching from Atlantic to Pacific to Arctic, with the world's longest coastline and sharing an even longer border with one southern neighbor—which North American power claims ten provinces and three territories?

The world's flattest and driest inhabited continent, the sixth-largest country by area, comprising a massive mainland, Tasmania, and countless smaller islands teeming with unique biodiversity—which island nation saw its Aboriginal ancestors arrive 50,000 to 65,000 years ago?

A Mediterranean peninsula crowned by the Alps, with nearly 800 islands including Sicily and Sardinia, the EU's third-most populous member with nearly 59 million people and Rome as its eternal capital—which European nation enclaves both Vatican City and San Marino?
Italy: Country in Southern and Western Europe

A West Asian nation historically called Persia, bordering Iraq to the west and Pakistan to the southeast, spanning five regions and 31 provinces with over 92 million residents, home to one of the world's oldest continuous civilizations—which country's capital Tehran anchors its economic heartland?

An island nation of over 60 satellite islands clustered just one degree north of the equator, off the Malay Peninsula's tip, bordering the Strait of Malacca and the South China Sea—which island microstate was historically a maritime emporium called Temasek?
Singapore: Island country in Southeast Asia

A Southern European kingdom commanding the Iberian Peninsula, extending to North African enclaves and Atlantic and Mediterranean archipelagos, the EU's fourth-most populous member featuring continental Europe's southernmost point—which European power straddles multiple ocean basins?
Spain: Country in Southern and Western Europe

A mountain plateau city between the Mediterranean and Dead Sea, one of humanity's oldest settlements, revered by Judaism, Christianity, and Islam alike, destroyed twice, besieged 23 times, and captured and recaptured 44 times—which contested metropolis do two nations both claim as capital?
Jerusalem: City in the Southern Levant

A landlocked Alpine nation at the intersection of Central, Western, and Southern Europe, 75 percent mountainous, with nine million people concentrated on the plateau hosting Zurich, Geneva, Bern, and Basel—which federal republic comprises 26 cantons?

A Northwestern European nation with overseas Caribbean territories, twelve provinces and three special municipalities, sharing land borders with Germany and Belgium, and maritime boundaries with the UK and Germany in the North Sea—which dual-continent country speaks Dutch and (in the Caribbean) Papiamento?
Netherlands: Country in Northwestern Europe and the Caribbean

A West Asian nation covering most of the Arabian Peninsula, 2.15 million square kilometers, the fifth-largest in Asia and the only country touching both the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf, home to over 100 million implicitly—which Middle Eastern kingdom anchors the region?
Saudi Arabia: Country in West Asia

An archipelagic Southeast Asian and Oceanian nation spanning over 17,000 islands including Sumatra, Java, Sulawesi, and portions of Borneo and New Guinea, the world's largest archipelago by land area, teeming with extraordinary biodiversity—which megadiverse nation straddles the Indian and Pacific oceans?
Indonesia: Country in Southeast Asia and Oceania
It's the only place we know with liquid surface water—and it covers nearly three-quarters of this planet's crust. What are we talking about?
Earth: Third planet from the Sun
Fifth-largest country by area and seventh by population—but the only place in the Americas where Portuguese is the official language. Which South American giant are we describing?
An island nation nestled between the East and South China Seas with mountains dominating two-thirds of its terrain. Known officially as the Republic of China, what is this East Asian nation?

The world's fifth-most populous nation and home to the second-largest Muslim population as of 2023—it's bounded by the Arabian Sea and shares borders with four major neighbors. Which South Asian country is this?
From the Baltic Sea in the north to mountain ranges in the south, this Central European nation is the fifth-most populous EU member. Which country extends from the sea to the Sudetes and Carpathians?
Home to 107 million people—making it the most populous Arab nation and Africa's third-most populous—this transcontinental country spans northeast Africa and southwest Asia. What is it?
With coastlines on both the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean, this Maghreb nation claims disputed territory and Spanish exclaves along its northern border. What North African kingdom is this?
Half of the Korean Peninsula, half of a divided people—but it's got the ninth most populous metropolitan area in the world concentrated in one gleaming capital region. What is this East Asian nation?
South Korea: Country in East Asia
The northern half of the Peninsula, bordered by China and Russia, sealed from the world by an heavily militarized demilitarized zone. Which reclusive East Asian nation is this?
North Korea: Country in East Asia
Second-largest country in South America, eighth-largest in the world—spanning the southern cone with coastline, mountains, and plains. Which South American nation is this?
Known as CR7, this Portuguese forward has won five Ballons d'Or and a record three UEFA Men's Player of the Year Awards. Who is widely considered one of the greatest players in football history?
Eight Ballons d'Or, 46 team trophies, and in 2025 crowned the All Time Men's World Best Player by the IFFHS—this Argentine forward just captains Inter Miami. Who is one of the greatest in history?
Renowned for his crossing and set-piece mastery, he's the only English player to win league titles in four different countries — who is he?

Ranked world No. 1 for a record 428 weeks, this Serbian tennis legend won 24 majors (including a record ten Australian Opens)—the only man to hold all four titles at once across three different surfaces. Who is this tennis icon?
Born in 2000 and already called the greatest Norwegian player of all time—this Manchester City striker is known for speed, strength, and finishing inside the box. Who is he?
At eighteen he became the second-most-expensive player ever with a €180 million move to PSG, prized for his blistering pace and finishing — who is he?

An eleven-time Pro Bowler and seven-time All-Pro tight end who's won three Super Bowls with the Kansas City Chiefs—he holds the record for most consecutive and most overall seasons with 1,000 receiving yards at his position. Who is he?

Six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls, legendary figure of the 1980s and '90s—and as of 2026, the wealthiest athlete of all time with a 4.3 billion dollar net worth. Who is widely considered the greatest basketball player ever?
Michael Jordan: American basketball player and businessman (born 1963)
One of only five players to score 100 goals with three different clubs, this dribbling wizard is Brazil's all-time top scorer — who is he?
At just 22 years old (born 2003), this Spanish prodigy has already won seven majors and completed the career Grand Slam—the youngest man to do so. Who is this rising tennis superstar?
Famed for acrobatic volleys and physical dominance, this Swedish striker won 34 trophies and found the net in four consecutive decades — who is he?

The highest-grossing live music artist and wealthiest female musician of all time—known for autobiographical songwriting and constant artistic reinvention across country, rock, and pop. Who is this cultural icon?

A short-lived rapper and SoundCloud icon born in 1998 who pioneered emo rap and SoundCloud rap as a genre—known for exploring everything from trap metal to indie rock. Who was this controversial musical innovator?

A Russian tech company with 72% market share in its home country's search space and the largest ridesharing service there—but founded in 1997 to handle information differently. What is this Russian tech giant?

Founded in 1998 by Larry Page and Sergey Brin, this multinational dominates search, email, cloud computing, and AI—called the most powerful company in the world by the BBC. What is this tech colossus?
Crowned the "Queen of Rock 'n' Roll," she first found fame in the 1960s as half of an explosive husband-wife R&B duo behind "Proud Mary" — who is she?

An Irish singer-songwriter (1966-2023) who drew attention to child abuse, human rights, and women's rights while openly discussing her activism and mental health struggles. Who released 'I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got' in 1990?
Sinéad O'Connor: Irish singer and songwriter (1966–2023)

Dubbed the 'King of Pop,' this dancer and entertainer brought the moonwalk and anti-gravity lean to the world—breaking American racial barriers through music and visual performance. Who is widely regarded as the greatest entertainer of all time?
Born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar to Parsi parents, this four-octave frontman defied every rock convention from behind his piano — who was he?
Freddie Mercury: British rock musician and songwriter (1946–1991)
Dubbed the "Queen of Power Ballads," this best-selling Canadian artist was discovered as a teen by her future husband and manager, René Angélil — who is she?

A Catalan politician and journalist who served as president of Catalonia from 2016 to 2017, holding an independence referendum that ended his political career in Spain. Who is this controversial Catalan leader?
Carles Puigdemont: Politician and journalist from Catalonia, Spain (born 1962)
Educated at Gordonstoun and Cambridge before serving in the Royal Air Force, this monarch was created Prince of Wales in 1958 — who is he?
The Prince Charles, Prince of Wales
Prince Charles Philip Arthur George, Prince of Wales
Prince Charles Philip Arthur George of Edinburgh
The Prince Charles Philip Arthur George, Prince of Wales
Charles III: King of the United Kingdom since 2022

Only one capital city on Earth has land borders with two other sovereign nations—a rare geographic quirk that makes it a bridge between three countries. Which river-hugging seat of government in Southwestern Europe claims this unique distinction?
Bratislava: Capital and largest city of Slovakia

Founded in the 5th century at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, this capital city once served as the seat of the Caucasus Viceroyalty under Russian rule. What centuries-old Georgia city stands as a bridge between continents?
Tbilisi: Capital and the largest city of Georgia (country)

Founded in 1088, it's the oldest university in continuous operation on Earth—and the Italian city that houses it has been a powerhouse since the Etruscans called it by a different name. What city claims the world's most venerable academic institution?
Bologna: Capital and largest city of Emilia-Romagna, Italy

Founded in 1538 by Spanish conquistador Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada, it became the political and economic heart of an entire region and northern continent. What South American capital serves as the primary hub for its nation and beyond?
Bogotá: Capital and largest city of Colombia

The fourth-most populous city in the United States sits near the Gulf of Mexico in Southeast Texas, and its city government remains uniquely unconsolidated with any county. What sprawling Texas metropolis covers nearly 1,700 square kilometers with 2.3 million residents?
Houston: Largest city in Texas, United States

This capital stands on the River Dâmbovița in southeast Romania as the ninth most populous city by city-proper population in the entire European Union. What Romanian metropolis ranks among the EU's most populated urban centers?
Bucharest: Capital and largest city of Romania
Grouped as New England, Middle, and Southern, these British possessions on North America's Atlantic coast broke away to form the United States — what are they collectively called?

The Thirteen Colonies were the British colonies on the Atlantic coast of North America which broke away from the British Crown in the American Revolutionary War, and joined to form the United States of America.
The Thirteen Colonies in their traditional groupings were: the New England Colonies (Province of New Hampshire, Province of Massachusetts Bay, Colony of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, and Connecticut Colony); the Middle Colonies (Province of New York, Province of New Jersey, Province of Pennsylvania, and Delaware Colony); and the Southern Colonies (Province of Maryland, Colony of Virginia, Province of North Carolina, Province of South Carolina, and Province of Georgia).
As a Princeton grad student this mathematician dreamed up an "equilibrium" concept that won him a 1994 Nobel in Economics — who was he?
John Forbes Nash Jr.: American mathematician and Nobel Laureate (1928–2015)
Greeks call it "the co-capital," a nod to its role beside Constantinople in the Byzantine Empire — which is Greece's second-largest city, on the Thermaic Gulf?

At 436,551 residents within the city proper, it's Switzerland's largest city and largest railway hub—yet evidence of human habitation stretches back more than 6,400 years. What lakeside Swiss metropolis has been a crossroads since prehistoric times?

Home to Africa's largest artificial port and the Royal Moroccan Navy's main base, this Moroccan economic powerhouse sprawls across the Atlantic coast with over 4 million people in its metro area. Which city?
Russell Crowe stars in this 2001 Ron Howard film about a Nobel Prize-winning mathematician's struggle with schizophrenia, based on Sylvia Nasar's biography. What's the title?
A Beautiful Mind is a 2001 American biographical drama film about the mathematician John Nash who won a Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences.

This actress, personal assistant, and record exec appeared in "Lost Highway" and "Ellie Parker"—and the film "Mulholland Drive" was dedicated to her memory after her tragic death in 2001. Who was she?
Jennifer Syme: American actress, production assistant, and record executive (1972–2001)
Founded in 1040, this Nordic capital spent centuries under personal unions with Denmark but became the seat of royalty around 1300. Which Scandinavian city is it?
Oslo: Capital and most populous city of Norway
One of the world's oldest cities with over 3,400 years of recorded history, this Mediterranean coastal capital is the southernmost capital city on mainland Europe. Which is it?
Athens: Capital and largest city of Greece
Covering 60,000 km² and home to 600,000 people, this landmass is the only part of Egypt in West Asia—a bridge between Africa and Asia between two major seas. What is it?
The Sinai Peninsula, or simply Sinai, is a peninsula in Egypt, and the only part of the country located in West Asia.
Oscar Wilde's only novel, published in 1890–91, centers on a portrait that ages while its subject stays eternally young—a Gothic meditation on vanity and corruption. What's the title?
The Picture of Dorian Gray: 1890 novel by Oscar Wilde
Perched at 1,000 feet above sea level in the Appalachian foothills, this Georgia capital is the 36th-most populous US city and anchors the sixth-largest metro area in the country. Which city?
Atlanta: Capital and most populous city of Georgia, U.S.
Nestled in the Nafud desert at 600 meters elevation, this Arabian Peninsula city evolved from an 18th-century walled town in the 1950s and draws 5 million tourists yearly. Which capital?
Riyadh: Capital and largest city of Saudi Arabia
Indonesia's sprawling de facto capital covers 662 km² and anchors the world's most populous metropolitan area with over 40 million people. Which city?
Jakarta: De facto capital and largest city in Indonesia
This African megacity home to nearly 10 million people counts the ancient Giza pyramids and Memphis within its modern sprawl—what is it?
Cairo: Capital and largest city of Egypt
The fourth-most populous German city sits on the Rhine River and anchors a metropolitan region—named by the river it's about 22 kilometers northwest of which former West German capital?
Cologne: Largest city in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany
UNESCO calls this Brazilian megacity the World Capital of Gastronomy, and the Globalization and World Cities Research Network ranks it as an alpha global city. What is it?
São Paulo: Most populous city in Brazil
Guided by the Roman poet Virgil through nine concentric circles of torment, which first part of Dante's Divine Comedy describes a journey through Hell?
Inferno (Dante) — Inferno (Italian for 'Hell') is the first part of the Italian writer Dante Alighieri's 14th-century narrative poem The Divine Comedy, followed by Purgatorio and Paradiso.
Founded in 1642 as Ville-Marie (City of Mary), this Quebec city takes its name from a triple-peaked mountain at its center. What is it?
Montreal: Largest city in Quebec, Canada
Climbers call this Karakoram peak the Savage Mountain because it 'tries to kill you'—it's the deadliest of the world's five highest summits. What is it?
Sitting where the Sava and Danube rivers meet, this Southeast European capital is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on the continent. What is it?
Belgrade: Capital and largest city of Serbia
This seven-decade music titan won 28 Grammys, a Tony, and an Emmy—he was born in Chicago, moved to Seattle after World War II, and became a legendary arranger and producer. Who is he?
Quincy Jones: American record producer and musician (1933–2024)
Founded in 1565 and later home to the Portuguese royal court in 1808, this second-most-populous Brazilian city sits on the Atlantic coast. What is it?
Rio de Janeiro: Second-largest city in Brazil
This Nordic capital stretches across fourteen islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic, and was founded in 1252 by statesman Birger Jarl. What is it?
Stockholm: Capital and most populous city of Sweden
The largest and most populous Greek island, this Mediterranean giant lies 100 kilometers south of the Peloponnese and has 1,046 kilometers of coastline. What is it?
Home to the European Central Bank, this German city is one of four institutional seats of the European Union and forms a continuous conurbation with Offenbach. What is it?
Frankfurt: Largest city in Hesse, Germany
This Spanish midfielder from the Barcelona youth academy joined at age 11 and made over 1,000 professional career appearances—widely regarded as one of the greatest of all time. Who is he?

Xavi (footballer, born 1980) — Xavi (born 25 January 1980), commonly known as xavi Hernndez or simply xavi, is a Spanish professional football manager and former player who most recently managed La Liga club Barcelona.
Born Saul Hudson in London and nicknamed by actor Seymour Cassel, this hard rock lead guitarist is considered one of the greatest in history. Who is he?

Slash (musician) — Slash (born 23 July 1965), known professionally as slash, is a British and American musician, best known as the lead guitarist of the hard rock band Guns N' Roses, with whom he achieved worldwide success beginning in the late 1980s.
This Italian birthplace of the Renaissance was a center of medieval trade and finance, and ruled by the powerful Medici family during its rise to influence. What is it?
Florence: Largest city in Tuscany, Italy
With 30 million people, this Chinese metropolis is now the fifth-largest city in the world and home to the world's busiest container port. What is it?
Shanghai: Municipality and largest city in China
Settled as a Viking fishing village in the 10th century and separated from a Swedish city by the Øresund strait, this Nordic capital became Denmark's seat in the early 15th century. What is it?
Copenhagen: Capital and most populous city of Denmark
Sitting on the Río de la Plata and classified as an Alpha− global city, this Argentine capital is known for eclectic European architecture and rich cultural life. What is it?
Buenos Aires: Capital and most populous city of Argentina
Founded in 1630 by English Puritan settlers on the Shawmut Peninsula, this Northeastern U.S. city serves as the cultural and financial center of New England. What is it?
Boston: Capital and largest city in Massachusetts, United States
Canadian artist born in 1988 who weaves sci-fi and feminism into electronic soundscapes and rose to prominence with 'Visions' in 2012—who earned a Juno for Electronic Album?
Grimes: Canadian singer, songwriter and record producer (born 1988)
Poland's sixth-largest EU city by population sits on the River Vistula, serving as the nation's political, economic, and cultural heart—what's this capital?
Warsaw: Capital and largest city of Poland
Fourth-most populous in North America, straddling Lake Ontario's northwestern shore—it anchors a metropolitan area of over 7 million—what's Canada's largest city?
Toronto: Most populous city in Canada
South Korea's capital (population 9.6 million) whose metropolitan area became the world's sixth-largest metro economy by 2022—founded in 18 BC—what's this city?
Seoul: Capital and largest city of South Korea
Thailand's megacity (9.1 million people) sprawls across the Chao Phraya River delta, with over 17 million in its metropolitan region—what's this economic powerhouse?
Bangkok: Capital and largest city of Thailand
Founded by the Teutonic Knights in 1255 and known as Königsberg until 1946, which Russian exclave city is its only ice-free Baltic port?

Kaliningrad (known as Knigsberg until 1946) is the largest city and administrative centre of kaliningrad Oblast, an exclave of Russia between Lithuania and Poland (663 kilometres (412 mi) west of the bulk of Russia).
American military police procedural that premiered on CBS in 2003, spinoff from JAG, now the first installment of a major franchise—what's this show?
NCIS (TV series) — NCIS is an American military police procedural television series and the first installment within the ncis media franchise.
Spain's capital and second-largest city in the EU (3.4 million), sits 660 meters above sea level on the River Manzanares—what's this political, economic, and cultural center?
Madrid: Capital and largest city of Spain
The Netherlands' capital, colloquially called 'Venice of the North' for its UNESCO-heritage canal system, grew from a 12th-century fishing village into a major world port—what's this city?
Amsterdam: Capital and largest city of the Netherlands
Czech Republic's capital on the Vltava River, twelfth-largest in the EU, former seat of multiple Holy Roman Emperors and Habsburg stronghold—what's this historic city?
Prague: Capital and largest city of the Czech Republic
Europe's second-longest river flows 2,850 km southeast from Germany's Black Forest through ten countries to Romania's delta—once a Roman frontier—what's this historic waterway?
Puerto Rican rapper (born 1994) credited with bringing Spanish-language rap to mainstream global popularity, earning him the title 'King of Latin Trap'—who?
Bad Bunny: Puerto Rican rapper, actor and record producer (born 1994)

The Great Fire of 1871 leveled several square miles of this Midwestern metropolis, which grew rapidly from its position near a historic portage between the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River watershed. Today it's the third-most populous city in the US—what is it?
Chicago: Most populous city in Illinois, United States

Home to nearly 2.9 million people in its metro area—about a third of its entire nation—this capital sits on the river that shares its name, nestled where the Alps' foothills give way to the lowlands. What's this cultural and political powerhouse?
Vienna: Capital and largest city of Austria

With 3.7 million people within its city limits—the highest in the EU—this German capital is uniquely small by area among the states it belongs to. Surrounded by Brandenburg, it's the seat of which nation's government?
Berlin: Capital and largest city of Germany

Spread across 1,287 square kilometers and home to 2.7 million residents, this capital lies along the Tiber Valley in the central-western Italian Peninsula. It's the third-most populous city in the EU by city limits—but which capital is it?
Rome: Capital and largest city of Italy

Standing on the Moskva River with over 13 million residents within its limits—the highest for any entirely-European city—this metropolis anchors an urban area of 19.1 million. What's the capital and largest city of Russia?
Moscow: Capital and most populous city of Russia

Formerly known as Petrograd and later Leningrad, this city sits on the Neva River where the Baltic Sea begins, and ranks as the fourth-most populous in Europe. It's Russia's second-largest city—what's this former imperial capital?
Saint Petersburg: Second-largest city in Russia
Known locally as Sagarmāthā in one country and Qomolangma in another, this mountain was measured in 2020 by joint survey as 8,848.86 meters tall. Which peak stands as Earth's highest above sea level?
Mount Everest (known locally as Sagarmth in Nepal and Qomolangma in Tibet Autonomous Region of China) is the highest mountain on Earth above sea level.

The second-most populous US city after New York with 3.87 million residents, it's the commercial and cultural center of a sprawling Southern California region of over 18 million people. Also known as L.A., which Pacific-coast metropolis is it?
Los Angeles: Most populous city in California, U.S.

Straddling two continents with about two-thirds of its 15+ million residents living in one and the rest in the other, this Turkish megacity sits on one of the world's busiest waterways. Which transcontinental city commands the Bosphorus?
Founded in a Seattle garage in 1994 selling books by mail, it now runs the world's largest cloud-computing business. Name it.
Two Stanford PhD students built its search engine in 1998; the parent company renamed itself Alphabet in 2015. Name the search company.
A Swedish teenager founded it in 1943 selling pens and wallets by mail order; it is now the world's biggest furniture retailer. Name it.
It began in 1971 as a single Seattle store selling beans, not drinks, and took its name from a character in Moby-Dick. Name it.
Founded in 1837 by a candle maker and a soap maker who had married sisters, it owns Tide, Pampers and Gillette. Name it.
A Japanese loom manufacturer spun off an automobile division in 1937; it became the world's largest carmaker. Name it.
Its founder sold vacuum cleaners door to door before launching a DVD-by-mail service in 1997 that later killed Blockbuster. Name it.
A Dutch company founded in 1891 making light bulbs, it later invented the compact cassette and co-invented the CD. Name it.
Founded in 1976 and named after a fruit, its first product was a circuit board sold without a case, keyboard or screen. Name it.
A Korean trading company started in 1938 exporting dried fish and noodles; it is now the world's largest maker of memory chips. Name it.
Its name is a portmanteau of the founder's surname and 'electronics'; it built the PlayStation and the Walkman. Name it.
Founded in 1903 in Milwaukee, it is the only major American motorcycle maker to survive the Great Depression. Name it.
A Finnish paper mill founded in 1865 that became, for a decade, the world's biggest seller of mobile phones. Name it.
This Italian carmaker's badge carries a prancing horse, given to its founder by the mother of a World War I flying ace. Name it.
Dolphins, porpoises, beaked whales and sperm whales all belong to this cetacean group that diverged from baleen whales around 34 million years ago — what's the collective name?

Toothed whale (also called odontocetes, systematic name Odontoceti) are a parvorder of cetaceans that includes dolphins, porpoises, and all other whales with teeth, such as beaked whales and the sperm whales.
At just 14 he became the youngest male ever to represent his country, and as the host nation's star he was the most successful athlete at the Sydney 2000 Olympics. Which Australian swimmer is he?
Ian Thorpe (born 13 October 1982) is an Australian retired swimmer who specialised in freestyle, but also competed in backstroke and the individual medley.

A Swiss pedagogue and educational reformer (1746–1827) whose motto was "Learning by head, hand and heart." He founded institutions across German- and French-speaking Switzerland and revolutionized education. Who is he?
Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi (12 January 1746 - 17 February 1827) was a Swiss pedagogue and educational reformer who exemplified Romanticism in his approach.
Dissolved in water it yields a notoriously corrosive acid, yet it's also the main industrial route to fluorine and a feedstock for Teflon-style polymers like PTFE — which colorless compound is it?
Hydrogen fluoride is an inorganic compound with chemical formula HF.
With the formula AgNO3, this colorless, highly water-soluble compound is the least expensive salt of a lustrous precious metal and a precursor to many similar compounds — name it?
Silver nitrate is an inorganic compound with chemical formula AgNO3.

Found naturally in many plants and abbreviated "Bz," this white crystalline compound is the simplest of the aromatic carboxylic acids and lends its salts to the world of food preservatives — what is it?
Benzoic acid is a white or colorless crystalline organic compound with the formula C6H5COOH, whose structure consists of a benzene ring (C6H6) with a carboxyl (C(=O)OH) substituent.
This steep-sided, flat-topped County Sligo mountain was carved into shape as a nunatak during the last Ice Age, and sits in an area locals fondly call "Yeats Country" — what is it?

Benbulbin is a steep-sided and flat-topped mountain in County Sligo, Ireland. Benbulbin (Irish: Binn Ghulbain), sometimes Benbulben or Ben Bulben, is a steep-sided and flat-topped mountain in County Sligo, Ireland.
Played since at least 1650 BCE and surviving today as "ulama," this ritual pre-Columbian sport likely resembled racquetball, the aim being to keep the ball in play — what is it?
Formed in Detroit in 1997, this two-piece — guitar plus drums — became a leading force of the 2000s garage rock revival before winning their first Grammys for the album 'Elephant.' Who are they?
The White Stripes were an American rock duo formed in Detroit, Michigan, in 1997.
Its name means 'Lady Moon,' but this Afghan archaeological site is really the ruins of a Hellenistic city founded by the early Seleucids and destroyed around 145 BC — what is it?
Ai-Khanoum (meaning 'Lady Moon') is the archaeological site of a Hellenistic city in Takhar Province, Afghanistan.
Three of this American novelist's books — including 'The Accidental Tourist' — were Pulitzer finalists, and 'Breathing Lessons' finally won the prize in 1989. Who is she?
Anne Tyler (born October 25, 1941) is an American novelist, short story writer, and literary critic.

Also called prussic acid, this highly toxic and flammable liquid boils just above room temperature at 25.6 degrees Celsius. It is produced industrially as a precursor to many chemical compounds, particularly potassium cyanide and adiponitrile. What is it?
Hydrogen cyanide (also called prussic acid) is a chemical compound with the formula HCN and structural formula HCN.
Often called the greatest Polish composer since Chopin, this 20th-century conductor wrote four symphonies and a 1954 Concerto for Orchestra — but, tellingly, never an opera. Who was he?
Witold Lutosławski (25 January 1913 - 7 February 1994) was a Polish composer and conductor.

She was made a Dame on her deathbed in 1979, but decades earlier this music-hall star ranked among Britain's top ten film stars of the 1930s, famous for never shedding her thick Lancashire accent. Who is she?
Gracie Fields (born Grace Stansfield; 9 January 1898 - 27 September 1979) was a British actress, singer and comedian.
Hailed as a defining work of electronica, this debut by Richard D. James drew on tracks he'd taped as a teenager and is credited with introducing techno to fans of indie music. What album is it?
Selected Ambient Works 85–92 is the debut album by the British electronic music artist and producer Aphex Twin, whose real name is Richard D. James.
A Harlem Renaissance poet and novelist, this writer also served from 1920 to 1930 as the operating leader of the NAACP — who was he?
James Weldon Johnson (June 17, 1871 - June 26, 1938) was an American writer and civil rights activist.
Beginning with dukkha and moving through craving and its cessation, this Buddhist framework is described as 'how things really are when seen correctly' — what is it?
Four Noble Truths: Formulaic summary of Buddhist doctrines.
Signed to Columbia in 1996, this Houston girl group helped shape contemporary R&B with their harmonies and empowerment themes before the trio era — who were they?
Destiny's Child was an American girl group formed in Houston, Texas, in 1990.

Its severe, chronic form is called beriberi — a name possibly borrowed from a Sinhalese phrase meaning "I cannot, I cannot," for the weakness it causes; a shortage of which vitamin (B1) is the culprit?
With the formula Na2CO3, this odorless white salt yields an alkaline solution in water and earned the name 'soda ash' because plant ashes once gave it up. What is it?
Sodium carbonate (also known as washing soda, soda ash, sal soda, and soda crystals) is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2CO3 and its various hydrates.

Fought almost entirely at sea from 1798 to 1800 after France began seizing American ships, this undeclared conflict pitted the young United States against the French First Republic — what was it called?
Quasi-War: Undeclared naval war between the United States and France, 1798–1800.
