Succeeding his father Babur at just 22, this second Mughal emperor lost his entire realm to a rival before reclaiming the throne shortly before his death in 1556. Who is he?
Humayun: Mughal emperor from 1530 to 1540 and from 1555 to 1556.

After his first wife, heir to the British throne, died in childbirth, this prince — offered the Greek crown following that country's war of independence — instead became first king of a newly independent European nation in 1831. Who was he?
Leopold I of Belgium: King of the Belgians from 1831 to 1865.
Leading the Argonauts on a quest for the Golden Fleece, this Greek hero married the sorceress Medea, granddaughter of the sun god. Who is he?
Jason: Greek mythological hero and leader of the Argonauts.
An investigative journalist and fierce critic of a former Ecuadorian president, this presidential candidate had once been jailed and exiled before running in the 2023 election. Who was he?
A former AFL quarterback turned nine-term congressman, this politician served as HUD secretary under George H.W. Bush before running for vice president alongside Bob Dole in 1996. Who is he?
Jack Kemp: American politician and football player (1935–2009)
Known by the art name Unam, this authoritarian leader served as South Korea's first president from 1948 until his resignation in 1960?
Syngman Rhee: President of South Korea from 1948 to 1960. Born in Hwanghae Province during the Joseon period, Rhee attended a local Methodist school, where he converted to Christianity.
Born in London to a Pakistani family, this Labour politician served as MP for Tooting before becoming the third mayor of London in 2016?
Sadiq Khan: Mayor of London since 2016. Sir Sadiq Aman Khan (born 8 October 1970) is a British politician serving as the third and current strategic authority mayor for London since 2016.
Styled Viscount Althorp until 1975, this British peer and courtier was the father of Diana, Princess of Wales, and maternal grandfather of Prince William and Prince Harry?
John Spencer, 8th Earl Spencer: Father of Diana, Princess of Wales (1924–1992)
Imprisoned and tortured during Stalin's Great Purge yet later rising to command Red Army forces, this general uniquely held marshal rank in two different countries' armies?
Konstantin Rokossovsky: Soviet and Polish general (1896–1968)
Alongside Abigail Adams, she is one of only two women to be both the wife of one U.S. president and the mother of another — who is she?
Barbara Bush: First Lady of the United States from 1989 to 1993.
Fought along the Suez Canal from 1967 to 1970 after Arab leaders adopted the 'three no's' policy, this conflict pitted Israel against Egypt, Jordan, and the PLO?
War of Attrition: 1967–1970 war between Israel and Egypt. Following the 1967 Six-Day War, no serious diplomatic efforts were made to resolve the issues at the heart of the Arab–Israeli conflict.
A former member of an elite Croatian police tactical unit, this fighter's ring nickname referenced that job, and he won the 2006 Pride Open-Weight Grand Prix?
Mirko Cro Cop: Croatian mixed martial artist (born 1974)
Serving since 2012, this Russian diplomat is best known as the official spokesman for President Vladimir Putin?
Dmitry Peskov: Russian politician and diplomat (born 1967)
A German aristocrat who served briefly as Chancellor in 1932, this monarchist is largely remembered for helping bring Adolf Hitler to power as his Vice-Chancellor?
This political ideology holds that Islam should shape government and society through the implementation of sharia and pan-Islamic unity — what is it called?
The longest-serving leader of the Labour Party, this British statesman was deputy prime minister under Churchill before becoming PM himself in 1945?
Clement Attlee: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1945 to 1951.
In Ovid's Metamorphoses, this legendary Cypriot sculptor falls hopelessly in love with a statue of his own making — who is he?
Pygmalion (mythology) (Ancient) was a legendary figure of Cyprus.
Writing mainly in Russian but also in his native tongue, this author is considered one of the most celebrated figures in Kyrgyz literature?
Chinghiz Aitmatov: Soviet and Kyrgyz author (1928-2008)
Nicknamed 'Da Vinci,' this Ukrainian commander became the youngest battalion leader in his country's army before being killed at the Battle of Bakhmut in 2023 — who was he?
As a child, this future Polish president starred in a 1962 film alongside his identical twin brother, and later died in the 2010 Smolensk air disaster — who is he?
Lech Kaczyński: President of Poland from 2005 to 2010.

As the eldest son of the last Austro-Hungarian emperor, this man became the last crown prince of Austria-Hungary in 1916 and later the pretender to those thrones until resigning his headship of the imperial house in 2007 — who is he?
Otto von Habsburg: Heir to the Austrian throne (1912–2011)
This Roman general became the first in the late Republic to march on Rome and win a civil war, later resigning his dictatorship after enacting constitutional reforms — who is he?
Sulla: Roman general and dictator (138–78 BC)
As Director of Intelligence for the IRA during Ireland's War of Independence, this revolutionary later served as both Minister for Home Affairs and Minister for Finance — who was he?

Michael Collins (Irish leader) (16 October 1890 - 22 August 1922) was an Irish revolutionary, soldier and politician who was a leading figure in the early-20th century struggle for Irish independence.
With 309 confirmed kills, this Soviet Red Army sniper is considered history's deadliest female marksman — she later toured the United States rallying wartime support. Who is she?
Barred from Russia's 2024 presidential ballot over disputed signatures, this opposition politician was a close ally of a prominent dissident assassinated in 2015. Who is he?
Twice imprisoned during a 1920s satyagraha protest, this Indian activist quit the Congress party in 1925 and went on to found the movement behind modern Dravidian politics. Who is he?
Periyar: Indian social activist and politician (1879–1973)
Born moments before his twin brother, who followed still gripping his heel, this hairy, red-skinned hunter of the Hebrew Bible is considered the ancestor of the Edomites. Who is he?
Esau: Older son of Isaac in the Hebrew Bible.
By leading a 2022 factional revolt that toppled Maharashtra's coalition government, this politician became the state's chief minister before later serving as deputy chief minister. Who is he?
Born in Montevideo during his father's exile, this Guatemalan sociologist-turned-politician co-founded the Semilla party and became his country's president in 2024 — who is he?
Bernardo Arévalo: President of Guatemala since 2024.
The longest-serving U.S. secretary of defense, this Cold War-era Pentagon chief championed systems analysis and escalated American involvement in the Vietnam War — who was he?
Robert McNamara: American businessman and government official (1916–2009)
Sparked by a disputed 2004 presidential runoff marred by fraud allegations, these Kyiv-centered protests forced political change in Ukraine that winter — what are they called?

Orange Revolution: 2004–2005 political protests in Ukraine. The nationwide protests succeeded when the results of the original runoff were annulled, and a re-vote was ordered by Ukraine's Supreme Court for 26 December 2004.
Before becoming the 70th U.S. secretary of state under Donald Trump, this Kansas congressman led the CIA and graduated from West Point in 1986 — who is he?
Mike Pompeo: American politician and diplomat (born 1963)
Raised in Brooklyn's Crown Heights, this Democratic congressman succeeded Nancy Pelosi to become House minority leader in 2023 — who is he?

Beginning at Mecca in June 1916 and backed by Britain's Egyptian Expeditionary Force, this Hashemite-led uprising against the Ottoman Empire sought a unified state stretching from Aleppo to Aden — what was it called?
Arab Revolt: 1916–1918 uprising against the Ottoman Turks.
Breached in the early hours of 6 June 2023 and blamed by Ukraine on a Russian rifle brigade, this event caused extensive flooding along the lower Dnieper in Kherson Oblast — what was it?

Destruction of the Kakhovka Dam: 2023 dam breach in Ukraine. The Kakhovka Dam was breached in the early hours of 6 June 2023, causing extensive flooding along the lower Dnieper river, also called the Dnipro, in Kherson Oblast.

A fierce journalist for the sans-culottes during the French Revolution, this physician-turned-radical published the periodical The Friend of the People and is linked to the September Massacres — who is he?
Co-owner of Macy's department store and briefly a U.S. congressman, this businessman died aboard the Titanic after his wife refused to leave the ship without him — who is he?
Isidor Straus: American politician, businessman, and Titanic sinking victim (1845–1912)
Born with haemophilia treated by faith healer Grigori Rasputin, this last heir apparent to the Russian throne was exiled with his family to Siberia in 1917 — who was he?
Alexei Nikolaevich, Tsarevich of Russia was the last heir apparent to the Russian throne (1904–1918).

Observed between dawn and sunset throughout the lunar month of Ramadan, this practice is the fourth of five foundational religious pillars, meant to build self-control, piety, and compassion — name this religious practice?
Fasting in Islam (called awm in) is the practice of abstaining from food, drink, sexual activity, and anything that substitutes food and drink.
Dubbed the 'Kingmaker' of 1960s Indian politics for elevating two future prime ministers to power, this former Chief Minister of Madras dropped out of school early — who was he?
Killed alongside Benito Mussolini by Italian partisans in April 1945, this woman was the Italian dictator's mistress — who was she?

Clara Petacci: Mistress of the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini (1912–1945). Clara "Claretta" Petacci (Italian: [klaˈretta peˈtattʃi]; 28 February 1912 – 28 April 1945) was a mistress of the Italian dictator Benito Mussolini.
Proclaimed emperor at just two months old, this Russian ruler was overthrown within a year and spent the rest of his life a prisoner before being killed — who was he?
Ivan VI of Russia was Emperor of Russia (1740–1741).
The 17th Chief Justice of the United States, he once served as managing editor of the Harvard Law Review before clerking for a Supreme Court justice — who is he?
John Roberts: Chief Justice of the United States since 2005.
After buying a small Texas hotel in 1919 and renting its rooms in eight-hour shifts during an oil boom, this magnate built the world's first international hotel chain — who was he?
Conrad Hilton: American hotel tycoon and politician (1887–1979)
The first Louisianian to serve as House majority whip since the early 1970s, he has represented Louisiana's 1st congressional district since 2008 — who is he?
Serving as his half-brother's standard-bearer at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE, he was killed attempting to bring water from the Euphrates to the besieged family of the Prophet — who was he?
Abbas ibn Ali: Son of Ali ibn Abi Talib (died in 680)
Formed from the union of Deira and Bernicia, this early medieval English kingdom once stretched from the Humber all the way to the Firth of Forth — which kingdom?
Northumbria: Medieval English kingdom. Northumbria was an early medieval English kingdom, existing between 654 and 1066 AD, spanning modern-day Northern England and Southern Scotland.
A close ally of President Macron, this French politician has served as Minister for Equality between Women and Men and previously as Minister for Solidarity and Family — who is she?
Aurore Bergé: French politician and Minister. Previously, Bergé represented the 10th constituency of the Yvelines department in the National Assembly since 2017.
He became the fifteenth ruler of an Arabian dynasty in 2020 after his cousin's death, having previously served for decades as Minister of Heritage and Culture — who is he?
Haitham bin Tariq: Sultan of Oman since 2020.
Sparked by an 1835 revolt against a Mexican president's new centralizing constitution, this sovereign nation lasted barely a decade before joining a much larger union — what was it?
Republic of Texas: Country in North America (1836–1846)
Known in Japan as the Nomonhan Incident, these decisive 1939 clashes saw Soviet general Georgy Zhukov combine tanks, aircraft, and infantry in tactics later reused at Stalingrad — what were they?
Battles of Khalkhin Gol: 1939 border clashes between Imperial Japan and the Soviet Union.
Also known as the Prince of Orange, he led the Dutch revolt against Spanish Habsburg rule that ignited the Eighty Years' War and eventually won the United Provinces their independence — who is he?
William the Silent: Dutch revolt leader (1533–1584)
Born Su Zhu, he succeeded Mao Zedong as China's top leader in the 1970s before being gradually eased out of power between 1978 and 1981 — who is he?
Hua Guofeng: Leader of China from 1976 to 1978.
Centered on the Abomey Plateau among the Fon people, this West African kingdom expanded to the Atlantic coast in the 18th century, gaining direct access to the slave trade — what was it?
This Korean admiral won all of his roughly 23 naval battles against Japan, most famously defeating a fleet of over 130 ships with just 13 of his own — who is he?
Taken as a Mughal hostage at age nine to enforce his father's treaty, this man later ruled from 1681 to 1689 as the second king of a major Indian empire — who is he?
Sambhaji: Chhatrapati of the Marathas from 1681 to 1689.
Co-founder of a wrestling promotion that grew into a multinational company, this former Small Business Administration head became the 13th U.S. secretary of education in 2025 — who is she?
Linda McMahon: American administrator and business executive (born 1948)
Known by the nickname Cak Imin, this Indonesian politician chairs the National Awakening Party and ran as a vice-presidential candidate alongside Anies Baswedan in 2024 — who is he?
In many religious traditions, this is described as the 'highest place' where souls, saints, or angels may reside or ascend to in the afterlife, standing in contrast to hell — what is it?
Heaven: Divine location in various religions.

Considered erotic poetry unlike other biblical books, this text narrates a passionate dialogue between a woman and her lover, warning the 'daughters of Jerusalem' not to awaken love too soon — what is it?
Song of Songs: Book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament.

Convicted in Israel after being identified as a notoriously cruel Treblinka guard nicknamed 'Ivan the Terrible,' this man was later convicted in Germany as an accessory to tens of thousands of murders at Sobibor — who is he?
John Demjanjuk: Ukrainian guard at Nazi death camps (1920–2012)
Raised alongside Achilles after being adopted by King Peleus, this Greek hero died in the Trojan War while disguised as his close companion, an event Homer immortalizes in the Iliad — who is he?
Born Gülbaran in 1955, this woman has served as Turkey's first lady since her husband became president — who is she?
Emine Erdoğan: First Lady of Turkey since 2014. Emine Erdoğan (née Gülbaran; born 16 February 1955) is the current first lady of Turkey as the wife of President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
This nontrinitarian Christian movement rejects the traditional three-in-one God concept, instead viewing Jesus Christ as a supreme moral teacher subordinate to a singular Creator — what is it?

Eldest son of a Nationalist Party leader, this politician studied in the Soviet Union as a teenager and later served as president of the Republic of China from 1978 until his 1988 death, ending martial law in Taiwan — who is he?
Chiang Ching-kuo: President of the Republic of China from 1978 to 1988. Born in Fenghua, Chiang was the eldest and only biological son of President Chiang Kai-shek.
President of Uganda since 1986, this leader ranks as the third-longest-serving non-royal head of state in the world today — who is he?
Yoweri Museveni: President and dictator of Uganda since 1986. Museveni unified the opposition under the National Resistance Movement and started the Ugandan Bush War.
Known as the 'Lion of Panjshir,' this Afghan commander led mujahideen forces against Soviet occupation before being assassinated in 2001 — who was he?
Ahmad Shah Massoud: Afghan military leader (1953–2001)
Produced annually by WWE since 1988, this event's signature match sees wrestlers enter the ring one at a time on a timer rather than all at once — what's the event?
Royal Rumble: World Wrestling Entertainment event series.
Founded by Anton LaVey with the 1966 creation of the Church of Satan in San Francisco, this belief system blends humanism, hedonism, and showmanship, drawing on Nietzsche and Ayn Rand — what is it?
LaVeyan Satanism: Religious movement founded by Anton LaVey.
This form of governance grounds legitimacy in scientific and technical expertise rather than the rule of the people — what's it called?
Technocracy: Form of government ruled by experts.

The eldest son of Henry the Fowler, this 10th-century king unified the German tribes and became Holy Roman Emperor in 962 after installing family members in the realm's most powerful duchies — who was he?
Otto the Great: Holy Roman Emperor from 962 to 973.
This Emir led Kuwait from 2006 until his death in 2020, having been the fourth son of a previous ruling sheikh — who was he?
Sabah Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah: Emir of Kuwait from 2006 to 2020.

This February uprising in Paris toppled the July Monarchy and forced King Louis Philippe I's abdication, giving rise to the Second Republic and inspiring similar uprisings across Europe that same year — which event was it?
French Revolution of 1848: Civil unrest in Paris, France.
This Indian politician serves as the 14th chief minister of Rajasthan and represents the Sanganer constituency as a member of the BJP — who is he?
Bhajan Lal Sharma: 14th Chief Minister of Rajasthan (born 1966)
The younger brother of a French emperor, this monarch ruled the client Kingdom of Holland from 1806 to 1810 after marrying his own step-niece, the daughter of Empress Josephine — who was he?
Louis Bonaparte: King of Holland from 1806 to 1810. Louis Bonaparte (born Luigi Buonaparte; 2 September 1778 – 25 July 1846) was a younger brother of Napoleon I, Emperor of the French.
Codenamed Project 17, this August 1990 military campaign began the Gulf War and led to a seven-month occupation before international forces intervened — which event?
Iraqi invasion of Kuwait: Beginning of the 1990–1991 Gulf War.
A viral video of him scolding sleeping city council members made this Japanese mayor an internet sensation before he placed second in the 2024 Tokyo governor's race — who is he?
Shinji Ishimaru: Japanese politician. Ishimaru ran in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election as an independent, but ultimately lost to incumbent Yuriko Koike.

Also called the House of France, this royal line founded in 987 by its eponymous king continued through cadet branches like Valois and Bourbon to rule almost continuously until 1848 — which royal house?
Capetian dynasty: European royal house of Frankish origin.

Serving the Umayyad Caliphate as governor of Iraq and the east, this administrator reformed coinage by minting silver dirhams bearing Muslim religious inscriptions instead of Persian designs — who was he?
Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf: Umayyad governor and viceroy (c1 June.661-1 June 714)
Suspended from office in 2025 and held at Marmara Prison amid politically charged legal proceedings, this politician has served as mayor of Istanbul since 2019 — who is he?
Ekrem İmamoğlu: Turkish politician and mayor of Istanbul (born 1970)

Beginning in 1881 with the crowning of a Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen prince as King Carol I and ending with King Michael I's 1947 abdication, this constitutional monarchy grew from an earlier union of Moldavia and Wallachia — which kingdom?
Kingdom of Romania was a constitutional monarchy that existed from 1881 to 1947.
This king surrendered his country to German invaders in 1940, sparking postwar controversy that nearly caused a civil war upon his return home in 1950 — who was he?
Leopold III of Belgium: King of the Belgians from 1934 to 1951.
Using the pseudonym 'Balraj' as commander-in-chief of the HSRA, this Indian revolutionary mentored Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev Thapar, and Shivaram Rajguru — who was he?
Around the year 1010, this Icelandic explorer followed Leif Eriksson's route to Vinland with his wife Gudrid in a short-lived bid to found a permanent settlement — who was he?
A leader of the Great Arab Revolt in the First World War who briefly ruled Syria before being expelled by the French in 1920, this Hejazi statesman went on to become King of Iraq — who was he?
Faisal I: King of Iraq from 1921 to 1933.
Serving as Speaker pro tempore for 22 days after Kevin McCarthy's removal, this North Carolina Republican chaired the House Financial Services Committee from 2023 to 2025 — who is he?
Adopted as Hadrian's heir after marrying his niece Faustina, this Roman emperor's peaceful 23-year reign saw a successful campaign in southern Scotland — who is he?
Antoninus Pius: Roman emperor from 138 to 161.
The only British prime minister born Jewish, this Conservative statesman clashed repeatedly with Liberal rival William Gladstone — who is he?
Benjamin Disraeli: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom (1868; 1874–1880)
According to Herodotus, this 6th-century BC queen of the Massagetae defeated and killed Cyrus the Great in battle — who was she?
Tomyris: 6th-century BC queen of the Massagetae. Tomyris became a popular subject in European art and literature during the Renaissance.
Serving as prime minister across three separate periods spanning nearly four decades, this politician is Cambodia's longest-serving head of government — who is he?
Hun Sen: Prime Minister of Cambodia (1985–1993; 1998–2023)
This legendary Germanic hero slew the dragon Fafnir and was later murdered after a quarrel involving his wife and another woman he had unknowingly helped deceive — who is he?

Conceived by Josh Wardle and launched on April Fools' Day 2017, this Reddit social experiment let users edit a single pixel on a shared canvas every several minutes — what was this collaborative project called?
R/place: Online social experiment on Reddit. r/place was a recurring collaborative project and social experiment hosted on the content aggregator site Reddit.
Head of the Soviet secret police at the height of the Great Purge, this Stalin-era official orchestrated mass arrests and executions before being arrested and executed himself in 1940 — who was he?
Nikolai Yezhov: NKVD director under Joseph Stalin (1895–1940)
In Greek myth, this master craftsman built the Labyrinth for King Minos and fashioned the wings that failed his son Icarus — who is he?
Originally an oral tradition composed over centuries before being written down in the Sasanian era, this is the core scripture corpus of Zoroastrianism — what is it called?
Avesta: Zoroastrian compendium of sacred literature.
A former flight attendant who later became a Royal Thai Armed Forces general and the king's bodyguard, she is the fourth wife and current queen of Thailand — who is she?

After German forces released a chlorine-and-bromine gas barrage on entrenched Russian defenders at Osowiec Fortress in 1915, the gassed survivors astonished the enemy by counter-charging and driving them back — what nickname did this battle earn?
Attack of the Dead Men: Battle at Osowiec Fortress during WWI.
This Umayyad commander crossed from North Africa to launch the Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula in 711, leaving his name forever attached to the rock where he massed his troops — who is he?
Tariq ibn Ziyad: Umayyad commander in Hispania (died c. 720)
The only queen to reign over a unified Spain, she took the throne before her third birthday after her father overturned the Salic Law to ensure her succession — who is she?
Isabella II: Queen of Spain from 1833 to 1868.
Singapore's first female speaker of parliament, she went on to become the country's eighth president in 2017, elected uncontested in a race reserved for Malay candidates — who is she?
Halimah Yacob: President of Singapore from 2017 to 2023.
Convicted for conspiring in the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing, this Michigan-born man briefly served in the U.S. Army alongside his co-conspirator before their plot together — who is he?
Born in 2007 as the youngest grandchild of Queen Elizabeth II, this British royal was known by a viscount's title until 2023 and is a nephew of King Charles III — who is he?
James, Earl of Wessex: Member of the British royal family (born 2007)
This Japanese samurai, who lived from 1574 to 1607, served as daimyō of the Fukui Domain in Echizen during the transition into the Edo period — who is he?
Yūki Hideyasu: Japanese samurai. Yūki Hideyasu (結城 秀康; 1 March 1574 – 2 June 1607) was a Japanese samurai who lived during the Azuchi–Momoyama and early Edo periods.
This French energy-technology giant, parent company of Square D and APC, was named the world's most sustainable company on the Global 100 index in 2025 — which corporation?
Schneider Electric: French multinational digital automation and energy management company.
This global industry devoted to building and maintaining infrastructure was worth over $11 trillion in 2022, about 13 percent of world GDP — which industry?
Construction: Process of building or assembling a building or infrastructure.
As the Army's most senior officer at the end of World War II, this German field marshal commanded Army Group A during the Battle of France and requested the Halt Order at Dunkirk — who was he?
Gerd von Rundstedt: German field marshal (1875–1953)
Appointed Russia's Presidential Commissioner for Children's Rights in 2021, this official had an ICC arrest warrant issued against her in 2023 over the deportation of Ukrainian children — who is she?
Founded in 2001 with the single goal of carving a new state out of Andhra Pradesh, this Indian party won that fight in 2014 and formed the new state's first government — which party?
Bharat Rashtra Samithi: Indian political party. BRS), formerly known as Telangana Rashtra Samithi (transl.
Born in Hong Kong and educated at Eton, this British former diplomat and MP walked solo across Asia after leaving the Foreign Office, and now co-hosts a podcast with Alastair Campbell — who is he?
Rory Stewart: British politician, academic and broadcaster (born 1973)

In 628 CE, an armed confrontation near a Jewish-populated oasis northwest of Medina ended with the Muslim army's victory after the defending commander was killed, reportedly by Ali ibn Abi Talib — what was this clash called?
Battle of Khaybar: 628 military campaign in the early Muslim period.
Though he died before ascending an 18th-century European throne himself, this crown prince's three sons who survived to adulthood all eventually became king — who was this royal heir?
Louis, Dauphin of France (born 1729): Heir to the French throne (1729–1765)
Often depicted as a beautiful woman with butterfly wings, this mortal-turned-immortal endured trials set by Venus to win back her husband Cupid in Apuleius's The Golden Ass — who is she?
Psyche (mythology): Wife of Cupid. Psyche is known from the ancient Roman proto-novel The Golden Ass (also known as the Metamorphoses), written by philosopher and orator Apuleius in the 2nd century.
Founded in 1949 as a breakaway faction from another Dravidian movement, this Tamil Nadu political party became the first non-Congress party to win a clear state majority, in 1967 — which party is it?
Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam: Political party in India. The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK; Tamil pronunciation: [t̪iɾaːʋiɖɐ munːeːtrɐk kɐɻɐɡɐm]; transl.
Venerated as a prophet across three major faiths, this biblical figure guided Israel's transition from the age of judges to kingship, first anointing Saul and later David — who is he?

Ruling an empire that stretched from northwestern Iran to the Punjab, this reputedly undefeated sultan carried the honorific 'Right Hand of the State' and laid groundwork for Persian culture to flourish in Lahore — who was he?
Mahmud of Ghazni: Ghaznavid sultan from 998 to 1030 (971–1030)
Nicknamed the 'Soldier King' for his role during World War I, this monarch succeeded his uncle Leopold II onto the throne in 1909 and later saw his country occupied by German forces — who was he?
Albert I of Belgium: King of the Belgians from 1909 to 1934.

While working at the RAND Corporation, this analyst leaked the top-secret Pentagon Papers to The New York Times in 1971, facing a 115-year maximum sentence before charges were dismissed over illegal evidence-gathering — who is he?
Coined by French peace campaigner Émile Arnaud in 1901, this opposition to war and violence was embodied in Gandhi's philosophy of steadfast nonviolent resistance, 'satyagraha' — what is it?

Pacifism: Philosophy opposing war or violence. Its effectiveness served as inspiration to Martin Luther King Jr., James Lawson, James Bevel, Thích Nhất Hạnh, and many others in the civil rights movement.

Promoted to Germany's DAX stock index in March 2023, this Düsseldorf-based company is the country's largest arms manufacturer, building everything from armored vehicles to warships via its Blohm+Voss subsidiary — what company is it?
Rheinmetall: German automotive and arms manufacturer.
Serving as Russia's de facto regent before becoming tsar in 1598 after the death of the last Rurik dynasty ruler, this leader's reign preceded the chaotic Time of Troubles — who is he?
Boris Godunov: Tsar of Russia from 1598 to 1605.

Fought from the 17th century to the end of the 19th, this long series of conflicts pitted European colonial powers, and later the United States, against native tribes primarily over land — what is this era of conflict known as?
American Indian Wars: Frontier conflicts in North America, 1609–1890s.
A member of the influential 'Eight Elders' in 1980s China, this revolutionary politician is also the father of the country's current top Communist Party leader — who was he?

Commanding seven 'treasure voyages' across Asia under two Ming emperors, this admiral was a Muslim-born eunuch who received a new surname from the Yongle Emperor — who commanded these historic fleets?
Zheng He: Chinese Admiral and diplomat (1371–1433/1435)

Representing the same Kerala constituency in the state assembly from 1970 until his death in 2023, this two-time chief minister became the longest-serving member in that legislature's history — who was he?
Oommen Chandy: 10th Chief Minister of Kerala (1943–2023)
According to Genesis, this Egyptian woman bore Abraham's firstborn son, Ishmael, and though unnamed in the Quran, Islam regards her as his second wife — who is she?
A two-time NCAA wrestling champion before entering politics, this Ohio congressman helped found the House Freedom Caucus and now chairs the House Judiciary Committee — who is he?
Equated with Hera in Greek myth, this Roman goddess of marriage was both sister and wife to Jupiter, sharing her sacred peacock symbol as part of the Capitoline Triad — who is she?
Juno (mythology): Ancient Roman goddess of marriage and childbirth.
This poet and broadcaster served as Ireland's president from 2011 to 2025, and his 2018 re-election landslide set a personal-mandate record only broken by his successor in 2025 — who is he?
Michael D. Higgins: President of Ireland from 2011 to 2025. Higgins was elected president of Ireland in 2011 after being nominated by the Labour Party.

This American fleet admiral commanded the U.S. Pacific Fleet in World War II and, as the Navy's top submarine authority, helped push through approval for the first nuclear-powered submarine — who is he?
Chester W. Nimitz: American naval officer (1885–1966)
Born in France and once a Marshal under Napoleon, this former French general became king of Sweden and Norway in 1818, founding the Bernadotte dynasty — who is he?
Charles XIV John: King of Sweden and Norway from 1818 to 1844.
According to the Hebrew Bible, this queen consort was first married to Uriah the Hittite, then to King David after he had Uriah killed, and became the mother of Solomon — who is she?
Bathsheba: Biblical figure and wife of David.

Originally referring to peoples near ancient Arabia, this medieval European term evolved after the rise of Islam into the standard Christian label for Muslims and the Muslim world broadly — what was the term?
Saracen: Archaic term for Arabs and later for all Muslims.

The third shōgun of a ruling dynasty, this Japanese leader closed the country's borders to Europeans and persecuted Christians during his 1623-1651 reign, a policy that lasted over two centuries — who is he?
Tokugawa Iemitsu: Japanese Samurai, Daimyo and Military leader of Japan from 1623 to 1651.
Born Namgyal Wangdi, this Sherpa mountaineer stood atop Mount Everest alongside Edmund Hillary in 1953, becoming one of the first two confirmed to reach the summit — who is he?
Trained as a classical ballet instructor and educated in Czechoslovakia, this monarch ascended the Cambodian throne in 2004, just a week after his father's abdication — who is he?
Norodom Sihamoni: King of Cambodia since 2004.

The granddaughter of a notorious 20th-century Italian dictator, she became in 2004 the first woman to lead a political party in Italy after earlier careers in film, modeling, and pop music — who is she?

Facing extradition from the UK to India over financial crimes, this businessman built his fortune as chairman of the country's largest spirits company and a sprawling conglomerate spanning aviation and real estate — who is he?
Vijay Mallya: Indian businessman and politician (born 1955)
Formed in 1993 by merging a party from West Germany with one from East Germany, this party held 85 of the Bundestag's 630 seats after Germany's 2025 election — which party?
Alliance 90/The Greens: Green political party in Germany.
This 10th-century king introduced Christianity to Denmark and united Jutland and Zealand under his rule, before being ousted by his own son — who was he?

Harald Bluetooth: 10th-century King of Denmark and Norway. Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson (Old Norse: Haraldr Blátǫnn Gormsson; Danish: Harald Blåtand Gormsen, died c. 985/86) was a king of Denmark and Norway.
This German Social Democrat served as Federal Minister of the Interior under Chancellor Olaf Scholz from 2021 to 2025, after leading her party's opposition in the Hesse state parliament — who is she?
Nancy Faeser: German politician, Federal Minister of Interior (born 1970)

Fought in 657 CE on the banks of the Euphrates, this clash pitted the fourth Rashidun caliph, Ali ibn Abi Talib, against a rebelling Levantine governor, ending in arbitration after Ali gained the upper hand — which battle?

Battle of Siffin was fought in 657 CE (37 AH) between the Iraqi Arab forces of the fourth Rashidun caliph Ali ibn Abi Talib and the Syrian Arab forces of the rebelling long-time governor of the Levant, Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan.
Detonated near a Japanese-controlled railway line in 1931, this staged, barely-damaging explosion became the excuse for invading Manchuria — what was it called?
Mukden incident: 1931 Japan false flag railway explosion.
Once expected to succeed his mother as India's prime minister, this politician died in a plane crash, clearing the way for his brother Rajiv to inherit the family's political mantle — who was he?

Spurned in childhood as an illegitimate son, this early-19th-century monarch transformed his kingdom's army into a formidable fighting force during his reign from 1816 to 1828 — who was this Southern African king?
Shaka: Zulu king from 1816 to 1828. King Shaka was born in the lunar month of uNtulikazi (July) in 1787, in Mthonjaneni, KwaZulu-Natal Province, South Africa.

Rooted mostly among rural Indigenous communities in Chiapas, this Mexican far-left group has been in a frozen conflict with the state since 1994 and takes its name from a revolutionary agrarian commander — which group?
Zapatista Army of National Liberation: Far-left political and militant group in southern Mexico.
Fill in the blank: “____ refers to a December 2008 assault that took place in Ansan, South Korea.”

Cho Doo-soon case refers to a December 2008 assault that took place in Ansan, South Korea. An eight-year-old girl known by the pseudonym Na-young (나영) was kidnapped and raped by Cho Doo-soon, a 56-year-old male, in a bathroom inside a church.
Founder of a Mumbai travelling theatre company in 1944, this actor became the patriarch of a Hindi-film dynasty spanning four generations — who is he?

Leading a Russian nationalist party since 2022, this politician also chairs the State Duma's Committee on International Affairs, a post that has drawn heavy domestic and international media scrutiny — who is he?
Leonid Slutsky (politician) (born 4 January 1968) is a Russian politician who has been the leader the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia since 27 May 2022.
Ruling Korea's Joseon dynasty from 1418 to 1450, this monarch is remembered above all for creating Hangul, the native Korean alphabet — who was he?

Sejong the Great: King of Joseon from 1418 to 1450. Sejong (Korean: 세종; Hanja: 世宗; May 15, 1397 – April 8, 1450), commonly known as Sejong the Great (세종대왕; 世宗大王), was the fourth monarch of the Koreanic state Joseon.

Sparked by a suppressed student demonstration in Prague on International Students' Day in November 1989, this peaceful transfer of power ended 41 years of one-party rule in Czechoslovakia — what was it called?
Velvet Revolution: Democratization process in Czechoslovakia in 1989.
Elected to Newark's council after a 10-day hunger strike in a tent, this Rhodes Scholar became the city's 38th mayor before becoming New Jersey's first African-American U.S. senator — who is he?
This Costa Rican diplomat took over UN climate negotiations six months after the failed Copenhagen summit and helped broker the 2015 Paris Agreement — who is she?
Killed during Hernán Cortés's seizure of Tenochtitlan, this ninth Aztec emperor presided over the empire at its largest territorial extent — who was he?
Moctezuma II: Tlahtoāni of the Aztec Empire until 1520.
Born a Lithuanian polytheist and known as Jogaila as Grand Duke, he converted to Catholicism in 1386, married Queen Jadwiga, and became sole ruler of Poland — who was he?
Władysław II Jagiełło: Grand Duke of Lithuania (1377–1434); King of Poland (1386–1434)
This nation, described in the Hebrew Bible as a staunch enemy of the Israelites, was founded by a grandson of Esau, and the Torah even commands that all memory of it be erased — name this nation?

Amalek (Biblical) was a nation described in the Hebrew Bible as a staunch enemy of the Israelites. The name "Amalek" can refer to the nation's founder, a grandson of Esau; his descendants, the Amalekites; or the territories of Amalek, which they inhabited.
Born to a murdered Arvernian aristocrat, this Gallic chieftain united the tribes of Gaul in a doomed revolt against Julius Caesar's legions — who was he?

This Indian businessman founded a sprawling conglomerate once called India's second-largest employer after the railways, before being arrested in 2014 over billions in unrefunded investor deposits — who is he?
Known as the 'Young Turks,' this secret society and political party pushed for constitutional reform in the Ottoman Empire and was persecuted by Sultan Abdul Hamid II — which organization?
Committee of Union and Progress: 1889–1919 Turkish political party.
A founder of the Grey Wolves, this Turkish economist has chaired the ultranationalist Nationalist Movement Party since 1997 — who is he?
Leading a team nicknamed 'The Untouchables,' this Prohibition agent worked to bring down Al Capone in Chicago — who was he?

A Venezuelan Marxist-Leninist protected by the Stasi and KGB, this notorious terrorist led the 1975 raid on OPEC's Vienna headquarters and later bombed targets to demand his wife's release from prison — who is he?
Carlos the Jackal: Venezuelan-born international terror operative (born 1949)
Serving briefly as prime minister before becoming Turkey's president from 2007 to 2014, he earlier joined forces with a fellow reformist named Erdoğan after his party split in 2000 — who is he?
Abdullah Gül: President of Turkey from 2007 to 2014. Abdullah Gül (born 29 October 1950) is a Turkish politician who served as the president of Turkey from 2007 to 2014.
Wrongfully convicted of spying for Germany in 1894 largely due to antisemitism, this French army officer was imprisoned on Devil's Island before evidence cleared his name — who is he?
The favorite of Jacob's two wives and mother of Joseph and Benjamin, her older sister Leah was Jacob's first wife — who is she?
Serving as Turkey's prime minister four separate times between 1974 and 2002, he also invaded Cyprus and lifted a ban on opium cultivation during his first term — who is he?
Bülent Ecevit: Prime Minister of Turkey (1974; 1977; 1978–79; 1999–2002)
The longest-serving chief minister of Punjab across three separate terms, this politician has twice served as Pakistan's prime minister, most recently since 2024 — who is he?
Shehbaz Sharif: Prime Minister of Pakistan (2022–2023; 2024–present)
In the Book of Genesis' Table of Nations, this son of Noah is named as ancestor of the peoples of the Aegean, Anatolia, and Greece — who is he?
Japheth: Biblical figure, son of Noah.
Born to a Cossack family in Poltava, this journalist-turned-revolutionary became Supreme Commander of the Ukrainian People's Army during the Ukrainian War of Independence — who was he?
This Swedish diplomat became the youngest UN Secretary-General ever at 47, oversaw creation of the UN's first peacekeeping forces in Egypt and the Congo, and died in a 1961 plane crash — who was he?
Dag Hammarskjöld: UN Secretary-General from 1953 to 1961.

This semi-nomadic Turkic people controlled the steppes of southeastern Europe and Crimea in the 9th and 10th centuries, waging war against the early Rus' state for over two hundred years — who were they?
Pechenegs: Extinct Turkic people. The Pechenegs or Patzinaks, were a semi-nomadic Turkic people from Central Asia who spoke the Pecheneg language.

Founded in 1961 by Gérard Mulliez, this French retail giant operates in Spain as Alcampo and in Russia as 'Ashan,' a name derived from the district of its very first store in Roubaix — what is this company called?
Auchan: French multinational retail company. Auchan (French: [oʃɑ̃]) is a French multinational retail group headquartered in Croix, France.
A banker who once served as CEO of Banco Guayaquil, this politician became Ecuador's 47th president in 2021 after years as a vocal critic of the Correa administration — who is he?
Guillermo Lasso: President of Ecuador from 2021 to 2023.
Appointed by Gavin Newsom in 2023 to fill the Senate seat left vacant by Dianne Feinstein's death, she became the first openly LGBT African American to serve in the chamber — who is she?
Laphonza Butler: American politician and labor union official (born 1979)
This Welsh Liberal led Britain through the First World War as prime minister and helped negotiate the creation of the Irish Free State — who was he?
David Lloyd George: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1916 to 1922.
Serving as foreign minister across the regimes of Louis XVI, Napoleon, and Louis XVIII, this crafty French diplomat represented his country at the Congress of Vienna — who was he?
Charles Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord: French secularized clergyman, statesman, and diplomat (1754–1838)

Organized by the Irish Republican Brotherhood and lasting six days in April 1916, this armed insurrection aimed to end British rule and saw sixteen of its leaders executed — what was this uprising called?

Easter Rising: 1916 armed insurrection in Ireland. The Easter Rising (Irish: Éirí Amach na Cásca), also known as the Easter Rebellion, was an armed insurrection in Ireland during Easter Week in April 1916.
Born in 2003 as the only daughter of Prince Edward and Sophie, she is King Charles III's youngest niece and was once eighth in line to the British throne — who is she?
Lady Louise Windsor: Member of the British royal family (born 2003)
The longest-serving prime minister in Slovak history, he has led the country across four separate terms since founding his left-wing party in 1999 — who is he?
Robert Fico: Prime Minister of Slovakia (2006–2010, 2012–2018, 2023–present)
This U.S. Army officer led E Company's assault on the Belgian town of Foy after the siege of Bastogne was broken, and later served as the American governor of a Berlin prison — who is he?
After narrowly losing the top job to Indira Gandhi in 1966, this Indian politician finally became prime minister in 1977, leading a coalition formed in the wake of the Emergency — who is he?
Morarji Desai: Prime Minister of India from 1977 to 1979.
Holding a Candidate of Sciences degree in history, she has served as the spokeswoman for Russia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs since 2015 — who is she?
Trapped by an anticyclone and windless conditions in December 1952, this coal-fueled pollution event over England's capital killed an estimated 4,000 people in less than a week — what was it called?
Great Smog of London: 1952 air pollution event. It lasted from Friday, 5 December to Tuesday, 9 December 1952, then dispersed quickly when the weather changed.
Serving alongside generals Wang Jian and Wang Ben under the ruler who unified China's Warring States, this military commander was great-great-grandfather to a noted Han-dynasty general — who was he?
This Soviet sniper killed 225 enemy soldiers during the Battle of Stalingrad alone, becoming a celebrated Hero of the Soviet Union whose exploits later inspired books and films — who is he?
Vasily Zaitsev (sniper) (23 March 1915 - 15 December 1991) was a Soviet sniper who served in World War II.

Published by Anton LaVey in 1969, this text serves as the foundational scripture of a philosophy whose adherents describe themselves as 'atheistic' believers who see supernatural figures as projections of personality — which book?
The Satanic Bible: 1969 religious text of LaVeyan Satanism.

A composite of earlier Welsh prophet figures named Myrddin and Emrys, this legendary wizard served as advisor to Uther Pendragon in tales popularized by 12th-century writer Geoffrey of Monmouth — who is he?
Merlin: Legendary Welsh wizard. Geoffrey's account presented Merlin as a prophet and royal advisor to Arthur's father, Uther Pendragon.

Serving as Turkey's 23rd prime minister from 1996 to 1997, this Islamist politician was later banned from politics for violating the constitution's secularism clause after founding a movement called Millî Görüş — who is he?
Necmettin Erbakan: Prime Minister of Turkey from 1996 to 1997.

Also known as 'the Great,' this Grand Prince of Moscow ended Tatar dominance with an 1480 victory over the Great Horde and began using the title tsar in his correspondence with other monarchs — who is he?
Ivan III of Russia: Grand Prince of Moscow from 1462 to 1505.

Led by the future Roman emperor Titus, an army encircled and breached the walls of this Jewish holy city, destroying the Second Temple after a bitter feud between rival factions cut off the population's own food supply — which historic event is this?
Siege of Jerusalem (70 CE): Part of the First Jewish–Roman War.
The only woman ever to serve as chief minister of Rajasthan, this Indian politician also held two Cabinet posts under Atal Bihari Vajpayee — who is she?

Vasundhara Raje: 11th Chief Minister of Rajasthan. Vasundhara Raje Scindia (born 8 March 1953) is an Indian politician, who has held the position of the chief minister of Rajasthan from 2003 to 2008 and 2013 to 2018.
Serving as prime minister under Charles de Gaulle before becoming French president in 1969, this leader championed the Concorde, the TGV project, and France's first minimum wage — who is he?
Georges Pompidou: President of France from 1969 to 1974.
Born to a poor Cossack family and later a close ally of Stalin, this Soviet cavalry commander founded the Red Cavalry and became the subject of patriotic songs — who is he?

Born in 2001 as the eldest child of Belgium's king and queen, this royal became heir apparent when her grandfather abdicated in 2013 and is set to become her country's first queen regnant — who is she?
Princess Elisabeth, Duchess of Brabant: Heir apparent to the Belgian throne (born 2001)
Ruling Kuwait from 1977 until his death in 2006, this emir led the country through the Gulf War against Saddam Hussein's Iraq with US backing — who is he?
Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah: Emir of Kuwait from 1977 to 2006. The 13th ruler in his family's dynasty, Jaber's reign oversaw the transition of a relatively traditional society into a modernized state.
Though he died before his father, this royal heir apparent's own son inherited the British throne in 1760 as George III — who was he?
Frederick, Prince of Wales: Heir apparent to George II of Great Britain (1707–1751)

A member of the Cherokee Nation who once ran his family's plumbing business, this politician moved from Oklahoma's House delegation to the Senate before becoming U.S. secretary of homeland security in 2026 — who is he?
Markwayne Mullin: American politician and businessman (born 1977)
Born in Paris to a family of Georgian political refugees, this career diplomat became the first woman ever elected president of her adopted country — who is she?
Serving under Jimmy Carter, this Minnesota senator became the 42nd U.S. vice president and the Democratic Party's presidential nominee in 1984 — who is he?
Walter Mondale: Vice President of the United States from 1977 to 1981.
Marrying Princess Ingrid of Sweden and later fathering the future Queen Margrethe, this royal reigned over Denmark from 1947 to 1972 — who is he?
Frederik IX: King of Denmark from 1947 to 1972. Frederik IX (Christian Frederik Franz Michael Carl Valdemar Georg; 11 March 1899 – 14 January 1972) was King of Denmark from 1947 to 1972.
Once considered Chairman Mao's likely successor, this Chinese leader served as president of China from 1959 to 1968 before being purged during the Cultural Revolution — who is he?
Liu Shaoqi: President of China from 1959 to 1968. Liu Shaoqi (Chinese: 刘少奇; pronounced [ljǒʊ ʂâʊtɕʰǐ]; 24 November 1898 – 12 November 1969) was a Chinese revolutionary and politician.
Born into a poor farming family before being adopted into a samurai household, this statesman became Japan's first prime minister and helped draft the 1889 Meiji Constitution — who is he?

Employed to paint glow-in-the-dark watch dials in the 1910s and 1920s, these American factory workers were told to point their brushes with their lips — ingesting a radioactive element that would reshape U.S. labor law. Who were they?
Radium Girls: American female radiation poisoning victims (1917–1978)
The first woman to become president of Peru, she took office in December 2022 after her predecessor's failed attempt to dissolve Congress, and was herself removed from power in 2025 — who is she?
Dina Boluarte: President of Peru from 2022 to 2025. Boluarte aligned herself with the right-wing majority of the Peruvian Congress, and received support from the Peruvian Armed Forces.
Nicknamed the 'One-Eyed Dragon' for his missing eye, this Japanese samurai warlord founded the modern city of Sendai — who is he?
Date Masamune: Japanese samurai and daimyō (1567–1636)

This political movement to end slavery saw Haiti become the only nation to fully self-liberate through revolution, while France had first outlawed the practice all the way back in 1315 — what movement is it?
Abolitionism: Movement to end slavery. Abolitionism, or the abolitionist movement, is the political movement to end slavery and liberate enslaved individuals around the world.
Traditionally regarded as the first king to unify Norway into one kingdom, this 9th-century monarch was succeeded by his sons Eric Bloodaxe and Haakon the Good — who was he?
Harald Fairhair: Legendary first king of Norway. Harald Fairhair (Old Norse: Haraldr Hárfagri; c. 850 – c. 932) was a Norwegian king.
Born in 1940, she is the eldest child of the last Shah of Iran and his first wife, Fawzia of Egypt — who is she?

This December 1989 uprising began in the city of Timișoara and ended with the swift trial and execution of a longtime Communist dictator and his wife — which nation's uprising, the only one of 1989 to end that way?
Romanian revolution: 1989 popular uprising in Romania.

This attorney served as US national security advisor under President Biden from 2021 to 2025, after earlier roles advising Hillary Clinton and serving as a policy director for President Obama — who is he?
Jake Sullivan: American attorney and advisor (born 1976)
Derived from a Sanskrit word meaning 'land' or 'country,' this term describes the peoples, cultures, and diaspora of the Indian subcontinent — what is it?
Desi: Endonym for the Indian subcontinent and diaspora.

Nicknamed 'the Just,' this 15th-century King of Hungary and Croatia was crowned at just fourteen after his brother's execution, and later added the crowns of Bohemia and the title Duke of Austria — who was he?
Matthias Corvinus: King of Hungary and Croatia from 1458 to 1490.
The younger sister of Japan's first great unifier, this Sengoku-period noblewoman was mother to three daughters who each became prominent in their own right — who was she?
Oichi: Historical figure in the late Sengoku period (1547–1583)
Owned by Cover Corporation, this virtual YouTuber talent agency manages dozens of streamers across three languages with a combined 80 million-plus subscribers — what is it?
Hololive Production: Japanese virtual YouTuber agency. In December 2019, Hololive was merged with Cover's male Holostars agency and INoNaKa music label under the unified "Hololive Production" brand.
Twice shot in the head fighting the Turks and surviving both times, this Russian field marshal defeated Napoleon in 1812 through attrition warfare and earned the honorific 'of Smolensk' — who was he?
Mikhail Kutuzov: Field Marshal of the Russian Empire (1745–1813)
As Austria's foreign minister from 1809 and chancellor from 1821, this conservative diplomat anchored the Concert of Europe until the 1848 revolutions forced him out — who was he?
Klemens von Metternich: Austrian diplomat, foreign minister and Chancellor (1773–1859)
Aided by two teenage accomplices, this Texas serial killer murdered at least 29 young men between 1970 and 1973 before being fatally shot by one of his own helpers — who was he?

This Scottish politician led the Scottish National Party and served as First Minister from 2014 to 2023, after training as a solicitor and once stepping aside in a leadership race to back Alex Salmond — who is she?
Nicola Sturgeon: First Minister of Scotland from 2014 to 2023. Born in Ayrshire, Sturgeon is a law graduate of the University of Glasgow.
This Sudanese military officer took charge of a transitional council after the 2019 revolution and later seized total power in an October 2021 coup — who is he?
Abdel Fattah al-Burhan: Leader of Sudan since 2019.
This Germanic people migrated south from near the Elbe river through the Danube region before conquering most of the Italian Peninsula between 568 and 774 AD — who were they?
Lombards: Historical ethnic group of the Italian Peninsula of Germanic origin.
This Prussian officer's unfinished treatise 'On War' coined the phrase 'fog of war' and stressed the psychological, political side of combat — who wrote it?
Carl von Clausewitz: Prussian military theorist (1780–1831)
Succeeding his kinsman as ruler of Novgorod, this Varangian prince extended control along the Dnieper to Kiev and led a successful raid on Constantinople before his death in 912 — who was he?
Oleg the Wise: Varangian prince, founder of Kievan Rus'
After an evangelical conversion in 1785, this Yorkshire MP spent two decades leading the parliamentary fight that ended Britain's slave trade — who was he?
William Wilberforce: English politician and abolitionist (1759–1833)
Ruling the Sheikhdom of Kuwait from 1921 until his death in 1950, he was the tenth man to hold that position — who was he?
Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah: Ruler of the Sheikhdom of Kuwait from 1921 to 1950.

One of the original five Marshals of the Soviet Union, this military officer and politician later served as the country's head of state from 1953 to 1960, having forged a close friendship with Stalin during the Battle of Tsaritsyn — who was he?
Kliment Voroshilov: Soviet military officer and politician (1881–1969)
The only president of Ukraine to serve two full terms, this former machine-building industry executive led from 1994 to 2005 amid economic stabilization but growing oligarch influence. Who was he?
Leonid Kuchma: President of Ukraine from 1994 to 2005. Kuchma took office after winning the 1994 presidential election against his rival, incumbent President Leonid Kravchuk.
Captured while trying to relieve the siege of Leningrad, this Red Army general defected to the Third Reich and became the nominal head of a collaborationist anti-Soviet liberation army. Who was he?
Andrey Vlasov: Soviet Russian general and politician (1901–1946)
He named his B-29 bomber after his mother, then flew it over Hiroshima to drop the first atomic bomb used in warfare. Who was this Army Air Forces pilot?
Paul Tibbets: United States Air Force general (1915–2007)

The only surviving son of Charlemagne and Hildegard, this Frankish co-emperor conquered Barcelona from the Emirate of Córdoba in 801 and briefly lost his throne for several months in 833–834. Who was he?
Louis the Pious: Emperor of the Carolingian Empire from 813 to 840.
Depicted driving a horse-drawn chariot across the sky in a radiant crown, this Greek sun god later became central to Emperor Julian's short-lived 4th-century religious revival. Who is he?

Helios: Greek god and personification of the Sun. In ancient Greek religion and mythology, Helios (Ancient Greek: Ἥλιος pronounced [hɛ̌ːlios], lit. 'Sun'; Homeric Greek: Ἠέλιος) is the god who personifies the Sun.
The first practicing Orthodox Jew to head Israeli military intelligence, this retired general later served as IDF Chief of General Staff from January 2023 to March 2025. Who is he?
Herzi Halevi: Chief of General Staff of the Israeli Defense Forces (born 1967)

Born from the War of the Sicilian Vespers in the late 13th century, this southern Italian realm was ruled by rival branches of the Angevin family — one of whose queens, Joanna I, was murdered by her own successor. Which state?
Kingdom of Naples: State in the Italian peninsula (1282–1816)

In 2012, this Austrian skydiver jumped from a helium balloon in the stratosphere as part of a Red Bull-sponsored project, becoming the first person to break the sound barrier during freefall without vehicular power. Who is he?
Felix Baumgartner: Austrian skydiver and extreme sportsman (1969–2025)
Founded by the Italian saint Francis of Assisi, this Catholic religious family includes the Order of Friars Minor for men and the Order of Saint Clare for nuns — what are its members called?
Franciscans: Group of religious orders within the Catholic Church connected with St. Francis of Assisi.
Recorded by the 12th-century chronicler Saxo as a Viking shield-maiden and onetime wife of the legendary Ragnar Lodbrok, this warrior may actually be rooted in myths about a Norse deity — who is she?
Lagertha: Legendary Viking shieldmaiden and ruler.

The longest-serving leader of Germany's Free Democratic Party, this politician served as Federal Finance Minister until his 2024 dismissal, and his cabinet exit is seen as the catalyst for his party's 2025 parliamentary wipeout — who is he?
As head of Nazi Germany's secret state police for most of World War II, this SS official attended the 1942 Wannsee Conference that formalized plans for the genocide of European Jews — who was he?
Heinrich Müller (Gestapo) (28 April 1900; date of death unknown, but evidence points to May 1945) was a high-ranking German Schutzstaffel (SS) and police official during the Nazi era.
Born a prince of the Cherusci tribe and once a Roman citizen himself, this chieftain masterminded the ambush that wiped out three Roman legions at the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 — who is he?
Arminius: Germanic Cherusci chieftain (18/17 BC – AD 21)

Emerging from the fragmentation of the Golden Horde around 1465, this Central Asian nomadic state eventually stretched from the Caspian and Aral seas to the Ural Mountains under Kasym Khan — what was it?
Kazakh Khanate: 1465–1847 Turkic state in Central Asia.

This Byzantine emperor's early reign saw the Persians overrun Syria and Egypt after a defeat at Antioch, yet he rebuilt his army and drove them all the way back, winning a decisive victory in 627 — who is he?
Serving as the 18th U.S. ambassador to NATO before rising to Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, this diplomat briefly served as acting deputy secretary of state in 2023 — who is she?
Regarded as Nazi Germany's 'most extreme executioner,' this war criminal commanded a notorious penal Waffen-SS unit before dying in Allied custody in 1945 — who was he?
Oskar Dirlewanger: German military officer and war criminal (1895–1945)
Born from a fire sacrifice performed for a king of Panchala, this Mahabharata heroine became the shared wife of five Pandava brothers in a divinely sanctioned marriage — who is she?
Draupadi: Heroine of the ancient Hindu epic Mahabharata.
This Elizabethan explorer and statesman helped defend England against the Spanish Armada while also playing a leading role in colonizing North America — who was he?
Walter Raleigh: English statesman and explorer (1552–1618)
This career diplomat briefly served as acting U.S. secretary of state for a single day in 2009, and later led the CIA throughout the Biden administration — who is he?

William J. Burns (diplomat) (born April 11, 1956) is an American diplomat who served as the 8th director of the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) during the Biden administration from March 19, 2021 to January 20, 2025.

Named as a single people by the ancient Greeks, this Indo-European group inhabited modern Bulgaria, Romania, and parts of Greece and Turkey, giving rise to tribes like the Getae and Dacians — who were they?
Thracians: Indo-European people in ancient southeast Europe.

Carried out from a blue 1990 Chevrolet Caprice by two shooters, John Allen Muhammad and teenage accomplice Lee Boyd Malvo, this three-week shooting spree terrorized the Washington metropolitan area in October 2002 — what is it known as?
D.C. sniper attacks: 2002 series of coordinated shootings in the Washington, D.C. area.
Elected in 2014 to the same Yamagata seat her father once held, this Japanese politician went on to serve as Minister of State in the Kishida Cabinet — who is she?
Nicknamed 'the Grey-Haired,' this decorated Russian colonel was tapped by Vladimir Putin to take over a mercenary group after its leader's brief rebellion in 2023 — who is he?
Once considered one of the finest ODI batsmen in the world, this Indian captain led three World Cup campaigns in the 1990s before a life ban for match-fixing ended his career — who is he?

Mohammad Azharuddin: Indian cricketer. Mohammad Azizuddin Azharuddin (born 8 February 1963) is an Indian politician and a former cricketer who also served as the Indian national cricket team's captain.

Known to the Rus as the Obri and to the Göktürks as the Apar, this nomadic confederation ruled a khaganate centered on the Carpathian Basin from the late sixth to early ninth centuries — who were they?
Pannonian Avars: Alliance of various Eurasian nomads – 6th to 9th centuries.
A journalist who once served a year in prison for defamation, this politician has served as Armenia's prime minister since 2018 while pushing for closer ties with Turkey — who is he?
Nikol Pashinyan: Prime Minister of Armenia since 2018. Nikol Vovayi Pashinyan (born 1 June 1975) is an Armenian politician who is serving as the 16th and current prime minister of Armenia since 2018.
As chief of the Wehrmacht High Command's operations staff throughout World War II, this officer was convicted at Nuremberg for signing the notorious Commando and Commissar Orders — who was he?
Alfred Jodl: German general and war criminal (1890–1946)
This US Army military intelligence officer commanded the Alsos Mission during World War II and retired with the rank of colonel — who was he?
Boris Pash: United States Army officer (1900–1995)

This British mining magnate served as Prime Minister of the Cape Colony in the 1890s, entered the diamond trade at Kimberley in 1871 with backing from the Rothschild family, and dreamed of a railway spanning Cape Town to Cairo — who was he?
Cecil Rhodes: British mining magnate and politician (1853–1902)

Widely regarded as one of the greatest Roman historians, this writer chronicled the empire from Augustus's death to Domitian's reign in two major works, and also penned an account of his general father-in-law's campaigns in Britain — who was he?
Born Kunihiro in Ehime, Japan, in February 1946, this actor is better known by his professional stage name — who is he?

After his father abdicated in 2006 following 34 years of rule, this Wheaton College graduate became, at 26, the world's youngest reigning monarch, later overseeing his country's transition to constitutional monarchy — who is he?
Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck: King of Bhutan since 2006.
The last president of Afghanistan before the Taliban takeover in 2021, he held a PhD in cultural anthropology from Columbia University and once taught at Johns Hopkins — who is he?

Ashraf Ghani (born 19 May 1949) is an Afghan former politician and economist who served as the 8th and last president of Afghanistan from 2014 until his government was overthrown by the Taliban in 2021.
Blind in one eye from glaucoma and known affectionately as 'Gus Dur,' this Islamic scholar served as Indonesia's fourth president from 1999 until his removal in 2001 — who is he?
Abdurrahman Wahid: President of Indonesia from 1999 to 2001. On 17 January 2000, Abdurrahman issued Presidential Decree No. 6 of 2000 to annul the previous instruction.
She became the first Black woman and first openly LGBTQ person to serve as mayor of Chicago, holding the office from 2019 to 2023 — who is she?
Lori Lightfoot: Mayor of Chicago from 2019 to 2023. Lori Elaine Lightfoot (born August 4, 1962) is an American politician and attorney who was the 56th mayor of Chicago from 2019 until 2023.

Triggered by confusion over the succession after Tsar Alexander I's sudden death, this failed 1825 coup by liberal military officers took place in Saint Petersburg — what was this failed uprising called?
Decembrist revolt: 1825 failed coup in the Russian Empire.

This Polish resistance leader deliberately got himself captured by the Germans in 1940 so he could infiltrate a notorious concentration camp and organize a resistance movement from within — who is he?

Born an infanta and married to her double first cousin Louis XIV in 1660 to end a long war, this queen of France saw five of her six children die in childhood and was often overshadowed by the king's mistresses — who was she?
Maria Theresa of Spain: Queen consort of France.
This British peer, author, and broadcaster is the younger brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, and the maternal uncle of Princes William and Harry — who is he?
Charles Spencer, 9th Earl Spencer: British peer (born 1964)
Trained as an aeronautical engineer and mathematics professor, this Spanish politician served as the EU's top diplomat and a European Commission vice-president from 2019 to 2024 — who is he?
This Scottish missionary-explorer's obsession with finding the source of the Nile was driven by his belief that fame would help him end the East African slave trade — who is he?
David Livingstone: British colonialist and missionary.

The first woman elected as both a judge and district attorney in New York's Westchester County, this television host went on to become the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia in 2025 — who is she?
Jeanine Pirro: American television host, author and attorney (born 1951)
This 1992 mass killing of Azerbaijani civilians by Armenian and allied forces in a Nagorno-Karabakh town became the deadliest single event of that conflict — what is it known as?
Khojaly massacre: 1992 mass killing of Azerbaijanis during the First Nagorno-Karabakh War.

A boilermaker before West Point, this U.S. general graduated in 1915 alongside Dwight Eisenhower in "the class the stars fell on" and later became the first chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff — who is he?
Omar Bradley: United States Army general (1893–1981)

One of three major ancient Paleo-Balkan peoples alongside the Thracians and Greeks, this Indo-European group gave their name to a western Balkan region first described by a 6th-century-BC Greek writer — who were they?

Punished in the underworld by standing in a pool beneath a fruit tree whose branches always pulled away from his grasp, this Greek mythological figure lent his name to the English word for teasing someone with something unreachable — who was he?
Tantalus: Greek mythological figure and son of Zeus.
This 2006 incident, believed to be the only human fatality from a stingray strike ever captured on camera, happened at Batt Reef off Australia during the filming of a nature documentary. What was it?
Death of Steve Irwin: 2006 animal encounter accident.

Nominated in 2019 by Alexander Gauland to become co-chair of Germany's far-right AfD alongside Alice Weidel, this Bundestag member is known for pro-Russian, eurosceptic foreign-policy views. Who is he?
Centered in what is now southwestern Iran, with its capital at Susa, this Bronze Age civilization was known to classical writers as Susiana. What was this ancient Near Eastern civilization called?
Elam: Ancient pre-Iranian civilization between 3200 and 539 BC.
This Roman general campaigned against Arminius in Germania, and his honorific title honored his father's own victories there before he was adopted by his uncle Tiberius. Who was he?
This French luxury marque split from its former parent company in 2014; its two-letter name nods to a classic executive car and puns on the French word for 'goddess.' What's the brand?
DS Automobiles: French premium car marque of Stellantis.
A computer engineer by training, this Mexican senator and former Mexico City borough mayor ran as a coalition's nominee for the 2024 presidential election. Who is she?
Holding the title Count of Mordano, this Italian Fascist-era politician also served his country as an ambassador. Who is he?

Highly regarded as a military strategist, this Vietnamese general led communist forces to victory across the decades-long Indochina wars, while also serving as minister of defense and deputy prime minister. Who is he?
Võ Nguyên Giáp: Vietnamese general and communist politician (1911–2013)

Waged by Julius Caesar between 58 and 50 BC against the tribes of Gaul, this decade of Roman military campaigns culminated in the Battle of Alesia and the Republic's total conquest of the region. What conflict is this?
Gallic Wars were waged between 58 and 50 BC by the Roman general Julius Caesar against the peoples of Gaul (present-day France, Belgium, and Switzerland).
Allegedly the first Syrian to hold the position, this militant leader served as the fourth so-called caliph of the Islamic State from November 2022 until his death in April 2023. Who was he?
Abu al-Hussein al-Husseini al-Qurashi: Islamic State leader from 2022 to 2023.

A German Army intelligence officer in occupied Warsaw during WWII, this man is credited with saving several Polish Jews, including pianist Władysław Szpilman — his story was dramatized in The Pianist. Who was he?
Wilm Hosenfeld: German army officer (1895–1952) and Righteous among the Nations.
Known as 'the eye of Ra,' this Egyptian warrior goddess of medicine is often linked with Hathor and Bastet — who is she?
Sekhmet: Ancient Egyptian goddess. Sekhmet is also a solar deity, sometimes given the epithet "the eye of Ra".

This passenger airliner was grounded worldwide for nearly two years after 346 people died in two crashes within five months, and grounded again briefly in January 2024 after an in-flight incident. What aircraft is this?

Boeing 737 MAX groundings was grounded worldwide between March 2019 and December 2020 after 346 people died in two similar crashes in less than five months, and briefly in January 2024 following a dangerous in-flight incident.
Born in 2005, this Scandinavian royal became heir apparent to his country's throne when his grandmother abdicated and his father ascended in January 2024 — who is he?

Christian, Crown Prince of Denmark: Heir apparent to the Danish throne (born 2005). Christian, Crown Prince of Denmark, Count of Monpezat (Christian Valdemar Henri John; born 15 October 2005), is the heir apparent to the Danish throne.
In the Book of Genesis, this unnamed woman falsely accused Joseph of assault after he spurned her advances, landing him in prison — later Islamic tradition names her Zuleikha. Who is she?
Potiphar's wife: Figure from Jewish and Muslim tradition.
After leading Turkey's main miners' union and briefly working at the World Bank, this engineer-turned-statesman served as prime minister before becoming president from 1989 to 1993 — who is he?
Turgut Özal: President of Turkey from 1989 to 1993. ANAP won a parliamentary majority in the 1983 general election and Özal subsequently became the prime minister of Turkey.

Born into a farming family, this Indian politician served as chief minister of Karnataka before a nearly 11-month stint as prime minister during a hung-parliament coalition in the mid-1990s — who is he?
H. D. Deve Gowda: President of Janata Dal (Secular)

After co-founding a coal brokerage company, this West Virginia politician served as governor before spending 15 years in the U.S. Senate, ultimately leaving the Democratic Party to become an independent in 2024 — who is he?
Joe Manchin: American politician and businessman (born 1947)
Nicknamed 'Father of Conquests,' this fourth Mamluk sultan led the army that inflicted the Mongols' first major defeat at the Battle of Ain Jalut — who was he?
Baybars: Sultan of Egypt and Syria from 1260 to 1277.
Set in 6th-century BC Babylon but likely written centuries later, this Hebrew Bible text mixes court tales with apocalyptic visions of the end times — which biblical work is it?
Book of Daniel is a 2nd-century BC biblical apocalypse with a 6th-century BC setting.
As second son and designated heir apparent to Iraq's dictator from 2000, this security official ran the Republican Guard and reportedly authorized torture against dissidents — who was he?
Leader of Spain's far-right Vox party since 2014 and president of Patriots.eu since 2024, this politician represents Madrid in the Congress of Deputies — who is he?
Nicknamed 'The Restorer' after reuniting a fractured empire in 1413 following a civil war among brothers, this Ottoman sultan lost a naval battle to Venice off Gallipoli in 1416 — who was he?
Mehmed I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1413 to 1421.
The eldest son of a U.S. president assassinated in 1865, this lawyer was the only one of his parents' four children to live past 18, and later served as Secretary of War — who is he?
Robert Todd Lincoln: American lawyer and politician (1843–1926)

Traditionally credited to an 8th-century BCE prophet but believed by modern scholars to blend the work of at least three authors across centuries, which text opens the major prophets of the Christian Old Testament?
Book of Isaiah is the first of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible and the first of the major prophets in the Christian Old Testament.

Established by Napoleon after his victory at Austerlitz, this alliance of German client states brought about the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire and lasted until his defeat at Leipzig in 1813 — what was it called?
Confederation of the Rhine: Napoleonic union of German client states.

This East African Muslim state, ruled by a hereditary sultan from 1856 to 1964, once controlled a coastal strip of Kenya before losing it and eventually being overthrown by revolutionaries — what was it called?
Sultanate of Zanzibar: 1856–1964 East African Muslim state. It was also involved in the shortest war in history, the Anglo-Zanzibar War, which lasted 38 minutes on the morning of 27 August 1896.

Installed in 1933 and developed by António de Oliveira Salazar, this corporatist authoritarian regime evolved from a 1926 military coup against Portugal's unstable First Republic. What regime is this?
Estado Novo (Portugal) (lit. 'New State') was the corporatist Portuguese state installed in 1933.

Following Hitler's suicide and the fall of Berlin, Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel signed Germany's unconditional surrender in Karlshorst on 8 May 1945 — what major historical event does this mark the conclusion of?
End of World War II in Europe
End of World War II in Europe
End of World War II in Europe: Final battles as well as the surrender by Nazi Germany.
End of World War II in Europe
This Wisconsin Republican served as the 54th Speaker of the House from 2015 to 2019 and was Mitt Romney's running mate in the 2012 presidential election — who is he?
This period of Japanese history spanned the entire reign of Emperor Akihito, beginning the day after his father's death in January 1989 and ending with his abdication in 2019 — what was it called?
Heisei era: Period of Japanese history (1989–2019). Thus, 1989 corresponds to Shōwa 64 up until 7 January and Heisei 1 (平成元年, Heisei gannen; gannen means "first year") from 8 January.
Governing from 1946 to 1958, this parliamentary government presided over rapid postwar economic growth fueled by the Marshall Plan, despite chronic cabinet instability. What was it called?

French Fourth Republic: Government of France from 1946 to 1958. It also saw the beginning of the rapprochement with France's longtime enemy Germany, which led to Franco-German co-operation and eventually to the European Union.
Emerging from a wave of 1848 revolutions that toppled the monarchy, this government lasted only four years before an emperor's proclamation ended it in 1852. What was it called?

French Second Republic: Government of France from 1848 to 1852. The republic existed from 1848, when the monarchy fell, until its dissolution only four years later in 1852 upon the proclamation of the Second French Empire.

This Indian tribal folk hero led a millenarian religious movement against British rule in the late 19th century, after converting to Christianity and later founding his own faith among his community. Who is he?
Birsa Munda: Indian tribal freedom fighter and religious leader (1875–1900)
As chairman of a football ownership group, this Emirati executive oversees Manchester City and other clubs worldwide, while also serving as Abu Dhabi's Presidential Special Envoy to China. Who is he?
Khaldoon Al Mubarak: Emirati investment manager.

Founded in 1922 in consultation with the Comintern, outlawed in 1925, and only legalized after World War II, this is Japan's oldest active political party, with 250,000 members as of 2024 — which party?
Serving as Japan's prime minister from 2001 to 2006, he ranks as the sixth-longest-serving head of government in his country's history and once held the health and welfare portfolio twice. Who is he?
