Originally announced under a name too similar to a rival's title before its 2012 rename, this free-to-play vehicular combat game from Gaijin Entertainment even claimed at first to be an April Fools' joke. What is it?
War Thunder: Vehicular combat multiplayer video game.
Narrated by a narcissistic Manhattan investment banker secretly moonlighting as a serial killer, this 1991 Bret Easton Ellis novel was later filmed with Christian Bale in the lead. What's the book?

American Psycho: 1991 novel by Bret Easton Ellis. The story is told in the first-person by Patrick Bateman, a wealthy, narcissistic, and vain Manhattan investment banker who lives a double life as a serial killer.
Famous for never removing his helmet, this taciturn armored bounty hunter served both the Galactic Empire and Jabba the Hutt before apparently meeting his end in a sarlacc pit. Who is he?

Flowers in the Attic: 1979 novel by V. C. Andrews.

In this 1987 novel by Haruki Murakami, a college student in late-1960s Tokyo looks back on his relationships with two very different women — one fragile, one vivacious — what novel is it?
Norwegian Wood (novel) (Noruwei no Mori) is a 1987 novel by Japanese author Haruki Murakami.
Author of the 'Life, Interrupted' column in The New York Times, her memoir 'Between Two Kingdoms' chronicled her battle with leukemia?
Suleika Jaouad: American writer and motivational speaker (born 1988)

Calligraphy: Visual art related to writing. Calligraphy (from Ancient Greek καλλιγραφία (kalligraphía) 'beautiful writing') is fine handwriting taken to the level of visual art.
The first woman admitted to Florence's Accademia di Arte del Disegno, this Italian Baroque painter worked in the style of Caravaggio and later served at the court of Charles I of England?
Author of the 1667 epic 'Paradise Lost' and the influential free-speech tract 'Areopagitica,' this English poet also served as a civil servant under Oliver Cromwell — who was he?
John Milton: English poet and civil servant (1608–1674)
The fifteenth mainline entry in this action RPG series takes place on the world of Eos, where the empire of Niflheim hunts a magical Crystal guarded by the royal family of Lucis — which game?
This American columnist and journalist spent eighteen months living as a man for research, chronicled in her 2006 book 'Self-Made Man' — who is she?

Written by thriller novelist Ken Follett and set during England's 12th-century civil war known as the Anarchy, this 1989 novel follows the building of a cathedral in fictional Kingsbridge — what's the book?
The Pillars of the Earth: 1989 historical novel by Ken Follett. The Pillars of the Earth became his best-selling work.
Twice shortlisted for the Booker Prize and dubbed a master of 'the new unpleasantness' by the New York Times, this English novelist wrote 'Money' and 'London Fields' — who was he?

In this 1819 Brothers Grimm fairy tale, four aging farm animals set out to become performers in a German city but never actually arrive, instead scaring off robbers and moving into their house — which tale?
Town Musicians of Bremen: German fairy tale. It tells the story of four ageing domestic animals, who after a lifetime of hard work are neglected and mistreated by their former masters.
Serialized in Galaxy magazine in 1969, this novel by Frank Herbert is the second installment in his six-book science fiction series, whose sequel was adapted into a 2003 TV miniseries — which novel?
Dune Messiah: 1969 science fiction novel by Frank Herbert. A sequel to Dune (1965), it was originally serialized in Galaxy magazine in 1969, and then published by Putnam the same year.

Heaven Official's Blessing: 2017 novel by Mo Xiang Tong Xiu. Heaven Official's Blessing (Chinese: 天官赐福; pinyin: Tiān Guān Cì Fú) is a Chinese novel written by Mo Xiang Tong Xiu (墨香铜臭).

A key founder of the Confessing Church who wrote 'The Cost of Discipleship' in 1937, this German pastor's outspoken resistance to the Nazi regime led to his arrest in 1943 and imprisonment at Flossenbürg — who is he?
Dietrich Bonhoeffer: German Lutheran pastor and theologian (1906–1945)
Published in 1998, this British fantasy novel follows a young wizard's second year at his magical school and sparked religious debate over its depiction of magic. Which book?
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets: 1998 fantasy novel by J. K. Rowling.
Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets
Set in Messina, this Shakespearean comedy pairs witty rivals who are each tricked into confessing their love for each other through overheard gossip. Which play?
Much Ado About Nothing: Comedy play by William Shakespeare.
In this 1993 dystopian novel, a 12-year-old boy is chosen to inherit all of society's suppressed memories from before it embraced colorless 'Sameness.' Which book?
The Giver: 1993 novel by Lois Lowry.
A playwright who used absurdist theater to mock the Communist system, this dissident became the last president of Czechoslovakia and the first president of the Czech Republic. Who is he?
Václav Havel: Last president of Czechoslovakia and first president of the Czech Republic (1936–2011)
Published in 1859 and drawing on evidence gathered aboard the Beagle, this foundational work by an English naturalist introduced natural selection as the driver of evolution. What book?
On the Origin of Species: 1859 book on evolution by Charles Darwin.
Voiced by Daniel Kaluuya in a 2023 animated multiverse film, this alternate-universe, rebellious rocker take on a famous web-slinging hero battles a version of Norman Osborn. Which hero?
In this 1962 Philip K. Dick novel, the Axis powers won World War II, and a book-within-the-book called The Grasshopper Lies Heavy imagines the Allies winning instead — which Hugo Award-winning title?
The Man in the High Castle
The Man in the High Castle

The Man in the High Castle: 1962 novel by Philip K. Dick. The Man in the High Castle won the Hugo Award for Best Novel in 1963 and was adapted to television for Amazon Prime Video as The Man in the High Castle in 2015.
The Man in the High Castle
Published in two parts in 1880 and 1881 by Swiss author Johanna Spyri, this children's novel follows a five-year-old girl living with her grandfather in the Alps — which book?
Heidi: 1880–1881 Swiss novel by Johanna Spyri. It is a novel about the events in the life of a five-year-old girl in her paternal grandfather's care in the Swiss Alps.
Part of the so-called Literary Brat Pack, this American novelist published Less Than Zero at 21 and later wrote the controversial bestseller American Psycho — who is he?
Bret Easton Ellis: American author, screenwriter, and director (born 1964)
Though unnamed in the New Testament, this stepdaughter of Herod Antipas famously danced at his birthday feast and then demanded the head of John the Baptist — who was she?
Salome: Daughter of Herod II and Herodias.
Published in 1979 by Michael Ende, this German fantasy novel was translated into English by Ralph Manheim in 1983 and later adapted into a film series — which book?
The Neverending Story: 1979 fantasy novel by Michael Ende and its franchise.

Standing just over four inches tall and carved from limestone tinted with red ochre, this Paleolithic figurine was unearthed in Lower Austria in 1908 and estimated to be 30,000 years old — what is it called?
Venus of Willendorf: Prehistoric figurine from Austria. The Venus of Willendorf is an 11.1-centimetre-tall (4.4 in) Venus figurine estimated to have been made c. 30,000 years ago.
Taken by Voyager 1 from over 6 billion kilometers away in 1990, this photograph shows Earth as less than a single pixel — championed by astronomer Carl Sagan, what is it called?
Pale Blue Dot: Photograph of Earth by Voyager 1.
A pioneer of modern dance who performed across Europe, the U.S., and Soviet Russia, she died in Nice when her scarf became tangled in a car's wheel — who was she?
Isadora Duncan: American dancer and choreographer (1877–1927)
Published in 2005 and selling almost seven million copies on day one, this penultimate novel in a wizarding series delves into the villain's early life — which book is it?
Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince: 2005 fantasy novel by J. K. Rowling.
Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince
D. H. Lawrence's final novel triggered a landmark 1960 obscenity trial in Britain that Penguin Books won, selling three million copies once the ban lifted — which book is it?
Lady Chatterley's Lover: 1928 novel by D. H. Lawrence.
After anchoring Weekend Update and serving as head writer on Saturday Night Live, this comedian has hosted his own NBC late-night show since 2014 — who is he?
Seth Meyers: American comedian and TV host (born 1973)
The longest book in a wizarding-school series, this 2003 novel follows its hero's fifth year of exams and a meddling Ministry as the villain quietly returns — which book is it?
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix: 2003 fantasy novel by J. K. Rowling.
Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix
This Italian blogger built a following with The Blonde Salad before a fundraising fraud scandal known as Pandorogate led to a €1 million fine and her split from husband Fedez — who is she?
Chiara Ferragni: Italian blogger and influencer (born 1987)
Written by a Filipino writer and activist under Spanish colonial rule, this Latin-titled novel ('Touch Me Not') exposed injustices by friars and government — what book is it?
Noli Me Tángere (novel) (Latin for "Touch Me Not") is a novel by Filipino writer and activist Jos Rizal and was published during the Spanish colonial period of the Philippines.
A former White House Communications Director under George W. Bush and senior advisor to John McCain's 2008 campaign, she now anchors Deadline: White House — who is she?
Nicolle Wallace: American TV political commentator (born 1972)
Married to Canada's 23rd prime minister in 2005 before their 2023 separation, this public speaker focuses on environmental and children's causes — who is she?
Sophie Grégoire Trudeau: Canadian TV presenter (born 1975)
Published in 1852 by Harriet Beecher Stowe, this anti-slavery novel became the best-selling novel of the 19th century after the Bible — which book?
Uncle Tom's Cabin: 1852 novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe. Uncle Tom's Cabin; or, Life Among the Lowly is an anti-slavery novel by American author Harriet Beecher Stowe.
Written in 2006 by Irish novelist John Boyne, this book follows a German commandant's son who befriends a Jewish detainee at Auschwitz — which novel?
The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas
The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas
The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas: 2006 novel by John Boyne. The book has received a divided response from critics, with positive reviews praising the story as an effective morality tale.
The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas

Nicknamed 'the Certaldese' after his hometown, this 14th-century Italian humanist wrote The Decameron, a landmark collection of short stories. Who is he?
Giovanni Boccaccio: Italian author and poet (1313–1375)

Founded in 1848 by seven English painters and poets partly modeled on the Nazarene movement, this group sought a return to the vivid color and intense detail of Quattrocento Italian art. What was it called?

Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood: Group of English painters, poets, and critics founded in 1848. Later followers of the principles of the Brotherhood included Edward Burne-Jones and John William Waterhouse.
Born in Boulogne-Billancourt, this French politician has served in the European Parliament since 2019 and co-leads the party Place publique. Who is he?

Dubbed the father of 'scientific history,' this Athenian general chronicled the war between Sparta and Athens without invoking the gods — who was he?
Thucydides: 5th-century BC Athenian historian and general.

Smuggled into circulation via underground samizdat presses before its official 1973 Paris publication, this three-volume work by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn exposed the Soviet forced-labor camp system — what is it called?
The Gulag Archipelago: 1973 non-fiction book by Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn.
Composed in 1946 by a German Lutheran pastor, this confessional poem condemns the silence of intellectuals and clergy as the Nazis picked off their targets one group at a time — what is its title?
First They Came: Statement and poem by Martin Niemöller.
This manga about a group of students fighting to survive a zombie outbreak was left unfinished after co-creator Daisuke Sato's death in 2017 — what's the title?
Highschool of the Dead: Japanese media franchise.

Released in 2003 for Windows, this first-person shooter simulates World War II infantry combat across American, British, and Soviet campaigns, launching what would become one of gaming's biggest franchises. What game is this?
Call of Duty (video game) is a 2003 first-person shooter game developed by Infinity Ward and published by Activision.

In the best-known version of this 19th-century British fairy tale, an uninvited golden-haired girl samples porridge, breaks a chair, and falls asleep in the wrong bed inside a father, mother, and baby's forest home — what's the title?
Goldilocks and the Three Bears: 19th-century British fairy tale. "Goldilocks and the Three Bears" is a traditional classic 19th-century British fairy tale of which three versions exist.

Diablo (video game) is a 1997 action role-playing game developed by Blizzard North and published by Blizzard Entertainment for Windows.
This American broadcast journalist co-anchored NBC's Today show from 2018 to 2025 and hosted its entertainment-focused fourth hour for nearly two decades — who is she?
Hoda Kotb: American journalist and author (born 1964)

Originally conceived as a screenplay before becoming a 2005 novel, this Cormac McCarthy story of a drug deal gone wrong was adapted by the Coen brothers into a film that won four Academy Awards. What book is this?

Created by writer Bill Finger, this Gotham City villain is really psychologist Dr. Jonathan Crane, who turned to crime armed with a hallucinogenic 'fear toxin' — who is he?
Scarecrow (DC Comics): Supervillain in the DC Universe.

Published in 1989 by Stephen Covey, this self-help classic argues that character ethic, not personality ethic, is the key to lasting personal growth, laid out through principles he identified as conducive to change — what is the title?

The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People: 1989 book by Stephen R. Covey.

Known posthumously as the 'father of Russian punk rock,' this singer-songwriter founded the post-punk band Civil Defense and was a central figure of the Siberian punk scene — who is he?

Stray (video game) is a 2022 adventure game developed by BlueTwelve Studio and published by Annapurna Interactive.
This British comedian co-created a BBC sketch series with her longtime partner Jennifer Saunders and later starred as a small-village clergywoman in a hit BBC sitcom — who is she?
Dawn French: British actress, comedian and writer (born 1957)
This Polish Franciscan friar volunteered to die in a fellow prisoner's place at the German death camp of Auschwitz during World War II, and was later canonized as a martyr of charity — who is he?
Maximilian Kolbe: Polish Franciscan friar and saint (1894–1941)

Released the same day as its more famous sibling Unity in 2014, this stealth-action game was the last installment in its long-running historical series to appear on seventh-generation consoles, later remastered for Switch and Stadia — what's it called?
Assassin's Creed Rogue: 2014 video game. Assassin's Creed Rogue is a 2014 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Sofia and published by Ubisoft.

Refused publication in the USSR for its critical stance on the Revolution, this 1957 novel by Boris Pasternak was smuggled to Italy for its first printing, winning its author the Nobel Prize in Literature. What novel is this?
Doctor Zhivago (novel) (zhiv-) is a novel by Russian poet, author and composer Boris Pasternak, first published in 1957 in Italy.
At the foot of the Mount of Olives in East Jerusalem, this garden is where the Gospels say Jesus prayed in anguish before his arrest. What is it called?
Gethsemane: Garden by Jerusalem's Mount of Olives. The garden is a place of great resonance in Christianity.

Written by George Bernard Shaw in 1912 and named for a Greek mythological sculptor, this play about a phonetics professor transforming a Cockney flower girl was later musicalized as My Fair Lady. What is this play called?
Pygmalion (play) is a play written by George Bernard Shaw in 1912, named after the Greek mythological figure.
This Portuguese poet wrote under roughly seventy-five invented alter egos he called heteronyms, three of which — Caeiro, de Campos, and Reis — became major voices in their own right. Who was he?
Fernando Pessoa: Portuguese poet, writer, and philosopher (1888–1935)

Abducted at seventeen by a serial killer who had already murdered at least ten women in the Tampa Bay area, she survived to help police catch him and later spent decades in law enforcement herself. Who is she?
Lisa McVey: American police officer and motivational speaker, kidnapping victim of Bobby Joe Long.

Arthur Miller's 1953 play dramatizes the Salem witch trials as an allegory for McCarthyism; its author was later convicted of contempt of Congress for refusing to name fellow attendees at political meetings. What is this play?
The Crucible: 1953 play by Arthur Miller. It is a dramatized and partially fictionalized story of the Salem witch trials that took place in the Province of Massachusetts Bay from 1692 to 1693.

Javier Bardem won an Oscar for playing this remorseless hitman antagonist in the Coen brothers' adaptation of a Cormac McCarthy novel — a performance later named the most realistic screen depiction of a psychopath. Who is this character?

Assassin's Creed Syndicate: 2015 video game. Assassin's Creed Syndicate is a 2015 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Quebec and published by Ubisoft.

Though he considered himself primarily a poet, this English writer first found fame for novels like Tess of the d'Urbervilles and Far from the Madding Crowd, chronicling the declining fortunes of rural England. Who is he?
Thomas Hardy: English novelist and poet (1840–1928)
In this 2013 survival horror game from Canadian studio Red Barrels, a freelance journalist investigates a remote psychiatric hospital deep in the Colorado mountains. What game is this?
Outlast: 2013 video game. Outlast is a 2013 first-person psychological survival horror video game developed and published by the Canadian independent studio Red Barrels.

A Dutch polymath fluent in three languages and holding degrees in medicine, philosophy, and literature, this fictional vampire hunter is the arch-nemesis of Count Dracula in Bram Stoker's 1897 novel. Who is he?
Abraham Van Helsing: Fictional character created by Bram Stoker.

Born into slavery in Virginia in 1856 and freed as a child during the Civil War, this educator became the founding leader of the Tuskegee Institute in 1881 and rose to national prominence with his 1895 Atlanta Address. Who is he?
Booker T. Washington: American educator, author, orator and adviser (1856–1915)
This dancer partnered Gene Kelly in On the Town and Danny Kaye in White Christmas — who is she?
Vera-Ellen: American actress, singer and dancer (1921–1981)
Close friend of fellow Tang-dynasty poet Du Fu, this master's work is one of the 'Three Wonders' alongside a swordsman and a calligrapher — who is he?

Katniss Everdeen: Main character in the Hunger Games universe.

Released in 2009, this Ubisoft Montreal game follows Desmond Miles reliving the memories of his ancestor Ezio Auditore da Firenze — which game?
Assassin's Creed II: 2009 video game. Assassin's Creed II is a 2009 action-adventure game developed by Ubisoft Montreal and published by Ubisoft.

The daughter of a 43rd U.S. president and granddaughter of a 41st, this NBC personality co-hosts the fourth hour of a long-running morning show — who is she?

Dorohedoro: Japanese manga series. The 23 volumes were published from 2010 to 2019.

Uncle from Another World: Japanese manga series by Hotondoshindeiru.

The Shining (novel) is a 1977 horror novel by American author Stephen King.

Voiced by Mike Rianda in a 2023 animated Spider-Verse sequel and played by Tahar Rahim in 'Madame Web,' which Marvel supporting character shares story arcs with Spider-Man and Silk?

Writing under a pen name, this French physician-novelist won the Prix Renaudot for his bleak 1932 debut, 'Journey to the End of the Night' — what name did he write under?

Carlos Páez Rodríguez: Uruguayan entrepreneur, motivational speaker and writer.

This manga follows a rejected, vengeful teenage mutant named Lucy, part of a horned species wielding telekinetic 'vectors,' and takes its title from a German poem meaning 'song of the fairies' — what's the series?
Elfen Lied: Japanese manga series by Lynn Okamoto.

George Gurdjieff: Russian Empire mystic and writer (c. 1866–1877 – 1949)

Sirius Black: Fictional character in J. K. Rowling's Harry Potter novels.

In this 2017 Metroidvania from Australian studio Team Cherry, a nameless insectoid warrior explores the fallen, disease-plagued kingdom of Hallownest — what's the game?

Published in 2005 as the first installment of a Greek-mythology-inspired series, this Rick Riordan novel got both a 2010 film and a Disney+ series adaptation from 2023-2024 — what's the book?

During an 18-month split between John Lennon and Yoko Ono that Lennon later called his 'Lost Weekend,' this former personal assistant became his companion and later wrote two books about the relationship — who is she?
This 1996 encyclopedic novel by David Foster Wallace is stuffed with hundreds of sprawling endnotes — some with their own footnotes — and has sold over a million copies worldwide. What is it?

Infinite Jest: 1996 novel by David Foster Wallace. Categorized as an encyclopedic novel, Infinite Jest is featured in Time magazine's list of the 100 best English-language novels published between 1923 and 2005.
Known as the 'Apostle of Cuban Independence,' this poet and essayist became a symbol of the island's 19th-century bid for freedom from Spain. Who was he?

12 Rules for Life: 2018 self-help book by Jordan Peterson. It provides life advice through essays in abstract ethical principles, psychology, mythology, religion, and personal anecdotes.
One of the four pillars of the Chhayavaad movement in Hindi literature, this poet was dubbed 'the modern Meera' and likened to Sarasvati by a fellow poet. Who is she?

Born Mileikowsky in Warsaw, this historian and Revisionist Zionism activist specialized in the history of Jews in Spain while teaching at Cornell University. Who was he?

Katie Piper: English television presenter and writer (born 1983)

Lu Xun: Chinese novelist and essayist (1881–1936)

The Last of the Mohicans: 1826 historical novel by James Fenimore Cooper. It is the second book of the Leatherstocking Tales pentalogy and the best known to contemporary audiences.
Originally released in six serial volumes in 1996, this Stephen King novel follows a death row supervisor's encounter with an inmate who possesses inexplicable healing powers — what novel is it?
The Green Mile (novel) is a 1996 serial novel by American writer Stephen King.

Painted by Jacques-Louis David in the months after his friend, a French revolutionary leader, was stabbed in his bathtub by Charlotte Corday in 1793, this Neoclassical work has been called by one historian the first modernist painting. What is it called?

The Death of Marat: 1793 painting by Jacques-Louis David. Created in the months after Marat's death, the painting shows Marat lying dead in his bath after his assassination by Charlotte Corday on 13 July 1793.

A Nobel laureate and Auschwitz survivor, this Romanian-born writer chronicled the Holocaust in his memoir Night and later spoke out on genocides from Rwanda to Darfur — who is he?
Elie Wiesel: American writer and activist (1928–2016)

Alias Slade Wilson, this DC mercenary gained enhanced abilities from an experimental super-soldier serum and became the archenemy of Dick Grayson and the Teen Titans after his son's death sparked a vendetta — who is he?

Rocket Raccoon: Marvel Comics fictional character.
Writing under the pen name Isak Dinesen, this Danish author penned an account of her years in Kenya and a story called 'Babette's Feast,' both later Oscar-winning films — who is she?

At an elite academy for the ultra-wealthy, a middle-class girl clashes with four powerful classmates known as the F4 in this manga serialized from 1992 to 2004 — which series?

Edens Zero: Japanese manga series by Hiro Mashima.

El filibusterismo: 1891 novel by José Rizal.

Laocoön and His Sons: Ancient sculpture excavated in Rome in 1506 AD. The figures are nearly life-sized, with the entire group measuring just over 2 m (6 ft 7 in) in height.

Foundation (Asimov novel) is a science fiction novel by American writer Isaac Asimov.
Crafted by a dramatist for a live audience across venues from Broadway to community stages, this scripted dramatic form is meant to be performed rather than merely read — what is it called?
Play (theatre): Dramatic literary form. A play is a form of theatre that primarily consists of script between speakers and is intended for acting rather than mere reading.

Born in Thetford, Norfolk, and aided by Benjamin Franklin in emigrating to the colonies in 1774, this Founding Father's 47-page pamphlet Common Sense galvanized the case for American independence — who was he?
Thomas Paine: English-born philosopher and author (1737–1809)

Set in a world of anthropomorphic animals where a cultural divide separates carnivores from herbivores and eating meat is strictly illegal, this manga by Paru Itagaki ran in Weekly Shōnen Champion from 2016 to 2020 — what series is it?
Beastars: Japanese manga series. Beastars (stylized in all caps) is a Japanese manga series written and illustrated by Paru Itagaki.

Also a playwright behind Endlings and The Seagull on The Sims 4, this Canadian filmmaker's directorial debut Past Lives earned Oscar nominations for Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay — who is she?

Graham Greene: British writer and playwright (1904–1991)
Jack London's 1903 adventure novel follows a stolen ranch dog named Buck as he's sold into sled-dog service during the Klondike Gold Rush and grows steadily more primal — what is this book called?

Banana Fish: Japanese manga series by Akimi Yoshida.
This universal human tendency to find things funny gets its name from ancient Greek medicine, which held that bodily fluids controlled a person's health and mood — what is it called?
Humour: Tendency of experiences to provoke laughter and provide amusement.

Sam Lake: Finnish video game writer and director.

Nier (video game) is a 2010 action role-playing game developed by Cavia and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360.
Written by Neil Gaiman and centered on a mysterious drifter named Shadow, this 2001 fantasy novel blends US folklore with global mythology and won both the Hugo and Nebula Awards — what's its title?
American Gods: 2001 novel by Neil Gaiman. The novel is a blend of Americana, fantasy, and various strands of ancient and modern mythology, all centering on the mysterious and taciturn Shadow.

The last Mughal emperor and an Urdu poet, this ruler was declared Emperor of India by rebel forces during the 1857 uprising before being exiled to Rangoon, ending a nearly 500-year dynasty founded by Timur — who was he?
Bahadur Shah Zafar: Mughal emperor from 1837 to 1857.

Edicts of Ashoka: 3rd-century BCE inscriptions in South Asia.

Rhodesian Bush War: 1964–1979 conflict in Southern Africa.

Developing the theory of 'offensive realism' at the University of Chicago, this political scientist argued in a 2007 book that a pro-Israel lobby wields outsized influence over American foreign policy — who is he?

This Thai princess, a practicing attorney, helped the United Nations craft the 'Bangkok Rules' on the treatment of incarcerated women — who was she?
In Arthurian legend, this traitorous nephew — later recast as King Arthur's villainous, incestuously conceived son — died alongside him at the Battle of Camlann — who is he?
Mordred: Character in Arthurian legend. Mordred or Modred ( or; Welsh: Medraut or Medrawt) is a major figure in the legend of King Arthur.
This ancient Levantine kingdom along the Dead Sea's eastern shore is known from the Mesha Stele, which records its victory over a son of Israel's King Omri — what was it?
Moab: Ancient kingdom East of the Dead Sea. Moab was an ancient Levantine kingdom whose territory is today located in southern Jordan.
Second only to Cameroon's leader in tenure among non-royal heads of state, this president has ruled Equatorial Guinea since ousting his uncle in a 1979 coup — who is he?
Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo: Dictator of Equatorial Guinea since 1979. Obiang was Chairperson of the African Union from 2011 to 2012.
Once the youngest press secretary in Pentagon history, this political strategist later became a co-host of a daytime talk show while also appearing as a CNN commentator — who is she?
Alyssa Farah Griffin: American political strategist (born 1989)
The son of one U.S. president and younger brother of another, this politician served as Florida's governor from 1999 to 2007 before an unsuccessful 2016 presidential run — who is he?
Jeb Bush: American politician and businessman (born 1953)

Referred to by names like Yahweh, Jehovah, or the Lord, this transcendent yet immanent being is understood by most adherents to exist as a Trinity of three Persons — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. What or who is this?
God in Christianity: Christian conception of God.

In July 1984, a lone gunman killed 22 people at a fast-food restaurant in a Southern California border town before a police sniper ended his 77-minute rampage — for years it held the record as the deadliest such attack by a single gunman in U.S. history. What is this event known as?
San Ysidro McDonald's massacre: 1984 mass shooting in California, U.S.
Educated at Eton and Oxford, this British Conservative politician chaired the eurosceptic European Research Group and later served as Leader of the House of Commons — who is he?
Possibly rooted in Neolithic Çatalhöyük, this Anatolian mother goddess was adopted by Greek colonists and arrives in myth via a lion-drawn chariot — who is she?
Cybele: Anatolian mother goddess. In Greece, Cybele met with a mixed reception.
This Croatian politician founded the Ustaše in 1929 and led a Nazi- and Fascist-backed puppet state carved from occupied Yugoslavia from 1941 to 1945 — who is he?
Ante Pavelić: Dictator of the Independent State of Croatia from 1941 to 1945.
Mentioned in the Book of Exodus as the wife of Moses and daughter of the Midianite priest Jethro, this woman was the mother of Moses' two sons — who is she?
Dated to begin about 5,200 years ago with the invention of writing, this scholarly record traces humanity's religious feelings, thoughts, and ideas across the millennia — what field of study is this?
History of religion is the written record of human religious feelings, thoughts, and ideas.
Nicknamed 'the Prudent,' this King of France defied his father in a 1440 revolt, married the Duke of Savoy's daughter against his father's wishes, and took the throne in 1461 — who is he?
Louis XI: King of France from 1461 to 1483.
Coregent with his stepmother Hatshepsut for 22 years before ruling alone, this pharaoh led between 17 and 20 victorious military campaigns that brought Egypt's empire to its peak — who is he?
Thutmose III: Pharaoh of Egypt from 1479 to 1425 BC.
This French historian of Russian history served as Perpetual Secretary of the Académie Française from 1999 until her death in 2023 — who is she?
Hélène Carrère d'Encausse: French historian (1929–2023). Carrère d'Encausse was a member of the European Parliament between 1994 and 1999, representing the Gaullist-conservative party RPR.

The eldest of nine children born into a family with presidential ambitions, this Navy pilot died in 1944 flying a secret mission called Operation Aphrodite, redirecting his father's hopes to his younger brother — who was he?
Joseph P. Kennedy Jr.: American naval aviator (1915–1944)
A key figure of Chile's Nueva Canción movement, this singer-songwriter was arrested and killed in the days following the 1973 coup that overthrew President Allende — who was he?
Víctor Jara: Chilean folk singer and activist (1932–1973)

A vocal critic of the Federal Reserve and mass surveillance programs, this Texas congressman ran for president as the Libertarian nominee in 1988 before seeking the Republican nomination twice more — who is he?
Reigning for barely seven months in 1016 while battling a Danish invasion led by Cnut, this English king was the son of Æthelred the Unready — who was he?
Edmund Ironside: King of England in 1016. Edmund's reign was spent fighting against a Danish invasion led by Cnut.
Born Rozbih Khwushbudhan and trained as a Zoroastrian magus, this companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad converted to Islam after meeting him in Medina — who was he?

Salman the Persian: Companion of the Islamic prophet Muhammad. Muhammad specifically said "Salman is part of my Ahl al-Bayt." In meetings with the other companions, he was often referred to by the kunya Abu ʿAbdullah.

Home to West Semitic migrants known as the Kaldu who arrived between the 11th and 9th centuries BC, this marshy southern Mesopotamian region is named in the Hebrew Bible as the land of the Kasdim — which region?
Chaldea: Small Semitic nation of ancient Mesopotamia.
Born to King Shantanu and the river goddess Ganga, this Mahabharata hero renounced the throne and vowed lifelong celibacy so his father could marry Satyavati — who was he?
Bhishma: Statesman and patriarch of Kuru kingdom in the Hindu epic Mahabharata.
Wounded in the face, an eye, and seven other places across three wars, this Victoria Cross recipient also survived two plane crashes and tunnelled out of a POW camp — who was he?
Adrian Carton de Wiart: British Army officer (1880–1963)

At 93, this Cameroonian head of state is the world's oldest sitting president and the second-longest-ruling leader in Africa, having taken power in 1982 after his predecessor's surprise resignation — who is he?
Paul Biya: President of Cameroon since 1982.
In 2024, this Manhattan district attorney became the first person to secure a criminal conviction of a former U.S. president — who is he?
Alvin Bragg: American lawyer and politician (born 1973)
Once a Janjaweed chief in Darfur, this Sudanese paramilitary leader now commands the Rapid Support Forces battling the country's regular army in a civil war — who is he?
Hemedti: Leader of the Rapid Support Forces (born c. 1974)
This revolutionary became the first president of an Asian constitutional republic, leading Filipino forces first against Spain and then against the United States — who was he?
Ruling as King of Bahrain since 2002, this monarch introduced the National Action Charter reforms and became the country's first king after its 1999 transition to a kingdom — who is he?

Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa: Emir/King of Bahrain since 1999. Hamad bin Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa (Arabic: حمد بن عيسى بن سلمان آل خليفة; born 28 January 1950) is the King of Bahrain, having reigned since 2002.

Reigning as Rama IV of the Chakri dynasty from 1851 to 1868, this Siamese king embraced Western science and technology, earning a posthumous title as his country's 'Father' of those fields — who was he?
Mongkut: King of Siam from 1851 to 1868. Mongkut (18 October 1804 – 1 October 1868), posthumously honoured as King Mongkut the Great was the king of Siam from the Chakri dynasty, titled Rama IV.
Serving as Bavaria's Minister-President since 2018, this German politician has also led the region's dominant conservative party since 2019 — who is he?
This paratrooper-turned-politician placed third in Russia's 1996 presidential race with about 14% of the vote, later governed Krasnoyarsk Krai, and died in a helicopter crash — who was he?
Alexander Lebed: Soviet and Russian military officer and politician (1950–2002)
Elected as Toronto's mayor in 2023, this former NDP member of Parliament was previously married to a fellow NDP leader who led the Official Opposition in 2011 — who is she?

Spanning roughly 14,000 to 300 BCE, this era of Japanese prehistory saw a sedentary hunter-gatherer culture, whose ancestors migrated from Northeast Asia, Korea, and China, eventually blend with the incoming Yayoi people — which period?
Jōmon period is the time between c.
This king of Sparta went to war after his wife Helen fled to Troy with the prince Paris, fighting alongside his brother Agamemnon — who was he?
Menelaus: King of Sparta, husband of Helen of Troy. In Greek mythology, Menelaus (Ancient Greek: Μενέλαος, Menélaos) was a king of Sparta.
Since October 2021, this French politician has led the La France Insoumise group in the National Assembly, representing Val-de-Marne's 10th constituency — who is she?
According to medieval European legend, this immortal man taunted Jesus on the way to the Crucifixion and was cursed to roam the Earth until the Second Coming — who is this legendary figure?
This former Navy SEAL took part in the 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden and later stirred controversy by claiming he alone fired the fatal shot — who is he?
Robert J. O'Neill: US Navy SEAL (born 1976)
Imprisoned by Israel since 2002 on charges tied to deadly attacks he denies involvement in, this Palestinian legislator has long championed a two-state solution — who is he?

The longest continuous military campaign of World War II, this naval struggle pitted German U-boats against Allied convoys ferrying supplies from North America to Britain and the Soviet Union — what's this campaign called?
Battle of the Atlantic: Attempt by Germany during World War II to cut supply lines to Britain.

This Nigerian general seized power in a 1983 coup and ruled as military head of state, then decades later returned to lead the country as its democratically elected president from 2015 to 2023 — who is he?

Worshipped from the Bronze Age onward, this Hellenized Near Eastern goddess was the Semitic counterpart to Ishtar and was carried by Phoenician traders all the way to their colonies on the Iberian Peninsula — who is she?
Astarte: Middle Eastern goddess, worshipped from the Bronze Age through classical antiquity.
Named after its Austrian founder, this weapons manufacturer is famous for polymer-framed pistols but also makes field knives, entrenching tools, and even horse-riding gear — which company?
Glock GmbH: Austrian light weapons manufacturer. Glock GmbH (doing business as GLOCK) is a light weapons manufacturer headquartered in Deutsch-Wagram, Austria, named after its founder, Gaston Glock.
India's first and longest-serving Minister of Education, this Congress leader and former Khilafat Movement figure has his birthday marked each year as National Education Day — who is he?
Maulana Azad: Indian politician and writer (1888–1958)
Posthumously awarded India's highest military honor, the Param Vir Chakra, this army captain died fighting Pakistani troops at Point 4875 during the Kargil War in 1999 — who is he?
Vikram Batra: Indian Army officer, recipient of Param Vir Chakra (1974–1999)
This eighth Umayyad caliph ordered the first official collection of hadiths and sent emissaries as far as China and Tibet inviting rulers to accept Islam — who was he?
Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz: Umayyad caliph from 717 to 720.
This Japanese term describes marginalized, often homeless youth — a mix of runaways and those seeking community after bullying — who gather in Kabukicho's back alleys. What is this subculture called?
Toyoko kids: Youth group in Tokyo, Japan.
Known as 'Light of the Faith,' this Zengid dynasty ruler governed Seljuk Syria from 1146 to 1174 and looms large in the history of the Second Crusade — who was he?
Nur al-Din Zengi: Emir of Aleppo (1146–1174) and Damascus (1154–1174)

Serving as French prime minister three separate times — twice in the 1930s and again under Vichy France — this politician was executed for treason as a Nazi collaborator after World War II. Who was he?
A member of India's storied Nehru dynasty, this Indian National Congress politician has represented Wayanad in Kerala in the Lok Sabha since November 2024 — who is she?
The son of Ramesses I and father of Ramesses the Great, this Nineteenth Dynasty pharaoh ruled Egypt from around 1290 to 1279 BC — who was he?
Seti I: Egyptian pharaoh. Menmaatre Seti I (or Sethos I in Greek) was the second pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty of Egypt during the New Kingdom period, ruling 1290 BC to 1279 BC.
This Athenian general switched sides repeatedly during the Peloponnesian War — advising Sparta after fleeing sacrilege charges at home, then defecting again to advise a Persian satrap — who was he?
Alcibiades: Athenian general and statesman (c. 450–404 BC)
Formerly named France Télécom, this French telecommunications giant's current brand traces back to a UK mobile operator acquired by Hutchison Whampoa in 1994 — what is it called today?
Orange Group: French multinational telecommunications corporation.
Ruling the Vijayanagara Empire at its political and cultural peak from 1509 to 1529, this emperor defeated the sultans of Bijapur and Golconda and conquered the Raichur Doab in 1512 — who was he?

Krishnadevaraya: Emperor of Vijayanagara from 1509 to 1529. Krishnadevaraya (17 January 1471 – 17 October 1529) was emperor of the Vijayanagara Empire from 1509 to 1529 and the third ruler of the Tuluva dynasty.
Daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, this goddess of the dawn opens heaven's gates each morning for her brother, the sun god, to pass through — who is she?
Eos: Greek goddess of the dawn. In Greek literature, Eos is presented as a daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, the sister of Helios and the moon goddess Selene.
Serving Emperor Justinian I, this Byzantine general reconquered the Vandal Kingdom of North Africa in just nine months and is often called one of the 'Last of the Romans' — who was he?
The first woman to hold her position, this French politician has led the National Assembly since June 2022 and briefly served as Minister of the Overseas before that — who is she?
A career scholar-official of the Goryeo dynasty, this military commander is best remembered for his victories in the Third Goryeo-Khitan War — who is he?
As East Germany's chief decision-maker for two decades, this communist leader demanded the construction of the Berlin Wall in 1961 despite Soviet reluctance — who was he?
Walter Ulbricht: Leader of East Germany from 1950 to 1971.
The only cabinet member to keep his post across two different chancellors, this German politician has served as Federal Minister of Defence since 2023 — who is he?
Whose foundations trace to the 17th-century discovery of gravity and 18th-century advances that gave rise to classical mechanics, this branch of science studies matter and energy — which discipline?
History of physics is a branch of science in which the primary objects of study are matter and energy.

Born in 1953, this woman has claimed headship of a deposed European imperial dynasty since 1992 as a great-great-granddaughter of Emperor Alexander II, though her right to the title remains disputed — who is she?
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia: Disputed head of the House of Romanov.
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia
A scion of the family behind the Hyatt hotel chain, this Illinois governor is the second-wealthiest U.S. elected official, trailing only the president — who is he?
JB Pritzker: Governor of Illinois since 2019.
United by King Masinissa after his victory over Syphax during the Second Punic War, which ancient Berber kingdom in Northwest Africa was later alternately a Roman province and client state?
Numidia: Kingdom in North Africa, 202 to 25 BC.
Nicknamed 'Father of the Flame,' which paternal uncle of the Islamic prophet Muhammad opposed him and is condemned by name in a chapter of the Quran?
Abu Lahab: Uncle of the Islamic prophet Muḥammad (c.549-c.624)
Central to the rise of both Jainism and Buddhism, which ancient Indian kingdom in the eastern Ganges Plain formed the core of the Mauryan and Gupta empires?
Magadha: Region and Mahajanapada in ancient eastern India.
The son of a freedman, this Roman emperor ruled for just 87 days in 193 AD before the Praetorian Guard killed him for trying to restore army discipline — who was he?
Pertinax: Roman emperor in 193. The son of a freedman, Pertinax rose from modest origins through a military career.
Niece and fourth wife of Emperor Claudius, and mother of Nero, which powerful Julio-Claudian woman was great-granddaughter of Augustus?
Agrippina the Younger: Roman empress from AD 49 to 54.
Once head of Taipei's state-owned agricultural marketing company, this retired army officer turned Taiwanese politician has presided over Taiwan's Legislative Yuan since 2024 — who is he?
Executed as a teenager for sabotage against Nazi forces in 1941, which defiant Soviet partisan was posthumously named a Hero of the Soviet Union?

Founded in 680–681 by a nomadic people led by Asparuh after they defeated a Byzantine army, which medieval Balkan state at its height stretched from the Danube Bend to the Black Sea and rivaled Byzantium for centuries?
First Bulgarian Empire: 681–1018 state in Southeast Europe.
This granddaughter of a Michigan governor chaired the Republican National Committee from 2017 until resigning in 2024, presiding over a string of election losses — who is she?
Known at home as the 'Great Power Era,' this 17th-century Baltic dominion began with Gustavus Adolphus's ascension in 1611 and collapsed after the Great Northern War in 1721 — which power?
Swedish Empire: Historical period in the history of Sweden (1611–1721)
This 3rd-century shamaness-queen ruled the land of Wa after decades of warfare, sending tribute to China's Cao Wei kingdom — who was she?
Himiko: 3rd-century Queen of Yamataikoku. Himiko (卑弥呼; c. 170–247/248 AD), also known as the Shingi Waō (親魏倭王; "Ruler of Wa, Friend of Wei"), was a shamaness-queen of Yamatai-koku in Wakoku (倭国).
Proclaimed by Hitler from Prague Castle on 16 March 1939, this partially annexed Nazi territory covered the Czech lands after their occupation — which entity?
Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia: Territory of Nazi Germany (1939–1945)
Named for a 1930s guerrilla leader who resisted US occupation, this Nicaraguan socialist party toppled the Somoza dynasty in 1979 and governed through the 1980s — which party?
Sandinista National Liberation Front: Nicaraguan socialist political party founded in 1961.
From 1922 until the 1952 revolution, this nominally independent North African monarchy still saw Britain control its military and foreign affairs — which state?
Kingdom of Egypt: State in Northeast Africa and Western Asia (1922–1953)
The first woman to serve as Philippine president, she led the 1986 People Power Revolution that ended Ferdinand Marcos's rule — who is she?
Corazon Aquino: President of the Philippines from 1986 to 1992.
This grandson of Genghis, whose army sacked Baghdad in the 13th century and ended the Abbasid dynasty, founded the Ilkhanate in Persia — who was he?
Hulegu Khan: Western Asian Mongol ruler (c. 1217–1265)
Founder of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters party, this politician led the ANC Youth League before his 2012 expulsion — who is he?
Established in 1922 under a treaty that ended a war of independence against British rule, this dominion comprised 26 of 32 counties while the remaining six opted out — what was it called?
Irish Free State: British dominion in Europe from 1922 to 1937.
Eldest son of a U.S. Attorney General and older brother of a future Health and Human Services secretary, this Massachusetts congressman founded a nonprofit heating-oil charity in 1979 — who is he?
Joseph P. Kennedy II: American businessman and politician (born 1952)
Nicknamed 'the Balkan Prussia' for its frequent wars, this Southeastern European tsardom was proclaimed in 1908 when Prince Ferdinand raised it from a principality — what state was it?
Kingdom of Bulgaria: State in southeastern Europe from 1908 to 1946.
This self-proclaimed Sapa Inca led a large Andean rebellion against Spanish colonial rule in Peru and later became a symbol of the independence movement — who was he?
Túpac Amaru II: Leader of an uprising in Peru.
This Norwegian adventurer drifted 8,000 km across the Pacific on a hand-built raft in 1947 to test his theory that South Americans settled Polynesia first — who is he?
Thor Heyerdahl: Norwegian anthropologist and adventurer (1914–2002)
This British Royal Navy officer reached the South Pole in January 1912, just five weeks after a Norwegian rival — but died with his men on the return journey — who was he?
Robert Falcon Scott: British Antarctic explorer (1868–1912)
Nicknamed the 'She-Wolf,' this queen of England served as de facto regent from 1327 to 1330 as wife of Edward II — who was she?
Isabella of France: Queen of England from 1308 to 1327. Isabella arrived in England at age 12 during a period of growing conflict between the king and the powerful baronial factions.
Led by Alexis Tsipras, who twice served as Greece's prime minister starting in 2015, this pro-European left-wing coalition was founded in 2004 — which party?
Syriza: Political party in Greece. It was founded in 2004 as a political coalition of left-wing and radical left parties, and registered as a political party in 2012.
This Indian revolutionary assassinated the former Punjab lieutenant governor in 1940 in revenge for the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre, of which he was a survivor — who was he?
Udham Singh: Indian revolutionary (1899–1940). Singh was subsequently tried and convicted of murder and hanged in July 1940.
Left disabled after a factory accident as a young man, this South Korean politician rose from mayor of Seongnam to become his country's 14th president in 2025 — who is he?
Lee Jae Myung: President of South Korea since 2025.

Formed in the wake of Greece's military junta collapsing in 1974, this liberal-conservative party has been one of the country's two dominant political forces for decades, long rivaling the Panhellenic Socialist Movement — what is it?

New Democracy (Greece) is a liberal-conservative political party in Greece. New Democracy and PASOK were created in the wake of the toppling of the military junta in 1974, ruling Greece in succession for the next four decades.
During the American Civil War, what was the name for the federal government and loyal states that refused to recognize the Confederacy after Lincoln's 1860 election?
Union (American Civil War): US federal government from 1861 to 1865.
Serving from 2017 to 2024 as France's Minister of the Economy, Finance, and Digital Sovereignty, this politician also briefly led the Ministry of the Armed Forces in October 2025 — who is he?

Serving as the Shinawatra family's main political vehicle since its founding as the third incarnation of a party ex-PM Thaksin Shinawatra started in 1998, this party has led Thailand's ruling coalition since 2023 — which party?
Pheu Thai Party (PTP or PT; lit. 'For Thais Party') is a major populist, liberal conservative political party in Thailand.

Surviving five assassination attempts and years of imprisonment and exile for his democratization activism, this opposition leader finally won election as South Korea's eighth president in 1997 — who is he?
Kim Dae-jung: President of South Korea from 1998 to 2003.
A Catholic priest revered as the Father of the Nation, he delivered the famous 'Cry of Dolores' on 16 September 1810 to launch Mexico's independence movement — who is he?
Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla: Mexican Catholic preacher (1753–1811)

Forced into exile as a child when Bulgaria's monarchy was abolished in 1946, this former Tsar returned five decades later to become the country's prime minister after winning the 2001 election — who is he?
Simeon II: Tsar of Bulgaria from 1943 to 1946, Prime Minister from 2001 to 2005.
Leading Greece's Syriza party from 2008, this leftist critic of austerity became prime minister in 2015 and then presided over the country's harsh third EU bailout program — who is he?
Alexis Tsipras: Prime Minister of Greece (2015; 2015–2019). A prominent leftist figure, Tsipras served as the leader of the Greek political party Syriza from 2008 to 2023.
A Catalan lawyer-turned-club president, he steered his team to a record six trophies in twelve months back in 2009 and returned to the presidency again in 2021 — who is he?
Forced to annul his marriage to a disabled cousin so he could instead wed Anne of Brittany and unite her duchy with France, this monarch reigned from 1498 to 1515 — who was he?

Louis XII: King of France from 1498 to 1515. Louis XII (27 June 1462 – 1 January 1515), also known as Louis of Orléans, was King of France from 1498 to 1515 and King of Naples (as Louis III) from 1501 to 1504.
Once a loyal Nazi admiral running Germany's military intelligence service, he turned to sabotage and resistance against Hitler — and was hanged for treason at Flossenbürg in 1945. Who was he?
This Pakistani general became the country's third president under martial law in 1969, and his tenure oversaw the war that led to Bangladesh's independence — who was he?
Yahya Khan: President of Pakistan from 1969 to 1971.
Despite never attending Germany's War Academy, this WWI balloon observer rose to become a highly decorated Luftwaffe field marshal in World War II — who was he?

In 1909, this Korean independence activist assassinated Japan's former prime minister in Harbin, China, an act that led to his execution the following year and a Catholic excommunication not lifted until 1993 — who was he?

The son of Empress Joséphine from her first marriage, this military officer became Napoleon's adopted stepson, served as viceroy of Italy, and commanded the Army of Italy during the Napoleonic Wars — who was he?
Eugène de Beauharnais: French statesman and military officer (1781–1824)
As Mexico's 51st president from 1934 to 1940, this former revolutionary general nationalized the country's oil industry and carried out sweeping land reform — who was he?

Lázaro Cárdenas: President of Mexico from 1934 to 1940. Born in Jiquilpan, Michoacán, to a working-class family, Cárdenas joined the Mexican Revolution and became a general in the Constitutionalist Army.
A far-right Polish politician who once chaired a nationalist youth organization, he ran for president in 2020 and now serves as Deputy Marshal of the Sejm — who is he?
Co-founded by Nigel Farage in 2018 as the Brexit Party before its later renaming, this British party now holds seven seats in the Commons — name it?
Reform UK: Political party in the United Kingdom.
The first African-American to complete the U.S. Navy's basic flight training program, this officer became the first Black naval aviator killed in the Korean War — who was he?
Jesse L. Brown: United States Navy officer (1926–1950)
Known by the Dutch acronym BBB, this agrarian right-wing populist party is headquartered in Deventer and currently led by Henk Vermeer — name the party?
Farmer–Citizen Movement: Political party in the Netherlands.
As founder of the antisemitic newspaper Der Stürmer and Gauleiter of Franconia, this Nazi propagandist became the first member of the regime convicted of inciting genocide at Nuremberg — who was he?
Julius Streicher: German publicist and politician (1885–1946)
Owned by Canal+, this French video-sharing platform was among the first to support 720p HD and now serves over 300 million users monthly across 183 languages — name it?
Identified by three Gospels as a member of the Sanhedrin, this biblical figure took responsibility for burying Jesus following the crucifixion — who was he?
Joseph of Arimathea: Biblical figure responsible for Jesus's burial.

Appointed in 1986 to lead the Soviet commission investigating the Chernobyl disaster, this Deputy Chairman of the Council of Ministers later oversaw relief for the 1988 Armenian earthquake — who was he?

Born at Windsor Castle with her grandmother, the queen, in attendance, this granddaughter of a British monarch married her father's cousin, a Royal Navy officer, and later became Marchioness of Milford Haven — who was she?
Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine
Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine
Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine: Marchioness of Milford Haven (1863–1950)
Princess Victoria of Hesse and by Rhine
Leading a 1980 military coup that deposed Turkey's prime minister and abolished its parliament, this general later served as the country's 7th president — who was he?
Kenan Evren: 7th President of Turkey from 1982 to 1989.
This German Marxist theorist and women's rights advocate represented the Communist Party of Germany in the Reichstag from 1920 to 1933 — who is she?
Nicknamed 'Kaka,' this politician served as the third Chief Minister of Chhattisgarh from 2018 to 2023 after years representing the Patan constituency — who is he?
The second woman ever to hold the job, after Dee Dee Myers, this commentator served as White House press secretary under George W. Bush before co-hosting Fox News's 'The Five' — who is she?
Dana Perino: American conservative political commentator (born 1972)

Once one of the nine members of China's most powerful decision-making body, this former security chief was arrested on corruption charges in 2014 after a career that began in the oil and gas industry — who is he?

A leader of the First Crusade, this nobleman became the first ruler of a newly captured holy city in 1099 but declined the title of king, choosing 'Advocate of the Holy Sepulchre' instead — who is he?
Godfrey of Bouillon: Ruler of Jerusalem from 1099 to 1100.
This Swedish service tracks real-time aircraft positions worldwide using a crowdsourced network of more than 40,000 ADS-B receivers — what is it?
This philosophical idea holds that all humans belong to a single community and should live as 'world citizens' guided by universal moral standards — what is it called?
Cosmopolitanism: Idea that all human beings are members of a single community.
Nicknamed the 'Grand Marshal of Ayacucho,' this Venezuelan general served as Bolivia's first president and was Simón Bolívar's closest lieutenant in the wars of independence — who was he?
Antonio José de Sucre: President of Peru and Bolivia (1795–1830)
Leader of the Hitler Youth from 1931 to 1940 and later Nazi governor of Vienna, this German politician was elected to the Reichstag in 1932 — who was he?
Baldur von Schirach: German Nazi politician (1907–1974)
Ordered by President Jimmy Carter, this failed 1980 military mission tried to free 52 American hostages in Iran but collapsed at a staging site called Desert One — what is it?
Operation Eagle Claw was a failed United States Department of Defense attempt to rescue 52 embassy staff held captive by Revolutionary Iran on 24 April 1980.
Once an altar boy, this Ugandan warlord founded a rebel militia in 1987 seeking to establish a Christian state under dominion theology, later designated a terrorist group by the UN — who is he?
Joseph Kony: Head of the Lord's Resistance Army (born 1961)

After the assassination of his predecessor in 2018, this pro-Russian politician became head of a self-proclaimed republic in eastern Ukraine — and critics point to his earlier role in a notorious Ponzi scheme — who is he?
The last monarch of a Middle Eastern kingdom, he took the throne at age three after his father died in a car crash, and was killed during the 1958 revolution that ended the monarchy — who was he?
Faisal II: King of Iraq from 1939 to 1958.

Elected monarch of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1674, this military commander first made his name fighting in the Swedish invasion known as the Deluge before achieving fame against the Ottomans — who was he?
John III Sobieski: Ruler of Poland–Lithuania from 1674 to 1696.
Founding the Kamakura shogunate in 1192, this samurai became the first shogun to hold true nationwide power in Japan, having defeated the rival Taira clan in a five-year civil war — who is he?
Minamoto no Yoritomo: Japanese Samurai, Daimyo and Military ruler of Japan from 1192 to 1199.
Notorious for humiliating defendants and handing down frequent death sentences, this German judge presided over the People's Court from 1942 to 1945 — who is he?
Forced to abdicate in 1907 after 43 years on the throne, this monarch began as the 26th king of Joseon and became the first emperor of the Korean Empire — who is he?
Gojong of Korea (8 September 1852 - 21 January 1919), personal name Yi Jaehwang, later changed to Yi Hui, also known as the Gwangmu Emperor, was the penultimate Korean monarch.
This French politician served as government spokesperson for the Attal administration in 2024 after being elected deputy for Hauts-de-Seine's 8th constituency — who is she?
In 1996, a gunman killed 35 people at a historic Tasmanian tourist site, leading to sweeping changes in Australia's gun laws — what is this tragedy called?
Port Arthur massacre: 1996 mass shooting in Tasmania, Australia.
United under King Burebista in 82 BC and centered on Transylvania, this ancient kingdom fell after Roman conquest in AD 106, its capital Sarmizegetusa Regia destroyed — what was this land called?
Dacia: Ancient kingdom in Southeastern Europe (168 BC – 106 AD)
In 2016, a former care-home employee killed 19 disabled residents in Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, in the deadliest mass stabbing the country had seen in decades — what is this attack called?
Sagamihara stabbings: 2016 hate crime in Japan.
Impeached by the Texas House in 2023 by a vote of 121–23 after securities-fraud charges dating back to 2015, this Republican has served as Texas attorney general since 2015 — who is he?
Ken Paxton: American politician and lawyer (born 1962)
Second in line to a now-deposed monarchy's throne before the 1979 Islamic Revolution, this son of Iran's last Shah later studied at Princeton, Columbia, and Harvard — who is he?

This German jurist joined the Nazi Party in 1933 and used his legal theories to provide ideological justification for the regime, though he fell out of favor with senior officials by 1936 — who is he?
Carl Schmitt: German jurist and political theorist (1888–1985)
In 2008, a rented truck plowed into pedestrians in a Tokyo shopping district before the attacker turned to a blade, leaving seven dead — which incident?
Akihabara massacre: Civilian attack in Tokyo, Japan.
One of the fifty Nereids and daughter of the sea god Nereus, this Greek sea nymph appears in the Trojan War cycle of myth — who is she?
Known in Japan as Miura Anjin, this English navigator became the first Englishman to reach Japan in 1600 and was later granted samurai status — who is he?

William Adams (samurai) (24 September 1564 - 16 May 1620), better known in Japan as Miura Anjin ('the pilot of Miura'), was an English navigator who, in 1600, became the first Englishman to reach Japan.
Beginning her political career in the Arizona Green Party, this senator later left the Democratic Party to become an independent in December 2022 — who is she?
Author of the influential Islamist tract "Milestones," this Egyptian theorist was a leading figure in the Muslim Brotherhood — who is he?
Sayyid Qutb: Egyptian political theorist and revolutionary (1906–1966)
In 2023, 1.3 million applicants competed for just 1,255 government job openings through this Indian constitutional body's exams — what is it?
Union Public Service Commission: India's central recruiting agency.
Leading a decades-long independence war against Ethiopia to victory in 1991, this leader has served as his nation's only president since 1993 — who is he?
Isaias Afwerki: President of Eritrea since 1993. The United Nations and Amnesty International have cited him for human rights violations.
Deposed after only 93 days on the throne due to declining physical and mental health, this Ottoman sultan supported converting the empire into a constitutional monarchy — who is he?
Murad V: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire in 1876. Murad; 21 September 1840 – 29 August 1904) was the sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 30 May to 31 August 1876.
Arrested by India's Enforcement Directorate in a land scam case in January 2024, this politician nonetheless returned to serve as Jharkhand's chief minister that July — who is he?
Hemant Soren: 5th Chief Minister of Jharkhand.
Founded in 1932 by Oswald Mosley, this far-right political party once claimed 50,000 members before a violent 1934 rally alienated much of its following — what was it called?
British Union of Fascists: 1932–1940 political party. In 1939, following the start of the Second World War, the party was proscribed by the British government and in 1940 it was disbanded.
Beginning in early 1863, this insurrection against Russian imperial rule sought to restore the sovereignty Polish lands had enjoyed before a failed 1830 revolt — what was it called?
January Uprising: 1863 Polish–Lithuanian revolt in the Russian Empire.
Born in the Ukrainian SSR, this politician served as Russia's ambassador to Malta and Greece before becoming Governor of Saint Petersburg and eventually chairing the Federation Council — who is she?
Born in 1927, this Iranian ayatollah has served as secretary of the Guardian Council since 1992 and previously chaired the Assembly of Experts. Who is he?
Ahmad Jannati: Iranian principlist politician (born before 1927)

Born in Egypt as Hossam Boutros, this French far-right economist and media personality became spokesman for the National Front's Horaces group before later joining Éric Zemmour's Reconquête party. Who is he?
Jean Messiha: French media personality, former politician and civil servant (born 1970)

This Iranian Revolutionary Guard commander led the Muslim Peshmerga during the Iran–Iraq War and played a major role in restoring Iranian control over Kurdish territory before his death in 1983. Who was he?

Taking office at age 36, this Montenegrin economist became the youngest president in his country's independent history and the world's sixth-youngest serving state leader after a landslide 2023 election. Who is he?
Jakov Milatović: President of Montenegro since 2023.

The first woman and youngest person ever to hold Slovakia's presidency, this lawyer and environmental activist won the 2016 Goldman Environmental Prize for fighting a toxic landfill in her hometown. Who is she?
Zuzana Čaputová: President of Slovakia from 2019 to 2024.
Known for grilling witnesses with a whiteboard during congressional hearings, this California Democrat represented the state in the House from 2019 to 2025 and later ran for the Senate. Who is she?
This ancient Arab people built their wealth on a trading network centered at Raqmu — today's Petra — before Emperor Trajan annexed their kingdom into the Roman Empire in 106 AD. Who were they?
Nabataeans: Arab people who inhabited northern Arabia and the southern Levant.
The eighth shogun of his family's shogunate, ruling from 1716 to 1745, this samurai is remembered for repealing Japan's ban on Western literature — who was he?
Tokugawa Yoshimune: Japanese Samurai, Daimyo and Military ruler of Japan from 1716 to 1745.
This 19th-century religious leader served as the second president of a major American church and doubled as the first governor of Utah Territory. Who is he?

Formed in 1230 by the union of two Iberian kingdoms, this medieval polity was tied to Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage of discovery and endured until Philip V's 1716 reforms dissolved it. What was this realm called?
Crown of Castile: Former country in the Iberian Peninsula from 1230 to 1715.
This high-ranking Nazi SS officer served as Hitler's liaison to Heinrich Himmler and became the Führer's brother-in-law-by-marriage through his wedding to Eva Braun's sister. Who is he?
Hermann Fegelein: German Nazi Waffen-SS commander (1906–1945)

Expelled from the Labour Party in 2003 over his outspoken opposition to the Iraq War, this British politician has since led two different smaller parties and now lives in self-imposed exile in Russia. Who is he?
George Galloway: British politician, broadcaster, and writer (born 1954)

Active from 1929 to 1941, this organized crime enforcement squad carried out between 400 and 1,000 contract killings for the National Crime Syndicate before being exposed by a turncoat member nicknamed 'Kid Twist.' What was this group called?
Murder, Inc.: American organized crime groups in the 1930s and 1940s.

This Ukrainian-born Israeli billionaire co-founded a major bank in 1992, served as a regional governor from 2014 to 2015, and later used his media holdings to back Volodymyr Zelenskyy's successful presidential run. Who is he?

Founded by followers of a Berber religious leader recognized as the Mahdi, this North African empire ruled much of the Maghreb and the Iberian Peninsula from the 12th to 13th centuries. What was this empire called?
Almohad Caliphate: 1121–1269 Berber empire in North Africa and Iberia.
As France's chief diplomat, he delivered a famous UN speech opposing the 2003 invasion of Iraq before becoming prime minister under Jacques Chirac — who is this French politician?
Dominique de Villepin: Prime Minister of France from 2005 to 2007.
A former professional basketball player turned artist and politician, he's the only person to win four consecutive terms as Albania's prime minister — who is he?
Edi Rama: Prime Minister of Albania since 2013.
Aboard a Soviet submarine during the Cuban Missile Crisis, this officer's lone veto blocked his two fellow commanders from launching a nuclear torpedo at U.S. ships — who was he?
Vasily Arkhipov: Soviet Navy vice admiral who prevented nuclear war (1926–1998)
This king moved Poland's capital from Kraków to Warsaw and was the first Polish monarch from a Swedish royal house — who is he?
Sigismund III Vasa: King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania (1587–1632), King of Sweden (1592–1599)
Once chief advisor to Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, he later served as Turkey's foreign minister before becoming prime minister and party leader from 2014 to 2016 — who is this Turkish politician?
Ahmet Davutoğlu: Prime Minister of Turkey from 2014 to 2016. The AKP lost its parliamentary majority in the June 2015 general election, though it remained the largest party.
Born in Brilon and once a corporate lawyer, this politician has led Germany's Christian Democratic Union since 2022 and became the country's chancellor in May 2025. Who is he?
Friedrich Merz: Chancellor of Germany since 2025. Joachim-Friedrich Martin Josef Merz (born 11 November 1955) is a German politician who has served as Chancellor of Germany since 6 May 2025.

Ruling the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy from 493 to 526 and later regent of the Visigoths too, this king received the old Western imperial regalia from Constantinople and was addressed by Italy's aristocracy as princeps. Who was he?
Theodoric the Great: King of Italy from 493 to 526. As ruler of the combined Gothic realms, Theodoric controlled an empire stretching from the Atlantic Ocean to the Adriatic Sea.
Claiming to be Catherine the Great's dead husband Tsar Peter III, this Cossack leader proclaimed an end to serfdom in 1773 and led a massive peasant uprising across the Volga-Ural region. Who was he?
Yemelyan Pugachev: Russian Cossack rebel leader (1742–1775)
A vocal champion of the crypto industry in Congress, this Minnesota Republican has served as House majority whip since 2023 after narrowly losing a gubernatorial bid in 2010. Who is he?

Having first crossed the Atlantic as a 'gentleman volunteer' on Columbus's second voyage, this conquistador later became the first governor of Puerto Rico and led the first European expedition to Florida in 1513. Who was he?
Juan Ponce de León: Spanish explorer and conquistador (1474–1521)

Serving the state of Zhao during the Warring States period, this general — one of Chinese folklore's 'Four Greatest Generals' — died in 229 BC and is remembered as a master of defensive tactics. Who was he?

Michigan's 49th governor, this Democrat gained national attention in 2013 for a state Senate floor speech in which she shared her own experience of sexual assault during an abortion debate. Who is she?
Gretchen Whitmer: Governor of Michigan since 2019.

After decades as a loyal hetman of the Cossack Hetmanate, this Ukrainian leader switched sides in 1708 to ally with Sweden's Charles XII against Peter the Great — a gamble that collapsed after the Battle of Poltava. Who was he?
Ivan Mazepa: Hetman of the Cossack Hetmanate from 1687 to 1709.
Leading Sweden's Moderate Party since 2017, this politician became prime minister in 2022 at the head of a minority coalition and went on to complete his country's accession to NATO. Who is he?
Ulf Kristersson: Prime Minister of Sweden since 2022. Kristersson became party leader after Anna Kinberg Batra resigned in 2017.
Nicknamed 'the Unifier,' this monarch renamed his Balkan kingdom partway through his thirteen-year reign — the longest of its three monarchs — before his assassination in 1934. Who was he?
Alexander I of Yugoslavia was King of Yugoslavia (1921–1934).

Formed in 2003 through a merger of several socialist factions and mentored by veteran leader George Fernandes, this Indian party won 12 seats in the 2024 general election as part of the BJP-led coalition. Which party?
Janata Dal (United): Political party in India.
Co-founding a Marxist-Leninist political organization with Bobby Seale in 1966, this activist later earned a PhD in social philosophy citing Plato's Republic as an influence — who is he?
Huey P. Newton: Founder of the Black Panther Party (1942–1989)
This Finnish Green League politician served as Foreign Minister from 2019 to 2023 and became the first openly gay candidate to run for his country's presidency — who is he?
Founded by Pieter Omtzigt in 2023, this Christian-democratic party in the Netherlands is commonly known by the initials NSC — which party?
New Social Contract: Political party in the Netherlands.
This retired Turkish general served as the 30th Chief of the General Staff of the Turkish Armed Forces before becoming Minister of National Defense — who is he?
Yaşar Güler: Turkish general and politician (born 1954)

Born in Manchester's Moss Side, this British activist organized the suffragette movement that helped women win the vote in 1918 and was later named one of Time's 100 Most Important People of the 20th century — who is she?
As personal adjutant to Heinrich Himmler and later a Waffen-SS tank commander, this German officer was convicted for ordering the WWII killing of American POWs at Malmedy — who is he?
Joachim Peiper: SS officer and war criminal (1915–1976)
Originally founded in 1964 as a trucking company before pivoting to charter flights and then the ultra-low-cost model, this Florida-based carrier ceased operations in May 2026 — which company?

Claiming to be Ivan the Terrible's youngest son, who had supposedly died in a failed 1591 assassination attempt, this imposter ruled as Tsar of Russia for eleven months before being killed in 1606 — who was he?
False Dmitry I: Tsar of Russia from 1605 to 1606.
Formed by the 1736 marriage of a French duke to Maria Theresa of Austria, this dynasty merged two royal lines, inheriting through the mother's family and the father's — which dynasty?
House of Habsburg-Lorraine: Austrian imperial dynasty.
In October 2021, this U.S. assistant secretary for health became the nation's first openly transgender four-star officer across all eight uniformed services — who is she?
Rachel Levine: American public health official (born 1957)
Dubbed the 'Champion of Farmers' for his land reform work, this Indian independence activist briefly served as prime minister from July 1979 to January 1980 — who is he?
Charan Singh: Prime Minister of India from 1979 to 1980. Singh was principally known for his land and agricultural reform initiatives, and was Member of Parliament (MP) for Baghpat.

Held every March in Austin, Texas, since 1987, this tech-film-music extravaganza also spun off an EDU conference and a London edition — what's this festival, often shortened to a three-letter abbreviation?
South by Southwest: American annual film and music festival.

Fought in central and western Mexico from 1926 to 1929, this Catholic uprising erupted after President Calles moved to strictly enforce anticlerical articles of the 1917 constitution — what's this conflict called?
This public servant held the title of White House cabinet secretary under Joe Biden after serving as Assistant Secretary of State for Educational and Cultural Affairs under Obama — who is she?
Serving twice as Czech foreign minister and once as chancellor to Václav Havel, this politician also ran for president in 2013 as leader of the TOP 09 party — who is he?
Karel Schwarzenberg: Czech politician and noble (1937–2023)

Born a Danish prince at Sandringham House in England, this future Norwegian king became heir apparent when his father was elected to the throne in 1905, and led as defence chief during WWII — who is he?
Olav V: King of Norway from 1957 to 1991.

This 19th-century Habsburg-Lorraine royal fathered two emperors — one who ruled from Vienna, the other who ruled Mexico — and was grandfather to the royal whose 1914 assassination triggered World War I — who is he?
Archduke Franz Karl of Austria (17 December 1802 - 8 March 1878) was a member of the House of Habsburg-Lorraine.

Breaking out in 1990 between Moldovan government forces and pro-separatist fighters backed by Russia's 14th Army, this conflict over a breakaway region ended with a ceasefire in July 1992 that still holds — which conflict?
Transnistrian War: 1990–1992 separatist conflict in Moldova. Cojocaru, the Moldovan defeat in this war directly led to implementation of Moldovan neutrality.

After eight years in UN-funded public health work, this Indian strategist helped re-elect Narendra Modi as Gujarat's chief minister in 2012 before founding his own party ahead of the 2025 Bihar election — who is he?
Prashant Kishor: Indian politician. Prashant Kishor (born 20 March 1977), colloquially known as PK, is an Indian politician, the founder of the Jan Suraaj Party and a former political strategist.

Once led by three-time Italian prime minister Silvio Berlusconi until his 2023 death, this centre-right party — now helmed by former European Parliament president Antonio Tajani — revived a movement originally founded in 1994 — which party?
Forza Italia (2013) is a centre-right political party in Italy, whose ideology includes elements of liberal conservatism, Christian democracy, liberalism and populism.
This American oceanographer discovered the wrecks of the Titanic, the Bismarck, and the USS Yorktown, and once said finding hydrothermal vents beat finding that famous ocean liner — who is he?
Robert Ballard: Retired US Navy officer and professor of oceanography (born 1942)

Serving as India's president from 2017 to 2022, he was the first person from Uttar Pradesh and the first member of the Bharatiya Janata Party to hold that office, after serving as Governor of Bihar — who is he?
Ram Nath Kovind: President of India from 2017 to 2022.
