Once known as Edessa and nicknamed the City of Prophets for its legendary link to Abraham, this southeastern Turkish city sits near Göbekli Tepe, the world's oldest known temple — which city?
Urfa: City in southeastern Turkey. The city was known as Edessa from Hellenistic times and into Christian times.
Standing 462 metres tall in a St. Petersburg neighborhood, this 87-story skyscraper is the tallest building in both Russia and Europe, and the world's second-tallest twisted tower — which building?
Lakhta Center: Skyscraper in Saint Petersburg, Russia. Construction of the Lakhta Center started on 30 October 2012, with the building topping out on 29 January 2018.
Nicknamed the French city of 'weapon, cycle and ribbon' for its industrial past, this city sits about 60 km southwest of Lyon in the Loire département — which city?
Saint-Étienne: Prefecture and commune in Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, France.
Founded in 1795 when Kamehameha I united several Pacific islands under one crown, this monarchy later gained diplomatic recognition from European powers before its fall in 1893 — which realm?
Hawaiian Kingdom: Country in the Pacific Ocean (1795–1893)
Perched on a bend of the Eresma River in Spain, this city's skyline features a Roman aqueduct, a Gothic cathedral, and a fortress-palace — which UNESCO World Heritage city?
Segovia: City in the autonomous community of Castile and León, Spain.
Rising 132 metres above the River Rhine near Sankt Goarshausen, this slate cliff has been blamed for centuries of shipwrecks, with legend pointing to a siren. What's it called?
Founded around 10 BC as Augustoritum on the River Vienne, this French city is the second-most populous in Nouvelle-Aquitaine after Bordeaux — which city?
Limoges: Prefecture and commune in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France.
Dubbed the 'Temple City' and home to Kalingan shrines dating from the 6th to 13th centuries, this is the capital of India's Odisha state — which city?
Bhubaneswar: City in Odisha, India. Bhubaneswar (/bʊbəˈneɪswəɹ/; Odia: [bʱubɔn̪eswɔɾɔ]) is the capital and the largest city of the Indian state of Odisha.
This landlocked 19th-century Boer republic in southern Africa, with its capital at Bloemfontein, surrendered to the British Empire at the end of the Second Boer War in 1902 — which republic?
Orange Free State: 1854–1902 Boer republic in Southern Africa. It is one of the three historical precursors to the present-day Free State province.

Wedged between Guangzhou and Shenzhen in the Pearl River Delta, this Chinese industrial city ranks just behind Shenzhen, Shanghai, and Suzhou in exports and is home to one of the world's largest shopping malls — which city?
Dongguan: Prefecture-level city in Guangdong, China.
Named after a 16th-century Spanish viceroy of Peru and visited by a Spanish navigator in 1595, this volcanic archipelago lies in French Polynesia in the southern Pacific — which one?
Marquesas Islands: Archipelago in French Polynesia. Archaeological research suggests the islands were settled in the 10th century AD by voyagers from West Polynesia.
Bordering Toronto's Etobicoke to the east and sitting on Lake Ontario's northwestern shore, this Peel Region city is Canada's seventh-most populous — which Ontario city?
Mississauga: City in Ontario, Canada. The growth of Mississauga was initially attributed to its proximity to Toronto.
Home to the oldest cathedral in the mainland Americas, built partly from stones of nearby Maya ruins, this Mexican state capital anchors the northwest corner of its peninsula — which city?
Mérida, Yucatán (Spanish; Yucatec) is the capital of the Mexican state of Yucatn, and the largest city in southern Mexico.
The world's second-highest capital city after Quito, this Bolivian city has also been known over the centuries as La Plata and Charcas — which city?
Sucre: Capital city in Chuquisaca Department, Bolivia.

Straddling the China–North Korea border, this active stratovolcano's 946 AD eruption was one of the most powerful in the last 5,000 years, and its caldera now holds the sacred Heaven Lake — which peak?
Mount Paektu is an active stratovolcano on the Chinese-North Korean border.
Nicknamed 'the French Manchester' for its industrial past, this Alsatian city near the Swiss and German borders is home to the world's largest automobile museum — which city?
Mulhouse: Subprefecture and commune in Grand Est, France.
Perched at 2,325 metres in Eritrea, this UNESCO World Heritage capital earned its listing in 2017 for well-preserved Italian colonial modernist architecture — which city?
Asmara: Capital and largest city of Eritrea. Asmara ( əs-MAHR-ə), or Asmera, is the capital and most populous city of Eritrea, in the country's Central Region.
Holder of the Guinness World Record for oldest continuously used national flag, this red banner with a white Nordic cross is linked by legend to a 1219 battle — which flag?
Dannebrog: Flag of Denmark. The Dannebrog (Danish pronunciation: [ˈtænəˌpʁoˀ], lit. 'Red cloth') is the flag of the Kingdom of Denmark.
Home to the Mahabodhi Temple in the Indian state of Bihar, this pilgrimage site marks where Gautama Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment beneath a sacred tree — where is it?
Bodh Gaya: Historical city in Bihar, India.
Its capital, Morelia, was renamed for a hero of the Mexican War of Independence — which Pacific-coast Mexican state takes its name from a Nahuatl phrase meaning 'place of the fishermen'?
Michoacán: State of Mexico. The state is divided into 113 municipalities and its capital city is Morelia (formerly called Valladolid).

Home to the dormant volcano Mount Scenery — at 870 meters, the highest point in the entire Kingdom of the Netherlands — this tiny Caribbean territory has a population of just over 2,000 — which place?
Saba (island) is a Caribbean island and the smallest special municipality (officially "public body") of the Netherlands.
Known as Toyohara under Japanese rule until 1946, this Russian Far East city is the administrative capital of an island north of Japan — which city?
Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk: City in Sakhalin Oblast, Russia.
Sitting atop an extinct volcano in West Java and reached by 370 stone steps, this sacred site's five terraces are lined with hexagonal columns — which site?
Gunung Padang: Megalithic site in West Java, Indonesia.
Recognized as one of the Seven Natural Wonders of Africa thanks to its massive migration, which Tanzania-Kenya region also boasts a legendary lion population?
Serengeti: Geographical region in Tanzania. The Serengeti ( SERR-ən-GHET-ee) is a geographical region in Africa, spanning the Mara and Arusha Regions of Tanzania and extending to southwestern Kenya.
Once the capital of a Deccan sultanate near Hyderabad, this fortified city gave its name to some of history's most famous diamonds mined nearby — which citadel?
Home to greater Los Angeles and San Diego County, this roughly 23-million-strong U.S. region includes ten counties and the arid Colorado Desert — which region?
Southern California: Geographic and cultural region of the US.
Rising in the Czech Republic, this river forms part of the Poland-Germany border before emptying into the Baltic Sea's Bay of Pomerania — which river?
Known for houseboats on Dal Lake and pashmina shawls, this city serves as the summer capital of a disputed Himalayan region — which city?
Srinagar: City in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir.
Nicknamed the 'Graveyard of the Atlantic' for its many shipwrecks, this string of barrier islands off North Carolina was also where the Wright brothers first flew in 1903 — which coastal region?
Outer Banks: Barrier islands in North Carolina and Virginia, United States.
Located less than a mile from the Gaza Strip, this Negev city was chosen in 2024 to pilot Israel's urban forestry initiatives — which city?
Sderot: City in Israel. In 2024, Sderot was chosen to serve as a model for Israeli cities in the implementation of urban forestry ideas.
Nicknamed 'Pom City,' this Coral Sea capital of Papua New Guinea was a key Allied staging point that Japan tried but failed to capture during World War II — which city?
Port Moresby: Capital and largest city of Papua New Guinea. Port Moresby (Tok Pisin: Pot Mosbi), also referred to as Pom City or simply Moresby, is the capital and largest city of Papua New Guinea.
Home to Palladio's Teatro Olimpico and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994, this northeastern Italian city sits about 60 kilometres west of Venice — which city?
Originally designed to house just 15,000 people when construction began in 1958, this Saharan capital's population has since swelled to nearly 1.5 million — which city?
Nouakchott: Capital and the largest city of Mauritania.
Historically known as Caesarea and long considered the capital of Cappadocia, this Turkish city sits at the foot of a dormant volcano rising nearly 3,917 metres — which city?
Kayseri: Metropolitan municipality in Central Anatolia, Turkey.
Divided from Siberia by the Ural Mountains, which densely populated western region makes its country the largest and most populous in Europe, despite that country's much larger Asian half?
European Russia is the western and most populated part of the Russian Federation.
Home to a safari zoo, water park, and mud-bath health resorts on the Sea of Azov, which Ukrainian port city, under Russian occupation since February 2022, sits in Zaporizhzhia Oblast?
Berdiansk: City in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine. It is on the northern coast of the Sea of Azov, which is connected to the Black Sea.
Located on the northwest coast of Crete, about 70 kilometers west of Rethymno, this Greek city anchors a municipality of over 111,000 people — which city?
Chania: City in western Crete, Greece.
Home to a Norse parliament established on the Tinganes peninsula in AD 850, this small Atlantic capital's name literally means 'Thor's harbour' — which capital?
Tórshavn: Capital and largest city of the Faroe Islands.
Bordering Scotland to the north and the Irish Sea to the west, this predominantly rural English ceremonial county's largest city is Carlisle — which county?
Cumbria: Ceremonial county of England. Cumbria is predominantly rural, with an area of 6,769 km2 (2,614 sq mi) and an estimated population of 510,680 in 2024.
Founded by the wealthy Demidov family to produce copper and silver, this Siberian city on the Ob River became a major hub for silver production and was granted city status in 1771 — which city?
Barnaul: City in Altai Krai, Russia.
Named for the Greek word for 'summit,' this canal city near Cleveland became known as the Rubber Capital of the World thanks to Goodyear and Firestone — which city?
Akron, Ohio: City in the United States.

Flowing from the Vosges mountains through France and Luxembourg before joining the Rhine at Koblenz, this river's terraced hillsides between the Eifel and Hunsrück produce some of Germany's finest Rieslings — which river?
Founded in 1822 by the American Colonization Society and named for U.S. President James Monroe, this Atlantic coast city is Liberia's capital — which city?
Monrovia: Capital, chief port, and the largest city of Liberia.
This affluent south-east London district lends its name to the Prime Meridian and Mean Time, and was the birthplace of Henry VIII and Elizabeth I — which place?
Greenwich: Town in south-east London, United Kingdom.
Rising in Mongolia and flowing past Lake Baikal before emptying into the Kara Sea, this river is the largest to drain into the Arctic Ocean — which river?
Yenisei: Fifth-longest river in the world.
Nicknamed the 'city that never sleeps' and sitting on the banks of the Vaigai River, this Tamil Nadu city hosted the third Tamil Sangam under the Pandyan dynasty — which city?
Madurai: City in Tamil Nadu, India. Madurai is a major tier II city in the Indian state of Tamil Nadu.
Nicknamed the 'City of a Hundred Bell Towers,' this west-central French city has hosted a university since 1431 that once counted René Descartes among its scholars — which city?
Poitiers: Prefecture and commune in Nouvelle-Aquitaine, France.
Renamed from Lourenço Marques in 1976, this port city on a natural Indian Ocean bay is the capital of Mozambique — which city?
Maputo: Capital and chief port of Mozambique. Maputo (Portuguese pronunciation: [mɐˈputu]) is the capital and largest city of Mozambique.
Sitting on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, this port city runs ferries to Famagusta in Northern Cyprus and rail links to Adana via Tarsus — which city?
Mersin: City and metropolitan municipality in Mediterranean, Turkey.

Granted a royal charter by Richard I in 1196 to hold a weekly market, this Warwickshire town sits at the southernmost point of the Arden area, near the northern edge of the Cotswolds — which market town?

Stratford-upon-Avon: Town in Warwickshire, England. It is situated on the River Avon, 91 miles (146 km) north-west of London, 22 miles (35 km) south-east of Birmingham and 8 miles (13 km) south-west of Warwick.
Home to Mulhacén, continental Iberia's highest peak, this Andalusian mountain range offers skiing near the Mediterranean's sunniest shores — which range is this?
Sierra Nevada (Spain) (meaning "snow-covered mountain range") is a mountain range in the Andalusian provinces of Granada and Almeria in Spain.

Hidden in a Guatemalan rainforest and declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, this ruined Maya capital dominated the region politically and militarily during its Classic-era peak — which ancient city?
Tikal: Ruins of major ancient Maya city.
This English seaside resort on the Fylde peninsula boomed once Lancashire cotton-mill workers took their 'Wakes Weeks' holidays there, and gained its own railway station back in 1846 — which town?
Blackpool: Coastal town in Lancashire, England.
Headquartered by fashion brand Benetton and considered the birthplace of tiramisù, this Italian city in the Veneto region also lent its name to a sparkling wine — which city?
Part of Greece's Dodecanese island chain, this island is the third largest there, after Rhodes and Karpathos — which island?
Kos: Island in Greece. Kos or Cos (Greek: Κως [kos]) is a Greek island, part of the Dodecanese island chain in the southeastern Aegean Sea.
Capital of the Netherlands' North Holland province, this city bordering the Randstad was granted city rights back in 1245 — which city?
Haarlem: City in North Holland, Netherlands. Haarlem (Dutch: [ˈɦaːrlɛm]) is a city and municipality in the Netherlands.
Stretching 550 miles from Pennsylvania to Georgia, this Appalachian range gets its hazy color from isoprene released by its trees — which range?
Blue Ridge Mountains: Mountain range in the Eastern U.S.
Founded in 1864 after gold was struck at Last Chance Gulch, this state capital had roughly 50 millionaires within its city limits by 1888 — which city?
Helena, Montana is the capital city of the U.S. Helena is the capital city of the U.S. state of Montana and the county seat of Lewis and Clark County.
Wales's second-largest city, this port on a bay of the same name has a principal area stretching across the Gower Peninsula — which city?
Swansea: City and county in Wales. Swansea ( SWON-zee; Welsh: Abertawe [abɛrˈtawɛ]) is a port and coastal city in Wales.
Nicknamed the 'Garden Isle,' this fourth-largest Hawaiian island is home to Waimea Canyon and the Nā Pali Coast — which island?
Kauaʻi: Fourth largest island in Hawaii. Kauaʻi, sometimes written Kauai, is one of the main Hawaiian Islands.
Located near Vrindavan in Uttar Pradesh, this city is revered as the birthplace of Krishna and ranks among Hinduism's seven holiest cities — which city?
Mathura: City in Uttar Pradesh, India. Mathura (Braj pronunciation: [mɐ.t̪ʰʊ.ɾäː]) is a city and the administrative headquarters of Mathura district in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.
Sitting between Rotterdam and The Hague, this Dutch city is famous for its blue-and-white pottery, the painter Jan Vermeer, and being considered the birthplace of microbiology — which city?
Delft: City and municipality in South Holland, Netherlands.
Sitting at the meeting of the Amur and Zeya rivers directly across from China's Heihe, this Russian city is the administrative center of Amur Oblast — which city?

Blagoveshchensk: City in Amur Oblast, Russia. Blagoveshchensk (Russian: Благовещенск, IPA: [bləɡɐˈvʲeɕːɪnsk], lit. 'City of the Annunciation') is a city and the administrative center of Amur Oblast, Russia.
Dubbed Greece's 'Gate to the West' for its busy port trade with Italy, this city in the northern Peloponnese is also revered as the site of Saint Andrew's martyrdom — which city?
Patras: City in Peloponnese, Greece. The city is built at the foot of Mount Panachaikon, overlooking the Gulf of Patras.
First recorded in 1018 as 'Zuarina' and granted city rights in 1160 by Henry the Lion, this lakeside city is the least populous of Germany's state capitals — which city?

Opened to the public in 2017, this 123-story supertall in Seoul is the tallest building in South Korea, with a rooftop sky-bridge deck set at the same height as an iconic New York skyscraper. Which building?

Lotte World Tower: Supertall skyscraper in Seoul, South Korea. It is the sixth-tallest building in the world, the tallest in OECD countries and in South Korea, and also the first in South Korea to be over 100 stories tall.
Rising in Spain's Montes Universales and flowing over 1,000 kilometers west to the Atlantic at Lisbon, this is the longest river on the Iberian Peninsula. Which river?
Tagus: Longest river on the Iberian Peninsula. The Tagus ( TAY-gəs; Spanish: Tajo [ˈtaxo]; Portuguese: Tejo [ˈtɛʒu]) is the longest river in the Iberian Peninsula.

Nicknamed the 'Jerusalem of the Balkans' for once boasting 365 churches — one for every day of the year — this North Macedonian lakeside city earned dual UNESCO Cultural and Natural World Heritage status. Which city?
Ohrid: City in southwestern North Macedonia.
Fought over by Portuguese, Safavid Persian and Omani forces before Bahrain's 1971 independence, this Persian Gulf capital built its wealth on pearling and trade — which city?
Manama: Capital and largest city of Bahrain. Long an important trading center in the Persian Gulf, Manama is home to a diverse population.

Historically a Staffordshire wool town that grew into a coal, steel and lock-making powerhouse during the Industrial Revolution, this West Midlands city sits about 12 miles northwest of Birmingham — which city?
Wolverhampton: City in the West Midlands, England. Wolverhampton (WUUL-vər-HAMP-tən) is a city and metropolitan borough in the West Midlands, England.
Completed in Warsaw in 1955 in the Soviet 'Seven Sisters' style, this 237-metre high-rise was briefly the world's tallest clock tower until a Tokyo building took over in 2002 — which landmark?
Palace of Culture and Science: High-rise building in Warsaw, Poland. The Palace of Culture and Science (Polish: Pałac Kultury i Nauki; PKiN) is a notable high-rise building in central Warsaw, Poland.
Evacuated in November 2023 ahead of a volcanic eruption near its harbour, this Icelandic fishing town sits just 5 kilometres from the Blue Lagoon — which town?
Grindavík: Town in Iceland. Grindavík (Icelandic pronunciation: [ˈkrɪntaˌviːk]) is a fishing town in the Southern Peninsula district of Iceland, located near Þorbjörn.
At 2,300 metres above sea level, this Yemeni capital is the seventh-highest capital city in the world, and its UNESCO-listed Old City is famed for geometric-patterned high-rises — which city?
Sanaa: Capital and largest city of Yemen.

Sitting at the confluence of the Yellow River and a tributary, this prefecture-level Chinese city in western Henan neighbors the provincial capital of Zhengzhou and has a population topping 7 million — which city?
Luoyang: City in Henan, China. By the end of 2022, Luoyang Municipality had jurisdiction over 7 municipal districts, 7 counties and 1 development zone.
Lying off the coast of Kefalonia in the Ionian Sea, this small Greek isle is traditionally identified as the home of Homer's wandering hero Odysseus — which island?
Ithaca (island) (Ancient), is a Greek island located in the Ionian Sea, off the northeast coast of Kefalonia and to the west of continental Greece.
Sitting on Nueces Bay roughly 130 miles southeast of San Antonio, this coastal city is the seat of Nueces County and the eighth-most populous city in its state — which city is this?
Corpus Christi, Texas (Latin for 'Body of Christ') is a coastal city in the U.S.
Once known as Frobisher Bay until its traditional Inuktitut name was restored in 1987, this remote city became the capital of Nunavut in 1999 and remains the northernmost city in Canada — which city?
Iqaluit: Capital city of Nunavut, Canada. It is the territory's largest community and its only city, and the northernmost city in Canada.
Sitting at a river mouth on Finland's northwestern coast, this port city is the third-northernmost city in the world with over 100,000 residents, trailing only two Russian cities — which city?
Oulu: City in North Ostrobothnia, Finland.
Named after a village in Spain's Seville province by a member of a 1568 Spanish expedition, this Solomon Islands island bears the indigenous name Isatabu — which island?
Guadalcanal: Principal island of Solomon Islands. It is the largest island in the nation of Solomon Islands by area and the largest by population, followed by Malaita.
This Greek city, capital of the Laconia regional unit, sits in the Evrotas Valley on the site of a legendary ancient city-state — which modern city?
Sparta (modern city) is a city and municipality in the Peloponnese region of Greece, serving as the capital of the Laconia regional unit.
Nicknamed 'The Queen of the Hills,' this Himalayan-foothill hill station near India's Dehradun drew over three million visitors in 2019 — which town?
Mussoorie: Hill station in Uttarakhand, India. Mussoorie (Garhwali: [məsuːɾiː]) is a hill station and a municipal board in the Dehradun district of the Indian state of Uttarakhand.
Once under Russian rule until 1867, this city spans two islands in the Alexander Archipelago and holds the title of largest U.S. city by total area — which one?
Sitka, Alaska is a unified city-borough in the southeast portion of the U.S.
Adopted in 1962, whose national banner pairs green and white vertical stripes with a red crescent and star symbolizing Islam?
Flag of Algeria consists of two equal vertical bars, green and white, charged in the center with a red star and crescent, a symbol of Islam as the nation's prominent faith.

Bordered by Lake Ladoga to the north and the Narva River to the west along the Gulf of Finland, this historical region was home to Finnic peoples and briefly saw its northern half become an independent state in 1919–1920 — what is it?
Ingria: Historical region in northwestern Russia.

At 8,516 meters, this Himalayan giant is Earth's fourth-highest peak, and its proximity to a taller neighbor across a deep col makes it the least prominent of all the eight-thousanders — which mountain?
Lhotse: 4th-highest mountain on Earth. With Everest to the north and Nuptse to the west, Lhotse forms the apex of the massive horseshoe-shaped arc of the Everest massif.
This historical region at the heart of the Arabian Peninsula includes Saudi Arabia's capital and stretches from the Hejaz in the west to the Rub' al-Khali in the south — what's it called?
Najd: Region in central Saudi Arabia. Administratively, Najd is divided into three main provinces.
Home to about 2 million people along Lake Geneva's Arc Lémanique, this is the French-speaking cultural region of Switzerland — what's it called?
Romandy: French-speaking part of Switzerland. In 2020, about 2 million people, or 22.8% of the Swiss population, lived in Romandy.
Nicknamed the 'Empty Quarter,' this roughly 650,000-square-kilometer desert covers the southern third of the Arabian Peninsula across four countries — what is it?
Rub' al Khali: Desert in the Arabian Peninsula. The desert covers some 650,000 km2 (250,000 sq mi), including parts of Saudi Arabia, Oman, the United Arab Emirates, and Yemen.
Standing 2,228 metres tall in the Snowy Mountains near Jindabyne, this peak is the highest point on mainland Australia — which mountain?
Mount Kosciuszko (Polish) is the highest mountain of mainland Australia, at 2,228 metres (7,310 ft) above sea level.
Founded as the Greek colony of Euesperides around 525 BC and later refounded as the Ptolemaic city of Berenice, this Libyan seaport is the second-largest city in the country — which city?
Home to a centuries-old 'Japanese Bridge' and a UNESCO-listed old town, this Vietnamese former trading port was merged into Da Nang during the country's 2025 administrative reforms — which city?
Hội An (city) is a former city of Qung Nam Province in Central Vietnam.
This former capital of the Mongol Empire from 1235 to 1260 lies in ruins in Mongolia's Orkhon Valley, right beside the country's oldest surviving Buddhist monastery — which city?
Karakorum: 1235–1260 capital of the Mongol Empire.
This Roman name for the Iberian Peninsula gave rise to the modern names of both a European country and a Caribbean island — what was it called?
Also known as the European Megalopolis or the Liverpool–Milan Axis, this discontinuous urban corridor across Western and Central Europe is home to around 100 million people — what's it called?
Blue Banana: High population and GDP corridor in Europe.
Named for its hot sulphur springs and mythologized as an entrance to Hades, this narrow Greek pass was where Spartan-led forces made their legendary last stand against the Persians — which pass?
Thermopylae: Ancient fortified passage in central Greece.
Bounded by the Kunlun, Pamir, and Tian Shan mountain ranges, with the Gobi lying just to its east, this arid basin sits in Southern Xinjiang, China — what's it called?
Taklamakan Desert is a desert in northwestern China. The Taklamakan Desert ( TAK-lə-mə-KAN) is a desert in northwestern China.
Sitting on a river and bordering Georgia to the south, this Volunteer State city was a crucial railroad hub during the Civil War — which city?
Chattanooga, Tennessee: City in the United States.
This ancient Iranian city served as the capital of Elam and later as the winter capital of the Achaemenid Empire — which city?
Susa: Ancient city in Iran. Susa ( SOO-sə) was an ancient city in the lower Zagros Mountains about 250 km (160 mi) east of the Tigris, between the Karkheh and Dez Rivers in Iran.
Just 120 kilometers north of Tashkent, this southern Kazakh city is one of only three 'cities of republican significance,' alongside Almaty and Astana — which city?
Shymkent: City in Kazakhstan. Shymkent serves as a regional cultural and economic center.
Located in what's now Saudi Arabia's Tabuk Province along the Gulf of Aqaba, this Hebrew Bible and Quran region was named for a son of Abraham and Keturah — which region?
Midian: Geographical place mentioned in the Torah.
Home to Monterrey, Mexico's second-largest metro area, this northeastern state shares a narrow border with Texas — which state is it?
Nuevo León: State of Mexico. Monterrey, the state's capital, is the most populous city in Nuevo León and the ninth-largest in Mexico.

Built between 1936 and 1939 as part of the 'Strength Through Joy' program, this string of eight identical buildings on the Baltic island of Rügen was never finished as the seaside resort it was meant to be — what is it?
Prora: Building complex in Rügen, Germany.
This London borough contains the Houses of Parliament, Buckingham Palace, and Downing Street, plus the West End's Oxford Street and Soho — which borough is it?
City of Westminster is a London borough with city status in Greater London, England.
This small resort island off the northwest coast of Panay in the Philippines was named Travel + Leisure's Best Island in the World in 2012 — which island?

Boracay: Island in the Philippines. It has a total land area of 10.32 square kilometers (3.98 sq mi), under the jurisdiction of three barangays in Malay, Aklan, and had a population of 37,802 in 2020.
Named by ancient Greek and Roman writers, this Pontic-steppe region was home to an equestrian nomadic people who spoke an Eastern Iranian language — what was it called?
Scythia: Region of Eurasia defined in antiquity.
Sitting on the Smotrych River in western Ukraine, this historic center of the Podillia region briefly served as the temporary capital of the Ukrainian People's Republic in 1919 and 1920 — which city?
Kamianets-Podilskyi: City in Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Ukraine.

This German state, ruled by the same royal house as Britain, was created by the Congress of Vienna in 1814 and shared a monarch with Britain until 1837, when a law barring female succession split the crowns apart — what state was it?
Kingdom of Hanover: 19th-century state in the German Confederation.
Sitting on the Euphrates just west of Baghdad, this Iraqi city became a major insurgent stronghold after the 2003 invasion, prompting fierce urban battles — which city?
Fallujah: City in Al Anbar, Iraq.
Formed in 1927 by merging an old fortress town with Castellamare Adriatico, this Adriatic coast city is the most populous in Italy's Abruzzo region — which city?
Pescara: Comune in Abruzzo, Italy. Pescara (Italian: [pesˈkaːra]; Abruzzese: Pescàrë; Pescarese: Piscàrë) is the capital city of the province of Pescara, in the Abruzzo region of Italy.
Named after a telegraph pioneer's wife, this Northern Territory town sits near Australia's geographic dead center and straddles the usually dry Todd River — which town?

Alice Springs: Town in the Northern Territory, Australia. The name Alice Springs was given by surveyor William Whitfield Mills after Alice, Lady Todd (née Alice Gillam Bell), wife of the telegraph pioneer Charles Todd.
Named for Bethlehem in Portuguese, this Brazilian port city serves as the gateway to the Amazon River, near where the river system meets Marajó Island — which city?
Belém: Capital and largest city of Pará, Brazil.
Home to the ancient Colossus, one of the Seven Wonders of the World, this Greek island's medieval citadel — built by the Hospitallers — is a UNESCO World Heritage Site — which one?
With around 56,000 residents, this southeastern Polish city sits where mountains meet lowlands along the navigable San River, and its Old Town is a listed Historic Monument — which city?
Przemyśl: City county in Subcarpathian Voivodeship, Poland.
Taiwan's second-largest city, this metropolis sits in a basin that was renamed 'Taiwan-fu' in the late Qing dynasty and later replanned during the Japanese colonial era — which city?
Taichung: Special municipality in Republic of China.
Also known as Calicut, this Kerala city on the Malabar Coast was crowned UNESCO's first Indian City of Literature in 2023 and earned the nickname 'City of Spices' — which city?
Shallowest and smallest by volume of the five vast freshwater bodies straddling the U.S.-Canada border, this one also has the only deepest point among them that sits above sea level — which one?
Lake Erie is the fourth-largest lake by surface area of the five Great Lakes in North America and the eleventh-largest globally.
A historic coal-mining hub that grew rapidly under Soviet-era industrial expansion, this city of nearly 500,000 is the fifth-largest in Kazakhstan — which city?
Karaganda: City in Karagandy Region, Kazakhstan.
Situated on the River Exe as the county town of Devon, this English cathedral city began as a Roman legionary base under the personal command of Vespasian — which city?

Centered in northern Manchuria and linked to the Yemaek people, the ancestors of today's Koreans, this ancient kingdom was later claimed as a forerunner by both Goguryeo and Paekche — which kingdom?
Buyeo: c. 2nd century BCE to 494 CE kingdom in north-east China.
Revered for freeing his kingdom from vassalage to the Toungoo Empire, this Ayutthaya monarch ruled from 1590 and later welcomed Dutch traders — who is he?
Naresuan: King of Siam from 1590 to 1605.

Founded in 1891 and now Australia's oldest active political movement, this centre-left force has governed federally since the 2022 election and rules five of the country's eight states and territories — which political movement?
Australian Labor Party (ALP) is the major social democratic political party in Australia.
Also known as the White Huns, this Central Asian people defeated the Kidarites in 450 CE before falling to a joint Turkic-Sasanian force in 560 — who were they?
Hephthalites: 5th–8th-century nomadic confederation in Central Asia.
Deeply in debt to Adolf Hitler for loans he'd borrowed, this aristocratic field marshal commanded Germany's army during the Battle of France and the invasions of Yugoslavia and Greece - who was he?
Walther von Brauchitsch: German Commander-in-Chief during World War II (1881–1948)

Nicknamed the 'Iron Minister' for his crackdown on protests, this Italian politician was prime minister during the 1980 Bologna station bombing and later served as president from 1985 to 1992 - who was he?
Francesco Cossiga: President of Italy from 1985 to 1992. Francesco Maurizio Cossiga (26 July 1928 – 17 August 2010) was an Italian politician who served as the president of Italy from 1985 to 1992.

This Ukrainian linguist and Svoboda party politician was a vocal advocate for Ukrainian-language education as an act of decolonization and an equally vocal critic of Ukrainians who spoke Russian - who is she?
Iryna Farion: Ukrainian linguist and politician (1964–2024)

Born in Ukraine but rising through Russian ranks, this colonel general has commanded Russia's airborne forces since 2022 and earned Hero of the Russian Federation honors during the First Chechen War - who is he?

A major theorist of the Négritude cultural movement, this poet-politician became independent Senegal's first president in 1960 after advocating for African rights within a French federal structure - who is he?
Léopold Sédar Senghor: First president of Senegal, poet, and cultural theorist (1906–2001)
The son of Odysseus and Penelope, this young man sailed to Pylos and Sparta seeking news of his father, then helped slay the suitors back home in Ithaca — who is he?
Telemachus: Mythological son of Odysseus. When Telemachus reached manhood, he visited Pylos and Sparta in search of his wandering father.
After Silvio Berlusconi's death, this Italian politician took over as leader of Forza Italia while also serving as his country's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister — who is he?
The first chairman of Gazprom and Russia's second-longest-serving Prime Minister, this 1990s politician became famous for malapropisms that turned into everyday Russian idioms — who is he?
This American private equity investor and retired naval officer completed the Explorers Grand Slam and then dove to the deepest point of all five oceans during a 2018–19 expedition. Who is he?
A five-time Socialist Party candidate for U.S. president, this labor leader co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World and led a major railway strike against the CB&Q line in 1888. Who is he?
Eugene V. Debs: American labor and political leader (1855–1926)
Serving as White House Counsel to Richard Nixon from 1970 to 1973, this attorney became a key prosecution witness in the Watergate cover-up and was disbarred after his guilty plea. Who is he?
John Dean: American author, Watergate figure (born 1938)
Trained as a lawyer, this conservative French statesman served three stints as prime minister before becoming president in 1913 — who is he?
Raymond Poincaré: President of France from 1913 to 1920.
This Ukrainian-born lawyer served as prosecutor of Crimea before becoming Russia's ambassador to Cape Verde and a State Duma deputy — who is she?
In Greek mythology, which Argive princess became mother of the hero Perseus by Zeus and was later credited with founding the city of Ardea in Latium?
This retired four-star general served as Turkey's defense minister from 2018 to 2023 after commanding NATO brigades in Bosnia and Kosovo — who is he?
Hulusi Akar: Turkish general and politician (born 1952)
A loyal Stalinist who rose through the Soviet hierarchy during the purges, this politician served as Premier of the Soviet Union from 1955 to 1958 — who is he?
Styled Earl of Rocksavage before inheriting his title, this British peer and filmmaker served as Lord Great Chamberlain of England for over three decades — who is he?
David Cholmondeley, 7th Marquess of Cholmondeley: British filmmaker (born 1960)
The eldest daughter of Emperor Peter I, she never took her homeland's throne herself, but her son became its emperor in 1762, after her younger sister's own reign came to an end — who was she?
Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna of Russia
Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna of Russia
Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna of Russia was a daughter of Peter the Great of Russia.
Grand Duchess Anna Petrovna of Russia
The last man ever promoted to Field Marshal in the German military during World War II, this commander became notorious among his own troops for his brutal treatment of deserters — who was he?

This doctrine holding that governing authority is legitimate to some degree — especially over taxation and production — gained traction in American political discourse during the 1930s and '40s, its opposite being anarchism — what's it called?

Statism: Doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree. In political science, statism or etatism (from French, état 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.
This American diplomat served as the 25th U.S. ambassador to the United Nations before becoming national security advisor from 2018 to 2019 — who is he?
John Bolton: American attorney and diplomat (born 1948)
A private first class with Easy Company's 506th Parachute Infantry in World War II, this soldier jumped with the Airborne again in Korea, twice earning decorations for gallantry — who is he?
Albert Blithe: United States Army soldier.
Practiced by early humans and often paired with a funeral ceremony, this method of laying the dead to rest involves placing a body into the ground or a mausoleum — what is it?
Burial: Ritual act of placing a dead person or animal into the ground.
The main executive leader of France's Directory regime from 1795 to 1799, this politician steered the country through the later years of the Revolution — who is he?
Paul Barras: French politician, nobleman and military officer (1755-1829)

The first politician with a neo-fascist background to hold Italy's second-highest office, this former Defence Minister has served as president of the Senate since October 2022 and once led the party Brothers of Italy — who is he?

Born to vaudeville performers and later a decorated Navy pilot, this founder of the American Nazi Party was assassinated in 1967 after building a reputation as one of the era's most notorious white supremacists — who was he?
George Lincoln Rockwell: American neo-Nazi activist (1918–1967)
This French-born Catholic queen consort of Charles I was never crowned due to her faith, and was widowed — and impoverished — by his execution in 1649 — who is she?
Henrietta Maria of France: Queen of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1625 to 1649.
Serving as the 13th director of Israel's Mossad from 2021 until 2026, this intelligence officer succeeded Yossi Cohen and was in turn replaced by Roman Gofman — who is he?
David Barnea: Chief of the Israeli Mossad.

Nicknamed 'the Hunchback,' this Ottoman sultan took power after suppressing the Patrona Halil rebellion in 1730, then spent leisure hours writing poetry while his viziers ran the government — who was he?
Mahmud I: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1730 to 1754.

Commonly known by his initials, this former Indonesian army major now leads the Democratic Party and serves as Coordinating Minister for Infrastructure — and is the son of a former president nicknamed SBY — who is he?
Capital in Yerevan, this short-lived state emerged in 1918 from the collapse of the Transcaucasian Federation, only to be squeezed to the shores of Lake Sevan by an Ottoman invasion — which nation?
First Republic of Armenia: 1918–1920 country in Western Asia.

A close aide to Egyptian presidents Nasser and Sadat, this official was allegedly a Mossad spy who fed Israel intelligence before the Yom Kippur War, then died mysteriously falling from a London balcony in 2007 — who was he?
Ashraf Marwan: Egyptian businessman and spy (1944–2007)
This movement campaigns for women to have the same legal right as men to go bare-chested in public, and also supports mothers' right to breastfeed openly — which cause?
Topfreedom: Social movement to allow female toplessness.
Twice queen consort of England through her marriage to Henry the Sixth, this daughter of the King of Naples personally led the Lancastrian side during the Wars of the Roses — who is she?
Margaret of Anjou: Queen of England (1445–1461, 1470–1471)
This Italian politician and businessman began in Christian Democracy, later serving as the country's Minister of Defence starting in 2022 — who is he?
Guido Crosetto: Italian politician and businessman (born 1963)
Born in August 1975, this independent lawmaker sat in Japan's House of Representatives — who is he?

This American politician represented Arizona's 8th congressional district until resigning in 2012 after surviving an assassination attempt, later becoming a gun violence prevention advocate — who is she?
Gabby Giffords: American politician and gun control activist (born 1970)

Born in what is now Syria, this Roman emperor reigned from 244 to 249 during an unusually stable stretch of a turbulent century, after being proclaimed ruler when his predecessor died in battle — who is he?
Philip the Arab: Roman emperor from 244 to 249. Philip I (Latin: Marcus Julius Philippus; c. 204 – September 249), commonly known as Philip the Arab, was Roman emperor from 244 to 249.
In the Vedic calendar, this eleventh lunar day of each waxing and waning cycle is observed within Vaishnavism through fasting and worship of Vishnu — what is it called?
Ekadashi: Eleventh day of the lunar fortnight. Ekadashi is popularly observed within Vaishnavism one of the major paths within Sanatana Dharma, commonly known as Hinduism.
In February 2024 she became First Minister of Northern Ireland after serving as Vice President of Sinn Féin since 2018 — who is she?
Michelle O'Neill: First Minister of Northern Ireland since 2024. O'Neill was previously deputy First Minister of Northern Ireland from 2020 to 2022.
In Greek myth, this Trojan princess was Hector's grieving widow, later taken as a concubine by Neoptolemus after her young son was thrown from the city walls — who is she?
Andromache: Wife of Hector in Greek mythology.
Resigning from Japan's Liberal Democratic Party after a 2024 indictment tied to a political slush-fund scandal, this lawmaker had served in the House of Representatives since 2003 — who is he?
Flourishing roughly 1550 to 1260 BC in northern Syria, this Hurrian-speaking kingdom shows unusual traces of Indo-Aryan influence among its ruling elite — which ancient state?
Mitanni: Ancient Hurrian-speaking state in northern Syria and southeast Anatolia.
Known in early Welsh sources by the name Gwalchmei, this Knight of the Round Table stars in a Middle English poem pitting him against a mysterious green-clad challenger — who is he?
Credited with coining the phrase 'sovereign democracy' while shaping Kremlin strategy for over a decade, this close Putin aide earned the nickname 'grey cardinal' — who is he?

Governing France during the childhood of Louis XV, whom he was related to as both great-nephew and first cousin twice removed, this early 18th-century regent married a daughter of Louis XIV — who is he?
Philippe II, Duke of Orléans: Regent of France from 1715 to 1723.
Serving as the BJP's 10th national president from 2020 to 2026, which close aide to Narendra Modi became India's Minister of Health again in 2024?
J. P. Nadda: Indian lawyer and politician (born 1960)
First ruled from 918 by Richard the Justiciar and later inherited by a cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty, which feudal territory belonged to the medieval Kingdom of France?
Duchy of Burgundy: Vassal territory of France, 918–1482.
Nicknamed 'The Stormin' Mormon' for his 7-foot-6 frame, which German-born NBA center led the league in blocked shots during the 1996-97 season?
Shawn Bradley (born March 22, 1972) is a German-American former professional basketball player.
As first Grand Inquisitor of the Spanish Inquisition from 1478, this Dominican friar was also a chief supporter of the decree expelling Jews from Spain — who was he?
Tomás de Torquemada: Grand Inquisitor of Spain (1420–1498)
A dependency of England and then Great Britain from 1542 to 1800, this island realm was administered from Dublin Castle by a Lord Lieutenant appointed by the English crown — what was it called?
Kingdom of Ireland: Dependency of England and then of Great Britain (1542–1800). The Parliament of Ireland was almost exclusively Anglo-Irish.
A Scottish heiress and socialite, this aristocrat became infamous for her scandalous, much-publicised 1963 divorce from her second husband — who was she?
Margaret Campbell, Duchess of Argyll: British socialite (1912–1993)

Ordered under a state of emergency as the Soviet Union was collapsing, this 1990 military crackdown on Azerbaijani independence supporters in Baku killed roughly 147 civilians — what is this event called?
Black January: Violent 1990 crackdown on anti-government/anti-Armenian movements in Baku, Azerbaijan SSR.
This Russian dissident and writer founded and chaired the Democratic Union party and sat on the editorial board of The New Times before her death in 2014 — who is she?

Driven by WWI war debts and reparations demanded under the 1921 London Schedule of Payments, the German Papiermark lost nearly all its value between 1921 and 1923 — what is this economic crisis called?
Hyperinflation in the Weimar Republic: Period of extreme inflation in Germany during 1921–1923.
Once Putin's deputy chief of staff overseeing security and energy, this close Kremlin ally has run Russia's state oil giant since 2004 — who is he?
Formed in 1980 from four merged Salvadoran guerrilla groups, this left-wing party fought the government throughout a civil war that lasted until 1992 — which group?
Farabundo Martí National Liberation Front: Salvadoran political party and former guerilla organization.
The son of a former Himachal Pradesh chief minister, this Indian politician served as a government minister overseeing sport and broadcasting, and once led his country's cricket board — who is he?
In 1888 this Norwegian polymath led the first ski crossing of Greenland's interior, and later during an 1890s expedition reached a record northern latitude of 86°14′ — who is he?
Codenamed Operation Vigilant Resolve, this 2004 U.S.-led military operation in Iraq aimed to apprehend those responsible for killing American contractors — which operation?

First Battle of Fallujah: Operation of the Iraq War. The battle, and especially the images of Iraqi civilians killed or injured in the fighting, caused many Iraqis to become resentful of the US presence.
Culminating with giant satirical monuments set ablaze after weeks of daily firecracker displays called the Mascletà, this UNESCO-listed March festival is Valencia's biggest celebration — which one?
Fallas: Traditional celebration in Valencia, Spain.
A graduate of Cairo University who briefly served as Japan's defense minister in 2007, this politician has governed Tokyo since 2016 — who is she?
Yuriko Koike: Governor of Tokyo since 2016. Yuriko Koike (Japanese: 小池 百合子, Hepburn: Koike Yuriko; born 15 July 1952) is a Japanese politician who has served as the Governor of Tokyo since 2016.
This French politician founded the history-themed Puy du Fou theme park in Vendée and ran for president in 1995 and 2007 under the banner of the Movement for France — who is he?
Philippe de Villiers: French politician and essayist (born 1949)
Named for the physicist who shared a 1903 Nobel Prize with Pierre and Marie Curie, this SI unit measures one radioactive decay event per second — which unit?
Becquerel: SI derived unit of radioactivity.
First proposed after the 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese, this psychological theory says people are less likely to help a victim when others are present — what's it called?
Bystander effect: Social psychological theory. Recent research has focused on "real world" events captured on security cameras, and the coherency and robustness of the effect has come under question.
Discovered in 1844 by Karl Ernst Claus and named in honor of Russia, which unreactive platinum-group element with atomic number 44 now caps extreme ultraviolet photomasks for chip lithography?
Ruthenium: Chemical element with atomic number 44 (Ru)
Accidentally discovered in 1967 by German chemist Karl Clauss at Hoechst AG, which calorie-free artificial sweetener is sold under the brand names Sunett and Sweet One?
Capable of living up to 177 years and weighing as much as 417 kilograms, which giant reptile — native to a chain of Pacific islands named for it — is the largest cold-blooded land animal alive today?
Galápagos tortoise: Species of reptile. The species comprises 15 subspecies (12 extant and 3 extinct).
Sold under the brand name Nexium, this proton pump inhibitor treats acid reflux by blocking an enzyme in the stomach's acid-producing cells — what is it?
Esomeprazole: Medication which reduces stomach acid.
Also known as the Mexican husk tomato, this nightshade fruit has been cultivated since pre-Columbian times and is the key ingredient in salsa verde — what is it?
Nicknamed the 'terror of Bengal' for choking waterways across the world, this South American aquatic plant is commonly known as water hyacinth — what is its scientific name?
Pontederia crassipes: Aquatic plant native to the Amazon basin.

This Swiss-American engineer was the only one of a famous physicist's three known biological grandsons to survive childhood, and later earned patents in electronics while working at Texas Instruments — who was he?
This term describes the bulk functional tissue of an organ like the brain or lungs, the filler tissue inside flatworms, and certain leaf cross-section layers in plants — what is it?
Parenchyma: Visceral tissue found inside organs of animals.
Distinguished by the male's large, transversely ridged curved horns, which wild goat species roams Eurasia and Africa?
Nicknamed the 'killer' variety for its aggressive defense of the hive, this hybrid pollinating insect escaped Brazilian quarantine in 1957 and reached Texas by 1990 — which insect is it?
Africanized bee: Hybrid species of bee. The African honey bee was first introduced to Brazil in 1956 to increase honey production, but 26 swarms escaped quarantine in 1957.
Which condition describes a total absence of speech that can result from injury, illness, trauma, or a developmental or neurological disorder — sometimes only temporary?
Muteness: Medical condition. In human development, muteness or mutism is defined as an absence of speech, with or without an ability to hear the speech of others.
Nicknamed 'Iron Annie,' which corrugated-skin transport plane began life as a 1930 civilian airliner before Nazi Germany converted it for military use?
Known for a widely viewed 2010 TEDx talk on shame and vulnerability, which academic wrote six consecutive number-one New York Times bestsellers, including Daring Greatly?
Brené Brown: American academic, speaker and author.
Divided in two by a central septum, this air-filled space sits behind the nose and forms the uppermost part of the respiratory system — what is it?
Nasal cavity: Large, air-filled space above and behind the nose in the middle of the face.
Hailed as a 'miracle worker' in 1955, this researcher refused to patent his polio vaccine so it could spread worldwide for free — who is he?
Jonas Salk: American inventor of the polio vaccine (1914–1995)

After resigning from Evergreen State College following 2017 protests over campus racial equity, this podcaster and former evolutionary biology professor was named part of the 'intellectual dark web' — who is he?
Bret Weinstein: American podcaster and author (born 1969)

Nicknamed the 'leopard slug' for its spotted grey-brown skin, this mollusc mates by dangling from a thread of mucus off a tree branch — which species, first spotted outside Europe in Philadelphia in 1867?
Limax maximus: Species of slug. It is among the largest keeled slugs, Limax cinereoniger being the largest.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.
Also known as the deer ked, this blood-sucking fly sheds its own wings once it lands on a host and burrows through the fur to feed — what species is it?
Lipoptena cervi: Species of fly. Lipoptena cervi, the deer ked or deer fly, is a species of biting fly in the family of louse flies, Hippoboscidae.

Made by every living organism and responsible for much of the sour taste in fruit, this dicarboxylic food additive's salt form also serves as a key intermediate in the cell's central metabolic energy cycle — what compound is it?
Malic acid is an organic compound with the molecular formula HO2CCH(OH)CH2CO2H.

Trained originally as a naval architect before becoming a self-taught nuclear physicist, this scientist directed the Soviet Union's atomic bomb program and earned the nickname 'father of the Russian bomb' — who is he?
This genus of over 200 stinging insect species, Solenopsis, includes 'ginger' and 'tropical' varieties named for their painful bite and reddish coloring — what are they commonly called?
Fire ant: Genus of red ants.
Also called the Persian silk tree or mimosa tree, this flowering species in the pea family is native to Asia — what is it?

Albizia julibrissin: Species of plant. Albizia julibrissin, the Persian silk tree, pink silk tree, or mimosa tree, is a species of tree in the Fabaceae family, native to southwestern and eastern Asia.
Appointed to the Supreme Court by Barack Obama in 2010, this former Harvard Law dean became the fourth woman ever to serve as a justice — who is she?
Elena Kagan: US Supreme Court justice since 2010.
Sometimes called 'poor man's pepper' or 'pepper grass,' this fast-growing herb has a peppery bite similar to mustard — which plant?
Garden cress: Species of edible herb.
Caused by mutations in any of sixteen genes that weaken the skin's structural attachment layers, this rare inherited condition causes painful blistering from the slightest friction — which disease?
Epidermolysis bullosa: Rare medical conditions that result in easy blistering of the skin and mucous membranes.
Nicknamed the 'miracle leaf' and 'life plant,' this Madagascar-native succulent sprouts tiny new plantlets right along the edges of its leaves — which species?

Kalanchoe pinnata: Succulent plant native to Madagascar. Kalanchoe pinnata, commonly known as cathedral bells, air plant, life plant, miracle leaf, and love bush, is a succulent plant native to Madagascar.
This mammal order today includes only small African and Middle Eastern hyraxes, but once boasted a species weighing up to 600 kilograms called Titanohyrax — which order?
Hyracoidea: Order of mammals. It includes the living hyraxes, placed within the family Procaviidae, and several extinct taxa.

First recorded in the 3rd-to-5th-century manuscript Sunzi Suanjing, this number-theory result lets you deduce what's left over after dividing by a product of coprime numbers, just from the leftovers after dividing by each one — which principle?
Chinese remainder theorem: About simultaneous modular congruences.

This family of 138 primate species — including baboons, macaques, and mandrills — split off from a separate lineage of primates some 45 to 55 million years ago, yet is the closer kin to apes of the two — which family?
Old World monkey: Family of mammals. Old World monkey genera include baboons (genus Papio), red colobus (genus Piliocolobus), and macaques (genus Macaca).
Found in cardiac and skeletal muscle and distantly related to hemoglobin, high levels of this oxygen-storing protein let diving whales and seals hold their breath longer — which protein?
Nicknamed golden root or Arctic root, this Crassulaceae plant is popular in herbal supplements even though the FDA has warned sellers against overselling its health benefits — which plant?
Rhodiola rosea: Species of flowering plant in the stonecrop family.
As West Germany's economics minister, he engineered the postwar 'Wirtschaftswunder' before becoming the country's second chancellor in 1963 — who is he?
Ludwig Erhard: Chancellor of West Germany from 1963 to 1966.
First added to the DSM in 1980 and diagnosed in women twice as often as men, this condition describes an intense, maladaptive reaction to a stressful life event — what is it?
Adjustment disorder is a mental disorder defined by a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor.
Sold under the brand name Pulmicort, this steroid drug treats asthma when inhaled but also comes as a nasal spray for allergies and a rectal foam for bowel disease — which medication?
One of the most intensively studied and intelligent cephalopods, this mollusk ranges from the Mediterranean and English coastline all the way to South Africa — which species?
Common octopus: Species of cephalopod. The common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) is a mollusk belonging to the class Cephalopoda.
Caused by HPV and appearing on the sole of the foot with tiny black dots visible on its surface, this painful skin growth is treated with salicylic acid or freezing — what condition is it?
Plantar wart: Medical condition. A plantar wart, also known as a verruca, is a wart occurring on the bottom of the foot or toes.
Described as the most economically important oxide of its element, this compound with the formula SO3 is a key precursor to sulfuric acid and to acid rain — what is it?
Sulfur trioxide: Chemical compound. Sulfur trioxide exists in several forms: gaseous monomer, crystalline trimer, and solid polymer.
Known in mineral form as gibbsite, this amphoteric white compound with the formula Al(OH)3 is a major component of the ore bauxite — what is it?
Aluminium hydroxide: Chemical compound. Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, meaning it has both basic and acidic properties.
This plant genus in the mallow family gives us cotton, humanity's primary natural fiber, with its name tracing to an Arabic word for a soft substance — which genus?
Gossypium: Genus of flowering plants in the mallow family Malvaceae.
About 70% of people infected with this parasite-caused sexually transmitted infection show no symptoms at all, though it can raise the risk of contracting HIV — what condition is it?
Trichomoniasis: Medical condition. Trichomoniasis (trich) is an infectious disease caused by the parasite Trichomonas vaginalis.
Known commonly as garden thyme or German thyme, this flowering plant belongs to the mint family — which species is it?
Thymus vulgaris: Species of flowering plant.
This mathematician founded set theory and proved that there are more real numbers than natural numbers, revealing an infinity of infinities — who is he?
This large, structurally diverse family of plant compounds includes flavonoids and tannic acid, some of which were historically used as dyes and for tanning garments — what are they called?
In 2013, this tech billionaire took his own computer company private in a $24.4 billion buyout, the largest since the Great Recession, before it went public again in 2018 — who is he?
First flown in 1947 with a distinctive V-tail, this single-engine aircraft holds the record for the longest continuous production run in aviation history — which model?
Beechcraft Bonanza: Family of single engine American light aircraft, first flown in 1945.
Featuring an R−O−O−R backbone where two oxygen atoms bond directly to each other, what name covers this class of molecules?
Peroxide: Chemical compounds with the structure R–O–O–R'
The second jet fighter to enter RAF service and the first powered by a single jet engine, this twin-boom aircraft flew with the Halford Goblin turbojet — which aircraft?

De Havilland Vampire: Fighter aircraft; first single-engine jet in RAF service. The de Havilland DH100 Vampire is a British jet fighter developed and manufactured by the de Havilland Aircraft Company.
Designated Alpha Carinae and located some 310 light-years away, this bright giant is the second-brightest star in the night sky, outshone only by Sirius — which star?
Canopus: Brightest star in the constellation of Carina.
This German physicist was the first to conclusively demonstrate the electromagnetic waves predicted by James Clerk Maxwell's equations — who is he?
This condition, caused by low blood potassium below 3.5 mmol/L, can bring on fatigue, leg cramps, and a dangerously slow heart rhythm — what is it?
Hypokalemia: Insufficient potassium in the blood. Normal potassium levels in humans are between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L (3.5 and 5.0 mEq/L) with levels below 3.5 mmol/L defined as hypokalemia.

Named for the Ancient Greek word for 'star' after its flower shape, this group of roughly 170 mostly Eurasian perennial plants is also known for its late-blooming 'Michaelmas daisies' — which plant group?
Aster (genus) is a genus of perennial flowering plants in the family Asteraceae.

First catalogued in 1729 by an Italian priest who thought its spore-forming structures resembled a holy-water sprinkler, this genus of several hundred mold species takes its name from the Latin word for 'to sprinkle' — which genus?
Aspergillus: Genus of fungi. Aspergillus is a genus consisting of several hundred mold species found in various climates worldwide.
Found in Central and South America, only three living species of this blood-feeding, leaf-nosed flying mammal exist, while two extinct relatives once roamed North America — which creature?
Generated in mitochondria via the TCA cycle, this dicarboxylic compound gets converted into fumarate by an enzyme that helps build ATP — which molecule?
Succinic acid is a dicarboxylic acid with the chemical formula (CH2)2(CO2H)2.
The largest structure inside a eukaryotic cell's nucleus, this site of ribosome assembly also helps form signal recognition particles and responds to cellular stress — what is it?
Nucleolus: Largest structure in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells. The nucleolus also participates in the formation of signal recognition particles and plays a role in the cell's response to stress.
Sold under trade names like Super Glue and Krazy Glue, this fast-acting adhesive family rapidly polymerizes the moment it contacts water — which chemical group?
Cyanoacrylate: Type of fast-acting adhesive. The cyanoacrylate group in the monomer rapidly polymerizes in the presence of water to form long, strong chains.
Produced by the enzyme 5α-reductase acting on a more familiar male sex hormone, this compound is a more potent driver of prostate growth, sebum, and body hair — which hormone?
Also nicknamed 'Cornish salmon,' this predatory fish is often netted alongside the Atlantic herring it preys on, and is heavily overfished across European waters — which fish?
Merluccius merluccius: Species of fish. Merluccius merluccius or the European hake is a merluccid hake of the genus Merluccius.
In this common vision condition, distant objects appear sharp but close-up objects blur because light focuses behind the retina instead of on it - what is it?
Farsightedness: Eye condition in which light is focused behind instead of on the retina.

Three of this crustacean's five pairs of legs bear claws, with the first pair often dramatically oversized, and its burrow-dwelling relatives include the Norway variety known as langoustine - which creature?
Lobster: Family of clawed marine crustaceans.
Native to southern China, this pear tree's fruit goes by dozens of names worldwide - Asian pear, apple pear, nashi pear - but is rarely baked into pies due to its high water content - which species?
Pyrus pyrifolia: Species of pear with round crisp grainy fruit.
This scientific discipline uses techniques from titration to mass spectrometry to identify unknown compounds and measure exactly how much of each substance is present in a mixture - which field?
Analytical chemistry: Study of the separation, identification, and quantification of matter.
This glycopeptide antibiotic is given intravenously for MRSA infections like endocarditis and meningitis, but taken orally - where it's poorly absorbed - to treat a common gut infection - which drug?
Vancomycin: Antibiotic medication. Vancomycin is also taken orally (by mouth) to treat Clostridioides difficile infections.
Native to Africa south of the Sahara, this domesticated bird has since been introduced everywhere from the West Indies to Australia — which species?
Helmeted guinea fowl: Species of bird. The helmeted guinea fowl (Numida meleagris) is the best known of the guinea fowl bird family, Numididae, and the only member of the genus Numida.
This plant genus includes both chicory, whose roasted roots make a coffee substitute, and true endive, the base for salad greens like escarole — which genus?
Cichorium: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae.
One of the oldest groups of eukaryotic seaweed, this phylum boasts over 7,000 species — mostly marine, though about 5% live in freshwater habitats. What group is it?
Red algae: Division of plant life.

This dental specialty treats misaligned teeth and jaws, a condition worldwide diets of softer foods have made even more common by leaving smaller jaws with less room to fit them. What specialty is it?
First isolated in 1820 from black nightshade berries, this glycoalkaloid poison also occurs naturally in potatoes as a built-in pest defense. What compound is it?
Solanine: Glycoalkaloid poison found in the nightshade family of plants.
Its thick bark gets harvested every 9 to 12 years for wine-bottle stoppers and cricket-ball cores — what species of oak, native to southwest Europe and Africa, is this?
Quercus suber: Species of plant. Quercus suber, commonly called the cork oak, is a medium-sized, evergreen oak tree in the section Quercus sect.
This American neuroscientist and primatologist, a Stanford professor across three departments, has spent his career studying the neuroendocrinology of stress — who is he?
This Japanese media artist and academic directs a research centre for 'Digital Nature' and holds visiting professorships at multiple Japanese art universities — who is he?
Yoichi Ochiai: Japanese academic, artist, and entrepreneur. Yoichi Ochiai (落合 陽一, Yoichi Ochiai; born 16 September 1987) is a Japanese media artist, entrepreneur, and academic.
This zodiac sign's Latin name means 'fishes,' and it's where the ecliptic crosses the celestial equator near the March equinox — which one?
Pisces (constellation) is a constellation of the zodiac. It is between Aquarius, of similar size, to the southwest and Aries, which is smaller, to the east.

First synthesized in 1940 by chemist Roger Adams via hydrogenation of THC isomers, this psychoactive cannabis-derived compound is sold in vaporizers despite never being drug-approved — which compound?
Occurring naturally as the mineral brucite, this poorly soluble white solid neutralizes stomach acid in a well-known antacid — which compound?
Magnesium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Mg(OH)2.
This British-American historian, a senior fellow at Stanford's Hoover Institution, writes on financial history and holds notably favorable views of the British Empire — who is he?
Named for an Indonesian island where an 18th-century naturalist first catalogued it, this pungent, oregano-scented succulent also goes by Cuban oregano and Indian borage — which plant?
Coleus amboinicus: Species of plant. Coleus amboinicus is a species of semi-succulent perennial plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Also called a kilopond, this deprecated gravitational metric unit equals exactly 9.80665 newtons — the weight of a one-thousand-gram mass under standard gravity. What is it?
Kilogram-force (kgf or kgF), or kilopond (kp, from Latin pondus, 'weight'), is a non-standard gravitational metric unit of force equal to the weight on Earth of a one-kilogram mass.
This American cultural anthropologist's 1928 fieldwork, Coming of Age in Samoa, made her a household name for exploring adolescence and sexuality in Pacific societies — who is she?

Named after Scottish naturalist Alexander Garden and first proposed in 1753 by botanist Jane Colden, this fragrant flowering genus in the coffee family is native to Africa, Asia and Australia — which plant genus?
Gardenia: Genus of flowering plants in the coffee family Rubiaceae.
Grown for its edible taproot in red or golden varieties and closely related to Swiss chard, this vegetable's leaves are eaten too, sold simply as "greens" — which root vegetable?
Beetroot is the taproot portion of a Beta vulgaris subsp.
Usually symptomless until it ruptures — causing sudden, severe abdominal or lower-back pain — this dangerous enlargement of the body's main artery is most common in the abdomen — what condition?
Aortic aneurysm: Excessive enlargement of the human aorta.

Named from the Greek word for "fish" because of its dry, scaly skin, this family of genetic skin disorders ranges from a mild type mistaken for ordinary dry skin to a rare, life-threatening form — which condition?
Ichthyosis: Family of disorders causing dry, thickened, scaly skin.

Branching from the windpipe at a landmark called the carina, these airway passages narrow progressively through several orders before losing cartilage support and changing name entirely — what are they called?
Bronchus: Airway in the respiratory tract.
Defined as a blood level above 5.5 mmol/L, this elevated-potassium condition can trigger a dangerous heart rhythm and even cardiac arrest — what is it called?
Hyperkalemia: Excess potassium in the blood. Normal potassium levels are between 3.5 and 5.0 mmol/L (3.5 and 5.0 mEq/L) with levels above 5.5 mmol/L defined as hyperkalemia.

Also called the moon jellyfish, this once-thought-cosmopolitan species was split into roughly 28 separate species in the 2020s and is now known to live only in the north Atlantic and off Argentina — which species?
Aurelia aurita: Species of jellyfish. The species now identified as A. aurita is only found in the north Atlantic and in Argentina, and is not dangerous to humans.

Grouping over 30 inherited disorders that cause progressive weakening and wasting of skeletal tissue — with the Duchenne form affecting roughly half of all cases in young boys — what's this disease group called?
Muscular dystrophy: Diseases in which skeletal and visceral muscles break down over time.
Starting at Capcom in 1990, this Japanese game director helmed the first Resident Evil and later founded both PlatinumGames and Tango Gameworks, directing The Evil Within in 2014 — who is he?
Shinji Mikami: Japanese video game designer, director and producer.
Encompassing reporting, dashboards, data mining, and analytics, this set of strategies and technologies helps companies turn raw data into strategic decisions — what's it called?
Business intelligence: Strategies for analysis and use of data.
Caused by excessive exposure to silver dust or compounds, this condition turns the skin a striking blue or blue-gray shade, especially in sun-exposed areas — what's it called?
Argyria: Medical condition. The most dramatic symptom of argyria is that the skin turns blue or blue-gray, and is usually most prominent in sun-exposed areas of the skin.

This neurological disorder involves excessive sleepiness or time spent sleeping, sometimes linked to seasonal affective disorder, and appears under sleep-wake disorders in the DSM-5 — what is it called?

Hypersomnia: Neurological disorder of excessive time spent sleeping or excessive sleepiness. It can have many possible causes (such as seasonal affective disorder) and can cause distress and problems with functioning.
This English inventor and industrial designer created the bagless vacuum cleaner using cyclonic separation, and by 2023 was the UK's fifth-richest person — who is he?
James Dyson: British inventor and businessman (born 1947)

Despite its common names, this evergreen conifer isn't a true member of the pine, spruce, or hemlock genera, yet stands as the tallest species in its own family — what is it?
Douglas fir: Species of tree. It is native to western North America and is also known as Douglas-fir, Douglas spruce, Oregon pine, and Columbian pine.
Damage to the sympathetic trunk nerves produces this trio of symptoms on one side of the face — a constricted pupil, a droopy eyelid, and reduced sweating — what is this condition called?
Horner's syndrome: Facial disorder due to damage of the sympathetic nerves.

This congenital heart defect combines four distinct abnormalities — including a hole between the ventricles and a narrowed pulmonary exit — and can trigger cyanotic 'spells' in infants — what is this condition?
Tetralogy of Fallot: Type of congenital heart defect. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), formerly known as Steno-Fallot tetralogy, is a congenital heart defect characterized by four specific cardiac defects.

Beginning as a tightly compressed gray sponge before expanding into a pitted yellow-brown honeycomb atop a hollow white stem, which springtime fungus is a prized edible found near old orchards and hardwoods?
Morchella esculenta: Species of fungus. The pits are rounded and irregularly arranged.
Made from a fermented batter of rice and black gram, which thin, savoury South Indian flatbread is traditionally served with chutney and sambar?
Dosa (food): Thin batter bread originating from South India.
Formed when acetic acid combines with a base, this ion is also nature's most common building block for biosynthesis — what is it?
Acetate: Salt formed from acetic acid and a base.
This biological process turns a primary oocyte into an egg cell capable of developing once fertilized, beginning during embryonic development — what is it called?
Oogenesis: Egg cell production process. Oogenesis or ovogenesis is the differentiation of the ovum (egg cell) into a cell competent to further develop when fertilized.
Marketed as Buscopan, this anticholinergic medication treats abdominal cramps, bladder and biliary spasms, and can ease respiratory secretions near the end of life — what drug is it?

Blurring the line between a single creature and a colony, this cnidarian is actually made of specialized zooids from one fertilized egg working together to float, feed and jet-propel — what is it?
Siphonophore: Order of colonial hydrozoans with differentiated zooids.
Derived from the chemical name for acetaminophen, this brand-name pain and fever reliever was part of Johnson & Johnson until spun off under Kenvue in 2022 — which product?
Tylenol: Medication. Tylenol is a brand of medication, advertised for reducing pain, reducing fever, and relieving the symptoms of allergies, cold, cough, headache, and influenza.
Considered sacred by Hindus and Buddhists, this tree native to the Indian subcontinent is also known as bael and is the sole member of its genus — which species?
Aegle marmelos: Species of tree, considered sacred by Hindus. It is present in India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, and Nepal as a naturalized species.
Unlike its bulb-forming relative, the common onion, this perennial vegetable never forms a bulb and owes one of its names to its hollow, tube-like leaves — which plant?
Allium fistulosum: Species of plant. The species is very similar in taste and odor to the related common onion, Allium cepa, and hybrids between the two (tree onions) exist.
Also called T4, this hormone produced by the thyroid gland acts as a precursor to the more active T3 and helps regulate metabolism, heart function and bone health — what is it?
Thyroxine: Thyroid hormone. It is the primary form of thyroid hormone found in the blood and acts as a prohormone of the more active thyroid hormone, triiodothyronine (T3).
Caused by a fungus that forms galls on maize plants, this disease produces an edible delicacy in Mexico known as huitlacoche, often stuffed into quesadillas — which condition?

This general term describes inflammation of the kidneys, affecting structures such as the glomeruli, tubules, or the surrounding interstitial tissue — what is the condition called?
